===== [avh 0005]
Admiral Arun Prakash (Retd), PVSM, AVSM, VrC, VSM
Former Chief of the Naval Staff
Indian Navy
Advances in technology have helped push the frontiers of
aviation in all dimensions, and aircraft today fly higher, faster and farther
than ever before. In the cockpit, the pilots) need greater mental agility
and crew coordination to manage the large quantum of inputs available.
Not only has the intensity of air traffic grown manifold, but its diversity
now ranges from high-performance airliners to light aircraft and
unmanned aerial vehicles. All this has brought with it, more sophisticated
navigation and landing aids, as well as stricter air-traffic regulations.
From my own experience of over half a century ago, I can say
that flying-training is, at the same time, one of the most challenging and
most satisfying learning experiences one can ever undergo. But the
'learning' process does not end when one acquires a licence in civil or is
awarded 'wings' in the military. To be a safe and competent professional,
a pilot must remain involved in a continuous process of acquiring,
retaining, refreshing and updating his aviation knowledge. In the air, it is
as much a pilot's flying skills, as his knowledge of the aircraft and
environment that can make the difference between safety and disaster.
The volume that you hold in your hands is a comprehensive
corpus of aviation knowledge, compiled, meticulously, over 17 years, by
Commander Thomas Tom. A Naval Aviator of high standing, a Qualified
Flying Instructor (QFI) and a DGOA Examiner, Thomas, in his years of
lying, has, no doubt, encountered the full gamut of contingencies that a
cockpit. Based on his experience, he has
painstakingly, assembled this compendium which, concisely but lucidly,
covers almost every aviation topic of relevance. This book is akin to a
'one stop shop', where 'rookies', as well as those aspiring for higher
qualifications can find what they need.
I commend Commander Tom, for undertaking this 'labour of love'
in order to provide a study guide or 'aide memoire', which will be useful,
not just for preparing for examinations and licences, but also for aviators
wishing to keep themselves up to date by dipping into the interesting and
well-illustrated pages of The Aviator's Handbook.
akrakash

Preface
Dear aviator, if you are starting out in your aviation career & want
to expand your professional horizons, or if a CPL/ATPL is your aim, then
you will have no choice but study from many voluminous & expensive
aviation books, such as:
- Oxford Aviation Academy Ground Training (14 volumes)
- FAA Handbooks for Aviation (multiple volumes)
- AP3456 - RAF Manual for Flying (14 volumes)
- Ground Studies for Pilots (6 volumes)
- ATPL 1000 Questions - Keith Williams (7 volumes)
- Flight Instructor School précis (5 volumes)
- Flight Without Formulae (AC Kermode)
- ICAO Annexes/Docs & DGCA CARS, & many more...
You may already have the PDFs of these books, but then, you will
still have to sift through the clutter, read, study & make notes; and have it
ready for revision before your exams. Who has the time for all this, these
days? This is where The Aviator's Handbook can help you. The topics in
this book are researched from all the books mentioned above.
This book is the culmination of more than 17 years of study and
research. It had its humble beginnings as my personal notes, which I
meticulously made & maintained throughout my flying career. Through
this book, I want to share with you my journey, what I learnt, and what
you will need to study. I hope this book will serve you as a strong
foundation on your quest for knowledge.
In the course of making this handbook, I adhered to three guiding
principles: use a language as simple as possible, all topics should be
fully covered & each topic should not exceed one page. As far as
possible, I have avoided the use of technical jargon & complex formulae.
Remember, every statement and line in this book is important and is a
possible question. This book is for people like you & me... the average
pilot; the busy aviator; the CPL/ATPL aspirant. Use this book as a CPL/
ATPL exam preparatory tool, or as a quick reference handbook of
aviation knowledge. Both experienced & inexperienced pilots will find
their own use of this book.
Rest assured, this book will save you a lot of time.
If you come across any error, or to provide any feedback/suggestion,
kindly send an email to: theaviatorshandbook@icloud.com.
After all, we all are here to learn, aren't we?
Visit theaviatorshandbook.com for the latest updates & corrections.
===== [avh 0013]
How can you benefit from this book?
Student Pilots
This book encompasses the entire gamut of professional
knowledge a budding aviator needs, & includes all the topics taught to
you during your initial pilot training, be it in the defence forces or civil
aviation. It also covers the entire DGCA syllabus for CPL/ATPL
exams. Carry this handbook to all your ground subject classes. Rather
than making any notes yourself, you could just tick-off the topics in this
book as and when they are covered in your course. Use the Index to look
up specific topics directly. And as you come closer to your exam dates,
you will soon realise that this book is your best friend.
Military Aviators aspiring for a CPL/ATPL
My colleagues, there is no question about it... you all are 'Top-
Gun'. You have flown high, close to the edge of space, and have pulled
countless Gs. You have flown low over the vast blue oceans in radio
silence to track that enemy targets. You have flown deep into the endless
deserts and jungles 'where even angels fear to tread"; to rescue countless
civilian lives by risking yours. But trust me. Civil aviation is a very different
ball game, in a different arena, run by a totally different set of rules. Here,
your knowledge of air regulations, performance, air-conditioning,
pressurisation & safety of passengers is more important than your
ability to do a perfect 'upward-clover'. This book will help you reduce
your burden while preparing for your ATPL exams, and align you
faster with your new career, by adding to your existing knowledge.
Experienced Civil Pilots
You are the stalwarts of aviation. And experience, just like vintage
wine, only gets better with age. However, age and memory do not always
go hand-in-hand, and we need to keep re-visiting our textbooks from time
to time. This book is just what you need. It is a reference manual for
aviation subjects and is an indispensable & invaluable encyclopaedia
that deals with all aspects of aeronautical information. Use the Index
at the end of this book to find answers to almost all the aviation questions
you may come encounter in your day-to-day life. It will help you brush up
on your facts and keep you at the top of your game, at all times.
Flight Instructors
My dear colleagues, you are the torch-bearers of this fine
profession, and an enormous burden rests on your shoulders to impart
quality training to your pupils. Each chapter in this book is laid out in an
optimal sequence, to allow students to progressively build from
foundational to more complex topics. You may also use this book as a
reference to set minimum standards of knowledge on each topic. As you
prepare for your lecture, a quick read of any topic in this book will help
refresh your memory. This book will also come in handy when you set a
question paper for trainee-pilots.
I wish all of you, the very best, godspeed, & happy landings.

Flight is freedom in its purest form,
To dance with the clouds which follow a storm;
To roll and glide, to wheel and spin,
To feel the joy that swells within;
To leave the earth with its troubles and fly,
And know the warmth of a clear spring sky;
Then back to earth at the end of a day,
Released from the tensions which melted away.
Should my end come while I am in flight,
Whether brightest day or darkest night;
Spare me your pity and shrug off the pain,
Secure in the knowledge that I'd do it again;
For each of us is created to die,
And within me I know,
I was born to fly.
- Gary Claud Stokor

Air Regulations
===== [avh 0032]
1 - 3  Regulations
° Aviation Conventions & Organisations
Important Historical Civil Aviation Conventions
1929 Warsaw Convention: It established 'operator liability limitations'
for passengers, baggage & freight.
1944 Chicago Convention: It established the 'International Civil
Aviation Organisation' (ICAO) as a UN agency, with its HQ at
Montreal, Canada. It has 7 regional offices in Bangkok, Cairo, Dakar
(Senegal), Lima (Peru), Mexico City, Nairobi & Paris.
О• ОАСІ • ИКАО
пения • →
ICAO Assembly
(Consists of 193 contracting States. They meet once in 3 years)
(Consists of 33 contracting States, elected by Assembly for a 3-year term)
Commissions & Committees  Secretariat
- Air Navigation Commission  - Air Navigation Bureau
- Air Transport Committee  - Air Transport Bureau
- Legal Committee  - Technical Assistance Bureau
- Finance Committee  - Legal Bureau
- Committee of Unlawful Interference - Administration & Services
- Committee for joint support of air-navigation services
- ICAO was formed to encourage the safe & efficient development
of international commercial aviation.
- SARPs Standards & Recommended Practises are technical
specifications adopted by ICAO, in the form of 19 Annexes, for
regulation & global uniformity of airspace, navigation, nav-aids,
safety, security, customs, etc. Docs are recommendations that
are not yet mature enough for inclusion in Annexes.
- Contracting States must enforce all SARPs unless they notify it in
their AIPs within 60 days. In India, it is published in AIP section 1.7
Jurisdiction of Offences Committed
- In the air: State in whose airspace the offence was committed,
has the right to prosecute.
- Over land: Rules of State above which a/c is flying will apply.
Over international waters: International law will apply.
- Over high seas: State of aircraft registry will prosecute.
1952 Rome Convention: It laid down rules w.r.t damage caused by a
foreign aircraft to third parties on the ground.
1963 Tokyo Convention: It laid down rules regarding offences & acts
committed on board an aircraft.
1970 Hague Convention: It established rules concerning hijackers.
1971 Montreal Convention: It laid down the authority of 'Captain of
aircraft' & rules against unlawful acts, i.e., destruction of aircraft
in flight, destruction of nav-aids, etc.
===== [avh 0033]
Regulations  1 - 4
ooo Aviation Organisations & their functions in civil aviation
IATA International Air Transport Association
IATA  - It is an international organisation that lobbies for the
interests of airline companies.
ECAC European Civil Aviation Conference
- It was established by ICAO in 1955 to institute
standard aviation policies & a safe/sustainable air
transport system in Europe.
EASA European Aviation Safety Agency
- It is the Aviation safety organisation in the European
Union & represents civil aviation regulatory authorities
of EU States. It was established in 2002 & took over
functions of JAA for establishing common regulatory
standards & procedures, licensing, etc.
Miation  JAA Joint Aviation Authorities
Authori  - It was a cooperation of aviation authorities in Europe,
established in 1970, for common certification
standards. It was disbanded in 2009. Only the
training organisation, JAA-TO, remains.
ITU International Telecom Union
ITU  - It is the oldest international organisation, established
on 17 May 1865.
- It is now part of the UN, with HQ in Geneva.
- They set up standards for 'radio-frequency spectrum
management'.
- Their main document is ITU RR (Radio Regulations).
DGCA Director General Civil Aviation
- It is the regulatory body for civil aviation in India.
- They issue CARs (Civil Aviation Requirements).
- They deal with:
- Licensing of pilots & ATC controllers;
DGCA
- Registration of aircraft, Airworthiness;
- Accident investigation;
- Amendments to Aircraft Act, Aircraft Rules, etc.
AAI Airports Authority of India
- It was formed in 1995 and deals with:
- Provision of ATS services in their airports;
sale Senor sore
- Provision of nav-aids, comm-aids;
- Publishes AIPS, NOTAMs, PIBs;
- Design, development & maintenance of
aerodromes.
WPC Wireless Planning & Coordination (India)
- It was set up in 1962 under The Ministry of
Wireless Planning
& Coordination  Communication to implement policies of ITU.

Regulations  1 - 6
°o National Law (India) (Ref: 1937 Aircraft Act, 1937 Aircraft Rules)
1920 Indian Aircraft Rules: It mainly provides rules regarding customs.
1934 Aircraft Act:
- It governs manufacture, operations, sale & import of aircraft. However,
Central Government can, by a 'Gazette', exempt anyone from this.
- These rules apply to - Citizens of India, wherever they are;
- Aircraft & passengers on an aircraft registered in India;
- Aircraft & passengers on an aircraft not registered in India, but
is currently flying over India;
- Aircraft operated by a non-Indian, but his place of business and
residence is in India.
- Govt has the power to detain any a/c & has wreck & salvage rights.
- Penalty of contravention to this Act: 2 years prison + Rs.10 lakh fine.
- Penalty for slaughtering animals/depositing rubbish within 10 km of
an aerodrome ARP: 3 years prison + Rs.10 lakh fine.
1937 Aircraft Rules: It lays down regulations for civil aviation in India.
- Amendment to these rules is published by DGCA in AIC.
- Some of the important Aircraft Rules are:
- Crew must communicate with a boom-mic when on ground &
receiving departure clearance or when engines are running or
when in air, aircraft is below TA/10000', whichever higher.
- Supersonic flight is not permitted in Indian airspace.
- Climb-cruise technique is not permitted in Indian airspace.
- No aircraft will fly over published 'Prohibited Areas'.
- Formation flying is not permitted for any civil aircraft in India.
- Military a/c formation must be within .5 nm laterally, 100' vertically
& formation must operate as a single unit for nav/position reporting.
Separation between a/c in formation is responsibility of flight leader.
- No Aerobatics is permitted within 6 nm of aerodrome & below 6000'
- Night Flying: Any flying ½ hr after sunset to ½ hr before sunrise.
- Petroleum in Bulk: Term used when petroleum qty > 900 litres.
- Succession of Command of crew is to be published by operator.
- Radio: No person without RTR licence will operate aircraft radio.
- Mail: No mail is to be carried in a/c without permission of DG Post.
- Hangar: Aircraft with fuel in their wings is to be parked in a well-
ventilated hangar, certified with non-inflammable materials.
1954 Aircraft Public Health Rules
- The PIC shall inform ATC at least 2 hrs before arrival if any person on
board the aircraft is suffering from infectious/quarantinable disease.
- Dead bodies with yellow fever, plague, anthrax are not allowed in a/c.
- Other dead bodies are allowed if they are properly enclosed in a coffin.
1994 Rules on obstructions/demolition w.r.t. buildings around aerodromes.
2003 Rules on the carriage of dangerous goods
2011 Rules on aircraft security
2012 Rules regarding aircraft accident investigation
International Air Transit Agreements: Various degrees of freedom are -
1st degree of freedom: Freedom to overfly another country.
2nd: Land in another country for technical requirements/fuelling.
3rd: Drop passengers in another country.
4th: Pick up pax from another country & drop in country of a/c registration.
5th: Pick up pax from another country and drop in a third country

1-7  Regulations
°o Personnel Licensing (Ref: DGCA Aircraft Rules 1937, Schedule II)
ICAO Annex 1
- Every aircraft in India will be flown by a crew who are licensed as per
Indian Aircraft Rules. If the aircraft is not registered in India, crew should
be licensed according to rules of the country aircraft was registered in.
- Type Rating: Issued to a pilot after completing a 'Type Rating' course &
demonstration of necessary pilot skills on that aircraft.
- Instrument Rating: Issued to a pilot after demonstration of necessary
IF skills. Its validity is 1 year. A valid night IR is a must for night flying.
- Max Age for commercial transport ops is 60 yrs, 65 if co-pilot age < 60.
Medicals
- Medical validity starts from the date of conduct of medicals.
- Validity expires in case of pregnancy or any prolonged illness > 21 days.
- If hospitalised for a duration > 12 hrs, crew has to inform the operator.
- A valid Class I medical certificate is mandatory for CPLATPL.
Class I: Its validity is 12 months till age 40 yrs (single pilot operations),
& 60 yrs (multi crew operations). After that it is 6 months.
Class 2: Its validity 5 yrs till age 40, 2 yrs from 40-50 & 1 yr from 50-60.
SPL Student Pilot Licence: Minimum age for SPL is 16 yrs.
- It is issued by flying clubs authorised by DGCA.
- A trainee may fly without licence in any aircraft with AUW < 1500 kg.
- A trainee cannot go solo without a supervisor.
- He can fly only in Indian airspace, provided:
- He is flying with a QFI  - Not carrying passengers or goods
- He is not flying for remuneration - He will fly under VFR rules only
- Aircraft has dual controls.
- No X-country permitted without passing Meteorology & Nav DGCA exams.
PPL Private Pilot Licence: Minimum age for PPL is 17 yrs.
- He can fly a private aircraft, but not for remuneration.
CPL Commercial Pilot Licence: Minimum age for CPL is 18 yrs.
- At the time of application, he should have the following:
- Passed 10+2 exams  - Valid RTR licence & FRTOL
- Passed all DGCA exams  - Valid ELP certificate
- Passed flying skill test  - Valid Class | medical certificate
x-country of minimum 300 nm
Flying hours Needed:  • 2 full stops at 2 aerodromes
- Total Flying: 200 hrs
- PIC: 100 hrs (incl 20 hrs *x-country), with 15 hrs in last 6 months,
5 hrs by night in last 6 months (incl 10 takeoff & 10 landings)
- Instrument Flying: 10 hrs (5 hrs of simulator IF may be used)
ATPL Airline Transport Pilot Licence: Minimum age for ATPL is 21 yrs.
- At the time of application, all requirements are same as for CPL.
Flying hours Needed:
- Total Flying: 1500 hrs (incl 500 hrsi-country & 100 hrs by night),
with 20 hrs in last 6 months
- PIC: 250 hrs (incl 100 hrsi-country & 50 hrs by night), with 10
hrs in last 6 months
- Instrument Flying: 75 hrs (actual + simulated), 50 hrs (actual)
Licence Validity: CPL/ATPL is valid for 5 years. Beyond 5 years:
- Between 7 to 8 yrs pilot has to re-do flying skill test & Air-regs exam.
- Beyond 8 yrs: Licence expired. Re-do all exams, as if for a new licence.

1-8
° Rules of the Air & General Definitions
(See also: Performance > Definitions)
ICAO Annex 2
Right of Way Rules
- Head-on: If two aircraft are converging head-on, both will alter to right.
- Converging: If two aircraft are converging, aircraft that has the other
on the right will give way by altering to the right.
- Overtaking: Overtaking is deemed when one aircraft is approaching
another from astern, 70° either side. Overtaking aircraft will alter right
& give way to aircraft being overtaken until she is well clear ahead.
- Landing: Aircraft in air/ground will give way to aircraft landing. If two
aircraft are landing, the one which is below the other has right of way.
- Take-off: Aircraft about to take-off has the right of way over an
aircraft on the ground.
- Taxiing: Aircraft taxiing has the right of way over aircraft being towed.
Priority Between Aircraft  Right of Way Between Aircraft

TA Transition Altitude
- It is the altitude at or below which QNH is set on an altimeter. TA IS
fixed by State. It must be minimum 1500' above the aerodrome.
- For two or more close aerodromes, a common TA is promulgated.
- In India, minimum TA is 4000°.
Transition Layer
- It is the airspace layer between TA & TL and is usually < 500' thick.
- Climbing through TA, QNE is set. Descending through TL, QNH is set.
- QNH < 1013, layer height is 1500'. If QNH > 1013, layer ht is 1000'.
TL Transition Level
- It is the 1s available FL above TA. It changes with QNH at aerodrome.
===== [avh 0038]
000  1 - 9  Regulations
OCA Obstruction Clearance Altitude
- It is the minimum altitude an aircraft can descend to, above aerodrome
elevation during an NPA, or above threshold elevation during a PA, to
comply with obstruction clearance.  (See also: AEM)
- OCA = Highest obstruction in final & missed approach area (or within
4 nm of aid for circling approach) + AEM, rounded to next higher 50'.
MDA Minimum Descent Altitude/DA Decision Altitude
• - OCA + a margin (caters for crew qualification, Met conditions, eqpt, etc).
MSA Minimum Safe Altitude (written as MSA 6000)
- It ensures 1000' obstacle clearance within 25 nm from a nav-aid.
- MSA does not guarantee nav-aid signal reception.
- Descending below MSA is permitted only if visual reference with
terrain/runway is obtained.
MEA Minimum En-route Altitude (written as FL065/6500)
- It is the lowest permitted altitude in a route between two nav-aids.
- It ensures obstacle clearance (of 1000' above obstruction & 2000'
above mountainous terrain) + nav-aid reception + RT coverage.
- For legs up to 100 nm, clearance ensured up to 10 nm either side of route.
For legs > 100 nm, clearance width is 10% of leg length, restricted to
* max 60 nm on either side of the route.
- In a TMA, clearance is ensured up to 5 nm on either side of the route.
MAA Maximum Allowed Altitude (written as MAA FL280):
- It is the maximum flight altitude allowed in an airspace or route.
MOCA Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude (written as 6500T)
- It is the lowest published altitude between 2 VOR fixes on an ATS
route, which ensures obstruction clearance of 1000' where elevation
< 5000' or 2000' if elevation > 5000'.
MORA (Route) Minimum Off-Route Altitude (written as 6500a)
- It ensures obstruction clearance of 1000' where elevation < 5000' or
2000' if elevation > 5000'; within 10 nm either side of route & 10 nm
radius at end of the route.
- It is an altitude derived by Jeppesen.
- It does not ensure nav-aid coverage.
MORA (Grid) Minimum Off-Route Altitude
- It is the MOCA within a defined Latitude-Longitude grid.
- MORA Grid ensures obstruction clearance from terrain & manmade
obstructions but does not ensure nav-aid coverage.
- It is an altitude derived by Jeppesen or is provided by State.
- When derived by Jeppesen, MORA Grid ensures obstruction clearance
of 1000' where elevation < 5000' & 2000' if elevation > 5000'.
- When derived by State, MORA Grid ensures obstruction clearance of
1000' above obstruction & 2000' above mountainous terrain.
- '+/-' written inside the grid means MORA has doubtful accuracy.
- 'Un-surveyed means incomplete or insufficient information.
- On a chart, a MORA Grid value below 10000' is printed in green ink
& a value above 10000' is printed in red ink.
RSA Route Safety Altitude
- It is the highest obstruction within 5 nm of track + 1000' (if elevation <
5000') or 2000' (if elevation > 5000'), rounded off to next higher 100'.
Mountainous Area
- An area where terrain elevation changes 3000' within 10 nm.

-ạiIn class F,G airspace, required visibility can be reduced to 1.5 km, provided
the aircraft is slow-moving & there is no collision risk.
- Helos operations may be permitted in vis < 1.5 km if there is no risk of collision.
- No VFR take-off/landing permitted if visibility < 5 km or cloud ceiling < 1550.
If a VFR flight is unable to maintain VMC, then:
- Land as soon as possible; or
- Ask for amended clearance as comfortable/change route; or
- Ask for Special VFR, or Ask for IFR.
VFR Visual Flight Rules
Unless authorised by ATC, a VFR aircraft cannot take-off or land in a
Control Zone (CTR) when meteorological conditions are below VMC
rules (cloud ceiling < 1550' or vis < 5 km).
VFR flights are not permitted in the following cases:
- In IMC conditions;
- 20 minutes after sunset to 20 minutes before sunrise;
- At transonic/supersonic speeds;
- At a height < 500' above ground or water;
- Over cities/open gatherings of people, at a height < 1000' AGL;
- Beyond 100 nm seaward from shoreline within controlled airspace;
- Above FL150 (DGCA) / FL290 (ICAO).
- Military aircraft can operate VFR till FL285.
MVFR Marginal Visual Flight Rules
* Area where cloud ceiling is 1000' - 3000' and/or vis is 3nm - 5nm, & VFR
operations can still take place. MVFR only exists for pilots to easily
identify areas where the weather conditions are approaching IMC.
SVFR Special Visual Flight Rules
- SVFR is a VFR flight cleared by ATC in CTR, below VMC conditions,
- ATC must ensure safety is not compromised & traffic volume is low.
- It is only applicable for VFR flights; into, out of & within a CTR.
- Minimum visibility required for SVFR is 1500 m.
IFR Instrument Flight Rules
- To fly in IFR conditions, a PIC should hold a valid IR on that aircraft.
- Min nav-eqpt needed for IFR flight is 2x VOR, 2x VHF, 1x ADF & 1x ILS.
- FR flight will not be flown below the published MEA. Where no such
altitude is prescribed, it will be minimum 1000' above highest obstacle
(2000 in mountainous terrain), within 5 nm on either side of the track.
- If 'Y' was not entered in 'Flight Rules' in the FPL, a pilot could still
change to VFR on RT. (See also: RT Phraseology > Changing to VFR)
- Change of flight rules only done at the request of the pilot, not ATC.
- Pilot must not cancel IFR unless reasonable time will be spent in VFR.
IMC Instrument Met Conditions: Whenever VMC conditions doesn't exist.

1 - 11  Regulations
000
ADIZ Air Defence Identification Zone (Ref: AIP ENR 1.12)
- It is an area where identification is required for all aircraft operating in
or approaching on such a heading that it may penetrate that area.
- India has promulgated 6 ADIZs: North, East, West, Centre, South
and Sub-South East (Andaman & Nicobar).
ADC Air Defence Clearance
- It is a clearance to enter/operate in an ADIZ.
- It is to be obtained minimum 10 mins before entering an Indian ADIZ.
- Obtaining ADC from FIC on RT after take-off is permitted.
- Validity is -15min to +45min of EOBT. Beyond that, fresh ADC is reqd.
- Valid for entire route & return, irrespective of no. of halts/FIR crossings.
- ADC is exempted for flights below 1000', within 5 nm from a/d ARP.
FPL Flight Plan  (See also: Procedure to fill a Flight Plan form)
- It is a written plan of the envisaged flight, in a specified format.
- It has to be filed at an ATS unit, up to 120 hrs (5 days) before aircraft
EOBT and at least 60 mins before departure (not EOBT).
- It is valid for flight delays up to 30 mins from filed EOBT.
- If filed in air, must be at least 10 mins before entering a Control Area.
- FPL needs to be filed for flights in:
- Where ATS services are required  - Advisory airspace
- Flight across international borders  - For ADIZ purposes
- RPL Repetitive FIt Plan: Can be filed only for IFR flights; If same flight
is planned daily or on same day of the week; for 10 consecutive days.
- Closing a FIt Plan: On landing, an arrival report needs to be made
at the destination, to the appropriate ATS unit, in person or by datalink.
EOBT Estimated Off Block Time
- Time an aircraft is expected to move from its bay prior departure.
ETA Estimated Time of Arrival: It is the expected arrival time of aircraft-
For VFR: overhead the destination aerodrome.
For IFR: over destination aerodrome nav-aid, before commencing IAP.
ETA Revision: Required if ETA changes > 12 mins or TAS changes > 5%,
passed by aircraft to ATC.
EAT Estimated Approach Time: Time ATC expects an aircraft to leave
the hold to commence an approach, following a delay.
- If delay < 20 min, "No delay expected" call is given by ATC.
- If delay > 30 min, the delay period is expeditiously passed to aircraft.
EAT Revision: Required if EAT changes > 15 mins, passed to a/c by ATC.
EET Estimated Elapsed Time
- Running time filled in FPL, from take-off, till a/c over initial approach fix.
Mandatory Position Reports to be given by aircraft on RT:
- On entering/leaving FIRs & control zones.
- At each designated reporting point in controlled airspace, under IFR.
- When crossing a coast line, outbound or inbound.
- Flying in foreign territory, in compliance with their reporting procedure
- When changing from one area of responsibility to another.
- When outside controlled airspace, a position report is needed every hour.
- When operating in a confined airspace, ops-normal call every hour.
- When not following an ATS route, 1s position report is to be given at
30 mins, after that every hour. (See also: RT Phraseology > Position Report)
===== [avh 0041]
Regulations  000 1 - 12
Aircraft Overdue (See also: Search & Rescue > INCERFA, ALERFA)
- Jet a/c is considered overdue if there is no RT contact with it at its ETA.
- All other a/c is considered overdue 30 min after its ETA (1 hour for
helicopters) or at the end of its notified endurance, whichever is earlier.
En-route RT Failure Procedure (See also: RT Phraseology > RT Failure)
- If flying in the vicinity of a controlled aerodrome, look for 'light signals'
from ATC.
- An aircraft repeatedly switching ON & OFF its 'landing lights' indicates
RT failure and that no other assistance is required.
- VMC: If aircraft is in VMC, despite having filed an IFR flight plan, then:
- Continue flying VMC & land at the nearest suitable aerodrome;
- Then inform the destination ATS unit by any means.
- IMC: If aircraft is in IMC & it is inadvisable to continue in VMC, then:
- Continue blind RT call at all places prefixing "Transmitting Blind
- Squawk '7600' irrespective of partial or complete RT failure.
- Maintain last assigned heading & level or MSA (if MSA is higher)
for 20 minutes (7 minutes if the aircraft is in radar controlled
area, following failure to report at a reporting point. This time
will allow ATC to resolve any conflicting traffic.
- After that, follow the filed flight plan. Try to make good all ETAs.
- When overhead destination, join the hold, descend in the hold.
- Commence approach as per filed ETA, complete a normal AP.
- Try to land within 30 minutes of filed ETA.
Fix Accuracy (Ref: Doc 8168, Jeppesen Air Traffic Control)
- Fix accuracy of aids is needed for designing obstacle clearance planes.
- Nav-aid fix accuracy is calculated by RMS (Root Mean Square) of ground
system tolerance + airborne system tolerance + flight technical tolerance
- NDB: Track accuracy RMS t6.9°
Tolerance
- NDB has poor tracking
accuracy but has good  Ground System
tracking overhead.  Air System
- VOR: Track accuracy RMS +5.2°  Flight Technical
- VOR has good tracking
accuracy but has poor tracking overhead (cone of confusion).
- ICAO regulations require VORs to have up to 50° overhead
tracking. But practically, tracking is available up to 80° overhead.
- ILS: Track accuracy +2.4°. Where more guidance accuracy is needed,
'Fan Markers' are used.  (See also: Nav-aids > NDB, VOR, ILS)
- DME: Accuracy ‡.25nm or 1.25% of the distance shown on DME.
- Terminal Radar: Accuracy t0.8 nm within 20 nm of radar transmitter.
- En-route Radar: Accuracy ‡1.7 nm within 40 nm of radar transmitter.
Accuracy Class Classification
- Bearing: A +2°  B +5°  C ‡10°  D > ‡10°
- Position: A 5 nm  B 20 nm  C 50 nm  D > 50 nm

===== [avh 0042]
000  1 - 13  Regulations
'Q' Codes  (See also: Abbreviations > Q Codes full list)
Q codes were initially used in 'the olden days' as brevity codes for ease
of communication during aircraft HF transmission, in Morse-Code. They
were promulgated on 05 Jul 1912, during the 3rd International Radio-
telegraph convention in London.
Series QAA - QNZ is allotted for aeronautical use
Series QOA - QQZ is allotted for maritime use
Series QRA - QUZ is allotted for common use
QFE : Barometric pressure at ARP, corrected for the temperature at a/d.
- When QFE is set, the altimeter reads 'O' at aerodrome datum.
QNH: It is the QFE (in hPa) corrected to MSL, using ISA conditions.
• QNH is rounded off to its lower value. 1013.6 is reported at 1013.
- When QNH is set, altimeter will read altitude above MSL.
- When flying outside a control zone, obtain local QNH from any
nearby aerodrome. If not available, set the lowest regional QNH.
QFF : It is the QFE corrected to MSL using prevalent Met. conditions.
- Surface synoptic charts are drawn on QFF.
QNE : What altimeter reads on landing when 1013 is set on altimeter.
- 1013 may be used for an aircraft altimeter that can't be set < 950.
- Outside controlled airspace, set QNE when above 3000'.
(See also: Meteorology > Pressure)
Fuel Dumping Regulations (Ref: DGCA CAR)
- Fuel-dump system should be able to dump fuel from
aircraft's max AUW to max landing weight within 15 mins.
- After dump, aircraft must be able to climb to 10000' & fly for 45 mins.
- No fuel dumping is permitted over towns/populated areas.
- Fuel dump should preferably be done over a water body.
- There must be no thunder showers or CB activity in the vicinity.
- Minimum aircraft height before dumping fuel must be 6000'; and no
other aircraft must be flying:
- 1000' above or 3000' below;
- 10 nm horizontally or 50 nm/15 mins behind;
- Through fuel dump area in the next 10 mins.
Operating Minima
Weather limitations (visibility) applied for AWO (All Weather Operations)
are called minima. For each approach procedure, approved minima are
indicated in the approach chart. A take-off/landing cannot be executed
below its approved minima. The different types of minima are:
AOM Aerodrome Operating Minima: It is the usability of an aerodrome
in restricted weather, below which it shuts down. AOMs are published
for takeoffs & approach procedures in terms of visibility, RVR & DA.
- Normal AOM applies to scheduled & general aviation operators.
- Restricted AOM applies to non-scheduled operators.
- Restricted AOM = Charted AOM + 100' (DA/H) & +400 m (RVR).
- OCAs in Jeppesen charts are normal AOMs & not restricted AOMs.
Operator Minima: Lowest minima an operator can use at a specified
airfield, following approval from DGCA.
Crew Minima: Lowest minima the crew is authorised to operate in,
depending on the crew qualification.
Aircraft Minima: Lowest minima which have been demonstrated
during aircraft certification.  (See also: AEM, PA/NPA Minima)

Interception by Military Aircraft (ICAO Doc 9433 Interception)
(See also: RT Phraseology > Interception)
- All International civil flights must carry an 'Interception Table'.
- Interception of civil aircraft is done only as a last resort, to identify
and, if needed, return the aircraft to track or divert it away from
prohibited/danger areas.
- If an aircraft is intercepted, a pilot must:
- Comply with instructions using appropriate visual signals.
- Attempt contact interceptor on VHF 121.5 MHz, or 243.0 MHz.
- Inform ATC if possible.
- Squawk 7700.

Signal  Aircraft on Ground  Aircraft in Air  O SO

& await clearance
Steady green  Clear for take-off  Clear to land
Flashing red  Clear r/w immediately  Aerodrome unsafe, do not land
Steady red  Stop immediately  Continue circling
White flashes  Return to the  Land at this aerodrome after

not land for the time being.

000  1 - 15  Regulations
Aerodrome Definitions  (See also: Aerodrome Characteristics)
Airfield: Large grass fields where runways may be marked.
Airport: Point of entry/exit of an aircraft from a country.
Aerodrome: A place where aircraft can land & take off.
International Aerodrome: Aerodrome where customs, immigration &
excise control is established on persons & cargo.
Controlled Aerodrome must have a control tower & a visual control room.
Aerodrome Elevation: Elevation of the highest point in the landing area.
ARP Aerodrome Reference Point: Geographical location of aerodrome.
Where an ATZ is established, it is the centre of the traffic zone.
Apron: A designated area for parking of aircraft, embarkation &
disembarkation of passengers, loading & unloading of cargo, etc.
Manoeuvring Area: Area including runway + taxiway.
Movement Area: Area including runway + taxiway + apron.
Signal Square is needed if aerodrome accepts non-radio aircraft traffic.
Minimum size is 9 m2 & must be visual 10° above horizontal at 3000'.
Rad-alt Area: An area 300 m (1000') before runway threshold, within 7%
gradient, extending 60 m either side of centreline, for Cat II/III ILS ops.
Isolated Parking Bay must be at least 100 m away from other bays.
Long Finals: When a/c is 8 nm from threshold, on a straight-in approach.
Finals: When aircraft is at 4 nm from the threshold.
Baulked Landing: A landing manoeuvre unexpectedly discontinued.
Flight in Vicinity of Aerodrome: All turns are to be made to left while
take-off/landing, except in a right-hand circuit.
Runway Definitions
Runway: An area prepared on land, where an aircraft can takeoff/land.
Runway Strip: An area of defined dimension; enclosing a runway &
taxiway, intended to provide safe take-off & landing for an aircraft.
Instrument Runway needs to be of minimum 1800 m (6000') length.
Near Parallel Runway: 2 non-intersecting r/w with convergence of < 15°.
Threshold: Beginning of usable portion of runway, for takeoff/landing.
Displaced Threshold: Threshold at a point other than beginning of r/w.
The portion behind it may be available for takeoff, but not for landing.
HST High-Speed Taxiway: A taxiway provided to expedite runway
vacation by aircraft at 50 kts (for a code 3,4 runway) & 25 kts (for a
code 1,2 runway). HST has to be at an angle of 30° (min 25°, max
45°) to the runway.
Runway Slope: Difference in threshold heights  Ht difference (tL) x 100
in %. Max permitted slope for a runway is 2%  TORA
Dry Runway: A runway that is neither wet nor contaminated.
Damp Runway: A r/w whose surface colour has changed due to moisture.
A damp runway doesn't affect a/c performance for take-off or landing.
Wet Runway: A runway whose surtace appears reflective due to the
presence of water but no significant standing water.
Contaminated Runway: A runway with more than 25% of its surface
covered with water or equivalent depth of 3 mm.
Equivalent depth = Actual depth × Specific gravity of contaminant
Flooded Runway: A runway with more than 50% of its surface covered
with water or equivalent depth of 3 mm.
See also: Airframe > Tyre > Aqua Planning)

Regulations  000 1 - 16
Large Aircraft: Any aircraft with AUW > 5,700 kg.
MEHT Minimum Eye Height over Threshold: Height between pilot's eye
& ground when the aircraft is over the threshold (height from threshold
to aircraft wheel + wheel to pilot eye).
MABH Minimum Approach Break-off Height: Lowest height above ground,
at which, if a missed approach is initiated, aircraft won't touch the ground.
Dropping of Items From Aircraft: Nothing to be dropped from a/c except:
- Fuel, cargo (only over non-populated areas) in case of a/c emergency.
- Markers, smoke - only for navigation purpose.
- Flowers, pamphlets - only if approved by district Magistrate.
A/c Weight Category Classification  Unmanned Balloon Classification
Light  AUW < 7000 kg  Light  Weight < 4 kg
Medium AUW > 7000 kg  Medium Weight 4-6 kg
Heavy  AUW > 136000 kg  Heavy > 6 kg or payload > 3 kg
Super Heavy AUW > 560000 kg
Aerodrome 'Watch-Hours of Operation' Codes
H24 Continuous Ops  HJ Sunrise to sunset  SR Sunrise
HX Irregular Ops  HN Night hours  SS Sunset
O/R Open on request  O/T Other times  HS For scheduled operators
PNR Prior notice reqd  PPR Prior permission read HO As per Ops requirement
LCN Load Classification Number
- A system of reporting strength of pavements and their ability to
support loads. It is obtained by doing pressure tests on the pavement.
Similarly, wheel load of an aircraft can also be expressed in LCN.
- If a/c LCN is > runway surtace LCN, it may damage the runway.
- LCN caters for local variations by placing LCN into groups.
ACN/PCN Aircraft/Pavement Classification Number
- ACN shows the relative effect of aircraft wheels on the pavement.
- PCN is calculated by taking into account a/c weight & tyre pressure.
- If PCN ¿«¿ACN, then aircraft AUW has to be reduced.
- 2 values for each (MTW & empty weight), for both rigid & flexible
ACN of aircraft will be mentioned in 'Pilot Notes'.
- Aerodrome ACN/PCN values are published in NOTAMs.
- Format of ACN/PCN (E.g. PCN 80/R/B/W/T)
80 : ACN/PCN value
R/F: Rigid/Flexible pavement
A/B/C/D: Pavement sub-grade strength (A high, B Med, C low, D Very low)
W/X/Y/Z: Tyre pressure (W-high) (X-med 217psi) (Y-low 145 psi) (Z-very low 73psi)
T/U: Technical evaluation/Usage evaluation with an actual aircraft.
ESWL/SIWL (Equivalent single wheel loading/single isolated wheel loading):
- Group of 2 or more wheels at the same pressure can cause more
damage than a single wheel. So, ESWL is calculated.

• Aircraft Operations
ICAO Annex 6
AOC Air Operator Certificate
- It is the authority for an operator to carry out commercial air transport ops.
- Before the grant of AOC:
- All aircraft belonging to the operator must be airworthy certified.
- Operators must demonstrate commercial viability & safety.
- Operators must ensure that planned destination & diversion aerodromes
are of an acceptable safety standard.
- Operator's main base must be fully established with support facilities.
- Operator must exercise full operational control of all flights & method
of control should be included & approved in their Operations Manual.
- All administrative posts as required by DGCA are to be maintained
by the operator, e.g.:
- Flight Operations Manager  - Maintenance System Manager
- Ground Operations Manager - Crew Training Manager
Contents of AOC
- Name and address of the operator;
- Date of issue and validity;
- Description of type of operations allowed & area of operations;
- Registration markings of the aircraft;
- Any limitations imposed;
- Special approval, if any (RVSM, RNAV, ETOPS, etc.).
Contents of Operations Manual
Part A: General  Part B: Aircraft Operations
- Administration & Control of Ops manual  - General info, Measurement units
- Organisation & responsibilities  - Limitations
- Operational control & supervision  - Normal/Abnormal procedures
- Quality system  - Procedure checklists
- Crew composition  - Performance
- Qualification requirements  - Flight planning
- Crew health precautions  - Mass and Balance
- Flight time limitations  - Loading
- Operating procedures  - Configuration deviation list
- Dangerous goods and weapons  - Minimum equipment list
- Security  - Survival, emergency equipment
- Handling, reporting of occurrences  - Evacuation procedures
- Leasing  - Aeroplane systems
Part C: Route & aerodrome instructions, Calculation of minima, AOM
Part D: Training methods and duties
MMEL Master Minimum Equipment List
- MMEL defines equipment on which certain flight failures can
be allowed & conditions under which this allowance can be accepted.
- It is published by the manufacturer, included in the flight manual,
approved by certifying agency & mentioned in the Certificate of
Airworthiness.
MEL Minimum Equipment List
- MEL defines whether a flight can commence or continue from any
stop, following failure/un-serviceability of any equipment
- It is published by the operator, included in the operations manual,
and approved by the DGCA.

Accident Prevention
- The State has to establish safety programs for all operators to:
- Identify & provide continuous monitoring of safety hazards;
- Ensure remedial actions to maintain minimum standards;
- Make continuous improvements for the overall level of safety.
- A 'Flight Data Analysis Program' is to be maintained by the operator
for all aircraft with AUW > 27000 kg.
• Before a flight (after any maintenance work has been done), the PIC
should check aircraft documentation to confirm the airworthiness of
the aircraft. He should check:
- Identity of the maintenance organisation;
- Date and time of maintenance;
- Details of maintenance done, referenced to approved books;
- Identity of the person signing the release.
Fuel Calculation: Fuel needed for a flight is to be calculated as
follows:
Taxi Fuel
+ Trip Fuel (fuel for take-off, climb, cruise, descend & IAP at destination)
+ Reserve Fuel (which consists of the following):
- Contingency fuel (5% trip fuel or fuel for 5 mins hold at 1500' at destination)
- Destination alternate fuel (Missed approach, climb, cruise, IAP at altemate)
- Final reserve fuel (30 mins hold (at hold speed) at 1500' at alternate)
- Additional fuel: Reserve for 2 hrs at cruise including Final Reserve Fuel,
if no destination alternate aerodrome is available. (e.g. remote islands).
+ Extra Fuel (At the discretion of Commander)
Lease: Dry Lease A/c is operated under permit of the borrowing company.
Wet Lease A/c is operated under permit of the leasing company.
Alcohol - No alcohol is to be consumed by the crew 12 hours before a flight.
- No alcohol must be served on domestic flights.
Smoking in Aircraft: Smoking is permitted in private aircraft if smoking is
certified in its 'Certificate of Airworthiness'.
- Signs must be displayed where & when smoking is prohibited/allowed.
- Smoking is not permitted during take-off, landing or refuelling.

Regulations  1 - 20
Crew, Duty, Passengers (Ref: CAR Section 7 Series J, PartI)
ICAO Annex 6
Introduction
- Minimum 2 pilots are required for night IFR operations for all turbojet/
turboprop aircraft with passenger capacity > 9.
- Operator must maintain crew duty-time records for the last 18 months.
- Transit time from home to work is not part of duty time or rest time.
oo Duty Period: Time from when crew reports to work, until free of all duties.
The duty period should be spread out as evenly as possible in a month.
oo Flight Duty Period: Time from when crew reports to work, until the aircraft
engines are switched OFF at the destination.
•o Flight Period: Time calculated from 'Chocks OFF' to 'Chocks ON'.
•o Standby Time: Time the crew spends as standby to other crew on duty.
- Max 12 hrs. Reduced to 8 hrs if no sleeping quarters provided for crew.
- If standby culminates into flight, then time spent as standby is added to
flight duty period. Otherwise, standby time is part of the duty period.
° Rest Period: Uninterrupted time given for the crew, free from all duties.
- Rest period should be as long as previous duty cycle or 8 hrs after
standby time or 12 hrs before flight duty period, whichever is greater.
- Rest period must be a minimum of 18 hrs if the aircraft has crossed 3
time zones & 36 hrs if the aircraft has crossed 7 time zones.
- ULRF flight crew has to be given 2 days rest away from base & 4
days rest at home base after ULRF, before rostering for next flight.
Unforeseen Extension: Duty time extension that can be given to the crew.
- Max 1.5 hrs flight period/3 hrs flight duty period, +1 landing, in a day.
- Max 4.5 hrs flight period/9 hrs flight duty period, +2 landing in 28 days
- If duty was extended, crew rest period should be double of duty time.
LRF Long Range Flight:
- Flights with flight period 12-14 hrs, or flight duty period up to 18 hrs.
ULRF Ultra Long Range Flight: (See also: Flight Procedures > Controlled Rest)
- Flights with flight period > 14 hrs, or flight duty period up to 22 hrs.
- ULRF flight requires a minimum of 4 crew; 2 of them should be PIC.
- In-flight rest plan: Crew must have at least 2 rest periods (one > 4 hrs).
- After rest, crew must return to duty only after freshen-up time (½ hr).
- Flight time can be extended if there is a bunk/rest seat, which is a
minimum of business-class seat standard, with a 40° recline.
Max Duty Cycle Periods in 24 hrs  Max Cumulative Duty Cycles

Night Duty: Any duty encroaching any portion of time 0000 hrs - 0500 hrs.
- Crew must not be rostered for 2 consecutive nights flight in / days.
- However cargo-ops permitted if 24 hrs rest is given to crew, in between.
===== [avh 0050]
Regulations
• Commander
A designated pilot amongst flight crew, who is a qualified PIC. He is the
final authority as to the disposition & safety of the aircraft. He may
delegate his duties to another pilot. He is responsible for ensuring:
Safety of all crew, passengers & aircraft while he is onboard.
Compliance with rules of the air  - Flight as per MEL
Flight planning, awareness of weather  - Offloading passenger/cargo
All relevant documents, manuals, charts (incl diversion), etc are on board.
He can refuse to carry deportee/cargo in the interest of flight safety.
- Ensure aircraft CG & weight limitations are catered for.
- Ensuring CVR/FDR Is not switched OFF, except in situations where CVR
data need to be saved and keeping it ON might over-write it.
PIC Pilot in Command: Pilot responsible for safety of aircraft during flight.
PF Pilot Flying: Pilot, who, for the time being, is on controls.
PNF Pilot Non-Flying: Pilot who is assisting PF.
- Flight crew must have their seatbelts ON whenever seated in cockpit.
• Cabin Crew  pre
- The minimum age for cabin crew is 18 yrs.
- Aircraft cabin crew requirement: 0 to 9 seats - nil,
10 - 50 seats - 1 crew, for every additional 50 seats +1 crew.
- When > 2 cabin crew on duty, one is appointed senior, reporting to PIC.
- Cabin crew cannot do duty on more than 3 types of aircraft at a time.
- Cabin crew must be seated at duty station during critical phases of flight.
Navigator: A navigator is required if an aircraft is without a nav-equipment
that can give instant & continuous position data & if flight is > 600 nm.
Crew shall not perform duties on an aircraft if:
- He is under the influence of any drugs/alcohol.
- If he knows or suspects that he is fatigued.
- Following blood donation or scuba diving > 30 ft, for a period of 24 hrs.
• Re-fuelling
- No passenger must be seated inside a/c while refuelling, unless no. of
seats inside a/c > 20. In such cases, the following must be adhered to:
- Passengers are not permitted to disembark/embark while refuelling.
- Seat belt signs must be turned OFF.
- No-smoking sign ON, 1 cabin crew must ensure pax do not smoke.
- No passengers must move around in the retuelling area.
- Provision for their safe & rapid evacuation must be established.
Ramp/ladders must be placed for passenger evacuation.
- Passengers should disembark if Jet B or AVGAS fuel is used.
- There must be no unauthorised person/building within 15m of refuelling.
- There must be no naked flame within 30 m of refuelling.
- Aircraft engines, ignition, radio & radar, must be OFF.
APU if reqd, must be started before fuelling & can run while refuelling.
Lights essential for refuelling can be ON.
- Baggage loading/unloading can be done during refuelling.
- No maintenance activity is permitted on aircraft that may cause a fire.
- No other aircraft jet blast should come within 43 m of refuelling.
- If fuel is spilt during fuelling, stop immediately. Before re-commencing
refuelling, spillage has to be cleaned & not just washed into drains.
Log All flight crew must maintain a personal flying logbook, preserved for
5 years from the date of last entry.
- It must be certified by an appropriate agency once in 3 months.
- Instrument Flying (IF) must be logged only by the pilot who was on
controls, for the duration that was solely flown on instruments.

Regulations  1 - 22
• Passengers (See also: Air Regulations > Security > Passengers)
- All passengers, before entering India, should have a valid passport.
- Operators must ensure crew & passenger are carried only in authorised
parts of a/c. Commander can permit temporary access to unauthorised
parts if he deems it necessary for flight safety considerations.
- Admission to flight deck is permitted only for operating crew and for
DGCA representatives for licensing, at discretion of the Commander.
- Prisoners: Carriage of prisoners are prohibited without written approval
of DGCA. Operators should have SOPs for the carriage of prisoners.
A law Enforcement Officer should always escort them.
- Deportees: The State has to bear the cost of travel of deportees.
- Inadmissible Passengers: If a passenger is inadmissible at the
destination (e.g. no visa/valid passport), the operator has to bear his
return cost. The operator may ask him for compensation and take
him to his State of departure or anywhere else he is admissible.
- Mental/Epilepsy Patients will not be carried onboard unless
accompanied by a doctor. The patient must be sedated if required.
- Transit Passengers may stay in the transit lounge for up to 48 hrs
and are not permitted to go outside the airport building.
- Carriage of birds/reptiles/animals in a/c are not permitted within India.
- Operator shall not deny any handicapped person; their aids/guide
dog, provided such person informs his requirement during check-in.
- If a State permits a passenger to enter that State without a visa, the
State of departure & other contracting States must not need any
other document other than his passport.
- All passengers must wear seat belts during take-off & landing &
whenever Commander deems it necessary.
Passengers Seating: Seats near an emergency exit must be allocated to
healthy people & must not be allocated to the blind, deaf, old, obese,
sick people, children, deportees or passengers with animals.
Passenger Briefing in an aircraft must include:
- Smoking regulations;
- Seat position and tray stowage;
- Location of emergency exits;
- Location and use of floor escape path markings;
- Stowage of hand baggage;
- Restrictions on the use of portable electronic devices;
- Location and contents of the briefing card.
Passengers are to receive a demonstration of:
- Fastening and unfastening seat belt;
- Use of oxygen equipment;
- Location and use of life jackets (if required to be used).
Standard Passenger & Luggage Weights used for performance calculations:
Operators must have a procedure for calculating passenger mass, where-in they
either weigh each passenger & baggage & use it for take-off mass calculation,
or use a standard value as per table below (which includes 6 kg cabin baggage)

Cargo: Cargo must be stowed in only the places designated for it.
- No baggage is permitted in the toilet, in the cabin or under seats
without adequate restraining straps.
- Baggage & cargo must not impede emergency evacuation routes.

1 - 23  Regulations
•° Aircraft Markings
ICAO Annex 7
- All aircraft has to be painted with a group of a Nationality/Common mark
& a Registration mark.
- Nationality/Common mark has to be painted on the underside of wings
(50cm wide), between wing/tail (30cm wide) & on tail (30cm wide).
- The State may temporarily exempt markings for prototype flights.
Nationality Mark: These are a group of letters/numbers selected from a
series of nationality symbols from the 'International Radio Callsigns'
allocated to the State registry by ITU. WPC then allots this to different
departments in India, Aircraft callsigns are notified by DGCA to ICAO.
Call signs allotted by ITU to India: ATA - AWZ, VTA - VWZ, 8TA - 8YZ.
Callsigns allotted for Indian aircraft: VT (civil) & VU (military).
Registration Mark: They are assigned by State/Common mark registry.
These could be any letters except the 5 letter codes from 'International
Code of Symbols' or 3 letter 'Q Codes' or SOS/PAN/XXX/TTT.
Common Mark: It is used for operators registered in more than 1 country.
It is allocated to ICAO by ITU (International Telecom Union), e.g., 4YB
is 'Arab Air Cargo' registered in Iraq and Jordan.
• Registration/Airworthiness
ICAO Annex 8 Part 3 (Ref: Aircraft Act 1934)
Aircraft Registration
- No one shall fly an aircraft unless it is registered and nationality/
registration marks are painted on the aircraft. Aircraft without
registration marks may be flown with written permission from DGCA.
- No aircraft registered in India will fly outside India unless it has a
valid permit from DGCA.
- Cat A Operator: A/c owned by Govt, or an Indian citizen/company.
- Cat B Operator: Aircraft owned by non-citizen but has his business/
residence in India.
Certificate of Registration:
- It is an official document certifying that State of registry has registered
the aircraft. It is valid until the destruction of the aircraft. It includes:
- Nationality & registration marks
- Type of aircraft  - Serial number
- Year of manufacture  - Name & address of owner
- If leased, name of lessee and lessor.
Certificate of Airworthiness
- CofA is issued/renewed/cancelled by the State of registration (DGCA)
- ICAO standard form of CofA includes nationality, registration marks,
designation of aircraft (e.g. Boeing 747-400) & serial number.
- CofA ensures a/c is developed & manufactured properly & is fit to fly.
- The State of the manufacturer has to ensure that aircraft standards
are equal to or above ICAO regulations.
- CofA is re-validated at periodic inspections of a/c, as per rules of State.
- If a/c is damaged, CofA has to be re-issued after repair & inspection.
- The State may temporarily exempt CofA for a prototype aircraft
- Defect record needs to be maintained for all a/c with AUW > 5700 kg.
===== [avh 0053]
1 - 24
• Facilitation
ICAO Annex 9
Introduction
- Facilitation deals with rules for arrival and departure of aircraft &
aircrew on international flights.
- International flights into, from & over Indian territory are subject to
Indian law.
- When arriving in a country, all flights must land first at, and depart
last from an international airport.
Facilitation of Aircraft
- It is a document that provides entry of aircraft into a country. It can be
electronic, type written or written in ink/indelible pencil.
- General Declaration: An internationally accepted form, containing
aircraft registration details, flight number, date & place of departure,
destination and number of crew/passengers. It is signed by the PIC.
Contracting States may not require more than 2 copies of General
Declaration, manifest & stores list.
- An oral declaration concerning passengers, baggage & crew is
considered sufficient. A random check will be acceptable.
- For a '2nd degree of freedom' flight, submission of flight plan 2 hours
before arrival is considered sufficient to land in another country provided
they land at an international airport.
- No customs charges will be levied to any a/c registered in another state.
Facilitation of Crew
- The crew of transit/connecting flights may stay temporarily without
being subject to inspection except during security eventualities.
- The State has to ensure that when crew baggage is checked, it is
done so expeditiously & without delay.
- States shall make provisions for expeditious & temporary entry of
technical personnel into a foreign country to repair an aircraft on the
grouna.
- If not stopping for passengers, the crew will be allowed to stay 'duty-
free' till such time as set by the State.
- CMC Crew Member Card:
CMC holders are exempt from customs, health & immigration.
CMC can be used as an ID when presented along with a valid
flight crew licence.
Any crew having a CMC will not require a VISA or passport to
stay in a city provided they will return back for his next
scheduled duty return flight.
Basic Flying Rules
1. Try to stay in the middle of air.
2. Do not go near the edges of it.
3. The edges of air can be recognised by the appearance
of ground, buildings, sea & interstellar space.
It is much more difficult to fly there.

1 - 25  Regulations
° Aeronautical Telecommunications
ICAO Annex 10 Vol II (Communication Procedures)
Aeronautical Fixed Stations are aeronautical stations on the ground.
Aeronautical Mobile Stations are aircraft in the air.
Types of Aeronautical Communication Service
1. Aeronautical Fixed Service: It provides tele-communication between 2
fixed points on the ground., e.g. between ATCs. It consists of:
1a. AMHS Air Traffic Service Message Handling Service: Used for
aeronautical ground-ground communications, e.g. for the
transmission of NOTAM, Flight Plans or Meteorological Data, etc.
1b. CIDIN Common ICAO Data Interchange Network: A network run
by ICAO to transmit text or binary messages for the purposes of Air
Traffic Control.
1c. AFTN Aeronautical Fixed Telecom Network: It is a worldwide
system of fixed circuits, to exchange messages & digital data
between ATC or other aeronautical stations like FIC.
• AFTN Letter Addressee Indicators
FIC  ZIZX  AFTN Office  YFYX
Area Control  ZRZX  NOTAM Office  YNYX
Approach Control  ZPZX  Airport Manager  YDYX
Tower  ZTZX  Local Meteorology Office YMYX
Military Aerodrome  YXYX Area Control Centre  ZQZX
e.g. Bangalore Approach Control: VOBLZPZX
Priority Designators of Messages in AFTN
SS  Distress messages
DD  Urgency messages
FF  Flight safety messages
GG  Meteorological messages  (TAFs METARS SPECIs)
GG  Flight regularity messages  (Administrative msgs to operators)
GG  AIS Aeronautical Information Service messages (NOTAMs)
KK Aeronautical administrative messages & service messages
AFTN Sample Message Format
ZCZC LAA005 12032000
DD VIDPZQZX
120900 VABBZQZX
[MESSAGE TEXT]
NNNN
Message Decoded
ZCZC: Unique start of message identifier. This code is always used.
LAA005: Transmission identifier
12032000: Message released on 12th month, 03rd day, 2000 UTC
DD: Priority of message
VIDPZQZX: DTG + Originator (Delhi Area Control centre)
120909 VABBZQZX: DTG, destination (Mumbai Area Control centre)
[Message]: Message in plain text
NNNN: Unique end of message identifier. This code is always used.
===== [avh 0055]
Regulations  000 1 - 26
2. Aeronautical Mobile Service: For communication system between units
on the ground and in air, e.g. VHF (118 - 136 MHz), HF communication.
RDARA Regional & Domestic Air Route Area
- These are fixed HF frequencies allotted for different regions/areas,
meant for en-route communication by domestic flights.
- 5 areas in India (N Delhi, E Kolkatta, W Mumbai, S Chennai, NE Guwahati)
- 3 fq per area, in 3, 6 & 9MHz range, e.g. Chennai 2872, 6655, 8909MHz.
MWARA Major World Air Route Areas
- These are fixed HF frequencies for regions across the world, meant
to be used for en-route communication by international flights.
- These cater to the lack of VHF coverage in remote areas, e.g.
Atlantic & Pacific.
- In MWARA, the world is divided into 31 overlapping contours.
- India has 3 of them:
Area  Frequency
MID II (Middle East II)  3467 5658  10018 13288
INO I (Indian Ocean !)  5634 8879 11300 17961
SEA I (South East Asia I)  3470 6556  10066 13318
3. Aeronautical Broadcast Service: 1-way broadcast communication.
3a. ATIS Automatic Terminal Information Service
- It is a continuous & repetitive terminal & weather information for an
aerodrome, transmitted on a VHF fq or VOR fq (never on ILS fq).
- Max ATIS transmission duration must be 30 seconds.
- One ATIS transmission will have information of only for 1 aerodrome.
- ATIS is updated every ½ hour or for significant change in weather
and is indicated by changing the 'ATIS designator alphabet.
- ATS unit is responsible for its preparation & dissemination.
Components of ATIS:
- Airport name  - Information code
- UTC Time  - Sky condition
- Visibility  - Temperature and dew point
- Wind  - QNH
- Runway in use  - Instrument approach in use
- Information code repeated
3b. VOLMET
- It is a continuous voice broadcast of weather information (TAF,
METAR, SPECI, SIGMET) for any aircraft in flight, on an HF fq.
- There are 8 VOLMET stations worldwide. 2 VOLMET stations are
in India (Mumbai & Kolkata), which transmits every ½ hour, on
11387, 66/6 & 2965 MHz.
- D-VOLMET: Data link VOLMET.
3c. AERADIO
A book published by AAI, to be used by operators. It contains info on:
- Aerodrome location indicators;
- Communication & nav-aid facilities available in airports;
- Aeronautical communication stations in India;
- AIR (All India Radio) fqs & their location information;
- Information on meteorological broadcast stations, VOLMETs & fqs.
4. Aeronautical Radio Navigation Service: Transmission of nav-aid
signals, e.g. VOR, DME, NDB, etc.

1 - 29  RT Phraseology
∞o General RT Techniques
- Controllers should not transmit to an aircraft during take-off, initial
climb, last part of final approach or landing roll unless necessary.
- The word 'Immediately' should only be used when immediate action
is required for flight safety.
- The words 'surface' (w.r.t surface winds), 'degrees' (w.r.t headings),
'visibility', 'clouds/height' (w.r.t Met reports) & 'hectopascals' (w.r.t
QNH) may be omitted, provided there is no ambiguity.
- Use of 'courtesies' (e.g. good morning) should be avoided.
- Frequencies: Use six digits, except where the last 2 digits of frequency
are both zero, in which case only the 1st four digits are transmitted.
- Inappropriate Words: The use of the word 'for' can cause confusion if
it is interpreted as the number 'four'. Similarly, the word 'to' directly.
before a climb/descent or change of heading can be confused with
"two'. It can be avoided by using the mandatory words 'flight level' or
'heading' immediately before the numbers.
ATC: Navy 237, climb to FL180.
ATC: Navy 237, turn left to heading 310 degrees.
∞o Conditional Clearance
- A conditional clearance allows an aircraft to execute the instruction
only after another event has taken place.
- They are only used when the aircraft concerned are seen by both
controller & pilot. Aircraft or vehicle causing the condition shall be the
first aircraft/vehicle to pass in front of the other aircraft concerned.
- The condition must relate to only one movement.
- Conditional clearance is given in the following order and must be
read-back in full and in the same sequence as given:
- Call sign;
- The condition;
- The clearance; and
- Brief reiteration of the condition.
ATC: Navy 237, after landing Airbus 321, cross Runway 08, after.
ATC: Navy 237, behind landing Boeing 757, line up runway 27, behind.
ATC: Navy 237, after passing 4000 feet, fly heading 030.
°o Mandatory Read-back of RT Clearances
- Read-back of clearances is vital for ensuring mutual understanding
between the pilot and controller of the intended plan for that aircraft.
- Whenever ATC says "cleared", the pilot has to read-back entire RT
call and in the order given. After read-back, repeat aircraft call sign.
- Writing down the clearance before read-back and ensuring that both
flight crew members listen to all clearances is vital.
- Listen & check ATC confirmation or correction of read-back.
- For weather information, only QNH & runway-in-use is read-back.
- The following clearances shall always be read-back:
- Taxi instructions  - Transition levels
- Departure/Take-off clearance  - Frequency changes
- Airways/Route clearances  - SSR instructions
- Level/Heading/Speed instructions  - Altimeter settings
- Approach/Landing clearance  - ype of radar service
- Runway in use, Runway Hold-short/cross/backtrack

Typical RT Calls
Readability Check/Time check
Pilot: Kochi Ground (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq).
Radio Check 12345, how do you read? / request time check.
ATC: Nine 1216. chi Ground, read you strength 3 with loud whistling noise/
Departure Information
Pilot: Kochi Ground (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
IFR to Mangalore, request departure information.
ATC: Navy 237, Kochi Ground, departure runway 18, winds 320/06 kts,
QNH 1012, temperature 28, dew point 26, visibility 6 km, time 27.
Pushback
Pilot: Kochi Ground (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
Stand 6 (position), Information D (ATIS), Request Pushback.
Pilot: Kochi Ground (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
Stand 6 (position), Security checks complete, POB 67 (POB),
Information D (ATIS), IFR to Delhi (destination), FL 100 (filed FL),
Request Start.
- All taxi clearances will contain a clearance limit, at which aircraft must
stop, till further permission to taxi is given.
- Complex/lengthy taxi clearances should be written down by the pilot.
- Before Taxi, runway in use, surface winds (magnetic), QNH, visibility
in direction of take-off, temperature & time check will be given by
ATC. Only QNH & runway in use is to be read-back.
Pilot: Kochi Ground (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (19),
Stand 6 (position), Information D (ATIS), Request Taxi.
ATC: Navy 237, Kochi Ground, taxi to holding point A1, runway 18,
winds 190/06 kts, QNH 1013, visibility 6 km, time 1010.
Pilot: Taxi to holding point A1, runway 18, QNH 1013, Navy 237.
Crossing an Intermediate Runway: If a taxi involves crossing a
runway, active or not, specific clearance to cross it is required.
ATC: Navy 237, cross runway 18 at A1, taxi to holding point C, runway 27.
Pilot: Cross runway 18 at A1, taxi to holding point C, runway 27, Navy 237.
*ATC may request aircraft to confirm when the runway is vacated.
Returning Back to Stand
Pilot: Kochi Tower (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
Stand 6 or Taxi link 'D' (position), message from despatch, 1 passenger
left behind, request taxi instructions back to dispersal, will switch off
engines/will disembark pax for security check, will call again for Start.
ATC Clearance or Departure Instructions
Pilot: Kochi Tower (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
Taxi link 'D' (position), request clearance to Delhi (destination), FL
100 (filed FL).
ATC: Navy 237, cleared to Delhi, via filed flight plan route, FL100, LEPTU1
departure, runway 25, straight ahead 1500', turn left 2000, further with
Kochi approach 119.7, Squak 1122.
Pilot: - Read back clearance verbatim -
Departure Delay Information: Departure sequence such as number 5
to depart' or 'expect departure in...' is NOT a take-off clearance.

1 - 31  RT Phraseology
Take-off & Departure
- The word 'cleared' shall only be used in connection with a clearance
to take-off or land.
- The word 'departure' is used for Departure/ATC clearance.
'Departure' is not an instruction for entering a runway or to take-off.
- The word 'Take-off is only used when issuing a take-off clearance. A
take-off clearance will always be issued separately. Pilots should not
use the word 'Take-off' till acknowledging ATC take-off clearance.
- Any instructions to 'hold, hold position' or 'hold short of' must be
read-back in full.
- Before Take-off, only significant change in visibility, weather & winds
(changes in headwind > 10 kts, tailwind > 2 kts or crosswind > 5 kts)
will be passed by ATC. This information need not be read-back.
Pilot: VUBFT, ready for departure.
ATC: VUBFT, runway 27, winds 270/17 kts, cleared for take-off.
Pilot: Cleared for take-off, VUBFT.
Immediate Departure: Sometimes, it is necessary for aircraft to take-
off immediately after lining up.
ATC: VUBFT, are you ready for immediate departure?
Pilot: VUBFT, Affirm.
ATC: VUBFT, Line up, be ready for immediate departure.
Amendment to Departure Clearance
If the aircraft is approaching a runway, any amended Departure
Clearance issued by ATC will begin with 'hold position'.
ATC: VUBFT, hold position, amendment to clearance, after departure
climb to altitude 6000 feet.
Pilot: Holding, after departure climb to 6000 feet, VUBFT.
Cancelling Take-off Clearance
If take-off roll has not commenced, the aircraft shall be instructed to
'hold position & cancel take-off' × 2, stating the reason.
ATC: VUBFT, hold position, Cancel take-off,
I say again cancel take-off, due to vehicle on the runway.
Pilot: Holding, VUBFT.
After commencement of take-off roll, the aircraft shall be instructed to
'stop immediately' × 2.
ATC: VUBFT, stop immediately, VUBFT, stop immediately!
Pilot: Stopping, VUBFT.
Reject Take-off: If the Pilot rejects a take-off, use the word 'stopping'.
Pilot: VUBFT, Stopping, dog crossing runway, request backtrack.
Initial Climb
Initial Call: Aircraft calling an ATS unit on first contact after take-off
must include call-sign (& wake turbulence category if 'heavy'), SID
procedure, current level & cleared level, speed (if assigned by ATC),
and other ATC clearances (if assigned by ATC).
Pilot: Kochi Radar (station called), VUBFT (your c/s), on 124.7 (fq),
LETPU-1 Departure (SID), Passing 2300 feet, climbing to 6000 feet.
ATC: VUBFT, Kochi Radar, radar contact.

1 - 33  RT Phraseology
En route
First contact with subsequent ATS unit must include call-sign (&
wake turbulence category if 'heavy'), current level & cleared level,
speed & other ATC clearances (if assigned by ATC).
ATC: Navy 237, Kochi Approach, climb 6000 feet, proceed direct MML,
contact Kochi Radar, 123.5.
Pilot: Climb 6000 ft, proceed MML, changing to Kochi Radar 123.5, Navy 237.
Pilot: Kochi Radar (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
passing 2300 feet (current Level), climbing to 6000 feet (final level),
direct MML (previous ATC clearance).
Position Report: It contains your current position, time & flight level,
next position & time and further ensuing position.
Pilot: Kochi Radar (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
Position LATID (position), time 0455 (time), FL 310 (FL),
VIRAM (next position), at time 0510 (time),
UGABA next (further ensuing position), Navy 237 (your c/s).
Air Report: Air Report is a Position Report + temperature, spot
winds, sky condition & turbulence. Air report is also to be given in-
case of visibility drop, turbulence, icing or wind shear. In case of CAT,
give an Air Report with 'Unable RVSM due turbulence' call.
Pilot: Kochi Radar (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
Position LATID (position), time 0455 (time), FL 310 (FL),
VIRAM (next posn), at time 0510 (time), UGABA next (ensuing posn)
#Air Reporti,
Temperature -20°C (temperature), Winds 260/35 kts (winds),
Sky Clear (sky condition), nil/mild/severe turbulence (turbulence), or
Experiencing severe turbulence, Unable RVSM due weather,
Request descend FL 270 (new level),
Navy 237 (your c/s).
Joining an ATS Route/Route Crossing Clearance: It is same as
'Position Report' + TAS, IMC/MC & "request joining clearance at
position & time" for the required ATS route.
Pilot: Kochi Radar (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
Position LATID (position), time 0455 (time), FL 310 (FL),
VIRAM (next posn), at time 0510 (time), UGABA next (ensuing posn)
TAS 250 (TAS), IMC (IMC/VMC),
Request Joining/crossing clearance W15 (route)
at BILUN (position) at 0410 (time)
Navy 237 (your c/s).
Changing ATS Route/Diverting: Route alteration can be done when
asked by ATC or due to bad weather en-route or when diverting to
another aerodrome. It is same as 'Position Report' + "Request alter
track",  ", new route, FL, ETAs, EET, endurance & revised alternate.
Pilot: Kochi Radar (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
Position LATID (position), time 0455 (time), FL 310 (FL),
Request Alter Track due to diverting/weather,
New Route W15 CIA, W15N to Mumbai (new route), FL 200 (new FL),
ETA MML 0220, GGO 0300 (new ETAs), Total EET 0230 (EET)
Endurance 0300 (endurance), Revised Alternate Goa (new alternate)
Navy 237 (your c/s).

• 1 - 36
Approach & Landing
Information passed by ATC on RT During Arrival
- On First Contact: Runway in use, surface condition, meteorological
info (in case of precipitation), changes in the status of nav-aids.
- Prior Entering Circuit Area: Runway in use, surface wind & QNH.
- Final Approach: Significant change in surface wind (changes in
headwind > 10 kts, tailwind > 2 kts or crosswind > 5 kts).
Radar Vector & ILS Approach
- The phrase 'cleared ILS approach runway xx' does not mean that
the aircraft is cleared to the altitudes depicted on the approach
chart. Clearances to descend after FAF will be given separately.
ATC: Navy 237, tum right heading 240, cleared ILS approach runway 27,
maintain 3000', report established localiser runway 27.
Pilot: Turning right heading 240, cleared ILS approach runway 27,
maintain 3000', report established localiser runway 27, Navy 237.
Pilot: Navy 237, established localiser.
ATC: Navy 237, cleared ILS approach runway 27.
Pilot: Cleared ILS approach runway 27, Navy 237.
Continue Approach
- A controller may delay landing clearance by issuing an instruction
to 'continue approach' when an aircraft reports 'finals, if runway is
obstructed but is expected to be available soon.
- An instruction to 'continue approach' is NOT a clearance to land.
- An aircraft may be permitted to touch down before a preceding
aircraft has cleared runway, provided there is no danger.
- Met info or winds on finals need not be acknowledged by the pilot.
Pilot: Kochi Tower, Navy 237, finals runway 27.
ATC: Navy 237, Continue Approach.
Pilot: Continue approach, Navy 237.
ATC: Navy 237, cleared to land, runway 27, wind 270/10 kts.
Pilot: Cleared to land runway 27, Navy 237.
Touch & Go: After touchdown, the aircraft will continue for takeoff.
Pilot: Kochi Tower, Navy 237, finals, touch & go / full stop.
Low Approach: Descend to an agreed altitude & fly I| along the runway.
Pilot: Kochi Tower, Navy 237, finals, low approach.
ATC: Navy 237, cleared low approach, not below 300'
Pilot: Cleared low approach, not below 300', Navy 237.
Low Pass: Fly past ATC Tower or any other point for a visual check.
Pilot: Kochi Tower, Navy 237, finals, low pass abeam ATC at 200.
Go-Around: Any RT for an aircraft to 'go-around' shall be brief.
ATC: Navy 237, go around.
Pilot: Going around, Navy 237.
Missed Approach/Cancelling VFR, go-around in Visual Approach
- Missed Approach is initiated by a pilot if runway is not visual at DA
or if runway is blocked or lost runway during a visual approach.
- In case of a Microburst/wind shear, give microburst/wind shear report.
Pilot: Kochi Tower (station called), Navy 237 (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
at DH, runway not in sight; or vehicle on runway; or
Cancelling Visual Approach due runway not visual,
Initiating Go around & missed approach,
Climbing to 2000' turning Right 260, establishing radial 240,
Joining hold at height 2000' (read out missed approach procedure).

00  1 - 37  RT Phraseology
Emergency Communications (See also: Search & Rescue > Distress/Urgency)
As soon as there is any doubt about the safe conduct of a flight,
request assistance from ATC immediately. Flight crew should declare
the situation early; it can always be cancelled later. Pilots should
attempt to speak slowly to avoid any unnecessary repetition.
MayDay & PanPan format is the same.
Make the first call on the frequency in use. If not possible, call on 121.5
MHz. Squawk 7700. Format of call:
- MayDay/PanPan, preferably to be spoken 3 times
- Addressee station call sign
- Aircraft call sign, calling frequency
- Nature of distress
- Intention of captain
- Additional Info: Position, Time, FL, Course, Speed, Endurance, POB
Pilot: MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY,
Kochi Control (station called), VUBFT (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq)
Right engine failure, (nature of distress)
Request immediate landing at Kochi (intention)
Position 35 nm north of Kochi, heading 120, FL80, descending,
POB 150, endurance 3 hours (additional information)
ATC: VUBFT, Roger MAYDAY, turn left heading 090,
Radar Vectors ILS runway 27.
ATC: All stations, Kochi Control, Stop transmitting, MAYDAY.
Pilot: Kochi Control (station called), VUBFT (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq)
Cancel MAYDAY; right engine restarted, resuming normal navigation.
ATC: Roger, all stations, Kochi Control, Distress traffic ended.
Sécurité Sécurité
It is a call usually used for navigation/meteorological warnings, e.g.
sighted volcanic ash, tsunami, or concerning safety of life at sea, yet
may not be particularly life-threatening.
Pilot: Sécurité, Sécurité, Sécurité
Kochi Radar (station called), VUBFT (your c/s), on 123.5 (fq),
Position SUKOS (position), at time 0455 (time), FL 130 (FL),
Observing a tsunami approaching coast (information)
Diverting to Coimbatore (intention)
Request Alter Track (new route), New ETAs, VUBFT (your c/s).
Tower : "Aircraft in holding pattern, say fuel state"?
Aircraft : "Fuel state".
Tower  : "Say again" ?
Aircraft : "Again".
After that the tower controller switches off his radio & climbs
down the stairs to drink coffee the rest of the afternoon.
