• ACAS Phraseology
Once a pilot reports an RA or if the aircraft departs from ATC
clearance to comply with an RA, ATC ceases to be responsible for
the separation between that aircraft and any other aircraft affected
as a direct consequence of the manoeuvre induced by the RA.
In such cases, the RT call would be:
Pilot: Navy 237, TCAS RA.
If an ATC clearance contradicts ACAS RA:
Pilot: Navy 237, unable, TCAS RA.
When aircraft is returning to assigned clearance:
Pilot: Navy 237, clear of conflict, returning to FL150 (assigned clearance).

- If RCF occurs during a climb, maintain current FL for 20 mins, & give
a blind call to that effect. After 20 mins climb to previous cleared level.
- Squawk 7600. Try raising other aircraft on 121.5 MHz.
- Continue giving blind calls at mandatory reporting points, including
for IAP.
* In case deviating from track, it will be a 'weather deviation without
RT contact' call.

Will climb to FL330 in 20mins, will transmit again at VIRAM (intention)

- Additional Info: Type/unknown, fast/slow-moving, climbing/level.

Regulations  1 - 40
000 Airspace
ICAO Annex 11, Chapter 2
FIR Flight Information Region
- All airspace in a State must be divided into FIRs.
- FIR is the simplest classification of an airspace. Only Information
Service & Alerting Service are available in it.
- FIRs usually coincide with national boundaries.
- FIR geographically identifies its location & with its ACC.
- ACC (Area Control Centre) may provide Area Control Service in FIR.
- FIC (Flight Information Centre) provides FIS (Flight Info Service) in FIR.
- Open FIR: An airspace that is not identified as CTA/CTR
- India has 5 FIRs: A Mumbai, I Delhi, O Chennai, E Calcutta+Guwahati.
CTA Control Area
- CTA is usually established in the vicinity of major aerodromes and at
the confluence of ATS routes. It is intended only for en-route traffic.
- It is a controlled airspace, upwards from a particular defined FL.
- Lowest possible level of a CTA is 200 m (700').
- Where a lower limit of CTA is defined, it will be a VFR level.
- ACC (Area Control Centre) provides Area Control Service in a CTA.
TMA Terminal Manoeuvre Area
- TMA is an area normally established at the confluence of ATS routes
and in the vicinity of one or more major aerodromes.
- TMA may contain one or more CTRs.
- TMA is called TCA (Terminal Control Area) in the USA & Canada.
CTR Control Zone
- CTR is established in aerodrome vicinity for arriving/departing traffic.
- It is a controlled airspace, from the ground, up to a defined upper
limit, or until CTA, if it exists.
- Where an upper limit of CTR is defined, it will be a VFR level.
- Approach Control provides Air Traffic Control Service in a CTR.
- CTR may encompass more than 1 aerodrome if they are close together.
- CTR should be a minimum of 5 nm around an aerodrome ARP.
ATZ Aerodrome Traffic Zone
ATZ is an airspace around an a/d for local flying, takeoffs & landings.
- Where no ATZ is promulgated, it is 5 nm around an a/d ARP, up to 3000.
• ATC Tower provides control services in an ATZ.

===== [avh 0070]
000  1 - 41  Regulations
UIR Upper Information Region
- Airspace established only for en-route traffic (no landing or take-off).
- Lower boundary of a UIR will be a VFR flight level.
- UIR may have the same or different rules from airspace below/above it.
- ACC provides Area Control Service in a UIR.
UPR User Preferred Routes
- UPR offers each aircraft a unique & most efficient flight path as per
their requirement, instead of flying established ATS routes.
- They are constructed via published waypoints & latitudes/longitudes.
The operator can choose his preferred waypoints for a route.
- Fight-time interval between 2 waypoints shall not exceed 30 mins.
- UPR may include traditional ATS routes also.
- Where established, UPR zone vertical limits are from FL280 to FL460.
- A/c flying UPR routes should be RNAV10 & ADS-C/CPDLC equipped.
- UPR has the following advantages:
- Improves aircraft and operator operational efficiency;
- Reduce flight times;
- Reduce environmental impact of aviation;
- It can be used routes to avoid weather.
Danger/Restricted/Prohibited Areas
- Prohibited (P): Overflying a 'prohibited airspace' is not permitted at
any time and under any circumstance. If an aircraft flies over a
prohibited area unknowingly, it should signal MayDay & land at the
nearest aerodrome.
- Restricted (R): Overflying is restricted in this airspace.
- Danger (D): Airspace is dangerous to overfly, at published times.
- Alternate red/green flares from the ground indicate that you are flying
in a danger/restricted area.
- Dimensions & locations of these areas are published in NOTAMs.
- They are depicted by a 3 letter code: Country identifier, followed by
FIR identifier, followed by area serial number.
e.g. VID-65: V (India), I (Delhi FIR), D (Danger), 65 (Serial No)
AFSRA Aeronautical Fixed Service Routing Area
- The world's airspace is divided into 22 regions by ICAO.
- Each regions has its location designator.
Indian & South East Asian FIRs is allotted the designator 'V'.
EG, NZ, SA, SC, Y

Regulations  • 1-42
SUA Special Use Airspace
Airspace wherein activities must be confined because of their nature. It
is a generic term used for Restricted/Danger/Prohibited areas, TRA & TSA.
TRA Temporary Reserved Area
Airspace temporarily reserved for a particular user, for a determined
period of time, through which other flights may pass with permission
from ATC
TSA Temporary Segregated Area
Airspace temporarily reserved for the exclusive use of a specific user
for a determined period of time, through which no other flights may pass.
OCA Oceanic Control Area
- Airspace above FL55 over large oceans of the world is termed OCA.
- Strict navigation procedures & rules are applied & enforced in an OCA.
• MNPS Minimum Navigation Performance Specification
MNPS was introduced in 1977 after establishing procedures for North
Atlantic operators to derive benefit from the improvement in capabilities
of latest navigation equipment while ensuring safety of operations.
NAT MNPS (North Atlantic Minimum Nav Performance Specification)
- NAT MNPS vertical limits are from FL285 to FL420.
- NAT MNPS vertical Separation (same direction) is 4000' & lateral
separation is 60 nm.
- NAT MNPS area include the following Control Areas:
- Reykjavik to the North Pole;
- Shanwick & Gander Oceanic;
- Santa Maria Oceanic, north of 27°N;
- New York Oceanic, north of 27°N but excluding area west
of 60°W & south of 38°30'N.
- For DGCA approval to fly in NAT MNPS airspace, LRNS Long
Range Navigation Systems (2 INS or 2 nav-systems using inputs
from one or more IRS or any other system complying with MNPS)
are required in the aircraft. These systems must:
- Be capable of coupling with auto-pilot.
- Provide a continuous indication of aircraft position relative
to track.

Airspace Classification - Classes of Airspace
A: Only IF flights are permitted. All flights are controlled.
Control & separation is provided for IF - IFR.
B: IFR & VFR flights are permitted. All flights are controlled.
Control & separation for IER - IER, FR - VFR, VFR - IFR, VFR - VFR
C: IFR & VFR flights permitted. Control & separation for IFR-IFR, IFR-VFR
VFR flights not separated from VFR but receive info on other VFR flights.
D: IFR & VFR flights permitted. Control & separation only for IFR - IFR
IFR & VFR receive information about other VFR flights.
E: IFR & VFR flights permitted. Control & separation only for IF - IFR.
All other flights receive as much info about other flights as possible.
F: IFR & VFR flights permitted. But no separation for any flights.
IF flights get Info Service. VFR flights get Info Service if requested.
G: IFR & VFR flights permitted. But no separation for any flights.
All flights get only Information Service, as far as possible.
- A to E: Controlled airspace. ATC control provided to all controlled flights.
- C & D: Control provided to VFR only when conflicting with IFR.
- F: Only Advisory Service available.
- G: Open FIR airspace. Only Information Service available.

- C & D: All airspace designated as CTA, TMA, CTR, ATZ are C & D.
- E: All airspace in designated ATS routes (other than CTA, TMA, CTR).
- F: All airspace outside CTR, CTA, TMA, ATZ, ATS routes.
- G: All other airspaces.

Regulations  1 - 44
000 Airways
ICAO Annex 11, Ch 2
Routes
- Width of published air-routes in India is 20 nm (RNAV 10) (Ref: AIP ENR3.1)
- Q routes are RNP5 routes in India, with a width of 10 nm.
- W routes are routes specific for Indian domestic operators only.
- Oceanic Routes: Width of Oceanic Routes are 20 nm (RNAV10) &
adjacent tracks are separated by 50 nm.
- SIDs & STARs are also classified as ATS routes.
- Lower ATS routes are routes below FL245.
- Upper ATS routes are routes between FL245 - FL460.
- No aircraft is to operate within 15 nm from an international border
unless following an ATS route or taking-off from an aerodrome
located within 15 nm of an international border.
- Any aircraft crossing an ATS route will:
- Do so at 90° to the route;
- Take ATC clearance at least 10 min before on VHF or 20 min on HF.
Route Designators
Route designators shall have 5 characters (maximum 6). 1 Char +
1 Prefix (if reqd) + 1 Suffix (if reqd) + a number 001-999.
Chars: A,B,G,R are used for non-RNAV regional routes between States.
L,M,N,P are used for RNAV regional routes (RNAV 10).
H,J,V,W are used for non-RNAV non-regional routes that do not
extend beyond national boundaries. H used for one-way routes.
Q,1,Y,2 used for non-regional RNAV routes. Q Routes are RNP5.
Prefix: U is used for upper airspace routes. (Say 'Upper' in voice RT).
S is used for supersonic routes (say 'Supersonic' in voice RT).
K is used for helicopter routes (say 'Kopter' in voice RT).
Suffix: F is used in routes where only Advisory Service is provided.
G is used in routes where only Information Service is provided.
Y used for RNP1 route above FL200. All turns within 22.5 nm radius.
Z used for RNP1 route below FL190. All turns within 15 nm radius.
e.g. UW456F: Upper airway W456 & only Advisory Service avlb.
CDR Conditional Routes: (Numbers 1,2,3 suffixed in a route designator)
1 used for permanently plan-able routes during designated times.
2 used for routes plan-able during designated times.
3 used for non plan-able routes. Usable only when directed by ATC.
R used to designate an RNAV route.
X used when 'non B-RNAV approved aircraft' can fly that route.
SLOP Strategic Lateral Offset Procedure:
- SLOP is established to mitigate wake turbulence that exist 15-30 nm
behind an a/c which has crossed 1000' vertically above in opp. direction.
- Following SLOP is also safer. Track-keeping accuracy of modern
aircraft is so high that 2 aircraft in opposite direction on same route, but
is inadvertently maintaining the same level, are very likely to collide.
- In SLOP offset, aircraft flies either 1 or 2 nm RIGHT of an ATS route.
- SLOP must be executed only by a SLOP capable aircraft & only in
SLOP authorised airspace. In India, SLOPs are applicable only in
oceanic airspace routes of Chennai, Mumbai & Kolkata.
- Decision to execute SLOP is of the flight crew. In SLOP approved
routes, the pilot need not inform ATC about SLOP execution.
===== [avh 0074]
1 - 45  Regulation
• Air Traffic Services
ICAO Annex 11
Doc 4444 - PANS ATM (Procedure for Air Nav Services - Air Traffic Management)
Air Traffic Service consists of 3 Services: AirTraffic Control Service,
Flight Information Service & Alerting Service.
1. Air Traffic Control Service:
- It prevents a/c collision in air/ground & facilitates expeditious traffic flow.
- Control service is provided to all IF flights in airspace classes
A/B/C/D/E & to all VFR flights in airspace classes B/C/D.
- It is also provided to all aerodrome traffic in controlled aerodromes
and to all special VFR flights.
- This service does not prevent terrain collision, except when the aircraft
is under radar vector.
- There are 3 types of Control Services: Area Control Service,
Approach Control Service & Aerodrome Control Service.
1a. Area Control Service
- ACC (Area Control Centre) provides Area Control Service. It
controls the traffic within a CTA/TMA & en-route traffic in FIR/UIR.
- ACC issues ATC 'departure clearances' before departure of an a/c
from an a/d, to ensure separation between all controlled flights.
- This clearance will be coordinated between various ATS units until
the aircraft lands in an aerodrome, or for a portion of initial flight.
- Clearance expiry indicates the time at which it will become void if
the aircraft has not commenced its flight.
1b. Approach Control Service (See also: Instrument Approach/Departure)
- It is the Control Service associated with arrivals & departures and
is usually established in a CTR (Control Zone).
- Sometimes two Approach Controls are combined if there are
more than one aerodrome in the vicinity.
- Approach Control is usually radar controlled, e.g., en-route radar,
radar vector, SRA, PAR, etc.
1b i. En-route Radar ensures minimum a 5 nm separation b/w 2 a/c.
It may be reduced in certain circumstances. (See also: Separation)
1b ii. Radar Vector: Before the commencement of radar vector,
aircraft may be asked to turn up to 30° heading for identification.
- Radar vectors start from 2.5 nm of the 'Radar vector area' edge.
- Pilot must follow the given hdg, not track. ATC will cater for drift.
- Max intercept hdg given to a/c for localiser interception is 45°
- When 'mode 1,2 parallel r/w ops' in force, intercept hdg is 30°.
- During radar vector, pilot maintains with radar controller through-
out, so he obtains landing clearance from tower & informs pilot
by 4 nm (latest by 2 nm). If the radar controller cannot obtain
landing clearance by 2 nm, initiate missed approach procedure.
- During radar vector, if radar contact is lost in the last 2 nm of
approach, pilot must initiate missed approach procedure.
===== [avh 0075]
• 1 - 46
1b iii. SRA Surveillance Radar Approach
- SRA is a Non Precision Approach, using Terminal Approach
Radar (TAR).
- Every SRA has a Radar Termination Range. In an RTR2 radar,
approach guidance will be terminated at 2 nm.
- During SRA, the height aircraft should be at, will be passed every
1 nm for RTR2 radar & at every ½ nm for an RTR1 radar.
- During SRA, the pilot maintains with radar controller throughout,
so he obtains landing clearance from tower & informs the pilot
by 4 nm (latest by 2 nm). If radar controller cannot obtain landing
clearance by 2 nm, initiate missed approach procedure.
1b iv. PAR Precision Approach Radar
- PAR approach is a precision approach done with a dedicated
Precision Approach Radar.
- During a PAR approach, a controller gives continuous talk
down to a pilot in vectors of heading & ROD.
- Controller asks for an aircraft landing configuration check at 3 nm.
- In PAR approach, pilot maintains with radar controller through-
out, so he obtains the landing clearance from tower & informs
pilot by 4 nm (latest by 2 nm). If radar controller cannot obtain
landing clearance by 2 nm, initiate missed approach procedure.
1b v. Instrument Approach (See also: Instrument Approach Procedure)
- Prior to final approach, the required radar separation is
achieved by controlling the aircraft speed. Maximum speed
change that can be applied is 20 kts, in multiples of 10 kts.
- No speed restriction can be applied within 4 nm to touchdown.
- If the pilot is unfamiliar with the instrument procedure, the
controller shall read out the complete procedure from the point
where IAP starts. Missed approach will be read out if required.
- If the pilot establishes visual references with the runway,
instrument approach must still continue unless he requests for
a visual approach & is cleared by the controller.
1c. Aerodrome Control Service
- It controls the traffic at an aerodrome from a control tower.
- Usually, only 1 aircraft is permitted to be on a runway at a time.
- Take-off: Succeeding aircraft will not be given take-off clearance
unless the preceding aircraft has crossed the upwind threshold
(DER departure end of runway) & has commenced a turn away
from runway direction.
- Immediate Take-off' clearance: Line up & take-off immediately.
- Arrival: Landing clearance issued at 4 nm, may be reduced to 2 nm.
- 'Land after' clearance is sometimes issued when another aircraft
is on the runway, on landing roll.  (See also: RT Phraseology ≥
- It is issued only during the day & when:  Conditional Clearance)
- Succeeding pilot has the aircraft on runway in sight;
- Runway surface is dry;
- Controller can see the entire length of the runway.
===== [avh 0076]
1 - 47  Regulations
2. FIS: Flight Information Service
- Flight Information Service is only provided in airspace classes C to G.
- It is established by FIC (Flight Information Centre).
- It provides advice & information for safe & efficient conduct of a flight.
- Information contained in FIS includes:
- SIGMET & AIRMET;
- Volcanic activity;
- Radioactive/toxic material in the air;
- Changes in status of nav-aids, conditions at the aerodrome;
- Weather report, forecast at destination aerodrome;
- Collision hazards in airspace classes C, D, E, F, G.
3. Alerting Service (See also: Rules of the Air > Aircraft Overdue)
- Alerting service is maintained by FIC & ACC, to act as a central node
& to forward alerts to appropriate rescue coordination agency, e.g. RCC.
- This service is the link between aircraft needing service & the service
provider.
- Alerting service will also be provided by any ATS unit.
- Alerting service has priority over all other services.
My helicopter crew was into its 7h hour of flying replenishments to a Navy battle group, off
the coast of Mumbai. When we approached a ship for landing, we were told to circle
overhead. Just as I was getting a bit nervous because of low fuel, my crew chief asked
me to fly down and hover along the ship's bridge. I obliged and I could see the captain of
the ship look at us, then frantically pick up the phone. Within seconds, we were given
clearance to land. "What did you do?" I asked the crew chief, amazed.
"Not much", he answered nonchalantly. "I just held the mail bag out of the door".

Instrument Departure
ICAO Doc 8168 - PANS OPS (Procedure for Air Nav Services - Aircraft Ops)
Vol 1 - Flight procedure during IAP (for flight crew).
Vol 2 - Construction of visual and IAP charts (for specialists).
• SID: Standard Instrument Departure
- SID is an instrument procedure for departing IFR aircraft. The pilot is
expected to carry all relevant charts in the aircraft.
- SID procedures assumes all aircraft engines are operating.
- SID layout is dictated by obstacle heights, ATC restriction & ATS routes.
- Pilots have to cater for winds to keep within the protection area of a SID.
But if a/c is on 'radar vector', follow headings given by the controller.
- SID provides an obstacle clearance of 0' at DER Departure end of
runway, increasing at 0.8% gradient, in the direction of flight,
assuming a maximum track divergence of 15°.
- SID terminates at an en-route waypoint, & is named after the
waypoint it is guiding the aircraft to.

• MOC: Minimum Obstacle Clearance - Departure
- Obstacle clearance is given in any instrument procedure. When track
guidance is given, the cross-section of straight leg track is divided into:
- Primary Area: ½ of route width. An MOC of 90 m (250') is available
below the primary area.
- Secondary Area: ¼ of route width, on either side of the primary
area. MOC reduces from a full 90 m at the inner edge to 0 at the
outer edge of the secondary area.
- During turns, where no track guidance is available, total route width is
considered as primary area & has full obstacle clearance of 90m(250*).

• Straight Departure
- A departure is called a straight departure if the departure track is
within 15° of the runway centreline.
- In a straight departure, routes are based on track guidance given by
NDB, VOR, etc., which has to be acquired within 20 km (11 nm) from
DER (Departure End of Runway).
• Turning Departure
- A departure is called a turning departure if the departure track deviates
more than 15° away from the runway centreline, to avoid an obstacle.
- Straight flight is assumed till 120m(400') above & 600m ahead of DER.
- At a turn, a MOC of 90 m is provided from the obstacle.
- Routes that are based on track guidance given by NDB, VOR, etc., are
to be acquired within 20 km (11 nm) from departure end of runway DER.
- Maximum aircraft speeds permitted in a turning departure are:
A/c class: A 120 kts, B 165 Kts, C 265 Kts, D 290 Kts, E 300 Kts
• Omni-Directional Departure
- It is a departure where track guidance is not provided during the
design of the procedure and initial departure tracks are undefined.
- When the aircraft is at the end of runway at a safe height, it can be
navigated in any direction.
- Straight flight is assumed till 120m(400') above & 600m ahead of DER.
- At a turn in any direction, MOC of 90 m is provided from the obstacle.
- Omni-directional departures may have sectors that need to be
avoided due to the presence of obstacles.
- Where obstacles do not permit omni-directional departures, a straight
or a turning departure needs to be published.
MOC: Minimum Obstacle Clearance - En-route
When track guidance is not provided en-route, or if the aircraft is outside
nav-aid coverage, primary obstacle clearance area splays at an angle
of 15° from its width, from the last point where track guidance was
available. Width of secondary area is progressively reduced to 'O'.
There is no 'maximum width' of this area. It continues to splay at 15°.
- MOC for primary area is 1000' where terrain elevation < 3000'.
- Where terrain elevation is 3000'-5000', MOC is 1500'.
- Where terrain elevation is > 5000', MOC is 2000'.

Joining a Hold:
- First aircraft arriving overhead a nav-aid holds at the lowermost level,
unless that aircraft prefers to hold at higher level due to the high fuel
consumption rates at low levels.
- If asked to hold at a non-standard hold fix, then do a left-hand hold.
- Aircraft must be at holding height min 5nm before reaching hold point.
- Depending on the aircraft approach heading to enter a hold, there
are 3 sectors and their respective procedures.
- Parallel Sector: On arriving overhead nav-aid, do a rate 1 turn, turn
out-bound along in-bound track, time-out for 45 secs. Then turn left or
right depending on hold pattern, come overhead aid again, join hold
- Offset Sector: On arriving overhead, do a rate 1 turn, turn outbound
30° away from in-bound track, time-out for 45 secs, then turn left or
right to intercept in-bound track, come overhead aid again, join hold.
- Direct Sector: On arriving overhead, directly turn outbound of the hold.
- Type of entry into hold is decided as per heading of a/c & not the track.
- A t5° flexibility is allowed on border of each sector, for type or entry.
- When approaching overhead, if a/c hdg is within +30° of outbound leg,
a/c can proceed direct outbound to commence IAP. No hold is reqd.
- Timing action when joining hold is done when aircraft is abeam the
nav-aid. If abeam cannot be determined, then time-out on rolling out.
- Still air flying time on o/b is 1min below 14000' & 1:30min above 14000.
- In hold, all turns are rate 1 or with 25° bank, whichever is less.
- In hold, pilot has to cater for winds to maintain within protection area.
Drift Correction: 3x drift angle on the outbound, 1x on the inbound.
Time Correction: 1/J 1 second for every kt of HW/TW on outbound.

Leaving a Hold
- Descend in a hold is permitted only with ATC clearance. The
procedure of changing aircraft height in a hold is called Shuttle.
- While leaving hold, commencement of descend on outbound track is
permitted only when the aircraft is within t5° of the outbound radial.
- Usually, lowermost aircraft leaves hold and commences approach
first unless another aircraft is on priority due to low fuel/emergency.
- An aircraft may be asked to leave hold & commence approach if the
preceding aircraft has reported that he can complete the approach
without encountering IMC & controller has the preceding a/c in sight.
- If an aircraft elects to hold for weather improvement, another aircraft
may be permitted to commence the approach. The 1st aircraft may be
asked to hold elsewhere or go to the top of the hold stack.
- Credit Time: If an aircraft was asked to reduce speed or hold en-
route, that time will be credited to him during hold stacking.
Segments of Approach
Every segment has primary & secondary MOC areas.
1. Arrival Segment
- It starts from a point where aircraft leaves en-route airway & ends at
IAF (Initial Approach FIx). It this segment is 25 nm away from the
aerodrome, a STAR (Standard Terminal Arrival Route) is published.
- Omnidirectional or sector arrivals have MOC of 1000' till 25nm of nav-aid.
2. Initial Segment
- It starts at IAF (Initial Approach Fix) & ends at IF (Intermediate Fix).
- Obstacle clearance of 300 m/1000' is provided in this segment.
- Track guidance to IF has a max intercept angle of 90° for PA & 120°
for NPA
- If no track guidance to IF is available, a DR segment of not more than
10 nm may be specified. But intercept angle will be restricted to 45°.
- A Track Reversal procedure established, if:
- No suitable IAF or IF is available to construct NPA, or if only 1
nav-aid is available for both IAF & MAPt (Missed Approach Pt).
- This procedure needs track guidance till a particular DME. Then,
a procedure turn/base-turn/race track procedure will be published.
All turns are at rate 1 or with bank 25°, whichever is less.
- Procedure Turn: In this, the outbound track is reciprocal to inbound
track. Then, either a 45°/180° turn (in which outbound time is 1  or Cat i
min for Cat A/B & 1:15 min for Cat C/D); or an 80°/260° continuous
turn (which takes 2 mins) is executed.
- Base Turn: Unlike a procedure turn, in a base turn, the outbound
track is not reciprocal to the inbound track. It is used when
accurate tracks can be given by a VOR/NDB.
- Race Track Procedure: It is used where an aircraft is required to
enter a hold pattern before approach & orientation of hold does
not allow a base turn or procedure turn. Race track entry
procedure is the same as standard hold entry procedure.

3. Intermediate Segment
- Starts from IF (Intermediate Fix) & ends at FAF (Final Approach Fix).
- This segment is used to adjust a/c speed & configuration for landing.
- Obstacle clearance is 300m/1000' at IF reducing to 150m/500' at FAF.
- If there is no FAF, this segment ends at final approach track intercept pt.
- Max ROD permitted on outbound for Cat A,B aircraft is 804'/min & for
Cat C,D,E aircraft is 1197'/min.
4. Final Segment
- It starts from FAF & ends at threshold/MAPt.
- Optimum distance for FAF is 5 nm.
For NPA: FAF is indicated by a 'Maltese Cross' on Approach charts.
- Aircraft is not to commence descend until it is within t5° of VOR
outbound radial or within t5° of NDB outbound track.
- Optimum descend gradient for an NPA final approach is 5.2% (3°).
- Max permitted descend gradient for Cat A,B aircraft is 6.5% (3.8°),
for Cat C,D,E is 6.1% (3.5°) & for Cat H is 10% (5.7°).
- High ROD approaches (> 6.5%) have to be authorised by State.
- For NPA with FAF, optimum distance is 5 nm, maximum is 10 nm.
- For NPA without FAF, only 1 available aid is used for IAP & MAPt.
- It is unlikely that NPA final approach track is aligned with r/w c/.
- Pilots have to maintain within ‡5° of final approach track for MOC.
- If there is no FAF, ROD on final approach for Cat A/B is min 394
fpm, max 655 fpm & for Cat C/D/E is min 590 fpm, max 1000 fpm.
For PA: FAF is where intermediate altitude intercepts localiser.
- PA starts when the glide slope is intercepted.
- Aircraft is not to commence descend until it is within ½ full-scale
deflection on ILS localiser.
- Pilots are to maintain within ½ full-scale deflection on ILS for MOC.
- If glide path fails during approach, that approach becomes an NPA.
- If localiser fails during approach, that approach becomes unsafe.
Execute a missed approach procedure.
- ILS final approach guidance distance is usually 3 nm - 10 nm.
- In ILS Cat I approaches, descend gradient is between 2.5° - 3.5°.
Final approach is flown on a pressure altimeter.
- In ILS Cat II/III approaches, descend gradient is fixed at 3°. Final
approach is flown on a radio altimeter and a flight director.
Straight in Approach: (Ref: DoC 8168 Vol II Part / Section 4,5.2 - Alignment)
- A/c is permitted to do 'Straight in Approach' if final approach track
& r/w centreline is within +30° for Cat A, B & t15° for Cat C, D, E.
• If the final approach track > +30° from runway centreline, execute
IAP followed by a Visual Circling Approach.

5. Missed Approach Segment: Consists of 3 parts -
- Initial Phase:
- It begins at MAPt and ends at Start of Climb (SOC).
- In this phase, pilot cleans up the aircraft & concentrates on climb.
- Minimum obstacle clearance MOC of 30 m/100' is provided.
- No aircraft turns are permitted in this phase.
- Intermediate Phase:
- It starts at SOC with 30 m MOC & ends when 50 m MOC is
obtained.
- Turns with up to 15° bank are permitted in this phase.
- Track change is permitted up to t15° from the initial track.
- A minimum of 2.5% climb gradient is required.
- Final Phase:
- It starts at 50 m MOC & ends when a/c reaches hold height.
- Turns with bank > 15° is permitted in this phase.

Approach Ban Point
- A flight will not continue to its destination unless latest meteorological
information indicates that, at ETA, the weather will be above minima
at the destination or the alternate aerodrome.
- PIC will not commence an IAP if reported RVR/Vis is below minima.
- After commencement of IAP, if RVR/Visibility falls below minima, the
approach shall not be continued beyond:
- FAF for a PA;
- Below 1000' for an NPA.
If RVR/Visibility falls below minima after the aircraft crosses FAF,
then the approach can be continued till DA/MDA, and aircraft can be
landed if the runway in sight at minima.
- If RVR is not available, CMV can be used as minima for NPA or Cat I
(See also: CMV)

°o Precision Approach (Ref: DGCA CAR - All Weather Ops)
ICAO Doc 8168 - PANS OPS
Introduction  (See also: Radio Aids > ILS)
- PA gives you vertical, horizontal & distance guidance on final approach.
- Obstacle clearance is ensured if aircraft is maintained within ½ full-
scale localiser & Glide Slope deflection.
DA Decision Altitude is the altitude at which missed approach must be
initiated when visual reference with r/w environment is not established
during the approach. DA caters for a height allowance the aircraft may
descend to, after the pilot has decided to initiate 'missed approach'. Actual
ht loss will depend upon pilot skill, a/c characteristics, altimeter errors, etc.
(See also: Rules of the Air Definitions > DA)
CAT I ILS
- Cat I ILS DA must not be < 200', and is based on pressure altimeter,
with datum as threshold elevation.
- Minimum RVR required for CAT I ILS is 550 m or Visibility 800 m.
- Minima published in IAP charts are RVR or CMV.
- A pilot may continue to descend below DH if visual reference is made
with runway, threshold, runway markings, r/w edge lights, PAPI, etc.
- For night Cat I ILS ops, at least r/w edge & threshold light must be ON.
- For Cat I ILS single pilot ops, min required RVR is 800 m unless it is
an autopilot coupled approach, in which case normal minima apply.
(See also: LVP)
CAT I| ILS
- Cat II ILS DA is b/w 200'-100' (based on rad-alt) & RVR not < 300 m.
- Auto-land system, if available, is preferred for Cat II ILS operations.
- For Cat I ILS, TDZ and MID RVR must be available.
- A pilot may continue to descend below DH if visual references made
with 3 approach lights or TDZ lights or r/w centre line or edge lights.
CAT I!! ILS  (See also: Instruments > Auto-pilot > Auto-land)
- Cat III ILS DA is between 100' - 0' & is based on radio altimeter reading.
- Unlike Cat I/II, Cat III minima do not provide sufficient visua
references for a manual landing. It only permits a pilot to decide if the
a/c will land at TDZ. Therefore Auto-land is mandatory for Cat Ill ops.
- For a Cat IIIA approach with Fail-passive Autopilot, aircraft may
descend below DH if reference made with 3 consecutive approach
lights or TDZ lights or runway centre line or edge lights.
- For a Cat IIIB with Fail-operational Autopilot, a/c may continue to
descend below DH if references made with at least one centreline light.
- For Cat IIIC approach, no visual references are required for landing.
- For Cat I|| ILS,  TDZ, MID & END RVR must be available.
- Landing lights are usually kept OFF during Cat II/III approach since
reflected light from fog & water drops may actually reduce visibility.

• Non Precision Approach
ICAO Doc 8168 - PANS OPS
(See also: Air Traffic Services > Radar Vector, SRA)
Introduction
- Non-precision are executed with guidance from ground equipment
that cannot provide height information. e.g. approaches made on
aerodrome approach aid like VOR/NDB.
- To ensure obstacle clearance, pilots have to cater for winds and
correct for aircraft drift while executing an NPA
MDA Minimum Descend Altitude: An altitude below which descend will
be made only if visual references have been established with the runway
environment and the aircraft is in a position to execute a normal landing.
MDA = OCA + a margin (caters for crew qual., Met conditions, eqpt, etc).
- Visual Reference means a pilot has, in his sight, all or any of the
following: runway, threshold, runway markings, runway centre/edge
lights, PAPI, etc.
- MDA applies to non-precision straight-in & circling approaches.
- Datum for MDA is calculated from aerodrome elevation.
(See also: Rules of the Air Definitions > MDA)

2D/3D Approach
2D Approach
- It is an NPA using lateral navigation guidance only, e.g., VOR approach.
- In this, the required vertical information is extracted from the approach
chart, and the pilot determines the necessary rate of descent.
- However, ICAO classifies a 2D approach to be a 3D approach if the
required vertical information is extracted from the aircraft navigation
system, e.g., a CDFA approach coupled with FMS VNAV.
3D Approach
- It is an approach that uses vertical guidance also. e.g., ILS approach.
- All precision approaches are 3D approaches.
===== [avh 0085]
1 - 56
Regulations
• CDFA Continuous Descend Final Approach
ICAO Doc 8168 - PANS OPS
Introduction
- CDFA is a flight technique and not a form of procedure design criteria.
- In this, final approach segment of an NPA is done from FAF, with a
continuous descent without level-off, to 50' above landing threshold,
where flare begins.
- All published NPAs are now CDFA unless specified otherwise.
- If FAF is not published, a pseudo-FAF can be calculated along the
inbound track, based on initial/intermediate approach altitude, distance
to the threshold (from DME/GPS) & a 3° glide path.
- Both CDFA & CANPA avoid Step Down Fix (results in stable approach).
- Steady ROD is to be maintained from FAF. If ROD > +300 fpm from
calculated ROD, approach is un-stabilised, go-around must be initiated.
- In CDFA, missed approach is executed on touching DDA. There is
no 'fly parallel'. Initiate (Climb) at DDA & left/right turn only at MAPt.
- If chart mentions an NPA as CDFA, the descend limit may be assumed to
be a DDA. Jeppesen assumes State has added height loss adjustment.
If the State hasn't specified it, Jeppesen will mention it as DAMDA.
- If the CDFA procedure is not flown, the pilot has to increase minimum
RVR requirement by 200 m for Cat A/B a/c & 400 m for Cat C/D a/c.
DDA Derived Decision Altitude: If a go-around Is initiated at MDA,
aircraft may sink below MDA due to its inertia. So, a minimum of 50' is
added to MDA to get DDA, so that if missed approach is initiated at
DDA, aircraft will not descend below MDA. The operator must establish
this safety margin (minimum 50') for each type of aircraft operated by
them & specify the documents where this value is derived from.
Why is 50' added to CDFA/NPA MDA and not to ILS DA?
ILS DA caters for aircraft sink while executing a missed approach. But MDA in
NPA is 'Minimum Descend Altitude'. During a CDFA, if you decide to initiate a
go-around when touching MDA, the aircraft may momentarily sink below it.
Advantages of CDFA
- No additional aircraft equipment needed.
- Integration with VNAV procedures possible.
- Constant angle approach, hence facilitates better visual cues for pilots.
- Approach, missed approach & go around manoeuvres similar to ILS.
- Minimises CFIT (Controlled FIt Into Terrain) caused by step down fixes.
- Increased safety due to the concept of 'stabilised approach'.
- Improved pilot situational awareness & reduced pilot workload.
- Improved fuel efficiency by minimising low-altitude level flight time.
- Reduced noise level by minimising level-flight time at high thrust.
CANPA Constant Angle NPA
CANPA is an old procedure similar to CDFA. A stable constant angle
approach is made until MDA. Then aircraft is flown level till MAPt. It
suits helicopters, who are allowed to do it.
Allowance used by procedures specialists for vertical displacement
Height loss/altimeter margin during initiating missed approach (Jeppesen Air Traffic Control, ICAO Doc 8168)

• Visual Manoeuvring (Circling) VM(C) or
Circling Approach or Circle to Land
ICAO Doc 8168 - PANS OPS
VM(C) or Circling Approach or Circle to Land is a visual manoeuvre, on
completion of an IAP, to bring the aircraft into a position for landing.
- It is an extension of lAP if a straight-in approach could not be made.
- It is also specified if:
- Runway alignment or descend gradient falls outside the criteria for
a straight-in approach. i.e., a/c is beyond t30° of r/w centreline, or
- Approach is made on one runway, but aircraft has to be landed on
opposite runway that doesn't have a published IAP.
- It is a visual manoeuvre keeping the runway environment (threshold/
approach lights/marks identifying runway, etc.) in sight at all times.
- If visual reference is lost while doing circling, initiate missed approach:
- Make a climbing turn towards the centre of the runway, then,
- When overhead, establish the published missed approach
procedure for the instrument runway.
- Minimum visibility needed for VM(C) is 2800 m (Cat A), 3200 m (Cat
B), 3600 m (Cat C/D), or NPA minima, whichever is higher.
- VM(C) is permitted only in published VM(C) areas.
- VM(C) area/circling radius is made around a runway by considering:
- Aircraft category, approach speeds & obstructions;
- Bank angles for turn (Cat A/B 25°, Cat C/D 20°, Cat E 22°), or
bank for rate 1, whichever is less;
- 25 kts of wind.
- Some sectors around the aerodrome may have VM(C) prohibited
areas due to the presence of obstacles.
VM(C) OCA = Highest obstn in circling area + Fixed MOC Margin (see table)
VM(C) MDA = OCA + Margin (Crew qualifications, Meteorological conditions,
airborne/ground equipment characteristics, etc).

===== [avh 0087]
Regulations  1 - 58
Visual Approach
ICAO Doc 4444 - PANS ATM
- It is the final approach done by an IFR flight when part of LAP is not
completed & approach is executed with visual reference to terrain (not
necessarily runway environment like in Circling approach)
- A request for a visual approach does not imply that the aircraft is
flying in VMC, but only that the specified requirements for a visual
approach have been met and the pilot can maintain visual reference
to the terrain. The flight continues in accordance with IF rules.
- Visual approach clearance is issued by ATC only if:
- Pilot has the aerodrome & preceding aircraft in sight; and
- Cloud ceiling is at or above initial approach level.
- If a runway has only a circling approach published, minimum visibility
required is 5000 m.
- For doing visual circuits, minimum visibility required is 5000 m.
• Stabilised approach
Following are the criteria for establishing 'Stabilised Approach' when an
aircraft is on various types of final approach:
- During NPA: Aircraft is stable in speed & ROD by 1000' AGL on finals.
- During PA: CDI indication is within 1 dot of localiser & glide slope.
- During VMC Visual Approach: Wings level by 500' AGL.
- During VMC Circling Approach: Wings level by 300' AGL.
- Speed: Within +20/-0 kts of reference speed (VREF)
- Max ROD on finals permitted is 1000'/min.
- Appropriate power settings are applied.
- Aircraft is in proper landing configuration.
- Crew briefings & checklists are completed.
Approach Speed  (See also: Performance > Approach Speeds > VAPP)
- It is the speed specified for approach and landing.
- Approach speed is calculated by adding VREF + a value, which depends
upon factors like headwinds, gust, ice accretion, etc.
- Usually, it is calculated as:
- VREF + ½ of steady headwind + full gust value, limited to 20 kts; or
- VREF + ⅓ of average headwind/gust-velocity limited to max 15 kts.

===== [avh 0088]
1 - 59  Regulations
Speed Control
ICAO Doc 4444 - PANS ATM
No speed control is enforced anywhere in Class A/B airspace & above
10000' in Class C airspace.
Speed Control Under Radar Surveillance
- Speed control is done to facilitate orderly flow of traffic & for spacing
between arrivals.
- If unable to comply, inform ATC about the minimum speed possible.
In such cases, ATC may remove an aircraft from the landing sequence
if it is not adhering to speed control.
- Speed control is achieved in steps of 10 kts below FL250 & 0.1mach
above FL250.
- 210 kts is considered minimum speed for a turbojet when aircraft is
below 10000' & in clean configuration.
Speed Control Under Non-Radar Environment
- Max speed permitted is 250 kts IAS below 10000' in Class C to G.
- Max speed permitted is 220 kts within 15 nm of a VOR.
- When traffic permits, ATC may issue a 'No Speed Restriction'.
Flights exempted from Speed Control
- Aircraft establishing a holding pattern;
- Aircraft encountering turbulent weather;
- Aircraft on CAT II/III ILS approach within 20 nm from touchdown;
- Any aircraft within 5 nm from touchdown;
- Aircraft carrying a VIP;
- Aircraft in an emergency;
- For all aircraft above FL390, without the pilot's consent.

===== [avh 0089]
Regulations  1 - 60
Separation
ICAO Annex 11, Doc 4444 - PANS ATM
Types of conflicting tracks between 2 aircraft:
- Same Track: Tracks converge/diverge +45° from behind preceding a/c.
- Reciprocal Track: Tracks converge/diverge t45° ahead of aircraft.
- Crossing Track: Tracks that intersect at any angle other than above.
Same  Reciprocal
Track  Track
Crossing
Track
- Essential Traffic: Traffic that should be separated but isn't. This
information is passed to another controlled flight when necessary.
(See also: RT Phraseology > Essential Traffic)
- If requested by an aircraft, agreed by another aircraft & sanctioned by
ATC, a flight operating in Class D & E airspace, if in VMC (even while
flying an IF flight plan), can climb or descend & maintain its own
separation, for a portion of the flight below 10000'.
- Aircraft can be cleared for visual approach if pilot confirms he is in VMC
& in visual contact with aircraft ahead & can maintain own separation.
Types of Separation
1. Radar Separation (2 aircraft separated on a radar)
- Beyond 60 nm from a radar, separation between 2 aircraft is 10 nm.
- 5 nm separation is ensured between 2 aircraft on a radar/ADS-B within
60 nm of radar.
- Separation may be reduced to 3 nm within 40 nm of a good radar.
- Separation is 2.5 nm when 2 aircraft are established on the same ILS
& within 10 nm of the threshold.
- Separation is 2 nm when 'Mode 2' parallel runway operations are in
force, between 2 aircraft on adjacent localisers.
• 2. Vertical Separation (2 aircraft separated in height)
- RVSM Separation: 1000' separation b/w flight levels until FL410.
- Non RVSM Separation: 1000' below FL290 & 2000' b/w FL290-FL410.
- ICAO flight level occupancy standard for an aircraft is +300' of the
cleared FL.
- An aircraft cruising at a FL has priority over another aircraft requesting
that FL. When 2 aircraft are at same level, the one ahead has priority.
• 3. Lateral Separation (2 aircraft separated side by side)
Geographical Separation: By keeping aircraft in different geographical
areas by position reports determined visually or by a nav-aid.
Track Separation:
- For aircraft using same nav-aid, 15 nm from the common aid with
track divergence of 15° for VOR, 30° for NDB & 45° for a DR fix.
- For aircraft using different nav-aids, separation is established by
ensuring that derived protected (buffer) airspaces do not overlap.
- In RNAV operations, separation is ensured by keeping 2 aircraft
on parallel tracks with sufficient separation in such a way that
their protected areas do not overlap.

• 4a. Longitudinal Separation (2 aircraft separated one behind the other)
DME Based
Same Level, Same Track
• 20 nm separation, provided both aircraft are on the same DME
• 10 nm separation it preceding aircraft is faster by 20 kts TAS
Same Level, on Crossing Track
• 20 nm separation, provided both aircraft are on the same DME.
- 10 nm separation if preceding aircraft is faster by 20 kts TAS.
provided each aircraft reports DME from a station located at the
crossing point & relative angle of track < 90°.
Same Level, on Reciprocal Track
- At least 10 nm separation when both aircraft pass each other
provided both aircraft are on the same DME.
Climb/Descend
- At least 10 nm separation when vertical separation doesn't exist,
provided both aircraft are on the same DME & 1 aircraft maintains
level flight.
• 4b. Longitudinal Separation - Time Based
Same Level, Same Track:
- 15 mins separation between 2 aircraft.
- 10 mins, if frequent determination of posn/spd is avlb from a nav-aid.
- 5 mins if both a/c departed from same aerodrome or if both a/c passed
over same reporting point & preceding a/c is faster by 20 kts TAS.
- 3 mins if both a/c departed from same aerodrome or if both a/c passed
over same reporting point & preceding a/c is faster by 40 kts TAS.
Same Level/Climb/Descend, on Crossing Track:
- 15 mins separation between both aircraft.
- 10 mins, if frequent determination of posn/spo is avib from a nav-aid.
Same Level/Climb/Descend, on Reciprocal Track:
- Aircraft has to maintain vertical separation for at least 10 mins
prior to & after the time another aircraft is estimated to have passed.
Climb/Descend through Level, on Same Track:
- 15 mins separation between both aircraft.
- 10 mins, if frequent determination of posn/spd avlb from a nav-aid.
- 5 mins, provided level change is commenced within 10 mins 2nd
aircraft has reported over same point.

===== [avh 0091]
Regulations  1 - 62
• 5. Visual Separation (Only in the vicinity of aerodromes)
- Application of visual separation between a/c increase aerodrome capacity.
- Normal separation standards between 2 aircraft may be reduced if:
- Both aircraft are continuously visual to the controller.
- Succeeding aircraft reports visual contact with preceding
aircraft & can maintain their own separation.
- Additionally, if requested by an aircraft, agreed by another aircraft &
sanctioned by ATC, a flight operating in Class D & E airspace, if in
VMC (even while flying an IFR flight plan), can climb or descend &
maintain its own separation, for a portion of the flight below 10000'.
• 6. Arrival Separation (Separation between 2 aircraft on approach)
• Landing clearance by ATC is usually given by 4 nm, latest by 2 nm.
- 'Land after' clearance may be given (only during the day) if succeeding
aircraft is visual with the preceding aircraft on the runway, provided
runway surface is dry & controller can see the entire length of runway.
- Succeeding aircraft may be cleared to commence approach if
preceding aircratt has reported that he can complete the approach
without encountering IMC & controller has the preceding a/c in sight.
- If an aircraft is executing an IAP but has not commenced base/
procedure turn, a departing aircraft may take-off in any direction.
- If arriving aircraft has commenced procedure turn but will take another
3 min to reach instrument threshold, departing aircraft may take-off in
any direction other than +45° of the reciprocal track of arriving aircraft.
- If arriving aircraft is in for a straight-in approach but will take another
5 mins to reach the instrument threshold, departing aircraft may take-
off in any direction.
• 7. Departure Separation (Separation between 2 departing aircraft)
Separation between two departing aircraft is 5 mins.
- Separation is 2 mins if both aircraft will be on same track & preceding
aircraft is faster by 40 kts TAS.
- Separation is 1 min if their departure tracks diverge by 45° or more.
- Separation is even lesser for parallel runway ops (See also: || r/w ops).
- Controller will clear an a/c to take-off when preceding a/c has passed
upwind end of runway (DER) & has turned away from runway direction.
- Departure clearance issued by ATC to an aircraft ensures separation
between all controlled flights & not just IF flights.
°° 8. Wake Turbulence Separation (Ref: Doc 4444, Jeppesen ATC chapter)
- Wake vortex exists behind every aircraft, including helicopters.
- In still air, vortex lowers by around 1000' & extends up to 9nm behind a/c.
- If a/c ht < 1000' AGL, vortex drifts out by upto 2 wingspan along ground.
- In crosswinds, the vortex can drift onto adjacent runways.
- To avoid turbulence due to wake:
- During Take-off: succeeding aircraft should lift-off before the lift-
off point of the preceding aircraft.
- During Landing: Succeeding aircraft should touchdown after the
touchdown point of the preceding aircraft.
(See also: Aerodynamics > Wingtip Vortex)

- It applies whenever an aircraft directly follows or crosses

- If both aircraft are using the same runway or a parallel runway
separated by < 2500'.

°o 8b. Wake Turbulence Time Separation - Landing
- Min time separation b/w 2 arriving a/c which are not radar-separated is:
- 2 minutes for M behind H;
- 3 minutes for L behind M/H & M behind SH;
- 4 minutes for L behind SH;
- No separation is needed between the same category aircraft.
• 8c. Wake Turbulence Time Separation - Take Off
- Minimum time separation for 2 departing aircraft is 2 mins for L/M
behind H and L behind M, if they are using:
- Same runway; or
- Parallel runway separated by < 760 m (2500'); or
- Crossing runway if flight path of 2nd aircraft will cross flight path
of 1st aircraft at the same altitude or < 1000' below; or
- Parallel runways separated by > 760 m (2500') or more if the
flight path of succeeding aircratt will cross the flight path of
preceding aircraft at the same altitude or < 1000' below.
8d. Wake Turbulence Separation -
Intermediate Take-off after a Full Length Take-off
- Minimum time separation between two departing aircraft is 3 minutes
for L/M behind H and L behind M, if they are using:
- Intermediate part of same runway; or
- Intermediate part of parallel runway separated by < 760m (2500').
Be. Wake Turbulence Separation -
Arrival/Departure with Displaced Threshold
- Additional minimum time separation between arriving-departing or
departing-arriving traffic if runway involved has a displaced landing
threshold is 2 minutes between L/M behind H and L behind M, if:
- Arriving L/M aircraft follows a departing H aircraft, or an
arriving L aircraft follows a departing M aircraft; or
- Departing L/M aircraft follows an arriving H aircraft, or a
departing L aircraft follows an arriving M aircraft; and
- If their flight paths are expected to cross.
8f. Wake Turbulence Separation -
Opposite Direction Use By Successive Aircraft
Minimum time separation of 2 minutes is required between L/M & H
and between L& M when the heavier aircraft is making a low or
missed approach & the lighter aircraft is:
- Using an opposite-direction runway for take-off; or
- Landing on the same runway in the opposite direction; or
- Landing on a || opposite-direction r/w separated by <760m (2500").
===== [avh 0093]
Regulations  1 - 64
000 Search & Rescue
ICAO Annex 12, ICAO Doc 7333 Search & Rescue
As per ICAO Convention:
- SAR in any airspace within a country is the responsibility of that country.
- SAR services in a State should be available 24x7.
- SAR region should as far as possible coincide with the FIR boundary.
- No overlap of SAR regions is permitted.
- Each contracting State should have similar procedures as its neighbours
& shall permit entry of SAR units from other nations into its own territory.
- In India, AAl is responsible for initiating SAR. RCC and its subcenters
are responsible for efficient SAR services.
- India has no SAR agreement with other countries but can seek assistance
from adjoining RCC.
- If a pilot observes a plane or ship in distress, he shall maintain visual
contact with it & pass its position to ATC unless he considers it
unnecessary or receives counter instructions from RCC.
- The first aircraft at the scene, even if it is not a dedicated SAR aircraft,
will take charge of on-scene activities. If he cannot contact RCC but
another aircraft that came in later can, the command of SAR is
transferred to the second aircraft until a dedicated SAR plane arrives.
- SAR a/c should have equipment for receiving & homing distress frequency.
Search & Rescue Process
- ELT (Emergency Locator Transmitter) transmits on 121.5 MHz,
243 Mhz & 406.025 MHz (Satellite fq).
- Satellites: 3 polar orbiting COSPAS & SARSAT sat. pick these signal
& relay the time & position (accuracy up to 5 nm) to 2 LUTs in India.
- LUT (Local User Terminal) at Bangalore & Lucknow re-transmit them
to MCC.
- MCC (Mission Control Centre) at Bangalore re-transmit them to RCC.
- RCC (Regional Co-ordination Centre): FICs of Delhi, Chennai,
Mumbai, Kolkata & Guwahati undertake duties of RCC. Additionally,
RCC sub-centres are also located at Kochi & Udhampur.
States of Emergency of Aircraft (See also: Rules of the Air > Aircraft Overdue)
Uncertainty Phase (INCERFA) is initiated when:
- There is uncertainty about the safety of aircraft & passengers;
- No RT contact from aircraft after 30 mins from a due position report.
Alert Phase (ALERFA) is initiated when:
- There is apprehension about the safety of aircraft & passengers;
- After an INCERFA, all communication efforts with aircraft has failed;
- Unlawful Interference in the aircraft is confirmed;
- Notified endurance of the aircraft is in doubt;
- Aircraft has not landed after 5 mins of being issued a landing clearance.
Distress Phase (DISTRESFA) is initiated following ALERFA when:
- Endurance on aircraft is over;
- Distress of aircraft is confirmed;
- Information has been received that the aircraft has force landed.

===== [avh 0095]
1 - 66
Regulations
• Accident & Incident Investigation/Report
ICAO Annex 13, ICAO Doc 9756 Accident Reporting
Introduction
- The purpose of accident investigation is to understand what went
wrong and to prevent further such accidents. Nothing else.
- ICAO must be notified of any accident/serious incident involving an
aircraft with AUW > 2250 kg.
- For aircraft with AUW > 5700 kg, a final report is to be sent to ICAO in
any ICAO working language, on completion of accident investigation.
Accident
- It is an occurrence where-in an aircraft sustains structural failure on
ground/air, requiring repair, except engine failure; or
- A person was fatally injured in flight; or has died within 30 days of an
accident due to an injury caused by the accident; or
- An aircraft is missing or inaccessible.
- All accidents must be reported to DGCA within 24 hrs of occurrence.
Serious Incident
- It is an incident that nearly caused an accident.
- They must be reported to DGCA within 24 hrs of occurrence.
Incident
- An occurrence other than an accident, associated with a/c operations
& its safety. It must be reported to DGCA within 48 hrs of occurrence.
- After an incident, only after DGCA clears the pilot can he commence
flying.
Accident Investigation
- The State in which accident took place must start the investigation.
- If State refuses, then the State of Registry or operator will investigate.
- If accident occurs in a non-contracting State or in international territory,
or if aircraft position is unknown, then State of Registry will investigate.
- A final report by the State conducting the investigation is to be sent to:
- State that started the investigation;
- State of aircraft registry/operator, aircraft design/manufacturer;
- State of which there were citizen casualties;
- Other States that provided help.
ATIR Air Traffic Incident Report
- It is a system for reporting, investigating and feedback of incidents
whilst an aircraft is under air traffic control. It is of 3 types:
- ATC Procedure Report: Procedural mistakes.
- ATC Equipment Report: Equipment malfunction.
00  - Air Proximity Report (AIRPROX): In the opinion of a pilot or controller,
the distance between 2 aircraft, their relative position & speed was
such that the safety of aircraft was compromised. Its categories are:
- Risk of collision  : There was serious risk of collision.
- Safety not assured: Safety may have been compromised.
- No risk of collision : No risk.
- Risk not determined: Insufficient information available.
- Initial report must be made on RT to ATC unless controller workload
doesn't permit so. In that case, pilot will be required to file it on landing.
- AIRPROX report must be confirmed in writing within 7 days.
(See also: RT Phraseology > AIRPROX)

- Width of each stripe is .9m for a PA runway & .45m for an NPA runway.
Runway Threshold Marking (Piano keys)
- Stripes that identify beginning of runway that is available for landing.
- Each stripe is 30m long, 1.8m wide & has 1.8m gap between stripes.
- No. of Stripes: 18m wide r/w - 4, 23m - 6, 30m - 8, 45m - 12, 60m - 16.
- Displaced Threshold is a threshold located at a point on the runway
other than its beginning, usually due to the presence of obstructions.
- It can be temporary or permanent. (Refer to the diagram above)
- Portion of runway behind it can be used only for taxi/take-off.
- Displaced threshold reduces LDA for a runway.
- It is marked by 10' wide white arrows along the centreline,
from beginning of the runway till the displaced threshold.
- Chevrons (yellow): It marks pre-threshold area that is unsuitable
for taxi, take-off or landing. It can be used as stop-way only.
Abandoned Runway: White 'X's marked along length of r/w, 1000' apart.
TDZ Touchdown Zone Marking
- Stripes 150 m (500') apart, identify TDZ where a/c should be landed.
- Markings within 900' of midpoint between thresholds are eliminated.
- Basic Pattern: Single row of stripe pairs. Runway > 900m has 1 pair,
900 - 1200m runway has 2 pairs, 1200 - 1500m runway has 3 pairs,
1500 - 2400m runway has 4 pairs, 2400m+ runway has 6 pairs.
- Pattern with Distance Coding: Similar to the basic pattern. But
instead of single pairs of touchdown zone markings, markings are in
groups of 3, 2 & 1 stripe pairs.

===== [avh 0097]
Regulations  000 1 - 68
Runway Aiming Point Marking
- These are 2 conspicuous broad stripes on runway, to serve as a visual
target for landing aircraft, where PAPI/glide slope, if available, intersect
- They are 30-60m long & 4-10m wide, placed 150m from the threshold
for a 800m runway, at 250m for a 800m-1200m runway, at 300m for
a 1200m-2400m runway & at 400m for a 2400m+ runway.
Runway Side-stripe Marking: A continuous white stripe painted on r/w
sides to provide visual contrast between runway pavement & ground.
Runway Shoulder Marking: A continuous yellow line to supplement
runway side stripes, to identify pavement areas adjacent to the
runway sides that are not intended for use by aircraft.
Runway Holding Point:
- Indicates where an aircraft must stop when approaching a runway.
- This line must never be crossed without explicit instruction from ATC.
- They are marked at min 75 m from runway c/l or 50m from runway edge.
extending across the width of taxiway or runway. Solid lines are
always on the side where the aircraft must stop. This is the pattem
closest to the runway if there is more than 1 runway holding point.
- ILS Critical Holding Point: Runway holding point for
Cat I/III ILS protection areas. It consists of 2 solid
yellow lines connected by pairs of vertical lines,
extending across the width of the taxiway. ATC will
ILS Holding Point
notify pilots when to hold short of an ILS critical area.
- Taxiway Intersection Holding Point: Single yellow  Taxiway Holding Point
dashed line extending across the width of the taxiway.
Non-movement Area Boundary Markings: It consists of 2 yellow
lines, 1 solid & 1 dashed. The solid line is located on the non-
movement area side (not under ATC control). Dashed yellow line is
located on the movement area side (ATC controlled).
2. Aerodrome Signs: All signs in an aerodrome must be frangible on impact.
- Mandatory Signs: Red board, white lettering, E.g. runway number.
- Information Signs: Yellow board, black lettering. E.g. taxi links.
- Location Signs: Black board, yellow lettering. E.g. taxiway designator.
- Dist. to-go Marker: Black board, white numbers, every 1000 along r/w.
- Signs showing numbers are always associated only with runways.

===== [avh 0098]
000  1 - 69  Regulations
3. Aerodrome Lighting System
- All lights in an aerodrome must be frangible on impact.
- Its max height must be below propellor height.
- Intensity of these lights should be controllable.
- Lights must be ON from night to day; or when visibility is < 3000 m.
- Aerodrome lights can be switched OFF provided they can be put ON
1 hour before ETA of the aircraft.
Aerodrome Beacon: These are flashing lights (24-30 flashes/min).
installed usually above ATC tower, that identify aerodrome location.
- Land Aerodrome: Flashing white & green beacon.
- Water Aerodrome: Flashing white & yellow beacon.
Taxiway Lights
- Taxiway Edge Lights are of blue colour, placed 60 m apart.
- Taxiway Centreline Lights are of green colour.
- Taxiway Leadoff Lights: Alternate yellow/green lights that lead
away from a runway centreline to a taxiway.
- ILS sensitive area: Taxiway lights of alternating yellow/green.
Runway Lights
Threshold Lights: 6 unidirectional green Its placed at r/w beginning.
- TDZL Touchdown Zone Lights: Installed on a Cat II/III ILS
runway with length > 1800 m. It consists of strips of white lights,
on either side of the centreline, from threshold till 900 m.
- RCLS Runway Centreline Lights: White lights, placed every 50'
along runway centreline.
- Last 900 m of r/w Its are red & white. Last 300 m Its are all red.
- RCLS is mandatory for a Cat II/III ILS runway.
- RCLS is required for low visibility take-off when RVR < 400m.
- REIL Runway End Identifier Lights: 2 synchronised flashing
unidirectional lights aimed 10° - 15° up.
- REDL Runway Edge Lights: White lights along runway edge, 60 m
apart for an instrument r/w & 100 m apart for a non-instrument r/w.
- Last ⅓ of runway or 600m whichever is less, is in amber colour.
- If the threshold is displaced, then REDLs are of red colour
from the beginning of the runway till the displaced threshold.
- Runway Guard Lights: 2 flashing yellow lights on both sides of
taxi holding point.

===== [avh 0099]
Regulations  000 1 - 70
4. Approach Lighting Systems
Simple Approach Lighting System
It is used for a non-instrument runway or for an NPA.
- It is a row of light extending from r/w centreline to minimum 420 m from
threshold & a cross-bar of 18 m or 30 m wide at 300 m from threshold.
Calvert Cat I Precision Approach
900 m from threshold. From 0 - 300 m, 1 row of centreline light;
300 m - 600 m, 2 rows; and 600 m - 900 m, 3 rows of centreline light.
Cat II/III Calvert Precision Approach
- It is the same as Calvert Cat I precision approach lights,
+ 1st segment augmented by 5 additional red lights on either side.
Cat I Precision Approach
- It consists of 720 m - 900 m long centreline barrette (3 to 5 rows of lights),
+ 1 cross-bar at 300 m (1000').
- Centreline barrette may be augmented with strobe lights.
Precision Approach Cat II/III
- Cat I precision approach lighting system
+ Additional 3 rows of red lights either side, from cross-bar to threshold.
+ Additional cross-bar at 150 m.
No ALS: No lighting system available at aerodrome; or
An ALS with length < 210 m + runway markings +
runway edge lights + threshold lights + runway end lights.
Basic Approach Lights: Any other approach lighting system:
An ALS with length between 210 m - 419 m HI/MI/LI + runway markings +
runway edge lights + threshold lights + runway end lights.
Intermediate Approach Lights: Simple approach lighting system:
An ALS with length 420m -719m single barrette HIALS + runway markings +
runway edge lights + threshold lights + runway end lights.
Full Approach Lights: Precision approach Cat I system:
An ALS with 720m HIALS distance coded barrette + runway markings +
runway edge lights + threshold lights + runway end lights.

Regulations  1 - 72
OIS Obstacle Identification Slope identifies obstacles that protrude
through it, within 15 km from an aerodrome, & obstruction lights are
placed a-top it. It is determined through a survey & is published in AIP.
- Low Intensity: A steady red light is used for obstructions < 45 m
height. A flashing red or yellow light is used for a mobile obstruction.
- Medium Intensity: A flashing white light is used for obstructions > 45 m.
- High Intensity: For obstructions > 150 m, sequential flashing white
lights (3 nos) are placed along the length of the obstruction.
- En-route Obstacles are objects > 150 m high, within 15 km radius
from an aerodrome.
Obstructions Markings within an aerodrome:
- Buildings: Marked with red and white squares.
- Vehicles: Aerodrome utility vehicles are painted yellow.
- Emergency Vehicles: Painted red or yellowish-green, e.g. fire trucks.

===== [avh 0102]
1 - 73  Regulations
000 Aeronautical Information Services
ICAO Annex 15, Doc 8126
Introduction
- As per ICAO, the State has to provide AIS or delegate it to a non-
government organisation. But the standards must remain the same.
- This service should be available 24 hrs. If not possible, it should be
available at least 2 hours prior to & 2 hours after arrival of the aircraft.
- All information published in AIS is in WGS 84 datum.
- Integrated Aeronautical Information Service consists of AIP, AIP
amendments, supplements, NOTAMs, PIBs, AIC and checklists.
AIP Aeronautical Information Publication
- AIP contains information of lasting nature, in cockpit friendly format.
- The State is responsible for the information published in AIP.
- In India, AAI publish AIP, amendments, supplements, NOTAMs & PIBs.
Vol I Part 1: GEN General: Regulatory & administrative information.
- GEN 1: Rules on entry, transit & departure of passengers.
- Rules that are different from ICAO are published here (GEN 1.7).
- Deals with aircraft instruments, documents, equipment, etc.
- GEN 3: Aeronautical Information Service.
- GEN 4: Changes in aerodrome, heliports, air navigation.
Vol I Part 2: ENR En-route: Information on flight planning.
- ENR 1: General rules of VFR & IFR
- Holding, approach, departure, interception procedures, etc.
- ENR 2: Airspace - UIR, TMA, etc.
- ENR 3: ATS routes, minimum flight altitude, etc.
- ENR 4: Radio, nav-aids, systems.
- ENR 5: Nav warnings, restricted, prohibited & danger areas.
- ENR 6: En-route charts.
Vol II: AD Aerodromes: Information on aerodromes.
- AD 1: Availability of aerodrome fire & rescue services.
- AD 2: Detailed information on aerodrome, refuelling facilities available.
- AD 3: Heliports (Not applicable in India).
AIP Amendments: Contains permanent changes to AIP, done by replacing page.
AIP Supplements: Contains temporary changes of duration >3 months or short
notice changes with extensive text/graphics, which cannot go in NOTAMs.
- A checklist of AIP supplements in force is published once every 30 days.
- Supplements have a serial number based on a calendar year.
- AIP supplements are printed on yellow coloured pages.
AIC Aeronautical Information Circulars: They are published by DGÇA.
They contain information that doesn't qualify in AIPs or NOTAMs, i.e.,
long-term forecast of major changes in legislation, rules, etc., e.g.:
- Information that is explanatory or advisory in nature;
- Information that is likely to affect flight safety;
- Amendment to 1937 aircraft rules.
PIB Pre-Flight Information Bulletin: It is a printed briefing folder for flight
crew, in plain language, and contains the following:
- Recap of current NOTAMs  - Met briefing  - Comm briefing
- En-route clearance, ADC/FIC - En-route nav-aids - Approach charts

===== [avh 0103]
Regulations  1 - 74
ooo NOTAM Notice to Airmen
- It is a notice containing info concerning establishment, condition or
change in any aeronautical facility, procedure or hazard, the timely
knowledge of which is essential to flight operations. They contain:
- Information on temporary changes of immediate nature at short
notice (except long texts/graphics, which will go in AIP Supplement)
- Information on permanent, operationally significant changes.
- They can be originated only by the 4 International NOTAM offices in
Chennai, Mumbai, Kolkata & Delhi.
- A list of NOTAMs in force is published on 1st day of every month & year.
- 7 days prior notice is needed for activation of danger areas in NOTAMs.
- Each NOTAM must talk about only 1 subject.
- Permanent NOTAMs are analysed at Jeppesen & included in charts.
- Temporary NOTAMs with validity < 90 days are not analysed/included.
- Temporary NOTAMs with validity > 90 days are analysed but may or
may not be included in charts depending upon their applicability.
Series/Classes of NOTAMs:
- A: Events that are likely to last > 2 hours, applicable for international flights.
• B: Events lasting from 30 mins to 2 hours.
C: Information for domestic operators only.
D: NOTAMs for military aerodromes.
• G: NOTAMs of lasting nature.
G NOTAM is issued only by NOTAM office Delhi, approved by DGCA.
NOTAM N: New NOTAM
- NOTAM R: Replaces previous NOTAM
- NOTAM C: Cancels old NOTAM
- SNOWTAM: Information on snow, ice or standing water on the runway.
- ASHTAM: Info on volcanic ash. Max validity is 24 hrs. ASHTAM codes -
- Red: Eruption in progress or dangerous, ash above FL250
- Orange: Eruption in progress or likely, ash not above FL250.
Yellow: Volcano active but currently not dangerous.
- Green: Volcanic activity ceased.
Sample NOTAM Format (Ref: Doc 8400 > NOTAM codes)
A1470/10 NOTAMN
Q)VOMM/QLBAS/IV/NBO/A/000/999/5129N00028W005
A)VOMM
B)1004282000
C)1006300800 EST
E)RWY09327L DUE WIP NO CENTRELINE AND TDZ LIGHTS AVBL
F)GND
G)12200M (40000ft) MSL
Sample NOTAM Decoded
A1470/10: Letter 'A' indicates Series. 4-digit is NOTAM number & 2-digit indicates year.
Q): NOTAM always starts with 'Q' qualifier, contains the following fields, separated by a f
VOMM: FIR (VOMM = Chennai FIR)
QLBAS: Q - start of Q group. 2nd+ 3rd & 4th+ 5th letters decoded from 'NOTAM codes'
in Doc 8400. If the code is not published, XX written & then further explained in
plain language. e.g. LB = aerodrome beacon, AS = unserviceable.
IV: (Significant to which traffic) I - IFR, V - VFR, IV - IFR & VFR
NBO: (Purpose) N- Attention of operators, B - Preflight information bulletins,
O - Operationally significant for IF flights
A: (Scope) A - Aerodrome, E - en-route, W - nav warning
010/280: Lower and upper limits of Flight Level affected
5129N00028W050: (Area of Influence), 50 nm radius around co-ordinates mentioned
A)VOMM: ICAO indicator of aerodrome or FIR (Chennai), can include more than one FIR
B)1004282000: DTG (UTC) of NOTAM effective. 2010, 04n month, 28h day, 2000 hrs.
C)1006300800 EST: Date/time group (UTC) when the NOTAM ceases to be effective.
All NOTAMs with EST written remains in force until cancelled or replaced.
D) Special period for changes being reported, otherwise omitted.
E) Plain text used to explain the 'XX' NOTAM content, if any.
F,G) Nav warning or air space restrictions if any, with reference datum & unit of
measurement. F = lower limit, G = upper limit
===== [avh 0104]
1 - 75  Regulations
• Security
ICAO Annex 17
Introduction
- It deals with rules concerning security of crew, pax & cargo, along with
airport design & access control. It is mainly intended to safeguard
international aviation, & if possible, apply it to domestic aviation.
- National security agency of the State has to provide a written version
of its 'security program for civil aviation', to other contracting States.
- Operators must not carry luggage of passengers who are not onboard a/c.
- Airside: Part of an airport in which security is controlled.
Passengers  (See also: Crew, Duty, Passengers > Passengers)
Potential Disruptive Pax: Deportee, inadmissibles, person in custody, etc.
- States must ensure procedures are in place & security personnel
are available during carriage of such passengers.
- These pax must board the aircraft before all other passengers.
- There must be no contact between them & other passengers. If
there was any contact, baggage screening must be re-done.
Armed Officers of the Law with weapons may be permitted to travel in
a civil aircraft by special sanction by State, provided:
- En-route State & destination aerodrome State has given permission;
- Destination airport is informed;
- The PIC is aware of his seat number;
- The weapon is stowed in an inaccessible area.
Carriage of Arms/Dangerous/Restricted Items
- Weapons must not be carried without permission of Central Govt.
- 'Operations Manual' must include procedures for such transport.
- Restricted items/arms must be stowed at a place not accessible to pax.
- Dangerous cargo can be carried in passenger cabin, if specified in the
technical manual. They should be clearly marked & properly packed.
- Consignor must provide a written note specifying nature & wt of cargo.
Hazard Class:  1 Explosive  2 Gas  3 Flammable liquid
4 Flammable Solid  5 Oxidising  6 Toxic & infectious
7 Radio Active  8 Corrosive  9 Miscellaneous
Unlawful Interference
- All a/c with >60 seats or AUW>45500 should have a cockpit door that
is lockable from inside & designed to withstand firearms/grenades.
- Admission to flight deck must only be for operating crew members &
representatives for licensing, at the discretion of the Commander.
- States must ensure that:
- Operators have a contingency procedure against hijackers;
- Aircraft experiencing unlawful interference are not denied ATC
services, permission to land, or use of nav-aids;
- If practical, hijacked aircraft should not be permitted to take-off
unless there is a risk of loss of life:
- Safety & provisions for the comfort of the crew and passengers
are ensured until the aircraft journey is continued.
• Actions by PIC During Unlawful Interference
- Unless conditions on a/c dictate otherwise, fly assigned track & hdg.
- If forced to depart track without informing ATC, then:
- Attempt RT on 121.5 Mhz;
- Squawk 7500 or 7700 if warranted. ATC may confirm on RT about
7500. If the pilot doesn't reply, then ATC assumes it is 7500.
- If no contingency procedure exists, fly 1500' from assigned FL.

VFR: FL035 to FL145 at 1000' separation (track 000-179 at odd levels &

RVSM Requirements for an Aircraft:
- 2 Independent altimeter (with cross-coupled static & icing protection)
- Altitude alert system (aural/visual warning if a/c deviates alt by ‡150')
- Altitude control system (which can hold altitude 150')
- Altitude reporting system (SSR Mode C with an encoding altimeter)
- ACAS Il equipment
RVSM In-Flight Procedures
- During preflight, set QNH. Max error must be < ‡60' from actual elev.
- When changing FL, a/c must not over/undershoot new FL by > ‡150.
- Every hour a crosscheck between 2 altimeters must be within +200'.
- Maximum a/c assigned altitude deviation from assigned FL is ‡300.
AAD Assigned Altitude Deviation: Maximum permitted deviation between
transponder Mode-C altitude & assigned flight level is 300'. This error
occurs if an incorrect altimeter setting was used or if aircraft is flying at
an incorrect flight level. ATC can identify this error.
ASE Altimeter System Error: This is caused by an error in the altimeter,
causing the aircraft to fly a flight level different to that displayed. This
error can only be identified by measuring actual aircraft height by external
means. Maximum permitted deviation between altitude indicated by
altimeter & flight level corresponding to ambient pressure is 245.
TVE Total Vertical Error: It is the sum of all errors, whether pilot induced
or equipment related, that can cause an aircraft to fly at a flight level
different than assigned. Maximum permitted TVE is 300'.
===== [avh 0106]
1 - 77  Regulations
oo RVSM Contingency Procedures are to be followed if the aircraft is
unable to maintain assigned FL due to:

===== [avh 0107]
1 - 78
Regulations
• ETOPS/EDTO (Ref: DGCA CAR EDTO, ETOPS)
ICAO Doc 10085 EDTO
ETOPS Extended Twin Engine Operations are flights conducted on a route
that contains a point farther than 1 hr flying time, at 'one engine inoperative
cruise speed', under standard ISA conditions, in still air, from an 'adequate
aerodrome'. It establishes safety regulations for 2 engine aircraft on routes
that were previously restricted to 3 or 4 engine a/c, e.g. transatlantic fits.
In 2012 ETOPS became EDTO Extended Diversion Time Operations to
include extended operations of 2, 3 & 4 engine aircraft. EDTO is intended
to design reliable aircraft, engines, systems & procedures for safe EDTO
diversions. CAO, however allows continued use of the term 'ETOPS' if
EDTO concepts are implemented. Maximum EDTO certified for an
aircraft is '787 Dreamliner' with an EDTO of 330 mins.
Adequate Aerodrome: An aerodrome that meets following requirements-
- Safety requirements of a/c landing & take-off at expected time of use.
- Aircraft requirements w.r.t. lighting, communication, nav-aids, etc.
- At least 1 IAP available (including ground radar based approaches).
Suitable Aerodrome: An aerodrome that is 'adequate' & has suitable
weather at the expected time of use.
Isolated Aerodrome: An aerodrome that has no destination alternate for a
given aircraft type.
Threshold Time: Singe engine flying time in standard ISA, in still air, to an
alternate aerodrome. Various approved 'Threshold Times' are as follows:
- 60 min for scheduled flights or 2 eng a/c with pax > 19, AUW > 45360kg.
- 90 min for non scheduled or 2 eng a/c with pax < 19, AUW < 45360kg.
- 120 min for aircraft with more than 2 engines.
- If diversion time is more than 60 mins threshold time, DGCA approval
is required. In such cases, aircraft systems requirements, operator
procedures & SOPs will be more stringent.
EDTO Entry Point: Point at which single-engine cruise speed under
standard ISA conditions in still air is more than threshold time (60 mins).
EDTO Significant System: Engine/system, whose failure will severely
affect EDTO flight. Max diversion time must not exceed EDTO significant
system's max working time, further reduced by a safety margin of 15 mins.
EDTO Critical Fuel: EDTO a/c should carry additional fuel as prescribed:
Fuel required for the following eventualities (whichever is greater):
- Rapid decompression and descent to oxygen safe altitude;
- Rapid decompression + engine failure & descent to oxygen safe alt;
- Engine failure and descent to DDA.
+ Fuel to fly to the alternate aerodrome;

RNAV systems, while offering very high accuracy similar to RNP
