RNAV Area Navigation
- RNAV routes specify the minimum equipment needed to satisfy
navigation accuracy along a flight path, for 95% of flight time.
RNAV1 means aircraft must be within 1 nm, 95% of the flight time.
- RNAV allows aircraft navigation in any desired path, within the
coverage of nav-aids or capability of self-contained nav system (INS).
E.g. FMS inputs - VOR/DME fix, DME/DME fix, GPS/WAAS, etc.
- RNAV is equipment based & doesn't need performance monitoring.
RNP Required Navigation Performance
- Like RNAV, RNP also has a number, indicating the size of containment
value. RNP1 aircraft must have a 95% probability to be within 1 nm.
- The difference between them is that, for RNP, aircraft needs to have
onboard performance monitoring & alerting (e.g. RAIM), whereas
RNAV doesn't need onboard monitoring.
- This allows a lesser reliance on ATC control & thus, is safer.
- RNP1 a/c may not be capable of RNP1 if nav-aid coverage is limited.
- RNP is performance based & may require more than just aircraft nav
capability. E.g. Communication: CPDLC, Surveillance: ADS-B/C, etc.
For RNP1, aircraft must be within 1xRNP value 95% of the time & within 2 x RNF
value 99.9999% of the time. Onboard monitoring must warn the pilot when
probability of TSE exceeding 2nm (2xRNP) is greater than 10-5 (0.99999%).

Advantages of RNP over RNAV
- Reduces ground-based nav-aid specific routes, thus reduces cost.
- Avoids the need for developing sensor-specific operations with each
new evolution of navigation systems, which would be cost-prohibitive.
- Helps in efficient use of airspace, fuel efficiency & noise abatement.
- Facilitates operational approval process for operators by providing a
limited set of navigation specifications intended for global use.

Advantages of RNAV/RNP Over Legacy Navigation
- Provides for local holding patterns;
- Reduces need for ground-based nav-aids;
- Reduces traffic congestion;
- Offers direct routes: saves fuel, time, and is environmentally friendly;
- Minimises RT: reduces pilot workload.
Nav-aids Used In RNAV/RNP
- GPS/WAAS: Operator must ensure RAIM availability.
- DME/DME: Accuracy depends on DME proximity & geometry.
- VOR/DME: Is less accurate than GPS or DME/DME fix.
- INS: Should be coupled with other nav-aids to improve accuracy.
Why is RNP 10 more restrictive than RNP 1?
RNP1 accuracy is logically more restrictive than RNP10. But in reality,
RNP1 requires lesser equipment than RNP10. An aircraft can be RNP1 capable
but not RNP10 certified. The reason for this is because of the difference in
airspace you use them in. RNP1 eqpt is intended to be used over land where there
are many ground/air-based nav-aids & thus, provides high accuracy. The further
you are from an airport (and land), the higher is the value of RNP required. RNP10
on the other hand,  IS used in oceanic airspace & requires more 'aircraft side'
equipment. For RNP10, you need at least 2 independent LRNS long-range nav-
systems (INS, IRS/FMS or GPS). Without GPS, accuracy time is limited to 6.2 hrs
due to IRS alignment drift beyond which a/c estimated position error is expected to
be > 10 nm. The time factor is also very important. For a 60 nm leg for RNP1 at 180
kts, accuracy must be maintained for only 20 mins. But for a 3200 nm RNP10 leg
(oceanic routes) at 480 kts, the required accuracy must be maintained for 400 mins.
This requirement is 10 times less accurate but has to be held for 20 times as long.

RNAV/RNP Waypoints
- Fly-by waypoints allow aircraft to turn prior (Turn Anticipation) to a

- Fly-over waypoints must be overflown by aircraft before starting a
turn. Usually MAPt & MAPt holding waypoints are the only fly-over
waypoints in an approach chart.

RNAV/RNP Legs
- Track to Fix: Leg is intercepted & flown as track to next waypoint.
ATC Instruction: "Direct Alpha, then on course to Bravo".
- Direct to Fix: Leg is described by a/c track from initial to next waypoint.
ATC Instruction: "Turn right, direct Bravo".
- Course to Fix: Leg is specified with a specified course to that fix.
ATC Instruction: "On course 150, to Alpha".
- Radius to Fix: Constant radius path from a point, terminating at a fix.
En-route RNAV/RNP Turns
Enroute RNAV/RNP turn tolerance is a circle with a radius equal to the
RNAV specs. Turn radius in RNP1 (routes Y & Z) is 15 nm below FL190
& 22.5 nm above FL200.
RNAV/RNP Separation
- Minimum separation is 80 nm between 2 RNAV10 aircraft.
- Separation reduced to 50 nm between 2 RNAV10 aircraft which are
on CPDLC or VHF contact.
- Separation is further reduced to 30 nm between 2 RNP4 aircraft on
RNP10 routes, which are on CPDLC/VHF & both reporting on ADS-C.
- Minimum 15 minutes separation is required in crossing situations.
RNAV/RNP Contingency
ATC unit should route non-RNAV aircraft (or during RNAV degradation)
via VOR/DME defined ATS routes; or, where practicable, provide
vectors until the aircraft is capable of resuming its own navigation.

===== [avh 0111]
Regulations  1 - 82
RNAV Specifications
ooo En-route
RNAV10 (Ref: DGCA Circular RNAV10 (RNP10))
- RNAV10 is used in oceanic space.
- Aircraft accuracy must be within 10 nm, 95% of the time.
- Width of RNAV10 tracks is 20 nm, with adjacent tracks at 50 nm.
- In RNAV10, no form of ATS surveillance is required.
- Minimum equipment required for RNAV10: Combination of 2
independent Long Range Nav Systems (LRNS) comprising of
either INS, IRS/FMS or GPS.
- For an INS/INS combination, the maximum flight time is 6.2 hrs
from when NAV mode was set to INS.
If a DME/DME fix is obtained, a/c can fly for another 5.9 hrs.
If a VOR/DME fix is obtained, a/c can fly for another 5.7 hrs.
- Radio fixes are usually automatically updated in FMS. Manual
updating of radio fix is not permitted unless specifically approved.
RNAV10 & RNP10 are the same, meaning RNP10, like other RNP specs,
does not require performance monitoring & alerting. ICAO decided not to
re-name RNP10 when in fact, it means RNAV10. This was because re-
renaming nav charts, operational approvals, etc, would be expensive.
000  RNAV5 (B-RNAV) (Ref: DGCA circular RNAV5 2014)
- RNAV5 is the original RNAV implementation for en-route navigation.
- RNAV5 aircraft accuracy must be within 5 nm, for 95% of the time.
- Although primarily intended in an ATS surveillance environment,
RNAV5 has been implemented in areas with no surveillance also.
- Minimum equipment required for RNAV5: Just one sensor
combination of VOR/DME, DME/DME, INS or GPS + 1 RNAV
computer.
- RNAV5 Nav-System Requirements
- Continuous indication of aircraft position relative to flight
track, bearing, distance, ground speed & time to waypoint.
- System should be able to store minimum 4 waypoints.
- An appropriate sensor failure warning should be available.
- RNAV5 Nav-aid Limitations
- DVOR can be used until 75 nm & CVOR until 60 nm.
- INS can be used only for 3 hrs from initial alignment.
- DME is considered sufficient to meet RNAV 5 standards.
- GPS should have RAIM function.
Terminal
RNAV1, RNAV2 (Ref: DGCA circular RNAV1, RNAV2 - 2014)
- RNAV1 (P-RNAV): Precision RNAV for use in terminal areas.
- RNAV2: Used in terminal & en-route areas.
- RNAV1 & 2 is intended for flights in radar surveillance environments
& applies to air routes, SIDs, STARs & IAPs, up to FAE.
- Minimum equipment required for RNAV1 & 2 are identical: GPS
(with RAIM), DME/DME, DME/DME/INS.
- ADME within a range of 3 nm - 160 nm can be used. They must
be within 30°-150° apart and 40° below the horizon.
- If DME coverage is not available, INS can have reasonable
accuracy within 2 nm up to 15 mins.

RNP Specifications
ooo En-route
RNP2: Used for en-route continental airspace. Accuracy required is 2 nm.
RNP4: Used for en-route oceanic/remote areas.
- Accuracy required is 4 nm. Adjacent tracks are at 30 nm.
- Aircraft uses GPS as primary nav-aid. It also must have 2 LRNS.
- Additionally, ADS-C & CPDLC are also required onboard.
RNP10: Same as RNAV10. (See also: RNAV10 Specifications)
o00 Terminal
RNP1: It applies to arrival/departure & initial/intermediate approaches.
- It is also intended where ATC surveillance is limited/not available.
- It uses GPS with RAIM as the primary nav-aid. DME/DME fix can
also be used where nav-aids are available.
- Where applicable, SBAS is also used.
Approach
RNP APCH (Ref: DGCA CAR LP/LPV minima, RNP APCH, APN/BaroNAV)
- It requires an accuracy 1 nm in terminal & missed approach, and
an accuracy of 0.3 nm in final approach.
- Procedures are titled RNAV(GNSS). It uses GBAS & offers several
minimas depending upon aircraft capability. Some of them are:
- LNAV/GPS: Basic GPS + VOR/DME approach (NPA).
- APV Baro VNAV: Approach with vertical guidance (NPA).
- (LP)LNAV Localiser performance. Uses SBAS for vertical guidance.
RNP AR APCH (RNP Authorisation)
- It provides high accuracy & nav performance.
- It uses GPS as primary aid & INS or DME/DME where required.
- Accuracy >1 nm in terminal/missed approach, .3 nm in final approach.
- Special authorisation is reqd for operator, similar to ILS Cat II/III.
A RNP (Advanced): It provides a single assessment of aircraft eligibility,
covering all phases of flight. Aircraft accuracy needed is 2 nm in
oceanic, 1 nm in en-route & terminal, and 0.3 nm in approach phases.
RNP0.3: Applies to helicopters. Accuracy .3 nm en-route, terminal & approach

Regulations
• Selection of Aerodromes
ICAO Annex 6 Ch.1, Doc 9976 Flight Planning & Fuel Management
Weather Conditions Required for Commencing a Flight
- For a VFR flight, Commander will take-off only if the meteorological
forecast indicates VMC along the route and at the destination.
- For an IFR Flight, Commander will take-off, or continue flight only
when the latest meteorological information available indicates that
destination or diversion aerodrome is within minima, at planned ETA.
Take-off Alternate
- Take-off alternate is used for landing in case of an emergency shortly
after take-off & it is not possible to land at the departure aerodrome.
- If weather conditions at take-off aerodrome are below landing
minima, there should be an alternate airport within landing minima,
within 1 hour flying time for a 2 engine aircraft and within 2 hours
flying time for a 3 or 4 engine aircraft, in still air at normal cruise
speed, with one engine inoperative.
En-route Alternate
- En-route alternate in needed for an aircraft experiencing abnormal or
emergency conditions en-route.
- The planned route should be such that there must be an adequate
aerodrome within 1 hour flying time at normal cruise speed and with
one engine inoperative, at every point on the route.
- If diversion time is more than one hour, it comes under ETOPS.
Destination Alternate
- Destination alternate is needed if it is impossible or inadvisable for the
aircraft to land at the planned destination.
- 2 Destination Alternate aerodromes are required for flight planning, if:
- No meteorological forecast is available for destination; or
- Forecast at planned destination indicates that weather is below
minima from 1 hour before ETA to 1 hour after ETA.
- 1 Destination Alternate is required within minima for all IF flights
even if the destination aerodrome is within planned minima at ETA.
- No Destination Alternate is required if:
- Destination is remote that no useable is diversion available; or
- 2 separate runways are available at destination, & meteorological
forecast indicates 5 km visibility & cloud ceiling above 2000 or
circling height + 500' whichever higher, for 1 hour before ETA
to 1 hour after ETA.
ETOPS Alternate: En-route alternate needed for emergency landing
during ETOPS operations.
Planning Minima for IF Flights: Minimas used while planning a flight

• LVP Low Visibility Procedures
ICAO Doc 9365 All Weather Operations
(Ref: DGCA CAR - All weather operations)
Introduction
- Any CatI/III ILS landing, Low Visibility taxi & LV Take-off is called LVP.
- Aerodromes that intent to operate in low visibility must develop Low
Visibility Procedures. These procedures must be certified by DGCA.
- Vis < 800 m or RVR < 550 m or cloud ceiling < 200' will trigger LVP.
- During LVP, if TDZ RVR is < 550 m, MID RVR also shall be given.
- If TDZ or MID RVR is < 300 m, END RVR also shall be given by ATC.
- ILS Cat II/III is permitted only if a/c & operator is certified by DGCA.
- Supervised take-off & landing are not permitted during Cat II/II & LVTO.
LVTO Low Visibility Take-off
- Takeoffs in RVR < 400 m is called LVTO. It requires DGCA approval.
- Foreign operators approved for LVTO must apply with DGCA again.
- Non scheduled operators require minimum RVR 400 m for take-off.
- Commander will take-off only if the weather at departure aerodrome
or at take-off alternate is within landing minima.
- If RVR is < 200 m, TDZ, MID & END RVR must be available for
LVTO. If TDZ RVR is not available, a pilot assessment is considered
sufficient, provided MID & END RVR is > 200 m.
- LVTO Minima (Minimum RVR & runway lighting required for LVTO):
- 400m: Runway edge Its or centreline marking available.
- 300m: Runway edge Its + centreline marking available.
- 200m: Runway edge Its + centreline Its available.
- 150m: Runway edge Its + centreline Its (min 30m spacing) + all 3 RVR avlb.
- 125m: HI r/w edge Its + centreline Its (min 15m spacing) + all 3 RVR avlb.
- 75m: HI r/w edge Its + c/l Its + all 3 RVR + lateral guidance available.
- HI centreline Its must be at 1 m interval & HI edge Its at 60 m interval.
- All 3 RVR (TDL, MID & END RVR) available.
- Aircraft requirements - Thrust reverser available for all engines;
- Windshield wipers, window heating & anti-skid operational;
- 90 m visual segment is available from the cockpit.
CMV Converted Meteorological Visibility
Visibility is reported at a site different from where a pilot makes an
approach & thus may be different from actual RVR. Therefore a CMV
value is derived from reported visibility, where RVR is not available.
CMV = Reported meteorological visibility multiplied by a factor:
If HIALS available  1.5 x Vis (day)  2.0 x Vis (night)
Any other lights available  1.0 x Vis (day)  1.5 x Vis (night)
No lights available  1.0 x Vis (day)
CMV is used only for  CMV not to be used for
- CAT I ILS or straight-in NPA  - Take-off
- Only used when IAP depicts RVR - For calculating RVR < 800 m
minima but tower only reports  - Minima for circling or Cat II/III appch
visibility & no RVR info available - When actual RVR is available
- No CMV is used if ALS is out
SP Safe-guarding Procedures: LVP will commence only after SP has been
completed, to prepare the aerodrome for CAT II/III approaches. They are:
- Inspection of airfield ground lighting;
- Termination of all work in progress & removal of all equipment from
localiser/glide path sensitive area, manoeuvring area & aprons.
SP shall be initiated when:
- RVR is < 1200 m & is forecasted to deteriorate to 800 m or less;
- The cloud ceiling is 400 ft and is forecast to fall to 200 ft or less.
===== [avh 0115]
1 - 86
Regulations
• Noise Abatement
ICAO Doc 8168 Departure Procedures
Introduction
- The State has to ensure that aerodromes identify noise-sensitive areas
around it & operators develop their noise abatement procedures.
- The procedure specified by an operator will be same for all aerodromes.
- No procedures are allowed if r/w conditions are snow, slush, oil or ice.
Types of Techniques/Procedures Used for Noise Abatement
- Use of noise preferential routes during departure & arrival.
- Use of noise abatement take-off or approach procedures.
- Use of noise preferential r/w to direct a/c away from sensitive areas.
But Commander can refuse a noise preferential r/w for safety reasons.
Noise Abatement Take-off
- Priority for noise abatement is secondary to obstacle clearance.
- Power settings during engine failure are at the discretion of the pilot.
- Visibility must not be < 1900 m for take-off.
Reduced thrust take-off (for noise abatement):
- It facilitates noise abatement and fuel savings.
- It extends engine life by reducing thermal stresses.
- Procedure: During take-off, maintain take-off thrust up to 25% less
from max power. This is permitted only when aircraft AUW < max
permitted & runway TORA available is much more than required.
- Reduced thrust take-off is not permitted if:
- Runway is contaminated/has ice/is slippery;
- Aircraft anti-skid or reverse thrust is inoperative;
- At night or when visibility is < 1 nm;
- Gust 15 kts; or tailwind 5 kts; or if wind-shear is reported.
Power reduction after take-off (for noise abatement):
- During initial climb, power reduction is to be done only above 800',
and after aircraft speed is > V½ + 20 kts. Above 3000', aircraft is
permitted to increase speed to cruise speeds.
- No procedures with turns coinciding with power reduction allowed.
- No procedures allowed during wind shear/microburst.
Noise Preferential Routes
- Turns to establish NPR must not be done until a/c is at least 500' above
obstruction along the flight path. Max bank must be restricted to 15°.
- Sufficient nav guidance must be available in noise preferential routes.
- NPRs & standard arrival/departures routes should be compatible.
Noise Abatement Approach
- Procedures must be only within 5nm of aerodrome or after crossing FAF.
- Noise preferential runway should not be used for landing unless they
have adequate visual & instrument guidance for landing.
- No procedure is allowed if cloud ceiling < 500' or visibility < 1900 m.
- No procedures are allowed during reverse thrust engagement.
- No procedures are allowed during wind shear, downburst activity.
- No procedures are allowed if crosswinds > 15 kts, tailwind > 5 kts.
- No procedures allowed if runway conditions are snow, slush, oil or ice.
===== [avh 0116]
1 - 87  Regulations
• Parallel Runway Operations
ICAO Doc 9643 Simultaneous Parallel Runway Operations
Near Parallel Runways are non intersecting r/w with convergence < 15°.
Sidestep Manoeuvre: A visual manoeuvre, at the completion of a precision
approach, for a straight-in landing, on a parallel runway < 1200' away.
NTZ No Transgression Zone: A 2000' wide buffer between adjacent
runway centrelines where no aircraft should enter during independent
approach. If any aircraft enters NTZ, the radar will instruct other aircraft
to discontinue approach, climb & turn away. Missed approach headings
of parallel runways should diverge by 30°.
If the threshold of 1 runway is displaced & is not abeam the threshold of the
other, then better ht separation is achieved during simultaneous || approach.
This allows for a reduction in distance between || r/w by 30 m for every 150 m
of displaced threshold. Absolute minimum distance between 2 || r/w is 1000'.
During simultaneous ops, radar separation is provided by a separate radar
controller on a separate RT fq, till visual separation is applied, or aircraft
has landed, or aircraft is 1 nm beyond the runway during missed approach.
Mode 1: Simultaneous || Independent Approach Without Separation
- They are approaches on | r/w without radar separation between a/c.
- In this, minimum width b/w both runway centrelines must be 1035 m.
- Each runway will have an alternating high-side & low-side, with 1000'
height separation between adjacent aircraft on parallel approaches.
- Separation can be reduced to < 1000' only if both a/c are on localiser.
- Thereafter, if there is a significant deviation, the radar will intervene.
- Only straight-in approaches are permitted. No track reversal allowed.
Mode 2: Simultaneous || Dependent Approach With Separation
- In this, minimum width between both runway centrelines must be 915 m.
- Radar separation is applied between 2 aircraft.
- An aircraft on a radar vector will be given a max intercept angle of 30°,
by at least 1 nm to localiser, & min 2 nm before glide slope intercept.
- 3 nm separation is applied between aircraft on the same localiser.
- 2 nm separation is applied between aircraft on the adjacent localiser.
- Only straight in approaches are permitted. No track reversal allowed.
Mode 3: Independent Parallel Departure
- It is the procedure for simultaneous departure from 2 parallel runways.
- In this, minimum width between both runway centrelines must be 760 m.
- If distance between || runway < 760 m, then wake turbulence criteria
will not be met & the runways will be considered as a single runway.
- All departing aircraft are identified by the radar by 1 nm from DER.
- Departure tracks must diverge minimum 15° immediately after take-off.
Mode 4: Segregated Departure/Arrival
- In this, 1 runway is exclusively used for arrival, the other for departure.
- Minimum width between both runway centrelines must be 760 m.
- An aircraft on a radar vector will be given a max intercept angle of 30°,
by at least 1 nm to localiser, & min 2 nm before glide slope intercept.
- For arrival, radar separation between 2 aircraft on the same localiser
is 3 nm until they have established on the localiser.
Mode 5: Semi Mixed Operations - Any combination of the above modes.
===== [avh 0117]
Regulations  1 - 88
• Operational Hazards
ICAO Doc 8168: Operator SOPs
Classification of Fire
- Class A: Fire due to wood, paper, cloth or plastic. Use water or DCP.
- Class B: Fire due to oil or fuel. Use CO2, foam, HALON or DCP.
- Class C: Fire due to electric equipment. Use Halon or DCP.
- Class D: Fire due to flammable metals, sodium, magnesium. Use DCP.
Classes A & C are the most common causes of an aircraft fire.
(See also: Airframe > Emergency Equipment)
Actions during Fire
- Cockpit/Cabin fire: Use CO2 or HALON & not water or DCP. During
cabin fire, emergency oxygen supply may get contaminated.
- Cargo-hold fire: Turn-off ventilation.
- Hot brakes: Release parking brakes, use DCP or water. Approach
the wheels from ahead/astern. Never from the sides.
Windshear  (See also: Meteorology > CAT > Wind Shear)
- It is called wind shear if there is a change in wind speed > 25 kts
within 500', > 40 kts within 1000', or > 50 kts within 1500':
- Low-level wind shear: Wind shear 1500' & below, on takeoff/approach.
- In case of encountering windshear/microburst, maintain aircraft
configuration, open maximum power & initiate climb.
- Any aircraft expected to be operated in suspected or actual icing
conditions shall not take-off unless the aircraft is inspected for icing.
- Such aircraft should have 'surface inspection lights' for night operation.
(See also: Meteorology > Icing)
Bird Strike: 90% of bird strikes happens below 1500 m.
- Most effective bird scarers are 'shell crackers'.
- If aircraft maintains 135 kts or less, it has been observed
that birds will fly away at least 2 seconds before a bird strike.
Pressurisation Failure: It is of 2 types:
- Explosive Decompression, caused due to large damage to airframe, &
- Slow Decompression, caused due to minor airtrame damage or
leak in the pressurisation system.
- In both cases, pilots must put on an oxygen mask &
descend below 10000' immediately.
Ditching Procedure  Winds  Best
If the sea is calm, ditch along the  Good
swell. If winds are > 40 kts, ditch  *  Good  Ditching
along a swell
into the wind. Fly onto the water
at the slowest possible speed.

1 - 89  Regulations
Flight Procedures
ICAO Doc 8168: Operator SOPs
Standard Checklists
- Checklists are to be used by crew for all phases of aircraft operations.
- Aircraft manufacturer checklist will be the basis of operator checklist.
- Items in the checklist must be restricted to those critical to flight safety.
- Operators should ensure that checklists are part of their SOPs.
- SOPs must cater procedures for checklist interruption.
Crew Briefings
- Proper pre-flight briefing must be done for individuals & combined crew.
Departure briefing should include:
- Runway in use, aircraft configuration - Take-off speeds.
- Taxi-out route, relevant hot spots  - Alternate aerodromes
- Navigation & communication setup  - Departure procedure & routes
- Aerodrome, terrain, noise restrictions - Standard callouts
- Minimum equipment list  - Emergency procedures
Approach briefing should include:
Minima, aircraft configuration, landing speeds
- Terrain restrictions  - Destination alternate  - Standard callouts
- Arrival routes  - Emergency procedures - Cold temp correction
- IAP/visual procedure - Taxi-in & hot spots  - Missed approach
Managing Cockpit Distractions (Ref: DGCA Circular - Distraction)
- Operator must include sterile cockpit rules in SOPs & in crew briefings.
- Sterile cockpit: No un-needed conversation among crew below 10000.
- When undertaking 'heads down' activity like handling FMS etc., that
pilot must announce: "My head down, you fly".
- In case of distractions like TCAS, visual obstructions, birds, etc., only
1 pilot should 'look outside'. Announce: "You fly, I watch".
- Be careful about completion of checklists & checklist interruption
procedures. Ask yourself, "where was I? What was I doing?"
- Ask for more time if required from ATC/crew, avoid being rushed.
• Controlled Rest (Ref: DGCA CAR Controlled Rest) (See also: Crew, Dutyi ULRF)
- Controlled rest is permitted for the crew on flight durations < 3 hrs.
- More than 1 rest is permitted if flight duration is > 3 hrs.
- Only 1 crew permitted for controlled rest at a time. The other pilot
becomes PF (Pilot Flying).
- Rest must commence only after reaching top-of-climb & ends 30mins
before TOD. Rest allowed only in reduced-workload phases of flight.
- Maximum duration of controlled rest is 40 mins + another 20 mins for
orientation. This 20 minutes can be part of the 30 mins betore TOD.
- Before resting, PIC should brief criteria for termination of controlled rest.
- Resting pilot should remain seated with seat belts fastened, with
seats pushed aft and must not interfere with the control column. He
can, however, use eyeshade or ear defenders.
- During controlled rest of one pilot, the other non-resting pilot will not
leave his seat under any circumstance, not even for toilet breaks.
- Autopilot and auto-thrust must be operational and engaged.
- FMS manipulations must be minimum during this period.
- Altitude changes are not permitted during controlled rest.
- Pilot must inform cabin crew about the controlled rest timings.
- Operators must have an SOP for the cabin crew to check on pilots
during their controlled rest.
- Cabin crew will call PF every 20 mins (night) & 30 mins (day) to check.
If there is no answer, he/she will go up to the cockpit to check.
- After controlled rest, non-resting crew will check full ops status of a/c.

3rd Digit: It is prefixed with a hyphen (-). It is the filing order of same
type of approach, as there may be many ILS approaches for
different runways in the same aerodrome.
4th Char: (Optional) It represents multiple SIDs, STARs or Apron.
- e.g. 11-3A means 1st a/d of the city, 1-ILS, 3rd procedure for ILS.
- CM Metric charts. They use metric system as units of measure.
Special charts, contains modified info for a specific company.

- Do not use a chart before 0901 UTC on the effective date.
- If no effective date is given, use the chart when received.

1 - 103  Regulations
00 Procedure to fill a Flight Plan Form
Doc 4444, Appendi suctions in Fight Plar
General Rules
- Use capital letters, one letter in each space of the field provided.
- Any data should be inserted only in the fields & spaces provided.
Leave unused spaces blank.
- All times should be in 4 figures UTC (e.g. 1800, 0930, etc.)
- There are a total of 19 items in a flight plan. Items 1 to 6 are to be
filled by ATC. Items 7 to 18 should be completed as explained below.
Item 19 is to facilitate alerting of SAR (Search and Rescue) services.
- Flight plan can be filed up to 120 hours before EOBT.
- Inform ATC about delay exceeding 30 minutes for flights in controlled
airspace or 60 minutes for flights outside controlled airspace.
- It is essential to advise ATC of cancellation, delay or changes to flight plan.
- RPL Repetitive FIt Plan: Can be filed only for IFR flights, if same flight
is planned daily or on same day of the week, for 10 consecutive days.
Item 7 Aircraft Identification (Max 7 characters)
- Aircraft registration letters: DAGXC or IN241; or
- Company designator followed by the flight number: AI441; or
- Tactical call sign (military): BRUNO12, SWIFT45, RED1
Item 8 Flight Rules & Type of Flight
1 for IFR  Y for IFR first, then VFR
V for VER  Z for VER first, then IFR
If Y or Z is filed, specify, point where a change in flight rules is planned.
Where there is more than one change planned, code will be for first
rule, i.e., use 'Z' for VFR to IFR then later to VFR.
Then insert Type of Flight:
S Scheduled operator  M Military
N Non-scheduled operator  G General aviation
X for any other categories, then specify it in item 18.
Item 9 Number, Type of Aircraft & Wake Turbulence
Number of Aircraft: Insert if there is more than one, else leave blank.
Type of Aircraft: Manufacturer's designator. If no designator is
assigned, or for formation of more than one type, insert 'ZZZZ' &
specify in item 18, preceded by 'TYP/'. E.g: TYP/3C182
Wake Turbulence: /L - Light /M - Medium  /H - heavy
Item 10 Equipment
COM/NAV equipment, followed by stroke '', suffix for SSR equipment.
N if no COM/NAV/approach aid is available, or if equipment is unserviceable.
S if standard equipment (VHF, VOR & ILS) is available & serviceable.
G GNSS  J1 CPDLC VDL  M1 Inmarsat
J2 CPDLC FANS A/1 M2 MTSAT
J3 VDL Mode A  M3 Iridium

Item 13 Departure Aerodrome and Time
Departure Aerodrome ICAO designator. If no designator specified,
insert 'ZZZZ' (and specify in Item 18 "DEP/") e.g. 'DEP/Ramnad"; or
DEP/5023N02214E (Coordinates); or DEP/BBG 180017 (Brg/Dist).
Departure Time (4 digit) Insert EOBT in UTC
Item 15 Cruising speed, Altitude/Level & Route
Cruising Speed TAS for the first or whole cruising portion of flight.
If KMPH, insert 'K' followed by 4 figures, e.g., K0220 = 220 kmph
If Knots, insert 'N' followed by 4 figures, e.g., N0175 = 175 kts
Cruising Level Insert first level required (maximum 5 characters)
If flight level, insert 'F' followed by 3 figures, e.g. F085 = FL085
If altitude in 10s of meters, insert 'M' in 4 figures, e.g. M0150 = 1500m
If altitude in 100s of feet, insert 'A',  i, e.g. A055 = 5500 ft
if cruise climb, insert 'C' point at which CC will start, e.g. C/BBG.
If it is a VFR flight, insert 'V'
Route Description
Flight in ATS Routes
- If departure a/d is located on an ATS route, insert designator of
first ATS route. If not, insert 'DCT, followed by the joining point of
first ATS route & designator of ATS route, e.g. DCT RONEX L617.
- Then insert each point at which there is a change of speed (5%
TAS), level, ATS route, and/or flight rules, e.g. BBG/N0200A080
IFR (at BBG you change speed to 200 knots, altitude to 8000 feet
and change flight rules to (FR).
- After each point, add designator of next ATS route segment, even
if it is the same as the previous one; or, insert DCT, if flight to next
point is outside a designated route, unless both points are defined
by geographical co-ordinates or by bearing & distance.
Co-ordinates (5 digit or 11 digit) e.g. 51N025E or 5220N03305E
Bearing & distance from a nav-aid e.g. BBG170020.
Flights Outside ATS Routes
Insert points not more than 30 minutes flying time or 200 nm
apart, including each point at which there is a change of speed,
level, track, or flight rules. Insert DCT between successive points
unless both points are defined by geographical co-ordinates.
Item 16 - Destination, EETS, Alternate Aerodrome
Destination & EET (maximum 10 characters)
Insert ICAO designator followed by EET, & not planned time of landing.
If no designator published, insert "ZZZZ" followed by total EET, and
specify in Item 18 tARR/) e.g. ARR/5417N02005E.
IFREET: Time from take-off till commencing IAF at the destination.
VFREET: Time from take-off till overhead destination aerodrome.

Item 19 Supplementary Information
It is not to be transmitted in the FPL message. But these details will be
helpful during a search & rescue mission.
E/ Insert 4 figure fuel endurance in hours and minutes, e.g. E/0430.
P/ POB Persons on Board. "P/TBN® (to be notified), e.g. P/005, not P/5
R/ (Radio):
- crossiU if UHF on frequency 243.0 MHz is not available.
- cross "V' if VHF on frequency 121.5 MHz is not available.
- cross "E" if an emergency locator transmitter (ELT) is not available.
S/ (Survival):
- cross all indicators if survival equipment is not carried.
- cross 'P" if polar survival equipment is not carried.
- cross "D" if desert survival equipment is not carried.
- cross "M" if maritime survival equipment is not carried.
- cross &J® if jungle survival equipment is not carried.
J/ (Jackets):
- cross all indicators if life jackets are not carried.
- cross "L" if life jackets are not equipped with lights.
- cross "F" if life jackets are not equipped with fluorescein.
- cross "U" or "V" or both to indicate radio capability of jackets, if any.
D/ (Dinghies):
- cross "D" and "C" if no dinghies are carried; or
- insert (NUMBER) - number of dinghies carried (example: 02)
(CAPACITY) - in persons, of all dinghies (example: 006)
(COVER) - cross C if dinghies are not covered.
(COLOUR) - insert colour of dinghies if carried.
A/ (Aircraft) insert colour of aircraft and significant markings.
N/ (Remarks):
- cross "N" if no remarks; or
- any other survival equipment carried and any other remarks.
C/ (Pilot) Insert name of Pilot-in-Command.

===== [avh 0138]
Aerodynamics
Part 2
Aerodynamics
===== [avh 0139]
2-3
• Terms & Definitions
Density: Mass per unit volume. (kg/m3) [ML-3]
Pressure: Force exerted per unit area. [N/m?]  Aerodynamics
Adiabatic Change: Change with no heat exchange from surroundings.
Isothermal Change: Change at a constant temperature.
Vector: A quantity with magnitude & direction.
Scalar: A quantity with only magnitude.  J M (mass) = W (weight)
Mass: Quantity of matter contained in a body.  g (gravity)
- 1 Mass = 1 force needed (in that direction) to move or stop a body.
Weight (Unit - Newton)
- Force with which a body is  J W (weight) = m (mass) x g (gravity)
attracted to the earth's centre.
Momentum (kg m/s) [MLT-1]  J Momentum = m (mass) x v (velocity)
- Tendency of body to continue
in motion after being placed in motion.
Inertia: Reluctance of a body to change its state of equilibrium (rest/motion).
- It is a quality related to its mass (thus scalar) & not its velocity.
- It refers to both stationary & moving objects.
- It should not be confused with momentum.
Force (Unit - Newton) (kg/s2) [MLT-2]  F (force) = m (mass) x a (acceleration)
- Force changes the momentum/ J
state of rest or uniform motion of body.
Q. Mass 60000 Kg. Find the lift force needed?
Ans. F = m x g => F = 60000 × 9.81 = 588600N of lift force needed.
Work (Unit - Joule)
- Force is said to work on a body when it moves along its line of action.
- If the body does not move, no work is done.
- If force 100N is used to move f W (work) = F (force) x d (displacement)
a mass of 10 kg or 100 kg for
10 meters, work done is the same.
f Power = F (force) x d (disp)
Power (Unit - Watt) (Joule/sec)  t (time)
- It is the rate of doing work.
- If 5000 N moves a mass (irrespective of what mass is) by 1000 m in
2 minutes, then the power used = 5000x1000/120 = 4167 watts.
Energy (Unit - Joule)
- It is the capacity of a body to do work.
- Energy a body has is measured in the amount of work it can do.
Kinetic Energy: Energy stored in a body due to its motion.
v2 = u2 + 2as  but, if a body starts from 0, then
v2 = 0 + 2as  u = initial velocity
v = final velocity
v2 = 2as => s = v2 / 2a........ (1)
Derivation  a = acceleration
but, KE  = F (force) x s (distance) or  s = distance
M x a x s. Substituting (1),
KE = Mav2 / 2a, or KE = Mv2 / 2
Potential Energy: Energy stored in a body due to its position.
m = mass
Energy = Force x Distance
PE=F x d=> m x ax d  but a = g (gravity)  d = distance
d = h (height)  a = acceleration
PE = m xg x h
===== [avh 0140]
2 - 4
• Newton's Laws of Motion
1. A body will remain in rest or uniform motion in a straight
line unless acted upon by an external force.
2. Rate of change of momentum is proportional to applied force &
change of momentum takes place in the direction of applied force.
3. Action & reaction are equal and opposite.
Equations of Motion

Aerodynamics
• Static Pressure  (See also: Instruments > Pitot System)
- It is the result of the weight of air on all surfaces of the aircraft.
- A lower altitude will have higher a static pressure.
- Static Pressure is denoted by 'S'.
• Dynamic Pressure
- Air in motion has KE (Kinetic Energy). But in a one-side open tube
(pitot tube), air is brought to complete rest & this KE is converted
into pressure energy. This pressure rise is called dynamic pressure.
- KE is proportional to density (p) of air & square of a/c speed (V2).
- Therefore, Dynamic Pressure = ½ pvz.
- If aircraft speed is doubled, dynamic pressure increases 4 times.
• Measuring Dynamic Pressure (Principle of ASI) (See also: Instruments > ASI)
- Total pressure acting in a pitot tube = ½ pv (Dynamic) + S (Static).
- Therefore, Dynamic Pressure = Total Pressure - Static Pressure.
- ASI is a pressure gauge that measures this Dynamic Pressure.
- As per Bernoulli's theorem for streamlined flows, this dynamic
pressure remains constant in every part of the stream.
- So, a pitot tube can be placed anywhere on the airframe, where
airflow is flowing at a higher or a lower speed than that of aircraft.
Provided static source is placed correctly without airflow interference
or obstructions and senses correct atmospheric pressure, an ASI
will always read correct.  (See also: Bernoulli's Theorem)
- As air density ! with 1 in altitude, mass of airflow over an a/c will .
So, to maintain the required lift force, speed of a/c has to t.

2. Lift by Momentum Theory (How a windmill works)
An aerofoil can produce an aerodynamic force by merely deflecting a
stream/jet of fluid/air. This force produced is proportional to the attitude
(AoA) of aerofoil in the air-stream and its curvature.

3. Lift by Circulation Theory (Magnus Effect)
- In an airflow around an infinite non-rotating cylinder, there
are equal streamlines above & below (see diagram below).
This causes equal pressure drop on top & bottom of the cylinder.
This pressure drop cancels each other out & no lift is produced.
- The point of stagnation where the air is completely brought to stop
is at points A & B (where air molecules don't move up or down).
- But, in a rotating cylinder, total velocity at A is in an upward sense,
and stagnation points are now at points A' & B' (below A & B). The
amount of downward shift of these points depends on the speed of
rotation. As the rotation speed 1, flow speed f & pressure l on top
of the cylinder (as per Bernoulli's theorem).
- As a result, a net force is produced upwards, & lift is generated.
B
Why does a golf ball lift?
A rotating cylinder creates lift due to Magnus Effect. But, if the cylinder
has a rougher surface, due to friction, the air in its vicinity also travels
with it, which induces additional circulation, thereby lift + further.
Why does a cricket ball swing?
- Normal Swing: One side of the ball is smooth (has laminar airflow).
The other side initially has laminar flow, but then the seam makes it
turbulent, causing a low pressure. Thus, the ball swings towards the seam.
Bowler controls the swing by keeping one side of the ball smooth by
constantly polishing it.
- Reverse Swing: If ball speed is > 90 mph, due to 1 in Reynolds
Number, laminar layer becomes turbulent layer earlier. Turbulent layer
on the other side of the seam becomes even more thicker & breaks
away from the ball surface. The ball now swings to the other side.
- Contrast Swing: Towards the end of a cricket match, when both sides
of the ball become rough, reverse swing can happen even at slower
speeds (< 70 mph).

• Viscosity  (For air, p = 1.79 x 10-5 kg/m/sec at ISA sea level)
- It is the tendency to j relative motion b/w adjacent layers of a fluid.
- Its unit is 'coefficient of viscosity' (|). (kg/m/sec) [ML-1T-1]
- In a gas, temperature 1 = viscosity 1 (due to 1 collision b/w molecules).
Aerodynamics  - In the atmosphere, altitude 1 = temperature | = viscosity | (till
tropopause). Viscosity remains steady in stratosphere.
- In liquid, temperature f = viscosity 1 (due to l cohesive forces).
Kinematic Viscosity (For air, "p = 1.46 x 10-5 m2/sec at ISA sea level)
- It is an alternative way to measure viscosity of gases.
- It is the ratio of 'coefficient of viscosity' to density (p)
- With 1 in altitude, I J. But p (density) | more. So, as altitude 1,
kinematic viscosity f, even in stratosphere.
Reynolds Number
- Reynolds Number is the ratio of inertial forces to
viscous forces within a fluid. It is dimensionless.
- RN is used to predict flow patterns in different fluid flow situations.
- A model aircraft (of smaller size) & an actual aircratt, it compared at
the same RN, will have the same aerodynamic characteristics.
- Low RN = Laminar layer = quicker boundary layer separation, 1 drag.
- High RN = earlier transition to turbulent layer = 1 KE in turbulent
layer = delayed separation layer = 1 drag.
- In airflow near leading edge on an aerofoil, RN is low (< ½ million);
thus laminar flow exists. Further down the surface (transition layer),
RN will 1 (1-5 million). When RN is > 10 million, turbulent flow exists.
- It may seem that turbulent layer has more drag than laminar layer &
that laminar layer is better for aircraft, but that is not the case.
Turbulent layer has high KE & thus delays boundary layer separation.
Laminar layer separates easily & the drag caused by a separated
laminar layer is more than the drag due to a turbulent layer.
- High RN causes: 1 CLMAX, † lift, 1 stalling AoA.
- RcRIT: RN at which there is a sudden shift in transition layer upstream,
creating turbulent layer & delays boundary layer separation.
† RN = pVI  0 = density I = Dimension of the body
V = velocity | = Viscosity
Scale Effect
- It is the variations in aerodynamic
characteristics with change in RN.
- Scale models have 3 drawbacks:
- Small model: Difficult to make it accurate.
RCRIT RN
- Large model: Difficult for wind tunnel testing.
- 10 Scale model = length 10, area 100 & mass 11000.
- If flow parameters over scale model are not same as on actual a/c,
then aerodynamics fundamental laws (L = C½ pV2) won't hold good
- If mass is not accurate, stall/spin characteristics will not be the same.
- To compensate for these, 'VL law' (velocity x linear dimensions L)
has to be applied & must remain constant. i.e., a 10 model of an
actual 400 kmph aircraft will have to be tested with at 4000 kmph.
- This is not practically feasible. However, if RN (wl) is kept constant
by 1p, then v can be J. Thus, if density is 1 25 times, then the VL
law is valid, and a wind tunnel testing speed of 160 kmph (4000/25)
should give accurate results.

• Aerodynamics Definitions
Aerofoil  : A shape capable of producing lift.

Mean Chord (c)  : Average chord.
Wing Span (b)  : Distance from wingtip to wingtip.
Wing Area (S)  : Surface area of wing (chord x span).
Leading Edge Radius: Radius of curvature of LE.

Aspect Ratio (AR)  : Span/mean-chord or span2/wing area. AR = s/c
Max Camber  : Maximum distance b/w mean camber line & chord.
Mean Camber Line : Line joining LE & TE, equidistant from upper &
lower surface.
Angle of Incidence: Angle between chord & horizontal datum of aircraft.
Angle of Attack : Angle between chord and RAF.
Dihedral  : Angle between 25% of chord & lateral axis of aircraft.
Sweep Back  : Angle between 25% of chord & perpendicular to chord.
Wash-in  : A wing twist, giving an † in AoA incidence towards tip.
Wash-out  : A wing twist, giving an I in AoA incidence towards tip.
Wing Loading  : Weight per unit area.
Load Factor  : Lift/Weight.
Lift  : AD force acting 90° to RAF or flight path.
Total Reaction  : Resultant of all AD forces acting on a wing, through CP.

• Centre of Pressure CP & Total Reaction TR
- CP is the point through which sum of all aerodynamic forces
(TR Total Reaction) of an aerofoil can be considered to act.
- Position of CP is a function of aerofoil camber, lift coefficient, & AoA.
- TR Is split into Lift & Drag. (See diagram on previous page)
- TR is always perpendicular to the aerofoil chord, & lies along CP.
- As AoA 1, pressure distribution peaks-up & moves forward, TR length
1 & CP moves forward causing nose to pitch up (unstable movement).
- CP is most forward at CL MAX, just before stall.
- At stalling AoA, TR magnitude reduces suddenly & CP moves back.
- In a cambered aerofoil, CP moves between 20-30% of the chord at
normal working AoA.
- In a symmetric aerofoil, CP remains fixed at approximately 25% of
its chord, and is independent of its AoA
- On a flat plate, as AoA 1, CP moves backward & nose pitches down
(stable movement).

- Aerodynamic Centre is defined as :
- Pt where pitching moment remains constant at normal working AoA.

- An aircraft pitches about its lateral axis, which passes

- In the end, the aerodynamic centre is calculated for its simplicity;
We may assume that lift forces act not at the 'centre of pressure' (a
varying point), but at the 'aerodynamic centre' (a fixed point), for
ease of calculations.

Subsonic (2D) Airflow on an Aerofoil
Here, we assume there is no 'span wise' airflow for ease of understanding. However, in
an actual aerofoil, airflow has 'span wise' flow, which causes 'Lift Induced Drag'.
Introduction  Aerodynamics
- Airflow pattern around an aircraft depends only on its shape,
altitude & RN (size, viscosity, density, speed)..
- Static & dynamic pressure will vary throughout the flow, but
the total pressure (static + dynamic) is always constant.
• Leading Edge (LE) Stagnation Point
- It is the point where part of the airflow hitting the front tip of the
aerofoil is brought to complete rest.
- At this point, flow velocity is zero, +ve pressure is maximum. Here,
total pressure = static pressure. Dynamic pressure is zero.
- From LE stagnation point, flow separates into top-flow & bottom-flow.
- Beyond LE stagnation point, speed of airflow 1 and its pressure..
- At the point of max camber on the top-surface, speed of airflow iS
max and its pressure is least.
- After this point, flow speed 1 & pressure 1 back to free stream value.
Upwash: As air flows towards an aerofoil, it will lift up towards the lower
pressure at the upper surface, known as upwash.
Downwash: After crossing aerofoil, airflow returns to its original direction.
• Boundary Layer: It is the region of airflow near the aerofoil surface
where flow speed is < 99% of the free-stream airflow speed.
- A typical boundary layer thickness is 2 mm at LE & 20 mm at TE.
- BL characteristics are determined by aerofoil surface condition & RN.
- Boundary layer does not contribute to lift in the normal operating
- Bouncay ayer erects a profound  ranges of AoA. But has a profound effect during high AoA.
- Wing high-speed characteristics.  - Value of form-drag.
- Wing stalling characteristics.  - CL MAX.
- A thin laminar flow called Sub-laminar Layer continues at a very
low level below the turbulent layer. This thin layer smoothens the
aerofoil surface & reduces skin friction drag.
• Laminar Boundary Layer  Turbulent Boundary Layer
- Exist before transition point  - Exist after transition point
- Smooth, steady, thin flow  - Unsteady, thick flow
- Low skin friction drag  - High skin friction drag
- Moderate velocity gradient  - High velocity gradient
- Low energy exchange  - High energy exchange
- In turbulent layer, the rate of change of velocity or mean speed is
higher than laminar layer; hence skin friction drag is higher.
- However, due to its high KE, turbulent layer is more resistant to
separation when meeting adverse pressure gradient. Thus, it is
preferable to a laminar layer.
- In icing conditions, ice accumulates on the aerofoil leading edge,
which has a laminar layer, but it easily breaks off in a turbulent layer.

Lift
• Introduction
- Lift is the component of Total Reaction which is 1 to flight path of a/c.
†  Lift = CL (pressure distribution) × ½ pV2 (dynamic Pressure) × s (wing area)
- AD efficiency of an aerofoil at a particular AoA = Lift/Drag at that point.
- In normal working AoA, CL is always much greater than CD.
- Best p is at 4° AoA. But max CL & min CD is not obtained at best b.
- Greatest contribution to overall lift comes from upper aerofoil surface.
- Speed of 'V' in any Lift/Drag equation is TAS, not IAS.
- Density of air is what makes lift possible. Low air-density makes lift
difficult. In vacuum/space, lift (and therefore flight) is not possible.
- As altitude 1, air gets thinner. So to maintain the same lift, same IAS
has to be maintained or TAS has to be increased.
- At 40000', density is ¼ compared to sea-level. So to maintain same
IAS & same lift, TAS has to be 2x.
- At the same altitude, if AS is increased 2x, AoA (CL) has to be l to
¼, to maintain the same lift.
- For the same IAS (same dynamic pressure), change in density will
have no effect on lift or drag.
• For same TAS, 1 in density = 1 lift, but also 1 drag.
1 in IAS (1 dynamic pressure) = 1 lift, but also 1 form-drag.
Minimum IAS required to fly Is determined by CL MAX.
• Lift Curves
- For any aerofoil, AoA 1, CL 1.
- For a symmetric aerofoil, at 0° AoA, CL = 0, produces no lift.
0 - As camber 1, CL MAX 1, stall AOA,, stall speed I, lifting force T.
2 - As aspect ratio 1, CL MAX 1, but Stall AOA T.
3- As sweep back 1, stall AoA 1 but CL MAX I, stall speed T;
- Lift vs CL graph for a +ve camber aerofoil intersect on the left of the
graph origin, & for a symmetric aerofoil, at the origin.
- It is better to use an aerofoil which is efficient at higher speed, by
temporarily † camber with flaps at lower speeds for takeoff & landing.

Drag
Introduction
- Drag is the sum of all aerodynamic forces which act parallel &  Aerodynamics
opposite to the direction of flight.
- It is of 2 types: Parasite Drag & Induced Drag.
• 1. Parasite Drag (Dp) (Zero Lift Drag)
- If an aircraft was flying at 'O' lift AoA,  Dp = ½ pV2 CDP S
only parasite drag would be present.
Dp = Parasite Drag
- It is of 4 types:  CDP = Coeff of parasite drag
1a. Skin Friction Drag
- It occurs due to the viscosity of air in the Boundary Layer.
- 1 in surface area of an aerofoil causes f in surface friction drag.
1b. Form Drag (Pressure Drag)
- It occurs due to the difference between the +ve pressure at LE
stagnation point & the -ve pressure at TE stagnation point. An
aerodynamic force will act in the direction of lower pressure.
- Profile Drag: Surface Friction Drag + Form Drag = Profile Drag.
- Streamlining: A means of 1 the fineness ratio, by l curvature of
the surface, thus, j adverse pressure gradient & thus 1 form drag.
- On a complete aircraft, total parasite drag is more than the sum of
drags caused by individual separate parts of the aircraft.
- When aircraft is producing lift, the boundary layer thickens &
become more turbulent, therefore creates more energy loss
where they mix; at wing-fuselage/engine-wing intersections, etc.
- Further drag is caused due to wake turbulence, causing a
pressure difference between the forward & aft surfaces.
1d. Increments in Parasite Drag
- Increment due to lift: Factors affecting parasite drag are transition
point & adverse pressure gradient. With f in lift, transition point
moves forward & adverse pressure gradient f, parasite drag f.
- Increments in interference drag: Occurs when lift 1.
- Change in frontal area: When aircraft AoA changes, either
because of speed change or due to manoeuvre, frontal area
presented to airflow change, consequently parasite drag t.
• Factors Affecting Parasite Drag Dp
- Speed: Dp is directly proportional to EAS2.
2x speed = 4x dynamic pressure = 4x parasite drag.
- Weight: Has no effect of Dp.
- Configuration: 1 in the aircraft frontal area (landing gear, flaps,
etc.) can 1 parasite drag up to 80%.
- Contamination: Airframe contamination (e.g. icing) 1 parasite drag.
- Altitude: At constant TAS, 1 in altitude = | dynamic pressure =
1 zero lift drag. At constant IAS, dynamic pressure remains the
same = induced drag remains the same.

Wingtip Vortex
- Since a wing has a finite length, whenever it produces lift, pressure
differential tries to equalise around wing tip, outward on the bottom,
flowing around the tip & inward on top. Where upper & lower
airflows meet, vortices form, smaller at the root & max at wingtip.
- The rotational velocity of the vortex is extracted from the main
airflow. This further adds to the induced drag of the wing.
- Greater pressure difference b/w top & bottom = larger vortex.
- IAS | = AoA 1, pressure gradient 1 = span wise flow 1 = vortex †.
- Wake vortex turbulence exists behind every a/c (helicopters also).
- In air, vortex lowers by ~1000' & extends up to 9 nm behind a/c.
- If a/c <1000' AGL, vortex drifts out up to 2 wingspan along ground.
- In crosswinds, the vortex can drift onto adjacent runways.

2 - 20
Stall
• Introduction
Aerodynamics  - Stall is caused by 'boundary layer separation' due to insufficient
kinetic energy in the airflow & high adverse pressure gradient.
- As AoA 1, adverse pressure gradient 1 & separation point moves
forward towards the leading edge. At CL MAX AOA, separation point is
very near the leading edge. Any further increase in AOA causes the
airflow to break down.
- During stall, CP of a normal aerofoil moves back. On a swept wing,
CP remains forward during stall.
(See also: Autorotation)
- On a small a/c, during stall, use rudder to pick up a dropped wing.
- On a swept wing, during stall, use aileron to pick up a dropped wing
• Critical Angle of Attack
- It is the angle of attack at which airflow over the wing breaks down.
- An aircraft will always stall at the same critical AoA, irrespective of
speed or attitude.
- All lift is not gone at critical AoA, but it is insufficient to support a/c.
Aerodynamic Symptom of Stall
- Buffeting occurs due to separated turbulent airflow over the tailplane.
- Amount of buffet depends on position of tailplane w.r.t. turbulent wake.
- If trailing edge flaps are lowered, the amount of buffet may reduce
because of increased downwash over the tailplane.
• Factors Affecting Aircraft Behaviour During Stall
- Aerofoil leading-edge curvature.
- Thickness/chord ratio.
- Camber.
- Point of maximum thickness & maximum camber of aerofoil.
- A sharp LE, thin wing & an aft position of maximum thickness will
cause a more abrupt stall.
• Methods to Get Favourable Stall Characteristics
- 1 LE radius, 1 camber, † thickness to chord ratio.
- Wing planform: In a rectangular wing, root stalls first. That is good.
- Washout: Reducing the angle of incidence from wing root to tip.
This causes wing root to stall earlier. Thus aileron (which is placed
outboard of the wing) will still remain effective during stall.
- Change in section: Greater thickness & camber at the leading edge.
- LE Slots, boundary layer blowing energises boundary layer.
- Root spoilers, stall strips on inboard of aerofoil leading edge.
- Vortex generators create small vortices & energise slow boundary
layer with fast-moving boundary layer present on top of the aerofoil.
- Boundary layer suction: Suck out slow-moving
boundary layer from top surface of the aerofoil.
Aircraft Design Requirements w.r.t. Stall  Vortex
Generator
- Aircraft should not abnormally pitch up during stall.
- It must be possible to produce roll & yaw by un-reversed controls.
- Positive longitudinal control should remain during stall.
- Aircraft roll caused due to stall must not be more than 20°.
- Stall warning should come ON 5 kts or 5% CAS before stall speed.

• Types of Stall
Deep Stall: When a normal wing stalls, CP moves backward. But on a
sweptback wing, CP tends to remain forward during stall, causing
the nose to pitch up. Now, if the tailplane on that aircraft is 'High-T'
Aerodynamics  type (e.g. C-17), the turbulent wake from the mainplane may interfere  with it, thereby reducing its effectiveness. Since elevators are now
ineffective, nose up attitude will continue holding aircraft in its stalled
condition. Rapid ROD that develops aggravates the condition even
further by f AoA & may make subsequent recovery impossible.
- Sweptback wing & T-tail configuration are the main contributory
factors of Super/Deep Stall.
- Stick Pusher: A device to prevent such aircraft from ever
stalling by physically pushing the stick forward before stall.
Pre Stall  Deep Stall
Shock Stall
- It occurs due to the sudden drop in CL. at M0.82, caused
by 'BL separation & -ve lift' behind top shockwave.
- It can happen at low AoA - high speed or at high AoA - low M no.
- Severity of stall depends on the shape of the wing section.
- This causes severe buffet like in subsonic airflow separation. But
unlike subsonic stall, this buffet can damage tail empennage.

Stall Recovery Procedure
- Lower the aircraft nose to reduce the angle of attack;
- Apply full engine thrust to increase air speed.
- When out of stall regime, stabilise altitude & aircraft contro
Autorotation
During stall, if there is a wing drop because of any reason (deliberate
or otherwise), drag on the down-going wing is greater than up-going
wing because relative AoA of the up-going wing is less than the down-
going wing. Now, beyond stalling AoA, any further increase in AoA will
only increase drag even further, including that of down-going wing.
Thus, the rolling tendency towards the down-going wing is even more.
Aircraft tends to roll (due to loss in lift) & yaw (due to increase in drag)
to the same side. This may cause a spin. That's why, during stall, a
pilot should never use an aileron to pick up a dropped wing. Use rudder
instead.

Tip Stall
- Wings are designed so that stall happens progressively from
root to tip.
- But in a swept-wing & a high-taper wing, although it allows a higher
maximum speed, they also have a higher tendency for tip stall.  Aerodynamics
- Tip stall is caused by the outward movement & thickening of the
boundary layer on the wig tips, making it susceptible to separation.
This causes a sudden reduction of CL at the tip.
- Tip stall is not preferred because:
- It reduces aileron effectiveness during stall.
- It causes large rolling moments if one tip stalls before the other.
It can cause pitch-up.
- To induce buffet on the tail surface, wing root must stall first.
Pitch Up
- It is a phenomenon that occurs in sweptback wings when its AoA 1
to the point of tip stall.
- When tip stalls, rapid pitch-up occurs due to longitudinal instability.
- Once this instability has set in, AoA continues to 1 causing more tip
stall, in a snowballing effect. It is caused by:
CP Movement
- As tip stalls, lift is lost from the outboard parts of the wing.
- This causes CP to move forward, giving more pitch-up moment.
- This results in the moment-arm between CP & CG to reduce,
causing even more pitch-up.
Change in Downwash Over Tailplane
- When tips are stalled, effective lift production is concentrated
on the inboard of wings. The resulting t in downwash causes
more airflow over the tailplane, thereby 1 its effectiveness
and f the tendency to pitch-up.
- This tendency can be reduced by careful placing of tailplane,
in line or below wing line.
Wash-out due to Flexure
- Occurs due to flexing of sweptback wingtips, when under load.
- It causes loss of lift at the tip, causing CP to move forward.

2 - 25
Aerodynamic Moments in a Spin
1. Rolling Moment
Rolling Moment due to Sideslip: Even at high AoA, the dihedral
effect induces a rolling moment in an opposite sense to sideslip.
In a spin, RAF is from the direction of the outer wing & results in  Aerodynamics
a rolling moment in the direction of the spin.
This is a 'pro-spin' moment.
Auto Rotative Rolling Moment: Normal damping-in-roll effect is
reversed at high AoA above stall. This is a 'pro-spin' moment.
Rolling Moment due to Yaw: Yawing velocity in spin induces a
rolling moment due to 2 reasons:
- Differences in speed of wings: Lift on the outer wing
increases more than the inner wing. It is a 'pro-spin' moment.
- Difference in AoA of wings: Yaw | AoA of outer wing & 1 AoA
of the inner wing. Because wings are stalled, CL of outer wing
is more & CL of inner wing is less. It is a 'pro-spin' moment.
Aileron Response: Ailerons produce a rolling moment even
though the wing is stalled. In-spin aileron is a 'pro-spin' moment.
2. Pitching Moment
Positive Longitudinal Static Stability: In a spin, the aircraft is in
a high AoA & the nose is pitched up. Positive longitudinal static
stability responds to this by a nose-down aerodynamic moment.
Damping in Pitch: When a/c nose is pitched up, tail pitches down
& its AoA is †. This produces a nose-down pitching moment.
Elevator Response: Elevator acts in a conventional sense & is
effective during spin. Down elevator increases nose-down
aerodynamic moment. It is an 'anti-spin' moment.
3. Yawing Moment
Positive Directional Static Stability: Rudder is a vertical surface
aft of CG, thus produces an aerodynamic yawing moment
tending to turn aircraft in line with sideslip. It is an 'anti-spin'
moment. Any vertical surface ahead of aircraft CG will give a
'pro-spin' moment.
Damping in Yaw: Rudder produces an aerodynamic yaw moment
to oppose the yaw.
Rudder Response: Rudders act in a conventional sense during
spin. In-spin rudder is pro-spin, out-spin rudder is anti-spin.

• Spin Recovery Actions:
Spin is caused due to 2 reasons: sideslip of rudder & stalled wings.
Spin recovery is aimed at stopping aircraft rotation by J pro-spin rolling
moment & 1 anti-spin moment. The sequence of recovery actions are:
- Close throttle, Neutralise ailerons.
- Full opposite rudder is applied to provide anti-spin moment & stop
side-slip. Rudder is effective during spin & is not in stalled condition.
- Give a pause: Rudder is initially shielded due to the downward motion
of aircraft & it takes some time for the anti-spin rudder to take effect.
- Stick progressively & centrally forward: It is done to un-stall
wings. But spin tightens initially. Why? When the elevator is moved
forward, 'q' (pitch angular velocity) is reduced, thus:
- L (Roll inertial moment)= (B-C)qr is reduced, anti-spin reduced;
- N (Yaw inertial moment)= (A-B)pq is reduced, anti-spin reduced;
- M (Pitch inertial moment) not effected as M = (B-C)pr
- : Anti-spin moment J, causing a slight pro-spin, & spin tightens.
- However, rudder gives high anti-spin moment to stop sideslip.
- Wings un-stall by this time & the aircraft recovers from spin.
• UPRT Upset (Unusual Attitude) Prevention & Recovery Training
In a transport aircraft, an upset is usually defined as:
- Pitch-up attitude > 25°; Pitch-down attitude > 10°; Bank > 45°; or
- Flight within parameters but speed is inappropriate for the conditions.
An upset is not necessarily a departure from controlled flight (i.e. a stall/
spin) but it does include abnormal attitudes & gross over/under-speed
conditions. Its avoidance & recognition are as important as knowing
recovery actions.
Basic Sequence of Recovery Actions:
- Check bank & pitch on the ADI.
- Cross-check with ASI/VSI/Altimeter before starting recovery.
For a nose-low case: Airspeed is probably increasing; altitude
is probably decreasing, VSI is probably indicating a descent.
For a nose-high case: Airspeed is probably decreasing; altitude
Is probably increasing, VSI is probably indicating a climb.
In both cases:
- Assess the aircraft energy state;
- Disengage autopilot and autothrottle;
- Retract speed-brakes (if extended);
- Apply flight & engine control inputs to recover, following the
manufacturers' & operators advice relevant to aircraft type.

Requirements of an Ideal Aerofoil
- High CL MAX: For lower landing speeds.  Aerodynamics
- Low CD MIN: Not only at a particular AoA but at a range of AoA, so
that aircraft can gain higher flight speeds.
- Good p ratio: Provides good efficiency, good weight carrying
capacity & less fuel consumption.
- High max value of C/CD: 1 C/CD = 1 power required = † endurance.
- Small & stable movement of CP: Greatest pressures on the wing
occur along the line of CP movement. A small & stable CP movement
therefore helps in reducing the structural weight of the wings.
Factors Affecting Performance of an Aerofoil
- Thickness, roughness, camber, leading edge shape.
Laminar Flow Aerofoils
- They are thinner than conventional wings.
- They are designed for making aeroplanes fly faster.
- Their thickest part is at 50% of chord (conventional is at 25-30%).
- They have maximum laminar flow, thus the transition point occurs
much later, and drag is considerably J.

- Airflow from canard may interfere with main/tailplane.

Stability
Introduction
Aerodynamics  - Stability is the tendency of an aircraft to return to a steady state of
flight after being disturbed by an external force, without any control
input from the pilot.
- Aircraft is in equilibrium (trim) when sum of all forces & moments is '0'.
- An aircraft is designed in such a way that its CG is just at the right
place to give optimum stability & controllability.
- More stability = Less manoeuvrability.
• Static Stability
- Static stability considers only the initial tendency of the aircraft after
it is displaced from equilibrium, due to any reason, e.g. a gust.
- Positive Stability: Aircraft automatically returns to equilibrium of
steady flight after a disturbance.
- Neutral Stability: Aircraft has neither the tendency to return to the
original state nor to continue deviation in the direction of disturbance.
- Negative Stability/Unstable: Aircraft continues to deviate in the
direction of the disturbance.
- Most a/c have +ve static stability in pitch, yaw & neutral stability in roll.
• 1. Longitudinal Stability (about lateral axis or pitching axis)
Tailplane is the principle surface contributing to longitudinal stability.

1b. Longitudinal Stability - Neutral
- Aircraft remains at the displacement to which it was disturbed to.
- If aircraft CG moves aft such that mainplane AC-CG moment is
equal to tailplane AC-CG moment, there won't be any overall up/
down moment & aircraft will remain in its new position.
1c. Longitudinal Stability - Negative
- Aircraft continues to pitch in the direction of the disturbance.
- Aircraft with -ve stability will have excessive response to controls.
Neutral Point
- At forward CG limit, stick forces are maximum & manoeuvrability
is minimum, as set by max permissible longitudinal static stability.
- At aft CG limit, stick forces are minimum & manoeuvrability is
max, as set by minimum permissible longitudinal static stability.
- At the aft CG limit, aircraft tends to be neutrally stable.
- If CG of an aircraft moves aft, the wing moment arm will 1 & tail
moment arm will J. Eventually, CG will reach a position where
wing moment arm = tail moment arm. That point is Neutral Point.
It is the point of reference in the study of longitudinal static stability.
- At neutral point, the aircraft is neutrally stable.
- If CG moves behind neutral point, aircraft will become unstable.
- In practice, a/c CG won't be allowed to move till the neutral point.
Static Margin: Margin between maximum aft CG limit & neutral point.

effective at large yaw/sideslip.

static stability.
- Ventral fins contribute to directional static stability but reduce
lateral static stability.
- So in an aircraft, dorsal fins are preferred to ventral fins.

- CG position has relatively negligible effect on directional static

Coupling of Directional & Lateral Stability
Till now, we discussed directional stability & lateral stability separately.
But in reality, for an aircraft in sideslip, the effect of directional & lateral
stability effects are coupled. They are:
- Rolling moment due to sideslip & damping in roll,  Aerodynamics
- Yawing moment due to sideslip & damping in yaw,
- Aerodynamic force due to sideslip,
- Moment of inertia of aircraft along roll axis, etc.
The complex interactions of these factors results in:
1. Directional Divergence
- In it, a small sideslip increases in magnitude until the aircraft is
broadside to the wind. † direction stability = I directional divergence
2. Spiral Divergence
- It exists when directional static stability > lateral static stability.
- When a sideslip exists to the right, a strong directional stability
tends to turn the nose into wind (right) while weak lateral static
stability lags in restoring aircraft laterally.
- Increased speed & lift on the outer wing further f bank to the right.
- Aircraft begins a slow spiral into the sideslip direction, gradually
increasing the spiral.
- It is usually controlled by the pilot.
3. Dutch Roll
It exists when directional static stability < lateral static stability.
When sideslip exists to the right, AoA of the right wing T, and a
strong lateral static stability will lift the right wing. But the
increased induced drag on the right wing will cause the aircraft
to yaw to the right. This causes Dutch Roll.
- Dutch Roll is more dangerous than spiral divergence.
- Yaw dampers are used to prevent Dutch Roll.
- If no yaw dampers exist, use ailerons & not rudder to correct for it.

• Flight Controls  (See also: Airframe > Flight Controls)
(See also: Stability)
Ailerons (fitted on main plane): Used for lateral control of aircraft.
Aerodynamics  - Deflection of ailerons produces a rolling moment.
- Deflecting control column to the right causes right aileron to move up
- In a steady banked turn, the outside wing travels faster, creating f lift.
But this is opposed by aerodynamic damping in roll due to lateral
stability. AoA of the down-going wing T, and up-going wing. Greater
the rate of roll, the greater is the damping.
- Eventually, rolling moment by ailerons is exactly balanced by damping
moment, causing a steady roll rate. Thus, ailerons areirate control.
- Smaller wingspan reduces aerodynamic damping & † rate of roll.
- Climbing with constant IAS will 1 rate of roll since damping 1 with ht.
- If aileron is moved down, stalling angle of the wing is decreased.
- Aileron Droop: On the ground, with controls neutral, ailerons are
slightly drooped (by design) below the wing line.
- When in the air, low pressure on the top surface sucks aileron up
into a position where they are aligned with the wing trailing edge.
- This droop 1/J symmetrically with flap deflection, to
augment flap area, for better lift during takeoff/landing.
Elevators (fitted on tail plane): Used for longitudinal control of a/c. D
- Displacement of elevators produce a pitch-up/down moment. When
the control column is moved back, elevators are deflected upwards,
aircraft tail develops a down-force, which moves the nose up.
- As AoA 1, tail down-force J due to aerodynamic damping in pitch.
- When aircraft reaches an equilibrium in pitch position, it will remain
in this position as long as the elevator is kept at that angle:
Thus, elevators are displacement control.
Rudder (fitted on vertical stabiliser): Used for directional control.
- If rudder is deflected to the right, aircraft will yaw to the right. This
will create a sideslip to the left & causing an RAF from the left. Inis
will cause a force on the vertical stabiliser, acting along aircraft CG
to the right, causing the aircraft nose to yaw left: damping in yaw.
- As yawing 1, damping force will t, When both becomes equal, aircraft
will remain at that yaw angle: Thus, rudder is a displacement control.
- A given rudder angle will provide a fixed yaw displacement.
- Fin Stall: If the sideslip RAF is more, fin may stall. It can be prevented
by adding a dorsal fin to rudder, thus | its aspect ratio († stalling AOR).
Spoilers: They are narrow flat plates fitted on upper side of wings.
- They are used to † drag and to | lift.
- Use of differential spoilers provide lateral control & prevent Adverse
Aileron Yaw.
- When spoilers on both wings operate together, they act as air-brakes.

Secondary Effect of Controls
Roll due to Yaw
- If right rudder is applied, aircraft will yaw to the right, left wing will
travel faster & lift on the left wing f. This causes the left wing to
lift up & aircraft will roll to the right, in the direction of initial yaw.  Aerodynamics
- Roll due to yaw is maximum at low speeds, with high AoA.

Methods to Prevent Adverse Aileron Yaw
- Differential Aileron: In this, the up-going aileron moves through
a larger angle than the down-going aileron. This f drag on up-
aileron & J drag on down-aileron. Thus, difference in drag
between both the wings are reduced.
- Frise Type Aileron: These are ailerons that have asymmetric
leading edge. Leading edge of the up-going aileron protrudes
below the lower surface of the wing, causing higher drag on that
side. Leading edge of the down-going aileron remains shrouded
& creates less drag. Thus differential drag is reduced.
- Aileron - Rudder Coupling: Aileron & rudder controls are inter-
connected. So, when ailerons are deflected, rudder automatically
moves to counter the adverse yaw.
- Roll Spoilers: During a roll, spoilers that deploy on the down-
going wing will increase drag on that side.

• Control Balance/Aerodynamic Balance
- The AD forces that act on control surfaces depends on:
- Area of control surface  - Its moment arm
- Amount of displacement  - IAS of aircraft
- For large & fast aircraft, these forces act on the control column
and may be too high for pilots to handle physically.
- This can be remedied with the use of hydraulic-powered/fly-by-wire
controls or by means of aerodynamic balancing.
- Aerodynamic balancing is done to make control surfaces easier to
move by using Tabs, Horns & Hinges.
Tabs  (See also: Airframe > Flight Controls > Hydraulic/Fly-by-wire)
Balance Tab: It is used to | stick load & J control surface effectiveness.
- They are 'hinged surfaces' on the trailing edge of control surfaces
& provide a force opposite to that of the main control surface.
- Balance tab moves in the opposite direction of control surface.
- It is not under pilot's control. Pilot moves surface, surface moves tab.
Anti Balance Tab: It is used to | stick loads, for more feel of controls
& to 1 control effectiveness.
- Anti balance tabs move in the same direction as control surface.
- It is not under pilot's control. Pilot moves surface, surface moves tab
Servo Tab: It is used for easier control surface movement by a pilot.
In this, pilot input does not deflect the control surface. Instead, it
deflects a servo tab, which produces a moment along its hinge line,
resulting in AD forces which in turn moves the main control surface.
- Servo tabs are sometimes used as trim tabs also.
- It can also be used as an emergency control surface during
hydraulic failure or a jammed elevator. But it works in opp. sense.
- But its effectiveness | at low IAS since deflection > 20° is not
effective. This problem can be corrected by using spring tabs.
Spring Tab: It is used to 1 control effectiveness of servo tabs at low
IAS. It is a modification on the servo tab, in which, the tab
movement is proportional to stick forces.
- In this, a spring is used, which is not compressed at low speeds.
- At high speeds, high dynamic pressure prevents control sunac
r from moving. So the spring is compressed by pilot input, whic
in turn moves the tab & the control surface.
Trim Tab: It is a small adjustable surface on the control surface TE,
controlled by a trim wheel/switch, to balance out residual AD forces
on the control surface, to relieve pressures on the control column.
- To maintain the control surface in its required position, the trim
tab is moved by the pilot in the opposite direction, until tab
movement balances the control surface hinge movement.
- A/c is trimmed if it maintains attitude & speed without pilot inputs.
- A/c has to be re-trimmed if speed, power or CG posn is changed.
Fixed Tabs: Non adjustable tabs, usually used in aileron & rudder.

Flight Mechanics
• Level Flight
- Lift is considered to act through CP, perpendicular, 90° to flight path.
- Drag is considered to act through CP, backwards, parallel to flight.
- Weight is considered to act through CG, vertically downwards.
- Thrust is considered to act through the thrust line, forward, parallel
to flight.
A LIFT
THRUST  DRAG
Y WEIGHT
• Balance of Forces
- For unaccelerated level flight, balance of all forces must be equal.
Thrust = Drag,  Lift = Weight
- If there is an increase in thrust, the aircraft will accelerate until drag
equalises thrust at a higher speed.
- CP moves forward with increasing AoA.
- CG moves with reducing fuel, configuration change, etc.
- Generally, CP is ahead of CG at low speed, giving a nose pitch-up
& behind CG during high speed, giving a nose pitch-down.
- Tailplane is designed to produce the necessary up or down-force as
required, to generate the necessary force to balance any pitching
moment arising from CP/CG movement.
- This causes additional drag: Trim Drag.
Reducing Speed & Stabilising at Low Speed
- When power is reduced, AoA is 1 to maintain the same lift initially.
- But as AoA 1, CP moves forward, thus reducing nose pitch down
moment.
- Thus, the stick has to be moved slightly forward again, to AoA, so
as to maintain level flight.
Factors Affecting Level Flight
Speed: If speed J, CL has to be 1 (t AoA) to maintain level flight.
Altitude: If weight is constant, the relationship between EAS & AoA
remains unchanged with altitude.
Weight: If weight is J (e.g., fuel consumption), lift must be, to
balance the new weight. To maintain the same AoA, speed has to
reduce.
A good landing" is one you can walk away from.
However, a "great landing" is one where you can use the airplane again.

Steady Climb
• During Steady Climb:
- Lift < weight because lift only has to support a portion of weight  Aerodynamics
(Wcose). This proportion l as the angle of climb f; and
- Thrust > drag, to additionally support backward component of weight.
- In pure vertical climb, no lift is needed. The full weight of the aircraft
is supported by thrust (Wsine).

Angle of climb & ability to climb depends on excess thrust.
• Best angle of climb will be at a speed that gives max difference
between thrust & drag, which is at speed Vy.
• For a piston aircraft, speed Vx is as low as 'safe unstick speed.
- For a jet aircraft Vx is VMD (since thrust does not vary with speed).
- Head Wind 1 = climb/descend angle 1, ground distance J.

POWER AVAILABLE VS POWER REQUIRED
(See also: Cruise > Little 'm)
Cruise Climb: It is a procedure used to f range & , tuel consumption of
an aircraft. For a constant weight & altitude, best range is achieved at
best TAS/Drag, which is 1.32 VMD. However, during flight, due to fuel
consumption, aircraft weight , AOA, drag | & 'total drag curve' lower.
Thus, to obtain best TAS/Drag, speed has to J, which we don't want to
do. Instead, aircraft is made to climb, keeping TAS constant at 1.19
Vp (IAS J). This procedure is called Cruise Climb. This is done till such
altitude where mach no. reaches M0.8. Beyond this speed, shockwaves
start forming. So, from then on, aircraft altitude is maintained constant
& TAS is reduced. This procedure, though efficient, may not be practical
in a busy airspace, where aircraft has to climb slowly, continuously,
unrestricted. So, another technique called 'Step Climb' is used.
Step Climb: As aircraft weight 1 due to fuel consumption, aircraft altitude
Is increased by 2000' higher than the optimum fuel economy cruise
altitude. This altitude is maintained until optimum cruise altitude
becomes higher than aircraft altitude by 2000'. Then aircraft altitude is
Increased by 4000' (from 2000' below to 2000' above optimum cruise
allitude). This process is repeated, maintaining within 2000' of optimum
cruise altitude. It gives up to 99% fuel efficiency as that of cruise climb.

Steady Descend
• During Steady Descend:
- Lift < weight because lift only has to support a portion of the weight  Aerodynamics

Steady Turn
