- Lift is resolved into forces 'equal & opposite to weight' & the 'centripetal

- But while in a bank, the vertical component of lift will 1 & will not be
able to balance the aircraft weight. The aircraft will start to descend.
- Therefore, AoA has to be increased to provide more lift, until the
vertical component of lift can balance aircraft weight.

• Cruise
- LRC Long Range Cruise: A speed that is 4% faster than 'still-air

- SAR Specific Air Range: It is the air distance covered per unit of

- GFC Gross Fuel Consumption: Fuel consumed in unit time.
- SFC Specific Fuel Consumption (GFC/Unit thrust): Fuel consumed per

* Littleim: It is the ratio between cruising IAS & VMD. (Little 'm'is used to

Practically, for best range, lower the cruise altitude = IAS 1 = 'm'1,
until m = 1.19 (for climb cruise) or until m = 1.32 (constant alt cruise).

Properties of Shockwaves
Normal Shockwave
- When a shockwave is 1 to airflow, it is called a normal shockwave.
Streamlines pass through it & there is no change in flow direction.
- Normal shockwave has higher compression & loss in total  Aerodynamics
pressure since kinetic energy is converted to heat energy.
- Behind a normal shockwave, mach no. is always subsonic.
Oblique Shockwave
- It is similar to a normal shockwave, but its orientation is more
than 90° to the flow direction.
- Crossing an oblique shockwave, the direction of airflow changes.
- Behind an oblique shockwave, flow may be subsonic or supersonic.
Expansive Shock
- Its properties are opposite to that of an oblique shockwave.
- Direction of flow change is gradual.
- No shock in an expansive wave means no loss of energy.

Why does airflow accelerate beyond M1.0 in a divergent duct?
As the airflow accelerates on top of the wing, it reaches maximum speed at
the point of maximum camber. Beyond that, the speed of flow should ideally
like in subsonic flow. But in supersonic flow beyond M1, speed of flow t. Why?
(1) At the point of max thickness and max speed, due to the presence of
shockwave, the pressure waves cannot transmit the pressure difference.
Also, aft of the point of max thickness, the area t. Due to the momentum of
air, it moves ahead & expands to fill this available space. Expansion of air
its temperature & density, causing its mach no. to increase.
("1) In a steady flow, mass flow remains constant. However, since velocity of
flow and area have increased, a further drop in density & pressure occurs.
As a result, mach no. increases further.

- Deflecting a control surface down in the transonic range will:
- 1 MCRIT due to accelerated airflow.

- Control Buzz: Presence of shockwave near 'control surface hinge'

shockwave helps to reattach separated airflow. It I shockwave

all-moving tailplane will not have this problem.
- Roll Control Spollers: Better control during roll in transonic region.

Transonic/Supersonic Stability
Longitudinal Stability
- Mach no. 1 = Longitudinal stability 1
- As mach no. 1 beyond M1.0, CP moves back & stabilises at 50%
of chord during transonic/supersonic flight.  Aerodynamics
- Thus, the distance between CP & CG 1, nose-down moment f,
+ve stability T.
- Presence of shockwave on the wing also I downwash over the
tailplane, causing 1 in its AoA & f in the pitch-down moment.
Lateral Stability
- Mach no. 1 = Lateral stability J.
- At MCRIT, one wing may drop due to the differential shockwave
position on the wings. On the wing which drops more, lift
increases causing more shockwave intensity, causing that wing
to drop further.
- So, the effect of 'dihedral stability', which was good in subsonic
flight, is now bad in supersonic flight.
- Sweepback: Positive effects of sweepback also reduce during
supersonic flight because of the same reasons above.
Directional Stability
- Mach no. 1 = Directional stability J.
- Fin effectiveness j at supersonic speeds.
- During sideslip, the strength of a bow shockwave that forms
towards RAF is more than the other side. Thus, pressure is more
on the side of RAF and the aircraft yaws away from that side.
- Moment arm j further in case of aft CG in a rear-mounted engine.
Cross-coupling of Inertia
Yaw Divergence
- It occurs if the aircraft has good longitudinal stability but poor
directional stability.
- When you pull up during a high-rate of roll, 'yaw due to roll'
caused during this pulling-up induces an increased upward
moment on the tailplane, causing a further yaw.
- It is caused due to high inertia in the pitching plane.
Pitch Divergence
- It occurs if the aircraft has good directional stability but poor
longitudinal stability, & the aircraft tends to face RAF.
- Now, due to yawing & rolling simultaneously, the pitch (when
inverted) goes down & due to poor longitudinal stability nose
continues to pitch down.
- It is caused due to high inertia in the yawing plane.
Methods to Avoid Cross-coupling
- Minimum inclination of inertial axis in normal flight conditions.
- Increase aircraft directional stability.
- Limit roll rate of aircraft.
The probability of survival is inversely proportional to the angle of arrival.
Larger the angle of arrival, smaller is the probability of survival and vice versa.

• Manoeuvre Envelope
Introduction
- Manoeuvre Envelop is a graphical representation of the operating
Aerodynamics  limit's of an aircraft. It is used to:
- Lay down design requirements for a new aircraft.
- Used by manufacturers to illustrate aircraft performance.
Parts of Manoeuvre Envelope
• CL MAX Boundary
- The curved line on the top & bottom depicts lift & load factor for a
given weight at max AoA & EAS.
- Pulling 'g' beyond this limit may stall a/c, but will not over-stress it.
- The speed at load factor '1' shows 'basic stalling speed.
• 'g' Limits
- It shows maximum +ve & -ve 'g' limits the aircraft can withstand.
- It generally has additional 50% safety margin before permanent
deformation (caution zone).
- Beyond this 50% margin, structural failure will occur.
- Since g = if/weight, if weight 1, g has to J to stay within safe limits.
• Max EAS
- A vertical line at right end of the graph indicates max safe speed.
- Exceeding this line may cause loss of panels, aileron reversal,
wing divergence, flutter or failure of the weakest structure.
- This line usually has a 5% - 10% safety margin (caution zone).
- As altitude 1, CL MAX J due to change in compressibility. So,
reduced stalling speed, 'g' limits & max EAS lines are re-drawn
for different altitudes.
• Rolling 'g' Limit
- Additional 'g' limits are imposed due to wing strength limitations
during rolls.
• Buffet Corners
- When a high 'g' manoeuvre is combined with high weight, the
weakest part may fail. So, the corners of the envelope are cut.
Information available on a Manoeuvre Envelop
- Available load factor for any height & speed
- Basic stalling speed
- Stalling speed at any height
- Compressibility mach no.
- Max available load factor
- Max EAS at any height
- Max EAS VNE.

Aeroelastic Problems
• Aileron Reversal
- Ailerons are fitted towards the wingtips to give max rolling moment.
- But if the wing has low structural stiffness, as IAS 1, dynamic
pressure on ailerons 1 & down-going ailerons may twist the wingtip,
reducing its AoA to a point that the twisted wingtip produces more
down-force than the up-force created by the down-going aileron.
- Thus aircraft rolls to the other side.
Elastic Wing
- It is most likely to occur in an aircraft
with fully powered controls.
- Remedy: Use Inboard ailerons;
Stiffening wings.
Divergence
- It occurs if wing has low stiffness & if its CP is ahead of flexural axis.
- Now, with 1 in IAS, high AD forces will twist the wing, which † its
AoA, moves CP forward, & further † distance between AC & flexural
axis. This causes the wing to continue twisting until it breaks.
- Divergence has no contribution from control surface movements.
- Remedy - Make aircraft wings stiffer. But this increases weight.
- Mass Balancing: Reduce moment arm between AC & flexural axis
(mounting engine ahead & below of wing, like a weight).
- Reduce chord length.
• Flutter
- It occurs when aerodynamic forces (gust/control input) interfere
with the natural vibrations of the wing, causing rapid & uncon-
trolled continuous oscillations, leading to a catastrophic failure.
- Flutter is caused by:
Flexural centre
- Low flexibility of wing.
- High aerodynamic & inertial forces.
Control Surface Flutter  Location of mass balance
- It occurs due to the oscillation of the control surface coupled with
oscillation in bending & twisting of the wing/tailplane.
- It develops if CG of control surface (aileron) is behind its hinge line.
Torsional Aileron Flutter (twisting of wings)
- An aileron displaced down will exert an upward force on the
aileron hinge. This causes the wing to twist about its torsional
axis, causing its TE to rise, taking the aileron hinge up with it.
- By the time aileron catches up, the wing has arrested the twisting
aerodynamic load on the aileron now causes the wing to twist in
the opposite direction. This cycle continues until the wing breaks.
- Remedy - Mass balancing ailerons;
- Make control surface irreversible: Powered controls.
Flexural Aileron Flutter (bending/flapping of wings)
- It is similar to torsional aileron flutter, but in a
flexural flutter, the wing as a whole moves up &
down (like bird wings flapping) instead of twisting.
- Remedy - Mass balancing of ailerons;
- Stiffening wings.  Flexural Alleron Flutter

• Propellor Theory
Blade Angle or Pitch: Angle between blade chord & plane of rotation.

Geometric Pitch
It is the distance a propellor would travel in one complete rotation as if
it were moving through air at that blade angle (like a screw thread).
Effective Pitch
In reality, a prop doesn't travel along its geometric pitch. Effective pitch
is the actual distance propellor would travel in one complete rotation.
Slip: Distance b/w GP & EP. Slip 'O' means props are at 100% efficiency.
Geometric Mean Pitch
It is the distance moved by a propellor when its AoA is 'O', or slip is 'O'.
As torward velocity of a propellor 1, its AoA,. At a particular point of
RAF, AoA becomes 'O'. However, the propellor is still producing thrust
due to its camber. The propellor advance per rotation, in this case, is
called GMP.
Experimental Mean Pitch
It is the distance moved by a propellor when producing no thrust. In
EMP, AoA will be even < GMP & thus advance will be even more.
EMP is always greater than GMP.
Helix Angle
It is the angle between the plane of rotation of a propellor & the path of
effective pitch. As prop rotates & advances through the air (following
line of effective pitch), actual path that blades follow describes a helix.
Blade Twist
Blade sections near the tip travel more distance in one rotation. So
blade angle must be 1 towards tip to give it constant geometric pitch.
This ensures constant thrust production throughout length of the prop.
AoA
It is the angle between the blade chord & RAF. Path of the propellor
through the air determines the direction of RAF.
Torque
It is the 'equal & opposite' reaction
of a propellor being rotated, which
generates a turning moment about
the aircraft longitudinal axis.  Thrust

Forces on a Blade
- Centrifugal Force: Tends to stretch a blade outward.
- Torque Bending Force: Tends to twists a blade.
- Thrust Bending Force: Tends to bends a blade forward.
- CTM Centrifugal Twisting Moment: It is a centrifugal force acting
on a blade leading edge & trailing edge, producing a moment
around pitch-change-axis, which tends to 'fine the blade'.
- ATM Aerodynamic Twisting Moment: Because blade CP is in
front of the pitch-change-axis, aerodynamic forces generate a
moment around pitch-change-axis, to coarsen the pitch. If AoA 1,
CP moves forward, thrust 1 & tends to coarsen pitch. It can be
considered akin to CP moving forward in a normal aerofoil.
- ATM is more than CTM during normal engine operations.
- In windmilling, ATM acts in same direction as CTM & will re-enforce it.

- This effect occurs only when aircraft pitches or yaws, and occurs

- In a tail-wheel aircraft, during takeoff rotation, tail-wheel comes up
& nose pitches down, causing precession & aircraft yaws to left.
- In air, a left yaw causes pitch-up & a pitch-up causes a right yaw.
- It can be eliminated by using contra-rotating propellors.

- Spiral slipstream generated by rotating props hits the tailplane
and creates a yawing moment to the left & roll to the right.

Airframe
===== [avh 0198]
3 - 3
Terms & Definitions
Aircraft: Any device intended for flight in air, including gliders, airplanes,
helicopters, balloons, etc.  (See also: Aerodynamics > Lift)
Aerofoil: A structure designed to produce a lifting force, caused by its
movement through air. E.g.: wings, rotor blades, propellors etc.
Fuselage: A structure within an aircraft, to provide space for crew, cargo
or passengers.
Stress: A force acting on a body, per unit area.  Airframe
Strain: Deformation caused due to stress. It is a ratio: Change in size
- It has no unit.  original size
Rigidity/Stiffness: Ratio of stress over strain (Young's Modulus).
Elastic Limit: Limit at which stress causes strain. When stress exceeds a
body's elastic limit, a permanent 'set happens. On the release of the
load, the body will not return back to its original shape.
Types of Loads
- Tension: A stress that tries to stretch a body. It is calculated by
dividing the load required to pull the body apart, by its cross-section
area. It is measured in Psi.
- Compression: A stress that tries to crush a body. It shortens/
squeezes aircraft parts. It is also measured in Psi.
- Shear: A stress that resists the force trying to cause one layer to
slide over another, e.g., loads on screws, bolts, rivets.
Combination of Loads
- Bending Force: Compression at the top, tension at the bottom.
- Torsion: Twisting force - compression at one end, tension at the
other. e.g., engine propeller rotation.
- Torsional Strength: Strength of a body to resist twisting.
Load Limits
- DLL Design Limit Load: Maximum load the aircraft designer
expects the airframe/components to experience.
- Proof Load: (DLL × 1.125) During proof load, aircraft structure must
not suffer permanent deformation. Flight controls/system should
function normally.
- DUL Design Ultimate Load: (DLL × 1.5) Airframe deformation may
occur, but aircraft structure must withstand DUL without collapse.
- Ultimate Stress: Load at which the airframe will collapse.
Design Philosophies
- Safe Life: A structure is designed to survive a pre-determined
number of flying hours, after which the component is replaced/
overhauled. If a crack is found, airframe is retired. This system
proved inefficient because predicting the rate of structure
deterioration is difficult.
- Fail Safe: Structure retains adequate strength until inspections are
planned. They are damage tolerant or has crack arrest features
(redundant load paths, long critical path lengths, etc.). This system
must have periodic inspection routines promulgated.
===== [avh 0199]
3 - 4
Metal Fatigue
- Stress at which metal cracks is called Ultimate Stress.
- However, multiple ON/OFF loads below ultimate stress can also cause
cumulative damage, which will eventually cause it to fail at a stress
below its calculated ultimate stress. This is called metal fatigue.
- Cracks usually form on surface discontinuities (screw holes, joints).
- Fatigue life of commercial aircraft is based on its pressurisation
cycle & not its landing cycle.
- Composite metals do not have this problem at stress levels less than
80% of its Ultimate Stress.
Airframe
Miner's Rule
- Miner's Rule estimates the cumulative fatigue damage due
to varying amplitude load cycles below Ultimate Stress.
- The 's-n curve' plots the no. of times different stress levels can be
applied on the body before the structure collapses.
- e.g., 80% of Ultimate Stress applied 102 (hundred) times can cause
failure. But 20% of Ultimate Stress has to be applied 10 million
times for the same failure to occur.
According to Miner's rule: N1
Measures to Reduce Fatigue  D1 N2+.= 1 at failure
- Reduce roller-landing/takeoffs;
- Avoid turbulence;  Design S-N
- Carry only fuel required for sortie;  curve
- Avoid tight 'g' turns;
- Minimise 'close formation' flying.
n1 02 N1  Nz  Endurance
Stages of Fatigue Failure
- Crack initiation: Occurs along joints, rivet holes, sharp corners.
- Crack moderation: Crack conditions deteriorate due to corrosion.
- Crack growth: Once crack reaches 1 mm, crack growth depends
less on the condition that caused it & more on stress levels.
- Final fracture will occur when the crack reaches a critical crack
length, at which point catastrophic failure will occur.

Airframe Construction
• Wing Construction Methods
Bi-Plane: Aircraft with 2 sets of wings. Old design, a/c speed < 200 kts.
Braced: It uses external braces to support the wings, e.g., Cessna.
Cantilever: Uses thick spars in a wing to support all loads. All modern
aircraft have cantilever wings. These are of 2 types:
- Mono Spar: Only one spar is used. Ribs and bulkheads supply
the necessary contour & shape for the wing.
- Multi Spar: Uses more than 1 spar.
Bi-Plane  Braced  Cantilever
Parts of a Wing
- Spar: It is the principle span-wise load-bearing member in a wing,
to withstand all bending & torsional loads.
- Stringers: They are span-wise add-on members to a spar, to prevent
buckling & bending of the wing. It works by stiffening the skin.
- Ribs: Transverse member, which supports skin & maintains its shape.
- Torsion Box: A box formed between front spar, rear spar, skin, ribs
& stringers. It resists bending & twisting loads.

• Fuselage Construction Methods
Truss or Framework: In this, metal tubes are welded in triangular
shapes called trusses. It is used in light/non-pressurised aircraft.
Monocoque: In this method, all structural and aerodynamic loads are
absorbed by the aircraft skin (also called stressed skin). It has light
frames inside to give it shape. It cannot tolerate dents & deformation.
Semi Monocoque: In this, additional structures reinforce aircraft skin &
provide shape & form to the fuselage. More sturdy than Monocoque.
Parts of an Airframe
- Longeron: Fore-aft airframe strengthening member.
- Stringer: Additional longitudinal member.
- Frames/Formers: For vertical strengthening. It opposes hoop stress.

Hydraulic System
• Introduction
- In an aircraft, a hydraulic system provides a means of operating
large & remote components that cannot be operated satisfactorily
by other means, e.g., undercarriage, flaps, brakes, etc.
- In a hydraulic system, fluid is only compressed by 1%, unlike a
pneumatic system, in which air is compressed by 99%.
- If a wrong hydraulic fluid is used in a system, it may lead to system
Airframe  - Hydraulic fluid, if found in milky appearance, means it has aeration.  failure due to leaks, blocked filters, high temperature or corrosion.
Such a system should be investigated.
• Working Principle
J Pressure (P) = Force  J Force (F) = Pressure x Area
Area
- Pascal's Law: When a force is applied by a piston to one end of a
column filled with fluid, pressure is transmitted in all directions & to
all parts of the system.
- Bramah's Press Principle: Smaller the area under load, the greater
the pressure generated. Larger the area under pressure, the greater
the load available.
Types of Hydraulic System
Open System
They are simple systems used in small aircraft where no constant
hydraulic pressure is needed during flight. An Engine Driven Pump
EDP runs continuously & pumps fluid, even when no service is
being operated. In this, only 1 service can be operated at a time.
Closed System
Constant Delivery: Pump delivers constant fluid volume whether it
is needed or not. Pump output is proportional to motor RPM. A
cutout valve operates when system pressure is higher than required
& diverts fluid to a reservoir. When the system pressure is low, an
accumulator is used to boost pressure.
Constant Pressure (Variable Volume): Pump varies delivery volume,
depending on the pressure in the system. When the required pressure
is achieved, pump stops. When pressure drops, pump turns back
ON. This system needs a pressure switch but not an accumulator.
• Advantages of Hydraulic System  Disadvantages
- Capable of transmitting high force.  - Prone to contamination,
- Rapid & precise response.  high temperature & aeration.
- Good power to weight ratio.  - Hydraulic fluid is hazardous.
- Simple & reliable.  - System is prone to leaks.
- Self lubricating.  - It is heavier than pneumatic.

• Parts of a Hydraulic System
- Reservoir: It is pressurised to reduce cavitation. It also
prevents fluid foaming, caters to small leaks & fluid
thermal expansion.
- Hydraulic Jacks: Actuators in a hydraulic system.
- Pump: It is used to pump the hydraulic fluid.
- Heat Exchanger: Cools the hydraulic fluid.
- Filters: Fitted in both pressure & return lines. It usually has a
pressure differential switch, to indicate a 'clogged filter'.
- Accumulators: They are used to:
- Store hydraulic fluid under pressure;  Airframe
- Dampen pressure fluctuations;
- Allow thermal expansion;
- For emergency pressure supply.
- Valves
- Shuttle Valve: It allows fluid supply on both sides of the
piston, to enable it to move in both directions.
- Restrictor Valve: Controls the rate of movement of a service.
- Automatic Cutout Valves: It stops the pump when the
required pressure is achieved.
- Non-return Valves: It ensures one-way flow of fluid.
- Pressure Relief Valves: It prevents mechanical overload of
the system.
- Stack Pipe in reservoir ensures fluid availability for emergency
services. Normal service uses a fluid feed from the stack pipe &
emergency service uses a fluid feed from the reservoir bottom.
- Hydraulic Fuse: It minimises fluid loss in case of a fluid leak. It is
fitted upstream from non-essential services.
- Hydraulic Lock: It prevents piston movement when the fluid flow
stops and makes the piston stationary.

Pneumatic System  10
• Introduction
- A pneumatic system works in a similar way to a hydraulic system.
But instead of hydraulic fluid, it uses air as the working medium.
- The required air is tapped from the engine compressor as bleed-air.
This bleed system needs to supply sufficient air quantity at low
engine RPMs & restrict excessive pressure at high engine RPMs.
- This is done by an HP shutoff valve that slowly opens when the LP
valve cannot supply sufficient air during low engine RPMs & close
at high engine RPMs.
- Bleed systems are protected by 'overheat' & 'over pressure sensors.
• Pneumatic systems are used in:
- Air conditioning  - Thrust reverser actuation
- Aerofoil & engine anti-icing  - Engine starting
- Cargo compartment heating  - Water tank pressurisation
- Hydraulic reservoir pressurisation - Cabin pressurisation
- Leading/Trailing edge flap operation
• Parts of a Pneumatic System
- Compressor: It compresses air.
- Ground Charging Valve: Used to supply compressed air on ground.
- Anti Freeze: Methanol is generally used as an anti-freeze. It is
vaporised by warm air from the compressor and is circulated
throughout system, to lower the freezing point of moisture.
- Oil/Water Trap: It collects moisture trapped in the system.
- It is mounted on the lowest part of the system.
- It has its drain valve at the bottom.
- Pressure Relief Valve: It relieves excess system pressure.
- Pressure Regulating Valve: It stops the compressor when requisite
system pressure is reached.
- Storage Cylinder: Stores compressed air.
Advantages of Pneumatic System
- Uses non-inflammable fluid (air) for its operation.
Open-loop system: used air is vented back to the atmosphere.
Less system weight  - Minor leak is not a problem
- Working fluid (air) is readily available - No filtration is required
Disadvantages  Actuator
• Precise & rapid response not available.
- Less system working pressure.
- High power handling not possible.

3 - 9
Landing Gear
Design Considerations in Making a Landing Gear
- Aircraft role & theatre of operations, e.g., STOL short takeoff/landing.
- Runway length & types of runway intended to be used.
- Aircraft cruising speed: Fixed landing gear will have more drag &
retractable landing gear will have more weight.
- Landing speed/aircraft weight determines the strength of landing gear.
• Arrangement of Landing Gear
Single Main: (e.g. U-2) It has a single main undercarriage, with smaller
tailwheel along the centreline. It is simple, light weight & has low drag.
Tail Dragger: (e.g. Dakota)
- In it, the main gear is placed ahead ahead of a/c CG & tail wheel.
- It is a simple old design, creates low drag. In it, wings are already
at high AoA during takeoft roll, giving high lift.
- But since main gear is ahead of aircraft CG, it has controllability
issues during takeoff & landing. It also has low pilot fwd visibility.
Bicycle Landing Gear (e.g. Sea Harrier)
- It has 2 main gears along centre line, forward & aft of aircraft CG.
- Additionally, it has 2 outriggers on the wingtips to provide stability.
- It is generally used in slender tuselages where there is no space.
- It has low weight/drag, but has controllability issues during landing
Tricycle Landing Gear: New design, most common configuration.
- In it, 90% of the aircraft weight is supported by the main gear.
Quadra-cycle Landing Gear (e.g. B-52, Strato-Fortress)
- In it, 4 main landing gears are mounted on an airframe, like in a car.
- In it, aircraft floor can be very close to the ground, however, It is
very sensitive to roll/crosswind during takeoff/landing.
Multi-bogey Landing Gear (e.g. Boeing-737)
- Multiple wheels are placed on the same gear bogey for safety &
steering control (safety during tyre burst).
- More the AUW/landing wt of aircraft, more the no. of bogeys used.
• Types of Landing Gear
Retractable Landing Gear: They fold into the fuselage, with hydraulics.
Since the tail-wheel has low drag, it is usually not retractable.
Fixed Landing Gear: Stronger, simpler, lighter, but has drag penalty.
- Split Axle: Axle split in between to enable obstruction clearance.
- Tripod: Consists of 3 members, 2 of them rigid, hinged to form a
triangle. On landing, these spread outwards & absorb the load.
- Spring Leaf: It has a strap of chrome-vanadium/spring-steel.
It bends upward on landing and cushions impact.
It has low maintenance & has a simple construction.
Single Shock Strut: Used in a low wing, fixed undercarriage a/c.

Shock Absorbers
Introduction
- Shock absorbers are used to dampen shocks of landing & taxiing.
- It is designed to never reach full extension or compression under any
operational load conditions because if they do, the strut momentarily
becomes rigid & will pass on the impact to the aircraft structure.
- Nose landing gear is subject to more movement/loads; thus it
generally has a 2 stage absorber for a greater range of operation.
Airframe
Oleo-pneumatic Shock Absorber
In this, a piston consisting of pressurised air/nitrogen (in chamber C) &
oil (in chambers B & A), are separated by a separator. In static
conditions, the weight of the aircraft is balanced by gas pressure (in
Chamber C) & oil pressure (in Chamber A). When a load is applied,
the piston moves up & oil (in chamber A) gets
compressed & flows through a clack valve into
chamber B within the piston. This causes the
separator to push down due to the increased oil
pressure above it. The separator will continue  Fluid
moving down until oil pressure above it equals gas  Clack
pressure below it. Thus, the compressing air (in  Valve
chamber C) absorbs the landing shock. After the
initial shock, air pressure in the piston (in chamber
C) is greater than what is required to support  Separator
the load. This high air pressure pushes the
Piston

to flow up through the clack valve back into
chamber A. This, in turn, causes the cylinder
upper head to move down & the oleo will extend.
Thus the restricted movement of oil through the  Oleo-pneumatic
clack valve slows extension & dampens rebound  Shock Absorber

Brakes
Drum brakes
Non-rotating metal drums are placed inside the wheel casing. A rubber
tube with metal plates is attached on top of it. When brakes are applied,
the air is pumped into rubber tubes, which press against the drum.
When brakes are released, a spring pushes back on brake pads.
Vanes placed inside the drum improve air circulation & pad cooling.
Disadvantages  Drum Brakes
- Causes vibration if the drum is distorted.  Cylinder
- Water may reduce brake effectiveness.  Airframe

Disc Brakes
• Anti-Skid Braking System
To minimise landing run, brakes should have maximum
braking force without causing wheels to lock & skid. Point
of skid depends upon runway surface, load applied by tyres
& braking force. A mechanical system senses the inertia of a small
flywheel which corresponds to the rapid change in wheel rotational
speed. During braking, when it senses a wheel lock/skid, system releases
hydraulic pressure, J braking effort & thus reduces skid. Hydraulic
pressure is re-instated when skid is reduced. This constant ON/OFF
braking is called Brake modulation. In electrical systems, sensors allow
controlled brake modulations, thus 1 braking efficiency by 15%. Anti-
skid usually deactivates automatically when aircraft speed is < 20 kts.
Advantages
- Most effective braking, ensuring minimum landing distance.
- Minimise tyre wear.
- Touchdown Protection: No brakes till touchdown & wheels start to spin.
- Skid Prevention: System maintains continuous braking force at a
level just below skid, at all speeds & surface conditions.
- Wheel Lock Protection: In case of wheel lock during braking, the
system releases brakes until the wheels spin up again.
• Auto Brakes:
- A system of automatic braking, during landing & reject takeoff.
- During landing, system applies max brake pressure automatically
when all power levers closed & aircraft speed is < 85 kts.
- System automatically disengages when speed < 20 kts or if anti-skid
fails or if power-lever is moved forward (incase of go-around).

3 - 12
Tyres
• Introduction
- Aircraft tyres are usually filled with nitrogen.
- Tyre wear can be reduced by taxiing at < 22 kts (40 kmph).
- Tyre Scrubbing: It occurs if the aircraft is made to do sharp turns
on the ground with a radius < minimum specified turning radius.
- If tyres are hot after taxi, tyre pressure may increase by up to 10%.
- Over Inflation causes excessive wearing of tyre centre.
Airframe  - Under Inflation causes excessive wearing of tyre shoulder. Tyre
under-inflation is one of the major causes of tyre failure. The tyre
will heat up faster and may cause a breakdown of rubber material.
Advantage of Tubeless Tyres
- Tyre pressure maintains longer because tyre lining is un-stretched.
- Tyre puncture will not cause rapid pressure loss.
- It is more resistant to impact blows.
- They are lighter because there is no inner tube (7.5% weight savings)
- Creep damage is eliminated.
Tyre Pressures
- Low Pressure Tyre: Pressure between 25 - 35 Ibs/sq in.
- Medium Pressure Tyre: Pressure between 35 - 70 Ibs/sq in.
- High Pressure Tyre: Pressure between 70 - 90 Ibs/sq in.
- Extra High Pressure: Pressure > 90 Ibs/sq in.
Standard Tyre Markings (marks that are printed on a tyre):
- Ply rating: It is not the no. of layers in a tyre, but its strength rating.
- Speed rating: Max permitted ground taxi speed, in knots.
- A red dot or triangle indicates the lightest part of the tyre.
- A green or grey dot on the tyre sidewall indicates AWL vents.
Tyre Creep: It is caused due to tyre rotating against the wheel hub.
- Creep may tear the inflation valve of 'tube tyres'.
- Creep is less likely to occur if tyre pressure is maintained correctly.
- Creep is very likely in new fitted tyres.
- Creep is measured by 'paint markings' on the tyre & wheel rim.
- Tubeless tyres have inbuilt valves and are not affected by creep.
Fusible Plugs: Fusible plugs are designed to melt and release air
pressure if excessive heat is generated during harsh braking. This
prevents excessive air pressure buildup inside the tyre & allows for a
controlled deflation, thereby prevents an accidental tyre blowout.

Wheel Hub: It is usually made of aluminium/magnesium alloy.
• Nose Wheel Control
Castoring: It is the ability of the nose wheel to turn to either side, which
helps in steering the aircraft, in response to differential braking or
aerodynamic forces.
Centering: Usually, there will be an auto-wheel-centering mechanism,
before the nose wheel is retracted.
Nose wheel Steering: It is usually controlled with hydraulics, or done
with a manual tiller.
Nose wheel Shimmy  Airframe
- Due to the flexibility of tyre sidewalls, an unstable rapid
sinusoidal oscillations may occur in the nose wheel while
taxiing/takeoff.
- Shimmy is also an indication of a broken torque link.
- It is reduced by using a 'double nose wheel' or by using 'Mastrad
tyres' (tyre with a deep cut in between, making it 2 halves).
• Aquaplaning (Hydroplaning)  (See also: Anti-Skid Brakes)
- It is the phenomenon of the tyre slipping (and not rotating)
over the runway surface, on a thin film of water.
- Water exerts hydrodynamic pressure on all surfaces, including that
of a tyre rolling on a wet runway. This pressure 1 proportionally to
the square of tyre velocity.
- As tyre speed increases, the inertia of water to move away from
under the tyre increases and forms a wedge. When hydrodynamic
pressure equals tyre pressure, it lifts up & aquaplaning starts.
- Once started, it can continue to a much slower speed than the initial
aquaplaning speed.
- Anti-skid brakes prevent aquaplaning.
Types of Aquaplaning  (See also: Air Regs > Runway Contamination)
- Dynamic: Tyre is lifted off runway surface due to standing water.
- Viscus: Occurs due to a thin film of water over a smooth runway.
- Reverted Rubber: Heat created during braking causes rubber to
melt and traps a layer of steam under it, causing a skid.
Factors Affecting Aquaplaning Speed
- Tyre Pressure: 1 tyre pressure = 1 aquaplaning speed.
- Water Depth: 1 water depth = 1 aquaplaning tendency.
- Tread Design: Deeper tread = J aquaplaning tendency.
- Tyre Condition: New tyre has J aquaplaning tendency.
- Speed: 1 speed = 1 aquaplaning tendency. Aircraft is to be
landed at a speed < aquaplaning speed.

3 - 14
Flight Controls  (See also: Aerodynamics > Flight Controls)
• Manual Control: It consists of a cable & pulley system, transferring
pilot control inputs to control surfaces. It consists of:
- Primary Stop: To set the range of movement of a control surface.
- Secondary Stop: To limit the movement range if primary stop fails.
- Fair Leads: To keep Tension cable straight & clear of aircraft structure.
- Tension Cable: Transmits pilot control input to control surfaces.
- It provides positive action in both directions.
Airframe  - They also remove backlash & reverse play.
- It compensates for temperature variations.
Inspection/Checks of control system should include:
- Correct cable tension  - Temperature compensation.
- Safety & locking at the ends - Correct range of movement.
- Always duplicate inspection of controls by another person.
Advantages of Cable System:
- Light, good strength-weight ratio.
- Less prone to impact damage.
- Occupy less volume, less no. of joints.
- Easy to route through aircraft
Aerodynamic Assisted Controls: Tabs assist manual controls.
(See also: Aerodynamics > Flight Controls > Aerodynamic Balancing)
• Power Assisted Controls:
- In this, a certain portion of force that is required to move
the control surfaces is provided by the hydraulic system.
- Natural feel of controls (proportional to IAS2) is retained with pilot.
- Power assisted controls are reversible at high aerodynamic loads.
• Fully Powered Controls (Fly by Wire):
- In this system, all the force that is needed to move the
control surface is provided by hydraulics. Transducers
convert mechanical movements of the control column to electric
signals, which are sensed by a computer & gives appropriate
movements to control surfaces.
- Pitch: Controlled by electrical elevator & stabiliser control.
- Roll: Controlled by electrical ailerons & spoilers.
- Yaw: Controlled by a mechanical rudder, electrical yaw
damping & trim.
- A pilot has no feel of aerodynamic forces. An artificial 'Q' feel
(proportional to IAS2) needs to be generated for the Pilot to retain
feel of controls.
- Aerodynamic loads on control surfaces will not move the control
column in the cockpit. Thus, fully powered controls are Irreversible
Controls'.
- 3 Computers (for redundancy) are needed for Fly by Wire systems:
- 2x ELAC Elevator Aileron Computer to control ailerons,
elevators & stabilisers.
- 3x SEC Spoiler Elevator Computer to control upper wing
surfaces, standby elevator & stabiliser.
- 2x FAC Flight Augmentation Computer for electric rudder control.
===== [avh 0210]
3 - 15
Parts of Powered Controls
Hydraulic Actuator: They move the control surface.
Artificial Feel Units: In powered control, the pilot doesn't
feel any aerodynamic loads & may over-stress aircraft.
Artificial feel units prevent that.
Spring Feel: It is just a spring that provides a basic 'feel' to
the pilot. They are adequate at low speeds. They are not
proportional to aircraft forward speed or aerodynamic loads. A
pilot may over-stress the aircraft at high speeds/loads.
'Q' Feel: Pitot & static pressure is supplied to 2 ends of a piston,
which provides a 'feel' to the pilot proportional to aerodynamic
forces. This system needs a large cylinder to generate adequate
dynamic pressures & is connected in parallel to controls. A pilot
needs to overcome this pressure on his control column.
Hydraulic 'Q' Feel: Hydraulic dashpots connected to the 'Q' feel
cylinder supply the necessary 'feel'. It is a smaller system than
'Q' feel. The system is adjusted for mach no. compressibility for
high-speed flights.
Electric 'Q' Feel: Computer feeds resistance 'feel' to control column.
'g' Feel: It is a system that produces stick forces independent of
forward speed & proportional to the 'g' forces applied. It is used
in fighter aircraft, to provide feedback to the pilot regarding 'g'
forces. It uses bob-weights & springs. It suffers from inertia &
turbulence error.
Requirements of Powered Controls
Performance
- Controls should produce satisfactory handling characteristics
throughout the aircraft flight envelope.
- The system should have a sufficient range of movement &
power to accomplish the task.
- Inadequate hydraulic power causes 'Jack Stall, where servo-jacks
cannot overcome the aerodynamic forces on control surfaces.
Feedback
- There should be a feedback loop capable of comparing pilot
control surface deflection & actual control movements.
- As stick forces increase proportional to the forward speed, 'Q'
feel has to be artificially synthesised.
- Stall warning & stick shakers are necessary.
Accuracy: System should be very accurate.
Stability: System should hold the control surface position & should
not deviate due to system errors.
Irreversibility: Effects of buffeting, flutter also must be stopped.
Sensitivity: System should be sensitive with small pilot inputs.
Takeoff Configuration Warning: It should come ON when power-levers
at TOGA & any of the following takes place:
- Stabiliser trim is outside takeoff range;
- Leading edge/Trailing edge flaps are not in takeoff configuration;
- Speed brake lever is not in the down position;
- All doors not fully locked;
- Flight controls are not unlocked.
===== [avh 0211]
3 - 16
Air conditioning
Air Condition System in an Aircraft Regulates:
- Temperature within 18°C - 24°C;
- Humidity at 30%;
- Quantity: Airflow of 10 cubic ft per minute per crew member;
- Quality: Max 1: 20000 ppm of carbon monoxide.
• Parts of Air Condition System
- Bleed Air (HP/LP valves): Taps bleed air from the compressor.
Airframe  - Temperature Control Unit: Controls the air temperature.
- Heat Exchanger: It is used for pre-cooling of bleed air.
- Water Separator: It removes moisture from bleed air.
- Cold Air Unit (Compressor/Turbine): It cools the air.
- Cabin Air Distribution System: Ducting for cabin supply.
- RAM Air Valves: Supplies cabin air directly from the atmosphere.
- Humidifier: Needed at high altitudes, to add moisture back to air.
Types of Air Condition Systems
Turbo Compressor
- It is the most popular 'old system'. It is used when 'high-pressure
bleed air' is not available.
- Low-pressure bleed air is 'Ram-air pre-cooled' in a heat exchanger.
- Then a compressor (which is run by engine-turbine) increases its
pressure, and enters a turbine where it expands & 'work' is extracted.
This causes a pressure drop & air cools, converting kinetic energy
of air to mechanical energy, thus cooling the air.
- A water separator extracts moisture.
- Temperature control valve adjusts hot/cold air before it enters cabin.
Brake Turbine
- It is used where HP bleed air is available.
- HP bleed air is pre-cooled (by ram-air) & enters the turbine where it
expands & 'work' is extracted. This causes a pressure drop & air cools.
- A compressor attached to the turbine acts as a brake/retarding
force for the turbine.
- It is a lighter system and has better mass flow.
- But it cannot be used to cool air when aircraft is on the ground.
Turbo Fan
- It is a refinement of the 'Brake Turbine' system.
- In it, instead of instead of the driving the compressor, the turbine
drives a centrifugal fan that sucks air for the bleed air pre-cooler/
heat-exchanger. This system can be used on ground too, as it
doesn't need Ram-air.

===== [avh 0212]
3 - 17
Pressurisation
Introduction
- Fatigue life of an airframe depends on no. of pressurisation cycles.
- Smaller the cabin, the higher is the airflow needed (1.5 kg/min per
passenger, 50% fresh + 50% recirculated air).
- Fighter cockpit needs 5 kg/min (80% around pilot + 20% for de-mist).
• Pressurised Areas in an aircraft: cockpit, cabin, fwd & aft cargo holds.
• Unpressurised Areas: Radome, nose & main landing gear bay, centre
section torque box, tail cone.
Hyperbaric: Maintains ground-level pressure till a/c operating ceiling.
Isobaric: Maintains cabin pressure at 8000' altitude (passenger a/c).
Hypobaric: Maintains cabin pressure at 25000' altitude, to reduce
the effects of rapid decompression caused by damage (fighter a/c).
• Pressurisation System Control
- Instruments needed in the cockpit of a pressurised aircraft: cabin
altimeter, cabin VSI, cabin differential pressure gauge.
- 8000' cabin altitude is most efficient in reducing airframe hoop stress.
So, in a passenger aircraft, max cabin altitude is maintained at 8000'.
- Maximum permitted rate of change of cabin altitude is 1500 fpm.
- If cabin altitude increases, pressure differential reduces.
- An aural & visual warning comes ON if cabin altitude is > 10000'.
- Pressurisation is controlled by having a constant mass flow of air
entering the cabin & varying the discharge rate of air into atmosphere.
- Outflow Valve: Closing this valve reduces air discharge & increases
differential cabin pressure. This valve has a thrust recovery nozzle
to regain the lost thrust energy from cabin exhaust air, during cruise.
- Outward Relief Valve opens if this pressure differential is > +25 Psi.
- Inward Relief Valve opens if -ve pressure differential is sensed in cabin
by 0.5psi - 1psi (e.g., during rapid descend below cabin altitude).
- Inward & outward valves are duplicated & placed above aircraft
flotation line, so that water doesn't enter the cabin during ditching.
- Dump Valve: Manually operated for emergency cabin depressurisation.
- Blowout Valve: Fitted between passenger & cargo compartment,
to prevent an excessive pressure difference between these areas.
(e.g., cargo door opening in flight).
- Ditching Cocks: It is used to shut outflow valves during ditching.
• System Operation
- During taxi, 'GROUND/FLIGHT switch' is selected to FLIGHT. Aircraft
is pre-pressurised to a differential pressure of 0.1 Psi, to ensure that
the transition to pressured flight is gradual & no pressure surge is
experienced on rotation & no engine fumes ingress into the cabin.
- During climb, outflow valve automatically controls the rate of change
of cabin altitude in proportion to ROC (between 300 - 500 fpm ROC).
- During cruise, a constant pressure differential is maintained.
Inflow = Outflow. Outflow valve is normally partially open.
- Small a/c altitude changes (t500') will not change cabin pressure.
- During descent, similar to climb, cabin descends at 300-500 fpm.
- By touchdown, differential pressure is 0.1 Psi.
- On the ground, outflow valve is fully opened to equalise pressure.
===== [avh 0213]
3 - 18
Ice & Rain Protection
(See also: Meteorology > Icing)
• Introduction
- Ice protection equipment is mandatory for all aircraft expected to
operate in icing conditions.
- An aircraft with frost on the airframe may be unable to get airborne
or may even stall immediately after takeoff due to reduced CL.
- Anti-Ice: Prevents ice accumulation by application of heat or fluid.
- De-icing: In it, ice is allowed to build up prior to removal. Ice removal
Airframe  is done by heat/fluid application or is mechanically removed.
- External De-ice: De-ice fluid is sprayed on aircraft on the ground.
Type-ll de-ice fluid is thicker than Type-l & stays on longer, but it
needs to be heated to 60°C before spraying. While undergoing
external de-icing, aircraft APU can be running but bleed air must be
OFF, to stop toxic chemicals from entering the cabin.
Ice Detection Devices
Ice Detection Head (Uses accretion principle)
- Teddington Ice Detector: It is a small protrusion on the
airframe, on which ice accrete, which is visible from the cockpit.
- Smith's Ice Detector: It consists of a hollow tube with 4 holes
placed on the airframe. If icing blocks these holes, it changes
the air pressure inside, which is sensed.
Mechanical Ice Detector
- Napier Ice Detector: Icing is sensed by an electric motor & a
blade. If ice accretes b/w them, motor needs more torque to run.
- Rose-mount Ice Detector: Vibration frequency of a vibrating
rod fitted on an airframe change if ice accretes on it.
• Ice Protection Devices
Wing Leading-edge Mechanical Pneumatic De-ice
- Span-wise rubber boots are fitted on the leading edge of wings,
which are connected to engine bleed supply lines.
- When OFF, boots are kept deflated by a vacuum pump or by engine
compressor 'venturi suction' keeping them stuck to LE, reducing drag.
- When ON, boots inflate & deflate in a cycle & break away the
ice. Used air is then dumped into the atmosphere.
Propellor Electric Thermal De-ice
- De-ice boots are usually installed on the inner ⅓ of props.
- It draws a large amount of current. A timer mechanism ensures
only 1 propellor is de-iced at any 1 time to prevent overheating.
- Propellor de-ice is to be done only when the props are running.
Fluid De-ice: De-ice fluid reduces the freezing point of water.
- De-ice fluid from a storage tank is sprayed along the wing LE.
- For props, fluid is delivered by a 'slinger ring' & pipes.
- Aircraft speed has to be low for this method to be efficient.
Hot Bleed-air De-icing: Hot bleed-air or hot engine oil is circulated
through plumbing to de-ice engine inlets, LE, TE, flaps, slats, etc.
Cockpit Window Electric Thermal De-ice: Electric current is passed
through an inner conductive coating of the cockpit windshield. It is
heated slowly to prevent thermal shock, for strength against impact
damage and to increase elasticity.
===== [avh 0214]

Composite Materials
Introduction
- Composites are made by mixing a matrix (resin) with fibre. Matrix is
the binder that transfers all the loads onto the fibre.
- Composites save weight & give additional strength to the airframe.
- Composites have different properties in different material directions.
Types of Orientation of Fibres in a Composite:
- Unidirectional  Airframe
Multidirectional
- Multidirectional

- Woven

Types of Composites
- Fibre: It uses a fibre & a resin.
(e.g. GRP uses glass fibre,
carbon, boron and a resin).
- Laminar: It uses layers of materials, sandwiched between a matrix
(e.g. plywood).
- Particulate: Powder/particles are embedded in a matrix (e.g.
concrete).
- Hybrid: A combination of the above.
Advantages of Composites  Disadvantages
- They are weight saving.  - Absorption of moisture.
- Offer resistance to corrosion.  - Inferior resistance to lighting strike
- Durable & reliable.  - Thermal fatigue.
- Good friction & wear properties.  - Less impact resistance.
- Improved dent resistance.  - Higher cost than metals.
- Low thermal expansion.
- Directional tailoring/aero-elastic tailoring possible.
Aeroelastic Tailoring
- It is a procedure for using tailored composite structures in the
construction of an airframe.
- In this, a material of required strength & property can be designed
by appropriate fibre angular orientation in each layer, by which, the
material can be made to twist in the desired direction when they are
stretched or compressed.
- This eliminates problems of divergence in swept-wing aircraft.
- It also reduces CP movement & flutter in unswept/swept-wings.
===== [avh 0215]
3 - 20
Fuel
• Introduction
- Changing the aircraft fuel type affects engine 'specific gravity setting',
requiring fuel-flow adjustment.
- Boiling point of fuel reduces with increase in altitude.
- Compensated Capacitance Fuel quantity indicator: Shows
correct amount of fuel in tanks, irrespective of fuel density.
- Capacitor Type fuel gauge compensates for aircraft attitude changes.
Airframe  - Waxing: Process of solidifying of heavy hydrocarbons (paraffin
wax) within the fuel at low temperatures.
- Vapour Lock: With an increase in aircraft altitude, boiling point of
fuel reduces, causing vapour to form, which may block fuel pipelines.
- If fuel looks foggy, it means it is probably contaminated with water.
• Fuel Octane Rating: It indicates fuel resistance to knocking/detonation.
- There are 2 chemically pure fuels:
- Iso-Octane: Good combustion, no detonation tendency, rating 100.
- Normal Heptane: Detonates reality, rating O.
- A mix of these 2 fuels gives a system of comparing a typical fuel's
detonation properties. E.g., a fuel rating of 95 means its detonation
properties are similar to a mix of 95% Iso-octane and 5% Heptane.
Requirements of an Ideal Fuel See also: Engines > Pre-Ignition, Detonation)
- Good flow at all conditions.  - 1 Sulphur content.
- Low fire hazard.  - Easy engine starting.
- High calorific value.  - Non corrosive.
- Complete combustion in all conditions  - Good lubrication.
• Fuel Additives
- FSII: Fuel System Icing Inhibitor.
- HITEC: A type of lubricant.
- Static Dissipators: Eliminate static electricity hazards.
- Corrosion & fungal growth inhibitors.
Fuel Types
MOGAS Motor Gasoline (Petrol). It is highly volatile.
- Carburettor icing & vapour lock is possible with this fuel.
AVGAS 80: Aviation Gasoline.
- It is red in colour. 80 relates to its antiknock properties.
AVGAS 100: It is green in colour. 100 relates to antiknock properties.
AVGAS 100LL: It is blue in colour (Low Lead content).
Jet A1 AVTUR: Aviation Turbine Fuel. It is clear or pale straw in colour.
- It is kerosene, with a specific gravity of 0.8 at 15°C.
- It has a flash point of 38.7°C & waxing point of -50°C.
JET A: It has a waxing point of -40°C.
JET B AVTAG: Aviation Turbine Gasoline.
- It is 'wide-cut' kerosene at a specific gravity 0.77 at 15°C.
- It has a flashpoint of -20°C & a waxing point of -60°C.

3 - 21
Aircraft Fuel System
Introduction
Aircraft fuel system comprises of the fuel system from the fuel tanks to
the engine HP fuel pump.
• Parts of Aircraft Fuel System
- Fuel Tank Types:
- Internal: Tanks inside wings. They can be rigid or flexible tanks.
- External: Fuel stored in external tanks on wing/airframe pylons.  Airframe
- Vent System:
- It is used to vent excess fuel & to equalise atmospheric pressure
in the fuel tanks.
- It should have a minimum of 2% of tank volume.
- Booster Pumps:
- These are centrifugal LP pumps that are used to transfer fuel
from tanks to engine, or to jettison fuel.
- They prevent Vapour Lock & Cavitation of HP fuel pumps by an
ensuring adequate supply of fuel.
- Fuel pumps are placed at the bottom of fuel tanks to prevent
them from overheating.
- Feeder Tanks:
- Fuel in feeder tanks allow for gravity feeding of fuel to engines.
- Fuel Dump:
- It dumps fuel from fuel tanks in case of an aircraft emergency.
- Regulations specify that after the dump, aircraft should be able
to climb to 10000' & thereafter fly for 45 mins.
(See also: Air Regulations > Fuel Dumping Requirements)
- Cross Feed: It supplies fuel from any tank to any engine.
- Shutoff Valves: LP shutoff valve stops fuel at the firewall.
- Baffles: They dampen lateral waves of fuel in a tank.
- Fuel Quantity Transmitter: Transmits fuel quantity in the fuel tanks.
- Fuel Drain: To drain fuel from the tanks when aircraft on the ground.
- Pressure Relief Valve: Relieves excessive pressure in fuel lines.
- Fuel Filter: Filters fuel.
Q: Where does a mountain climber keep his plane?
A: In a cliff-hangar.

3 - 22
• Emergency Equipment
(See also: Air Regulations > Aircraft Equipment Requirements)
Emergency Equipment
First Aid Kit: 1 kit for 0-99 pax. 1 additional kit for every 100+ pax.
Loud Hailers: Minimum 1 is needed for all aircraft with a passenger
capacity 61 - 99. 2 needed if passengers > 99.
Torch: 1 torch is needed near each floor level exit & at crew stations,
with a serviceability indicator LED flashing every 4 seconds.
Life Jackets: Adequate no. of life jackets must be available for all
pax, if aircraft is operating 50 nm away from land.
Life Rafts: Adequate no. of life rafts must be available for all pax, if
aircraft is operating 120 mins or 400 nm away from land.
Life Saving Equipment (including food): Needed for all pax when
operating in remote areas (arctic/desert).
Break-in Marks: Mandatory for all aircraft with AUW > 3600 kg. A 3 cm
line is to be painted on exterior fuselage, to indicate cut-out areas.
Emergency Lighting: Aircraft with > 9 pax needs emergency lighting,
powered by essential Bus. It should last minimum 30 mins.
Crash Axe: 1 is needed for all aircraft with AUW > 5700 kg or pax > 9.
If pax > 200, 1 additional axe is to be placed near a/c rear section.
ELT: 1 per aircraft. 2 if pax > 19. One of them must be automatic,
with an 80 nm range & should work for 48 hrs.
Fire Extinguisher: Engine fire extinguisher agent is FREON.
At least 1 on flight deck. Cabin: Pax 7 to 30 - 1, 31 to 60 - 2, 61 to
200 - 3, 201 to 300 - 4, 301 to 400 - 5, 401 to 500 - 6, 501 to b - 1.
NOMEX gloves must be available in aircraft to assist in tire igning.
Toilet fire extinguisher is activated by high temperature in its vicinity.
Emergency Oxygen System
- Normal Mode: Supplied oxygen-air ratio increases with
aircraft altitude. At 34000' supply is 100% oxygen.
- Emergency Mode: 100% oxygen in a continuous flow, by positive
pressure, irrespective of aircraft altitude.
- Pressure Demand System: Each crew has a demand regulator.
- Continuous Flow System: No regulator. Just plug-in mask for supply.
- Oxygen masks should come down automatically when cabin
altitude > 14000'.
- Chemical generators in aircraft provide oxygen for 15 mins.
- Portable oxygen cylinders must be charged to 1800 Psi & should
last for 15 mins.
- To test the oxygen system, acid-free soap & distilled water is used.
- Graphite is used for the lubrication of threads of the oxygen system
components.
Smoke Detection: Smoke detectors must be fitted in the toilets, cargo
compartment & electric bays. Smoke sensing principles are:
- Light Detection: Sensed by the change in visible light due to smoke.
- Light Refraction: Refractivity of light changes in smoke.
- lonisation: Senses ionisation of air due to smoke.
- Change in Resistance of a semiconductor due to heat/smoke.
Fire Detection System
- Melting Link Detector: Old system. A fuse melts due to heat.
- Differential Expansion Detectors
- Continuous Fire Detectors: Increase in temperature causes more
current to flow in a conductor with 'negative coefficient of resistance.

===== [avh 0219]
4 - 3
Piston (Reciprocating) Engine
• Parts of a Piston Engine
- Cylinder: A chamber within which the piston moves. It is made of
aluminium alloy, to withstand temperatures upto 2000°C.
- Cylinder Head: Top end of the cylinder which houses inlet/exhaust
valves and the spark plug.
- Piston: It transmits combustion force of power stroke to crank shaft.
- Piston Rings: It makes the piston airtight within the cylinder.
- Connecting Rod: It converts reciprocal piston motion to rotary motion.
- Crank Shaft: Attached to connecting rod, to connect multiple cylinders.
- Crank Case: Houses crank shaft & engine oil (in wet sump system).
- Inlet/exhaust Valves: For charge intake & exhaust of burnt gases.
- Spark Plug: Provides spark for the ignition of the air-fuel mixture
- Camshaft: It opens & closes inlet/exhaust valves at the correct time.
• Definitions
- TDC Top Dead Centre: Topmost position of the piston in a cylinder.
- BDC Bottom Dead Centre: Bottom position of the piston in a cylinder.
Stroke: Movement of the piston from any Dead Centre to the other.
- Bore: Internal diameter of a cylinder.
- Swept Volume: Volume enclosed between TDC & BDC.
- Clearance Volume: Volume above piston when it is at TDC.
- Tidal Volume: Volume above piston when it is at BDC, i.e., SV + CV.
- Compression Ratio: (Clearance vol + Swept vol) / Clearance volume.
- Charge: Air-fuel mixture drawn into an engine cylinder.
- CHT Cylinder Head Temp: Temperature of the hottest cylinder.
- MAP Manifold Absolute Pressure: Pressure entering inlet manifold.
- Rated Power: Power at which engine can be operated for long periods.
- Rated Altitude: Altitude till which sea-level power can be maintained.
- IHP Indicated Horse Power: Power developed inside a cylinder.
- BHP Brake HP: Power delivered by engine, for useful work.
- THP Thrust HP: Power produced at the propeller.

• Strokes in a 4-Stroke Engine (Otto Cycle)
4 - 5
Intake Stroke (A-B): During intake stroke, charge is drawn into
the cylinder by the down-going piston. Charge temperature 1.
Compression Stroke (B-C): In this stroke, charge is compressed.
Charge pressure 1, temperature 1.
Combustion (C-D): At TDC, spark plug ignites & flame propagation
happens quickly. Max pressure occurs keeping volume constant
before the piston moves down. Hence called 'constant volume cycle'
Power/Expansion Stroke (D-E): In this, expansion of gases push the
piston. Pressure J, temperature I. At E, the exhaust valve opens.
Exhaust Stroke (E-A): In exhaust, piston expunges the spent gases.

- Air Cooled Engine: It is used low speed engines, where ram-air is

- Liquid Cooled Engine: In it, a coolant fluid/oil is circulated through
cylinder jackets to absorb heat. It is then sent to a radiator, where
air-baffles cools it. Faster the aircraft speed, better is the cooling.

Multi Cylinder Engines
- In a multi cylinder engine, if all the cylinders produce its power stroke
at the same time, it will cause excessive engine vibrations.
- So, in it, the sequence of power stroke of each cylinder is staggered,
so as to give a constant engine power output at all times.
- In 4 cylinder engine, the 1st power stroke is from the 1st cylinder,
thereafter 3rd, 4th & 2nd.

- J Efficiency. Only 28% fuel energy converted to power output.
- Low airspeeds due to propeller RMP limitations.

Gas Turbine Theory
• Introduction
- Gas turbine engine is essentially a heat engine', which uses air as the
fluid to produce thrust, as per Newton's 3rd law.
- Its working cycle is similar to a piston engine: induction, compression,
combustion & exhaust. But unlike in a piston engine, all these happen
simultaneously, and combustion happens at constant pressure. Hence it
is called a 'constant pressure cycle'.
- Advantages:
- It can deal with much larger amounts of air & energy compared
to a piston engine.
- It is rotational engine, hence, has smooth operation.
- It generates a continuous supply of power, unlike a piston engine
where 3 strokes absorb power & only 1 stroke produce power.
Ideal Gas Turbine Cycle  Assumptions
1-2 Frictionless adiabatic compression  - Air is an ideal fluid
2-3 Frictionless constant pressure heating  - Heating & heat rejection - Isobaric
3-4 Frictionless adiabatic expansion  - Compression/expansion - Adiabatic
4-1 Frictionless constant pressure heat rejection - Gas equation (PV/RT) is valid
- Exhaust is at atmospheric pressure
Actual Gas-Turbine Cycle (Brayton Cycle)
1-2' Adiabatic compression occurs with friction.
2'-3' Combustion involving pressure loss.
3'-4' Adiabatic expansion with friction.
4'-1 Rejection of heat at constant pressure.

- Although this 1 engine efficiency & power output, the limiting factor

Thus, the actual cycle efficiency is only about 50% of the ideal cycle.
- Greater the entropy (S), lesser the energy that can be extracted.

Turbojet Engine
• Introduction
- It was invented by Air Commodore Sir Frank Whittle, RAF, in 1930.
- Jet Engine imparts large acceleration to a small mass of air.
- Thrust results from pressure & momentum changes of gas stream
passing through the engine & reacting on its rotating components.
These forces are forward & backward. The amount by which forward
forces exceed backward forces is called 'rated thrust' of the engine.
- Thrust is maximum at the start of takeoff run. Thrust reduces as
aircraft forward speed increases because Thrust = M (V - VA).
However, thrust recovers at higher speeds due to ram-pressure
recovery' (increased ram air compression at inlet at higher speeds).
Momentum Thrust = M x (VJ - VA)  M = Air mass flow rate
Pressure Thrust = A x (Pc- Po)  V = Exhaust gas velocity  Engines
Additional thrust that is produced when  VA = aircraft velocity
nozzle becomes choked, thus producing  A = Nozzle area
a pressure difference across exit nozzle  Pc= Nozzle exit pressure
Total Thrust = M x (V - VA) + A x (Pc - Po)  Po= Atmosphere pressure
- Afterburners 1 thrust by adding fuel to exit gas, thereby increasing
exit gas velocity. Modern high bypass engines can 1 thrust with
afterburners by up to 80%. However, this thrust comes at extremely
high fuel consumption.
• Performance of Jet Engines
- Forward speed: As velocity of aircraft 1, (VJ-VA) J. Thus, thrust j. But
if speed > 500 kts, ram-air compression 1, mass flow † performance 1.
- Altitude: Altitude 1 = density l, temperature J, pressure J. Although
l temperature is favourable for engine performance, | in pressure at
high altitudes has a bigger -ve effect, thus performance j. Above
tropopause, temperature is constant, performance l even further.
- Temperature: Temperature 1 = density l, performance J.
- Density: Density 1 = performance 1.
- Piston engine is more affected by density than a jet engine.
Propulsive Efficiency of Jet Engines
- Thermal Efficiency (NTH)  Rate of 1 of KE
- Propulsive Efficiency (Np) = Rafe of fuel energy release
Propulsive power produced or  Work done on aircraft
Rate of 1 of KE & Gas  Work done on airflow + work waste in exhaust
- Overall Efficiency (No) = (NTH) x (Np) = Propulsive power produced
Fuel power consumed
Why flat rating?: At lower temperatures, too much thrust may be generated, and
pressure within the compressor may exceed beyond limits. Flat rating limits the
engine power generated, & increase engine life.

Turbofan Engine (Bypass Engine)
• Introduction
- This is a type of turbojet, in which only part of the airflow (core flow) is
passed into the combustion chamber by compressor. Remaining air
is compressed (to a lesser extent, as per fan pressure ratio) by a fan
placed ahead of the compressor & bypasses combustion chamber.
- This fan provides a cold jet of greater mass flow & at relatively lower
speeds directly into the hot exhaust jet. Thus, temperature l, total
mass flow t, propulsive efficiency of the engine at lower speeds 1,
and overall exhaust jet velocity is 1.
- In a turbofan engine, majority of thrust comes from this bypass air.
- Bypassed air is also used for cooling the combustion chamber.
- High-bypass Engine: Bypass airflow is directly vented to atmosphere.
Engines  - Low-bypass: Flow rejoins downstream of turbine, at the exhaust.
- Bypass Ratio = MFAN / MCORE (Cold stream / Core stream)
Low bypass = Ratio < 1.5 High bypass = Ratio > 1.5 Vc = Vel core
Thrust = MFAN X (VJB - VA) + MCORE (VJC - VA)  V. = Velocity jet
VA = Vel aircraft
VJB = Vel by-pass
How can we increase propulsive efficiency?
By reducing kinetic energy loss. KE = ½ MV2 or ½ M (VJE - VA)2.
To maintain the same thrust, we can 1 M (mass flow) & 1 exit velocity (VE).
So, a bypass engine is more efficient, where mass flow is high and exit
velocity of gases is low. The fan thus produces additional thrust without an
increase in fuel flow. Here we assume that the thermal efficiency is constant.
Total jet energy = (Thrust x aircraft speed) + lost KE
= (VJ - VA) X VA + ½ (VJ - VA)2
= VJVA - VAR + ½ V2 + ½ VAR - VJ VA
Derivation  = ½ VJ - ½ VAR  = ½ (VJ - VA) (VJ +VA)
Ratio of useful power = Thrust x a/c speed = (V. - VA) x VA = 2VA
(Propulsive efficiency)  Total power  ½ (VJ-VA) (Vs+VA) (Vs+VA)
• Advantages
- Turbofan has better takeoff performance & better SFC.
- It has better efficiency over turbojets at slow speeds. But at higher
speeds, increased engine frontal area creates additional drag.
- With increasing forward speed, turbofan thrust does not fall as
quickly as a turboprop.
- It has a 20% - 25% dB reduction in noise levels over turbojets.
- Turbofan engine compressors are less prone to damage by FOD
ingestion as most of the debris is sent out into the bypass duct.

Turboprop / Turboshaft Engine
• Introduction
- In a turboprop, energy is extracted from turbines to run propellers,
leaving less residual thrust at the nozzle, unlike a turbojet, which
only extracts sufficient energy to drive the compressor & remaining
goes out as thrust.
- Turboprop engine gives small acceleration to a large mass of air.
- It is more efficient than jet engines at low alt & at speeds < 350 kts,
as props waste less kinetic energy in its slipstream than jet exhaust.
- For a turboprop, maximum thrust is when the aircraft is stationary.
As aircraft forward 1, propellor AoA J, thereby thrust J.
- At higher speeds, prop-tip reaches 1.0 M & performance 1 further.  110 M & perfor usel sas energy
- Turboshaft engines are the same, except that all useful gas energy
is taken out to produce rotary shaft power (helicopter/hover-craft  Engines
engines). In these engines, exhaust thrust is negligible. These
engines can be mounted in any orientation on an airframe.
• Turboprop Performance
- Turboprop has higher propulsive efficiency than turbojet, till 350 kts.
- Turboprop has higher power to weight ratio & greater fatigue life.
- ESHP (Equivalent) = SHP (Propeller thrust) + Jet thrust (exhaust).
- Effect of Speed: Speed 1 = ram-compression 1 = mass flow 1 =
better SFC. But speed 1 = prop-efficiency l. Thus, net thrust
produced 1 at low speeds & J at higher speeds (> 350 kts).
- Effect of Attitude:
- Altitude † = density 1 = mass flow | = SHP J, thrust J.
- Also altitude 1 = temp | = density 1 = mass flow 1 = thrust T.
- So, as altitude 1, density effect is slightly offset, but overall thrust j.
• Types of Turboprop Engines  (See also: Turbines > Free Turbine)
Direct Drive Turbine: Simplest design. Turbines run compressor directly,
& surplus power is transmitted to props through a reduction gear.
Free Turbine: Engine acts as a gas generator to supply high energy gases
across a free turbine, which in turn is connected to a propeller shaft.
- It offers easy engine start due to the absence of any propeller drag.
- Shafts can maintain their optimum speed independently of propeller.
- Most turboshaft engines are free turbine engines.
Compound Engine: Two spool engine, with props connected to LP spool.
(See also: Compressor > Multi Spool)

Types of Engine Control
- Turboprop engines operate at high RPM for maximum efficiency.
- Any 1 in RPM = 1 pressure ratio across compressor & affects SFC.
- There are 3 types of engine control:
Integrated RPM & Fuel Control:
- Power lever adjustment increases propeller RPM. Power lever
also simultaneously increases fuel flow to match RPM.
- Propeller constant speed unit (CSU) adjusts propeller pitch to
absorb the extra power produced.
- It is suitable tor compound-turbine engines.
Direct Control of Fuel Flow (Alpha Mode)
- Power lever movement adjusts fuel flow only.
- † fuel flow = 1 RPM = 1 power at free turbine.
- Propeller RPM is maintained by CSU by increasing blade angle,
which produces extra thrust.
- It is suitable for free-turbine engines.
Direct Control of Blade Angle (Beta Mode)
- Power lever movement controls blade angle.
- Propeller speed governor adjusts fuel flow to maintain constant
Propeller RPM.
Prop Synchronising & Synchrophasing
Synchronising: Each rotating propeller creates its audible frequency,
which is proportional to its RPM. This frequency interferes with the
frequency of a nearby propeller. The sound is amplified if the props
run even at slightly different RPMs. These beat noises can be
eliminated by running all propellers at precisely the same RPM.
This is called synchronising the RPM.
Syncrophasing: Further noise reduction can be achieved by
syncrophasing. This is because most of the noise produced is due
to interactions between blades of adjacent propellers, which is max
when adjacent blade tips are directly opposite each other. Maintaining
an optimum angular difference (phase difference) between props
minimise vibration levels. Maintaining these correct phase difference
is called syncrophasing. Pickup heads placed on each propeller
measure & maintain the proper phase difference.

Intake
• An Ideal Intake Should:
- Provide the engine with the correct amount of air, at the right speed;
- Provide air at all operating mach no., altitudes & throttle settings;
- Evenly distribute air at the engine compressor face;
- Minimise external drag;
- Provide air with minimum pressure loss. But losses occur due to:
- Tendency of the flow to separate from the intake boundary wall;
- Friction in the duct.
- Provide initial air compression & assist compressor by 'Ram effect'.
Ram Effect
- Since mass/weight of air passing through the engine is proportional to
thrust, f intake pressure = 1 weight of air = 1 thrust of the engine.
- By a suitable design, it is possible to do this by compressing air at
the intake. This additional compression f with f in forward speed. At
1.0 M, ram-compression is almost equal to compressor compression.
Beyond 1.0 M, ram-compression is more than the compressor.
- Ram Pressure Recovery: When aircraft is on the ground & engines
are running, pressure at intake is below ambient pressure because
of the high air velocity of air through the intake. When aircraft
moves forward, pressure at inlet rises due to 'ram-effect'. Point at
which inlet pressure = ambient pressure is
known as ram-pressure recovery.
Subsonic Intake  Subsonic  Pitot Intake
- At a constant density below mach 1.0,
velocity 1 = static pressure J, temperature l.
- So, a subsonic pitot intake must capture the required airflow & deliver
it at the compressor face at the required speed by converting
dynamic pressure of airflow to static pressure using a divergent
duct, to l air velocity & 1 static pressure.
- Thick well-rounded intake lips prevent flow separation.
Critical Operation (Ao / A1 = 1): Intake delivers correct air amount to
the compressor. Critical operation should occur at cruising speed.
Subcritical Operation (Ao / A1 < 1):
- Engine requires less air than what intake
is delivering.
- Back-pressure is felt at intake, causing  Design speed
excess air to spill out.  Critical operation
- It is undesirable as it 1 drag forces.
Supercritical Operation (Ao / A1 > 1):
- Engine demands more air than what intake
is delivering. This suction can cause
boundary layer separation & air starvation.  High speed
Subcritical operation
- It is caused by low aircraft speed + high  Intake spilling

- This is overcome by using auxiliary intake
doors that open during high engine demands.

Supersonic Intake
- Supersonic inlet duct must operate in 3 speed zones: subsonic
transonic & supersonic; and deliver air at the compressor face at
0.5 M, with minimal loss of energy.
- This is achieved by slowing the air with a combination of shocks at
the intake:
- Normal Shockwave is 1 to airflow - more pressure loss.
- Oblique Shockwave is at an angle to airflow - less pressure loss.
- Problems with intake start when aircraft nears mach speeds. At
these speeds, shockwaves form, which, if not controlled, will induce
loss of pressure & airflow and cause 'Intake buzz'.
- Intake Buzz: Airflow instability caused by shockwave being rapidly
swallowed & expelled at the inlet of an intake.
Critical Operation: (Ao / A1 = 1)
Engines  - Shockwaves rests on intake lip. A1 - Intake Cross-section
Subcritical Operation: (Ao / A1 < 1)
- Engine requires less air than what intake is delivering.
- This will push shockwaves forward & spill air out of an intake.
- Severe sub-critical can cause 'intake buzz'.
Supercritical Operation (Ao / A1 = 1. It can never exceed 1)
- Engine demands more air than what intake is delivering.
- This suction causes normal shockwave to form inside the intake.
- This is preferable to subcritical operation since no shockwave
drag is generated. But it may cause some instability inside the
intake.

Types of Intakes Designs
Pitot Intake
- It is a simple & efficient design with a
single round intake in front of the aircraft.
- For supersonic speeds, it uses a single normal shock across the
lip. Mach no. of airflow is instantly dropped to < 1 by the shock.
- Rounded lips prevent boundary layer separation by 1 its MCRIT.
- It is best suited for aircraft speeds < 1.5M. However, at speeds >
2M, pressure recovery is very poor.
Side Intake
- There are 2 separate intakes for  Side Intake
2 separate engines/compressors.
- In this, fuselage boundary-layer (slow-
moving air) may enter the intake & may  Diverter
cause compressor stall. This air has to be bled away by using:
- Diverter: Intake border is placed a few centimetres away from
fuselage skin, using ramps & ducts to divert slow boundary layer.
- Fence: A fence prevents slow boundary layer from entering intake.
- Bleed: Boundary layer is bled away to a low-pressure region
using slots inside the intake.
Divided Intake
- In this, there are 2 inlets placed on both  Divided Intake  Sea Harrier
sides of the airframe for a single engine/
compressor.
- When aircraft yaws, loss of ram-pressure may occur on 1 side of
the aircraft causing uneven airflow distribution at the compressor.
External Compression Intake (refer to the diagram on the previous page)
- They are needed for aircraft operating at higher mach no.
- In this, one or more oblique shocks (weak) & one normal shock
is used to bring airspeed < 1M.
- 2 Shock Intake: Simplest construction. One oblique shock is
formed by a wedge surface, followed by one normal shock.
- 3 Shock Intake: 2 oblique shocks + 1 normal shock.
- Isentropic Intake: Multiple oblique shocks + 1 normal shock. It
is achieved by suitable curved compression surfaces.
Variable Geometry Intake
- Fixed geometric intakes although simple, only operate efficiently
at its 'design mach no'. At any other speed, if oblique shock is
not placed on the lip, subcritical or supercritical operation may
occur (shock angle depends on mach no). This is not desirable
for operating on a wide range of mach no. A variable geometry
intake adjusts shockwave to rest on the lip as per aircraft speed.
Variable Position Intake (Modern fighter aircraft):
- Face of intake can pivot, creating a favourable intake at high AoA.

Compressor
• Introduction
- A compressor is needed to compress air to a predetermined value
& pass it on to the combustion chamber. It works by 1 kinetic energy
of air by a rotor/impeller, then diffusing its energy into static pressure
rise by a stationary diffuser.
- 50% pressure rise occurs at the rotor, 50% at the stator.
- One stage of compressor comprises of 1 rotor + 1 stator.
- Mass flow & pressure 1 depends on speed & diameter of rotor.
- Rotor (Impeller)
- Turbine rotates an rotor/impeller at high speed & sucks in air.
- 1 in mass flow can be obtained by 1 impeller diameter but rotati-
onal velocity has to be j to maintain impeller tip speed < 500 m/s.
Engines  - Resonance & vibration may occur if the rotor tip is too close to
the stator. It will cause aerodynamic buffeting & unsteady flow.
- Shrouding of blade tip is done to minimise compressor vibration.
- Stator (Diffuser)
- Guide vanes in a diffuser are divergent & tangential to impeller. it
converts kinetic energy (air velocity) into pressure energy.
- This passage between diffuser is designed in such a way that
the air entering the combustion chamber has the correct pressure.
- At a stator, air velocity J, pressure 1, temperature t.
- A greater pressure rise is obtained by compressing cold air.
- Compressor blades are fit loose in its hub to cater for expansion/
centrifugal forces.
- They are twisted from root to tip to maintain correct AoA along its
entire length.
- Compressor idling speed of an uncompensated engine will † with †
in temperature.
- EPR Engine Pressure Ratio: Ratio of LP Turbine outlet pressure
LP compressor inlet pressure
Centrifugal Compressor
- In a centrifugal compressor, air leaves impeller tip 1 to the intake
direction at a higher velocity & is sent to a diffuser.
- 1:4 compression ratio achieved for 1 stage centrifugal compressor.

• Axial Flow Compressors
- In an axial flow compressor, air leaves impeller tip parallel to the
intake direction at a higher velocity & is sent to a diffuser.
- Rotors in a compressor impart kinetic energy to the air.
- Stator (divergent passage between consecutive rotors) converts
kinetic energy into pressure energy & guides air to the next stage,
keeping mean air velocity constant.
- IGV Inlet Guide Vanes directs incoming air onto 1st stage rotor.
- OGV Outlet Guide Vanes are the last set of vanes. It directs air
into the combustion chamber.

- One stage of compressor comprises of 1 rotor + 1 stator.
- At each stage, pressure ratio increases 1:1.2. Any higher pressure
rise will cause air to break away from compressor walls & flow back.
Final pressure is result of multiplying pressure rise at each stage.
- Cross-section area of compressor stages is progressively reduced to
maintain a constant volume of air with increasing density/pressure
as each stage is working with an increasing pressure gradient. Net
effect is constant mean velocity & small smooth f in pressure energy.
- Multi-spool Engines: It is advantageous to split the compressor
into pressure sections, powered by co-axial shafts & different set of
turbines. e.g., turbofan engines where LP compressor handles large
quantities of air and passes on a proportionate amount of air to the
HP compressor & remaining to bypass.
- Average compressor ratio for a single spool compressor is 10:1 &
for a multi-spool compressor is 25:1.
