4 - 20
• Compressor Stall
- A compressor is designed to operate between certain limits
of RPM, pressure ratio & mass flow. Any operation outside
these limits may breakdown flow at compressor blades.
- Compressor stall happens the same way like an aerofoil stall. AoA
of relative airflow falling onto a compressor blade increases to a
point where flow breaks away.
- At constant RPM, J in mass flow causes I VA (axial velocity), which
causes AoA to t. Beyond critical AoA, flow breaks away & blade stalls.
- This unstable air now 1 AoA on adjacent blades causing partial flow
breakdown. This stall cell may either move around or may increase
to affect the whole compressor stage, or may dissipate.
- Stall Indication
- Rapid rise in JPT & fall in engine RPM.
- Stall will be accompanied by muffled rumbling noises or abrupt
Engines  explosions & vibrations from the engine.
- Causes of Stall
- Distorted intake, e.g., due to bird hit;
- Sudden aircraft manoeuvres;
- Damaged compressor/turbine;
- Flying through exhaust of another aircraft, e.g. close formation;
- Excessive fuel flow during abrupt engine acceleration;
- Lean fuel-air mixture during abrupt deceleration.
• Compressor Surge
- Surge happens when all compressor blades stall. It is a complete
breakdown of flow through compressor, with loud bangs.
- Slam opening throttle where acceleration control does not adequately
restrict fuel also may cause a surge.
- If a surge happens, slowly close the throttle of the affected engine,
adjust aircraft attitude to un-stall the engine, slowly re-open throttle.
Design Point: It is the particular engine RPM at which mass
flow & pressure ratio gives the best efficiency for a compressor.
Operating Line: A line joining various designs points.
Surge Point: It is the combination of RPM & pressure ratio at which
the compressor stalls. It is caused by a reduction of mass flow due
to a distorted Intake, aircraft manoeuvre, etc.
Surge Line: It is a line joining the various airflow & pressure ratios for
different surge points. For high-efficiency engines, operating line is
very close to the surge line. The 'bend' in a surge line is also called
a 'knee' & is typical in high-pressure ratio engines.
Surge Margin: Area between operating line and surge line.

- Airflow in front of a compressor depends on flow resistance.

Combustion Chamber
• Introduction
- 15:1 air:fuel ratio gives the greatest heat release during combustion.
- In a combustion chamber, the velocity of flame propagation (rate of
speed of flame) is low, ~ 2 to 4 m/s. It varies with the mixture ratio.
- Swirl Vanes: Used to slow down air, to prevent an engine flameout.
- Although combustion is at constant pressure, there is a pressure
loss of 3% - 8% due to turbulence & mixing in combustion chamber.
- Maximum permitted temperature in combustion chamber is limited
by turbine construction material & TET (Turbine Entry Temperature).
- Igniters are used to start engine ignition.
- Drain Tubes are used to drain unburnt fuel in case of a false start.
It is usually kept closed by chamber gas pressure.
Engines  - Primary Air: 20% of compressor air is mixed with fuel and is burnt.
- Secondary Air: 20% of air is introduced separately & is mixed with
primary air flowing through swirl vanes to stabilise & anchor flame.
- Tertiary Air: 60% of air is progressively introduced to cool the
combustion chamber & to dilute gases. It also cools chamber walls.

• Types of Combustion Chambers
Multiple: Multiple individual chambers placed around the engine.
- Chambers are ted by individual ducts from a compressor.
- They are interconnected to equalise delivery pressure.
Cannular/Tubo Annular:
- Although it has individual flame tubes displaced radially around
the engine, it doesn't have an individual air casing for each tube.
- This maintains close control of airflow in the combustion chamber.
- It is weight saving & has ease of construction.
Annular: Uses the whole area between compressor & turbine.
- Advantages: Has 75% less engine length than the other 2 types.
- Has less flame tube area & thus 15% less cooling air is needed.
- Combustion efficiency 1, no unburnt fuel, pollution ..
- It is a structural member of the engine.
- It has even gas distribution, no flame propagation problems.
- Simple to manufacture and is lightweight.
- Disadvantages: Difficult to develop/research/design/replace.
- Uneven thermal stress in the chamber when heated.
- Poor control of gas flow & burning.

Burners: They are used to introduce fuel into the combustion chamber in a
state where it can burn efficiently at all operating conditions, altitudes
& temperatures. It is of 2 types: Atomisers, Vaporisers.
1. Atomisers: They create a highly turbulent flow at their nozzle. The fuel
spray disintegrates into minute droplets of 20-200 microns, thus
provides a large surface area for burning. They are of different types:
Simplex Burner: Old type of burner.
- Fuel is forced through tangential holes into swirl chambers before
being sprayed out of its orifice.
- A shroud of air through peripheral holes provides 2 functions:
prevents carbon formation & assists in atomisation.
- Disadvantage: Fuel flow is directly proportional to 'square of
the product of nozzle areas' & 'square root of the pressure
difference across orifice.
Duplex Burner: It has 2 independent orifices, 1 big, 1 small.
- Small orifice is operated at low pressure, large one at high pressure.
- Duplex burners are more efficient at a wide range of operations.
Spray Nozzle: It mixes a portion of primary air with injected fuel.
- Thus, local concentration of air-fuel mixture is avoided.
- It reduces carbon formation & smoke.
Spill Type Burner: It is a simplex burner with an additional passage in
the swirl chamber to spill away excess fuel.
- Thus it is possible to supply fuel at high pressure to the swirl
chamber continuously. As fuel flow rate reduces with high altitude,
excess fuel can be spilt away.
- This ensures efficient atomisation at all times.
Lubbock Burner: It consists of a rod with a lot of tangential holes.
- As fuel pressure f, it acts against a piston which exposes more
holes through which fuel can pass into the swirl chamber.
- Disadvantage: Piston may stick due to impurities in the fuel.
2. Vaporisers: In this system, primary air is fed into a vaporising
chamber, mixes with fuel and then goes into the combustion chamber.
- Advantages: Can provide a wide range of operations;
- Provides complete combustion, less smoke produced;
- System does not depend on fuel pressure;
- Vaporisers are located behind the flame. Thus, combustion zone
is shorter (flame is stabilised before the combustion chamber).
- Disadvantage: Starting system needs spray nozzles with ignitor
plugs.

4 - 24
Requirements of an Ideal Combustion Chamber
Reliability: It has to withstand high temperatures/stress/vibration.
High Rate of Heat Release in a Small Area
- High combustion chamber pressure will f rate of heat release.
- Ignition lag has to be minimised.
- Dead space must be minimum (area near chamber walls where
temperatures are low).
High Combustion Efficiency
- Combustion efficiency is the % of chemical energy in the fuel
that has been converted into heat during combustion.
- Complete combustion will convert all carbon into CO2. Incomplete
combustion creates CO (Carbon Monoxide).
Flame Stabilisation: Flame instability will lead to flame-out.
Combustion Stability: There is a weak & a rich mixture limit for any
combustion chamber, beyond which the flame will be extinguished.
Engines  - Flame extinction is most likely when gliding at idle power
settings: high airflow & low fuel flow.
- Velocity of flame propagation is low; ~2-4 m/s & varies with
mixture ratio. But the speed of airflow through the chamber is
almost 10 times that speed. Thus a sheltered region for
recirculation of low-velocity air must be provided.
Even Distribution of TET Turbine Entry Temperature
- Max temperature in combustion chamber is limited by TET, due
to limitations of stress & creep characteristics of blade material.
- Poor temperature distribution across turbine face may cause hot
spots, reduce blade clearance & reduce turbine blade life.
Minimum Carbon Formation
- Carbon formation is caused due to an over-rich mixture in the
combustion chamber during conditions of low turbulence,
insufficient atomising & mixing. It increases air pollution & is also
a reason for visible detection of a fighter aircraft. It is of 2 types:
- Chamber Blocking: Hard coke build up in combustion chamber.
- Soot Formation, which is ejected through exhaust smoke.
Minimum Pressure Loss
- Turbine engine operates on a constant pressure cycle & any
change in pressure during combustion will result in a drop in
thermal efficiency.
- Hot Loss: (non-isentropic process)
- When heat is added to a constant area, total pressure drops.
This is called 'fundamental loss due to heat addition'.
- It is a function of combustion system inlet mach no & temp ratio.
- Hot losses are low compared to cold losses.
- Cold Loss:
- They are losses due to friction & mixing and is proportional to
gas velocity from inlet to combustion chamber.
- It occurs due to skin friction at various cooling holes & baffles.
- But some amount of pressure loss due to turbulence is
required for flame stabilisation & burning.

Turbine
• Introduction
- Turbine is a rotating assembly that converts kinetic energy &
pressure energy of combustion gases into mechanical energy.
- Power absorbed by the turbine drives the compressor.
- LP turbine drives LP compressor; HP turbine drives HP compressor.
- Large centrifugal stress exist on turbines due to high rotational speeds.
- Diameter of each turbine stage increases rearward to control gas
velocity as the gas expands into a larger area.
- In a turbine, gas velocity initially 1 then l, pressure l, temperature l.
- Usually, TET is up to 1700°C & stage temperature drop is ~ 200°C.
- Turbine blades are twisted from root to tip so that exhaust gas
does equal work on its entire length.
- Turbine blades are fitted to its hub by a loose 'fir tree' root. It is
made a 'tight fit' by the centrifugal force when the turbine rotates.
- Shrouds on top & bottom of a turbine form a smooth passage for
airflow. It avoids tip leakage, increases rigidity.
- Losses: At a turbine, around 8% pressure loss & 3.5% aerodynamic
loss occurs. 1.5% pressure loss occurs at NGV.
- EGT Exhaust Gas Temperature: It is the temperature measured
by parallel thermocouples, at the LP turbine outlet.
NGV Nose Guide Vane
- 1 turbine stage = 1 NGV + 1 turbine.
- NGVs are used to improve efficiency, J losses & 1 vibration.
- NGVs have an aerofoil shape & convergent passage to convert
pressure energy into kinetic energy. Pressure drop occurs at NGV.
- In a turbine, gases expand & increase in velocity. Thus NGVs
operate under choked conditions.
- NGV is also subject to temperature & stress fluctuations caused by
uneven flow distribution from the combustion chamber.
• Turbine Construction: On a blade root, faster air acts better as 'impulse'
& tip works better as 'reaction', with a smooth transition in between.
Impulse Turbine
- NGV are convergent and accelerates airflow onto the turbine.
- Airflow hits turbine blades & changes direction, turning the blade.
- Principle similar to a water wheel.  Impulse Turbine  Reaction Turbine
- It is used in starter turbines & APUs.

===== [avh 0242]
4 - 26
• Types of Turbine Installations
- Single-spool: Turbine connected to compressor directly.
- Multi-spool: Used for engines with more than 1 compressor. Each
turbine runs its corresponding compressor.
- Direct Coupled: Turbine shaft extends beyond compressor to run
propellers directly as well.
- Free Turbine: A free turbine is not connected to any compressor. It
is generally used in turboshaft engines.
Creep: Permanent elongation of blade due to high temp & tensile loading.
- A creep curve is plotted against time, when a given strain is
maintained at a fixed temperature.
- A small value of creep is allowed to keep optimum tip clearances.
Stage of Creep:
- Primary Stage: Relative rapid expansions, but at a decreasing rate.
- Secondary Stage: Creep expands at a constant rate.
Engines  - Tertiary Stage: Rate of expansion accelerates, leading to fracture.
- Primary stage is of main interest as it forms a part of the total
extension reached in a particular time.
Turbine Blade Cooling
- Convection Cooling: It is done by supplying cool air through
longitudinal holes emerging from hollow blade sections.
- Film Cooling: It is done by passing a thin film of air above the blades.
It is more effective than convection cooling, but manufacturing it is
expensive. Thus, it is only done on a portion of the blade, on leading
edge & trailing edge.
Turbine Disc (Hub) Cooling
- Disc is heated up due to radiation & heat conduction from blades.
- HP air from compressor is used to cool the front face of turbine disc.
- Rear face of the disc is protected by exhaust cone & some bleed air.
- HP air is also used to pressurise the seal between NGV shroud &
turbine disc, to prevent hot gas leakage.
- Cooling airflow will also pressurise the space around the shaft to
prevent high-temperature gases from escaping.
Turbine Faults
- Loss of Tip Clearance: Due to high temp, creep & bearing wear,
metal expands & clearance b/w shroud & turbine blade tip reduces.
- Buckling/Cracking/Distortion: They are caused by the hotspots
that form on turbines due to faulty blade cooling or cracking of NGVs.
- FOD: Turbines may be damaged by breakaway pieces of combustion
liner/carbon pieces.
- Turbine Blade Containment: Turbine blades that detach from the
disc have a destructive force and may damage engine & fuel tanks.
Requirements of Turbine Blades
- High strength  - Must handle high rotor RPM
- Good creep resistance  - Less turbine weight & size
- Resistance to thermal shock - Handle high turbine entry temperature
- Resistance to corrosion  - Handle high outlet temp & velocity
- Economic to manufacture  - High power output

Exhaust
• Introduction
- In a turbojet engine, exhaust gases must exit in the correct direction
& at optimum velocity.
- In a turboprop, temperature & back-pressure at the turbine is
controlled by the exhaust.
- Exhaust temperatures are generally 550°C - 850°C.
- Afterburner increases exhaust temperature up to 1500°C.
Components of Exhaust  It may also include
- Exhaust cone  - Thrust reversal
- Jet pipe  - Noise suppression parts
- Propelling nozzle  - Nozzle vectoring
1. Exhaust Cone  Engines
- It creates an increasing 'X-section' of jet pipe. Thus a divergent duct
is created, thereby, decelerating airflow & reduces pressure losses.
- It also protects rear surface of the turbine disc from overheating.
• 2. Jet Pipe
- Conveys exhaust gases from exhaust cone to propelling nozzle.
- In a bypass engine, bypassed air is also mixed here.
- Jet pipes are manufactured from heat resistant alloys.
- They are double-walled & has a gap between them. Air is passed
through it, to cool it.
3. Propelling Nozzle: They are of 3 types:
Convergent Nozzle
- Velocity of exhaust gas should ideally be < .5M to limit turbulence.
- Convergent nozzle accelerates the gas flow until 1M. At this
speed, the nozzle is said to be choked. (See also: Chocking)
- Jet speed can be further accelerated in a convergent nozzle by
increasing gas temp, i.e., after burning, thus increasing LSS.
- Gas exit pressure is usually more than atmospheric pressure
while exiting from the nozzle. This is undesirable because that
gas energy has exited the nozzle without acting on it. This
phenomenon is called under expansion loss. Thrust is lost.
Convergent Divergent Nozzle
- Adding an additional divergent section makes it possible to reduce
exit pressure to atmospheric pressure, thus avoid expansion loss.
- Reduced pressure also accelerates gases beyond LSS, thus,
momentum 1, thrust 1.
- But this will only operate optimally over a particular pressure
ratio, e.g., rockets. Operation outside design speed causes
severe over expansion - pressure less than atmospheric
pressure. This causes shockwaves inside a divergent duct.
- Thus, for practical reasons, aircraft will have variable geometry
nozzles.

Variable Geometry Nozzle: Design Types:
- Ejector Nozzle: It is an old nozzle design, when metallurgy was
not so advanced. It has no moving parts, & has f weight penalty.
- In it, a fixed primary nozzle is surrounded by a shroud, whose
area matches to that required when 'full thrust' is applied at
maximum speed.
- At low speeds, secondary air is supplied to secondary nozzle,
to control (reduce) the effective secondary nozzle area.
- Plug Nozzle: A plug is moved in & out to adjust nozzle diameter
from a convergent to high-area-ratio (Con-Di).
- Disadvantage: Reheat system cannot be accommodated,
since the plug is heavy & will have overheating problems.
- Advanced Variable Geometry Nozzle: A new design, made
with titanium honeycomb. Nozzle area physically changes.

- After-burner operations: Use of afterburner causes gas expansion in
the jet pipe & 1 static pressure. But this may cause a surge. Thus,
variable geometry nozzle is opened when after-burner is lit.
- Surge Control: Varying nozzle area also allows compressor
pressure ratio to be controlled, to avoid a surge.
- Noise Reduction: On high bypass engines, most of the noise
comes from LP fan. If nozzle area is J, turbine pressure will !, LP

- Taxiing: Nozzle is opened to max thereby reducing thrust for taxi.
- Thrust Vectoring: Nozzle exit direction can be varied up to 20°.

- Improved manoeuvrability in the air

- At a nozzle, Venturi-effect accelerates airmass flow. As pressure
differential increases, mass flow increases turther.
- When speed of mass flow reaches 1M, pressure waves cannot
transmit pressure difference information between both sides of the
nozzle anymore & thus, mass flow remains at 1M.
- This condition is called 'choked nozzle'.

Thrust Reversal
Requirements of Thrust Reverser
- Adequate amount of reverse thrust should be obtainable.
- Reverser should not affect normal working of the engine.
- Reverser should not cause debris/hot air into the intake.
- Discharged gases should not cause vibration & heating on a/c parts.
- Must be a non fire hazard, should not fall on lubrication/hydraulic system.
- Weight & complexity must be minimum.
- Safety: accidental reverse selection should be impossible.
- Failure in reversal system should not accidentally operate reverser.
- System should be fail-safe.
• Types of Thrust Reverser
Clamshell Door Type
- A clamshell door is stowed around inside of jet pipe, forming a
part of the inner wall. When operated, it rotates to deflect gas
forward through ducts that were previously covered.
Bucket Type
- Buckets fitted on jet pipe deflects outgoing gases forward.
- A pneumatic motor deploys these buckets.
Cold Stream Recovery
- Majority of thrust from high-bypass engines are produced by the
bypass air & that is deflected.
- This air is relatively cool; thus, it is called a cold stream reverser.
Reverse Pitch Propeller
- Provides reverse thrust by varying the blade angle of propellers.
- On the ground, this can also be used to taxi the aircraft in reverse.

4 - 30
Thrust Augmentation
Introduction
- Thrust of engine = M (V - VA). If speed of exhaust gas 1 = Thrust t.
- But exhaust can never exceed the speed of sound (nozzle choked).
- However more speed can be achieved by increasing the LSS, by
increasing air temperature, which is done by adding fuel in the jet
pipe (re-heat). Thus, if the speed of exhaust gases f = Thrust t.
- This provides a temporary 1 in thrust during takeoff & combat.
- Reheat is usually activated at 100% engine RPM.
- SFC: After-burning † SFC because an increase in temperature
increases the velocity of jet, and thus, propulsive efficiency reduces.
- But as mach no. 1, SFC J, and at M2.5, after-burning is efficient.
Afterburner Control
Engines  Pilot Controls Nozzle Area
- Nozzle control & re-heat is effected through pilot's throttle lever
movement ahead of maximum RPM position.
- As re-heat is applied, pressure ratio across compressor will t.
Thus, mass flow J, moving the operating point closer to surge line.
This is unacceptable & is avoided by the increasing nozzle area.
- As nozzle area 1, fuel flow is increased. Fuel flow is adjusted to
maintain a constant pressure ratio. Thus engine is un-affected.
- This system gives fast response.
Pilot Control of Fuel Flow
- Moving throttle ahead of max RPM position f fuel flow, causing a
sudden rise in jet pipe pressure which alters the engine pressure
ratio. This is sensed by PRCU (Pressure Ratio Control Unit) & it
1 nozzle area.
- When after-burning is completed, nozzle area returns to normal.
- This system has a slow response, but is more efficient.
Types of Afterburner Ignition Systems
Catalytic Ignition:
- A platinum/rhodium rod is placed in the exhaust & fuel is sprayed
onto it. A chemical reaction lowers flashpoint of the fuel and
spontaneous combustion occurs.
- This system is reliable, but slow.
Hotshot Ignition:
- It has one or two fuel injectors. One is placed inside combustion
chamber; other is in exhaust unit.
- A streak of flame initiated from the fuel injector in the combustion
chamber increases in length & flows into the exhaust unit, where
it ignites the air-fuel mixture.
- In this system, the turbine is not over-heated because:
- This hot streak has low energy;
- Some fuel is vaporised during this process, reducing temp;
- It is only used for a short time duration.
Spark Ignition: A spark ignites afterburner fuel.
- When the flame stabilises, ignition spark is stopped.
- It is, however, less reliable than catalytic ignition.
===== [avh 0247]
4 - 31
• Turbofan After-burning
- Turbofan after-burning is much more efficient than turbojet after-
burning because turbofan after-burner also receives pure bypass-
air, which contains more oxygen.
- Thus more fuel can be added to achieve the correct stoichiometric
ratio.
- Up to 50% thrust augmentation is achieved.
- Types of Turbofan After-burning:
- Gas-generator After-burning: Only the hot gas stream is after-
burned.
- Mixed Stream After-burning: Both hot & cold streams are
mixed & are re-heated in a common after-burner. Pressure of
both streams should be equal to avoid mixing pressure loss.
- Hot/Cold Stream After-burning: Both streams are after-burned
separately.
Engines
• Water Injection After-burning
- Thrust depends on mass flow. As air density 1, thrust 1. But density
| with 1 in altitude and † in temperature.
- Water injection into the system increases mass flow & thrust can be
restored up to 30%.
- Water should be as pure as possible to reduce scaling.
- Pure alcohol may be added to water as an anti-freeze. Alcohol
burning will add some heat back into the mixture to compensate for
heat loss due to water evaporation.
- Types of Water Injection After-burning:
- Compressor Inlet Injection:
- Water is injected into the diffuser case of the engine.
- Evaporation of injected liquid extracts heat from inlet air; thus
temperature is reduced.
- Thus compressor pressure ratio 1, mass flow f, exhaust
nozzle pressure ratio 1.
- Thrust 1 by up to 25%.
- Combustion Chamber Ignition:
- It is generally used in axial-flow turbofan engines.
- Water is directly injected into the combustion chamber.
- Mass flow & pressure through the turbine 1 relative to the
compressor.
- This causes exhaust temperature l, jet pipe pressure 1, thus
thrust 1.

4 - 32
Auxiliary Power Unit
• Introduction
- It is a small gas-turbine engine, generally fitted in the tail of aircraft.
- APU is started by battery power.
- APU is usually a 'free turbine'.
- It cannot be paralleled with other power supplies and can be used
only when there is no other source feeding the bus-bar.
• APU can provide
- Air-conditioning on the ground.
- Air for engine starting.
- Electrical power to aircraft on the ground.
- Emergency power supply in air.
- Emergency hydraulic power.
Engines
Ignition/Start System
• High Energy Ignition Systems
- They are used for starting engines & for engine re-light during a
flameout.
- They are high-volt, high-current systems, with an output of 12 Joules.
• Low Energy Ignition Systems
- They are used while flying through precipitation, to prevent engine
flameout. It has an output of 6 Joules.
• Problems During Engine Start
Hot Start
- It occurs when EGT exceeds temperature limits during start.
- It is caused by excessive fuel flow during start, due to:
- Presence of residual fuel in combustion chamber from
previous shutdown; or
- Tailwind during start; or
- Residual heat from a quick shutdown & restart.
- If EGT exceeds by even 1°C beyond prescribed limits, the
engine is deemed unserviceable and must be serviced.
Hung Start
- It occurs when ignition starts, but the engine does not reach self
sustaining RPM.
- It is caused by a faulty starter or low battery voltage during start.
- It is not caused by faulty igniters.
- Indications: High EGT, idle fuel flow, low RPM.
Wet Start
- During start, fuel flow starts & engine RPM reaches max starter
RPM, but EGT does not rise.
- It is caused due to a faulty igniter.
- A dry-start is required before the next start, to drain fuel.

Engine Fuel System
(HP Pump to Engine)
• Parts of Engine Fuel System
- HP Pump: Raises fuel pressure to ensure efficient burner operation.
- Fuel Flow Meter: Placed between HP shutoff valve & fuel nozzle.
- FCU Fuel Control Unit: Regulates fuel flow.
- Temperature Limiter: Limits max temp by controlling pump output.
- Power Limiter: They are sensors that prevent engine over-
stressing due to excess compressor output at high-speed low-
altitude' flights, by varying fuel pump rate.
- Drain Valves: They are used to drain fuel from the combustion
chamber after a wet start. These drain valves are generally kept in
closed position by combustion chamber pressure operated NRV.
. - Engine Acceleration Control:  Engines
- OSG Over Speed Governor: It acts as a fuel bleed valve when
maximum engine RPM is reached.
- BPCU Barometric Pressure Control Unit: As altitude f,
density J. Thus mass flow through the engine J. BPCU
maintains correct air-fuel ratio by reducing the fuel flow.
- MBPU Minimum Burner Pressure Unit: As altitude 1, density
1, mass flow through engine . To maintain correct air-fuel ratio,
BPCU reduces fuel flow. But that may cause flame extinction
due to lean mixture on closing throttle. So MBPC eliminates this
possibility by maintaining a minimum fuel pressure for
satisfactory operation. However, this causes idling RPM to f.
Requirements of an Engine Fuel System
- Engine RPM & fuel flow should be constant at pilot selected value.
- No flame extinction should occur during:
- Acceleration: No surge, overheating or rich mixture flame extinction.
- Deceleration: No lean mixture extinction flame extinction.
- It should increase idling RPM as aircraft altitude increase.
- It should assist in easy engine starting.
- It should be safe when the engine is overloaded.
Types of Engine Fuel Systems
Open Loop Fuel System: It maintains constant engine RPM for a
particular throttle position. It has no feedback.
Closed Loop Fuel System: It maintains engine RPM after cross-
checking against the desired RPM. It is error corrected.
Pressure Controlled Fuel System
- Pressure in the fuel line proportional to aircraft altitude. This is
achieved by a variable stroke pump.
- Pump delivers constant pressure at a given ambient condition
regardless of throttle position.
- Fuel pressure only changes with altitude/speed/atmospheric
conditions.
Flow Controlled Fuel System
- Fuel flow is controlled by throttle posn by a variable stroke pump.
- Additional orifices sense pressure drop & control burner pressure.
- Hence life of this system is more than pressure controlled system.

Lubrication
• Introduction
- Lubrication system lubricates, cools & cleans engine & bearings.
- Oil is also used for propeller pitch control & torque indication.
- Synthetic oil is preferred since it can handle high temperatures better.
- Unlike piston engine, turbojet engine has high oil consumption. So
oil is not replaced, just periodically added, to top-up the oil tank.
- Compressor bearing seals are pressurised by HP air. This ensures
oil does not leak out.
- Oil Pressure is measured after the oil pump.
- Oil Temperature is measured downstream of the oil cooler. If oil
temperature is high, it means air intake of the oil cooler is blocked
or oil quantity is low.
Engines  - Less engine RDT with high oil consumption means bearing seal is bad.
Types of Oil System
- Expendable Oil System: Lubrication oil expended or burned in the
combustion chamber. It is generally used in rockets & missiles.
- Wet Sump: It is a simple system, in which oil is stored in the crank
following drawbacks:
- Not efficient and oil cooling is low.
- Less lubrication during manoeuvres, inverted flight dangerous.
- Oil supply limited by crank case capacity
- Oil oxides easily, due to contact with continual hot engine
- Dry Sump: There is a separate oil tank, oil cooler, etc. Aviation
engines generally use a 'dry sump' system.
• Parts of a Dry Sump Engine Oil System
- Oil Tank: Stores oil.
- Oil Pump: Pumps oil from the tank to the engine for lubrication.
- Scavenge Pump: Oil circulated for lubrication is collected and
pumped back into the oil tank by one or more scavenge pumps.
- Fuel/Oil Cooler: This system warms fuel & cools oil simultaneously.
- Chip Detector: It detects the presence of metal chips in oil pipelines.
This could be a warning before a bearing failure.
- Oil Filter contains a mesh filter before & a fine filter after the pump.
- Centrifugal Breather & Vent: It is used to prevent excessive air
pressure within the gearbox & bearing.
- Oil Temperature/Pressure Gauges

FADEC Full Authority Digital Engine Control
Introduction
- In legacy engines, FCU controls the engine mechanically.
- In modern engines, FCU is replaced by a '2-Channel FADEC' (2
channel for redundancy). It is a digital system in which all engine
parameters are controlled digitally.
- FADEC has no manual override. If FADEC fails, the engine fails.
- A 'built-in test' in each channel analyses engine data independently
& compares results with each other to detect & isolate failures. The
healthiest channel with least faults automatically takes control of the
- FADEC will swap command to the stand-by channel if a fault occurs.
- If a malfunction of engine control prevents FADEC to move them, it
will attempt to move the controls to an optimum & safe position &
display relevant warning in ECAM/ECAS.
Inputs to FADEC
- Thrust lever angle  - Ambient temperature
- Altitude  - Engine inlet temperature, EGT
- Mach number  - Engine air demand
FADEC performs the following functions
Engine Control & Overspeed Protection
- Fuel control regulation for all stages of flight
- Power control management
- Fuel metering unit
Engine Stall & Surge Protection
- Variable bleed valve control
- Variable stator vane control
- Rotor active clearance control
- LP turbine active clearance control
- HP turbine active clearance control
Engine Aircraft Integration
- Automatic & manual engine starting & restarting
- Thrust reverser
- Auto thrust management
- Engine indications
- Data collection
Advantages of FADEC
- Provides precise fuel control
- It maximise engine efficiency & performance
- It extends engine life
- System is fault tolerant
- It monitors engine input/output
- It provides automatic engine emergency response
- It reduces pilot workload

Rockets
Solid Propellant Rockets
Motor Body
- Motor body must be as light as possible and must be capable of
withstanding high pressure & temperature.
- The propelling nozzle is attached directly to combustion chamber.
- The entire system generally has no moving parts or pumps.
Propeller Charge
- Fuel & oxidiser are combined to form the solid propellant.
- The propellant is housed within the combustion chamber itself.
- It is physically & chemically stable at ambient temperature. It
burns smoothly when ignited, giving out hot gases continuously.
Burn Rate & Grain Geometry
- Rate at which the propellant is consumed is dependent on the
Engines  chemistry of propellent & pressure inside the chamber.
- Thrust is proportional to the 'burning surface area' of propellant.
- If burning area is constant, it is called 'neutral rate'. If area f, it is
called 'progressive'. If burn area, it is called 'regressive rate'.
- Cigarette/End burning: Burning occurs at one end & the burn
surface area remains constant. But in this, thrust levels are low
& rocket body may overheat. Rocket CG will shift during buming.
- Radial/Internal burning: Burning is initiated along the whole
surface of an internal hollow part. It provides high thrust, has no
overheating problems & its CG remains constant.
Ideal Propellent Charge Characteristics  Ignition Solid
- Cheap to manufacture  - High density  Charge  Fuel  Nozzle
- High release of energy rate - Ease of handling
- High physical strength  - Non toxic exhaust
- No deterioration during storage - Predictable burn rate  Solid Propellant
- Safe handling characteristics  Rockets
Liquid Propellant Rockets
- Fuel, oxidiser, catalyst to aid chemical reaction & water for cooling
are carried in separate tanks.
- Mono-propellant: Propellant containing oxidant & fuel is contained in
a single substance, e.g. hydrogen peroxide + alcohol/nitromethane.
- Bi-propellant: Oxidant & fuel are carried separately & is mixed only
in the combustion chamber.
- Cryogenic Engines: Liquid oxygen at -172°C & liquid hydrogen at
-252°C offer very high performance as rocket propellent, but their
cold storage inside the rocket body is a problem.
Advantages  Disadvantages  Fuel Oxidiser Chamber  Nozzie
- Stop, restart possible  - More parts in a rocket
- Throttle control possible  - Expensive
- Higher thrust  - Handling/storage  Liquid Propellant
- Ability to cool nozzle  Rockets
Combustion Chamber: It is where propellants are burnt.
Nozzle: The nozzle is usually cooled by pumping the liquid propellant
through jackets around the nozzle before it enters combustion
chamber.
- Conical Nozzle: Simple construction, but there is a tendency for
flow separation to occur due to over/under expansion.
- Bell Nozzle: It provides a uniform velocity profile for exhaust
gases. But it is expensive to manufacture.

Other Engine Types
Ramjet
- Ramjet is just a conical duct with no compressor or turbine.
- By a suitable divergent intake design, air velocity is j to subsonic.
Air static pressure is maximum & velocity is minimum at the end of
the intake.
- Static pressure of free stream air can also be increased through an
oblique shockwaves at the intake.
- Compression & pressure rise of incoming air is achieved in combustion
chamber by ram-effect. Ram-effect 1 as forward speed of aircraft f.
- Injectors spray a fuel mist into the compressed air & a spark ignites
the mixture in the combustion chamber. A grill type flame holder
provides a barrier for the burning mixture. If there is no sufficient
forward speed, exhaust gases will come out of both sides of the
engine.
- After combustion, temperature rises and reaches max at the nozzle.
- At 1M, there is sufficient thrust to operate a ramjet, but is not efficient
until 2M. At 2M compression is 7:1, at 3M - 28:1, at 4M - 70:1.
- Since there are no turbines, there is no problem of TET until 5M.
- At 5M, temperature rise is too high & disassociation of air takes
place into nitrogen and oxygen & Ramjet efficiency reduces.
- Ramjet has no moving parts - no need for lubrication, no energy losses.
- As compression is totally dependent on ram-effect, ramjets are only
used at high speeds. † compression = † efficiency = | SFC.
- As altitude 1, ramjet thrust J.
- Ramjets are also used in missiles, where normal jet engines initially
accelerate it to the required higher speed for ramjet operation.
- Turbo-ramjets combine turbojet for lower speeds & ramjet at higher
speeds.
Scramjets (Supersonic Ramjets)
- Beyond 5M, air disassociates into nitrogen & oxygen atoms due to
excessive temperature rise & ramjet efficiency reduces.
- To prevent disassociation, in a Scramjet, air is not slowed down to
subsonic speed. Combustion occurs at supersonic velocities & the
combustion chamber achieves maximum pressure recovery.
- In a scramjet, the fuel used is hydrogen.
- Scramjets provide viable thrust up to 24 M.

Pulse-jets
- Pulse-jets are similar to ramjets. The difference is that
airflow is intermittent through the engine.
- In a Pulse-jet, air enters through a grid of input valves.
- The valves close & air is burnt in the combustion chamber.
- Expansion of exhaust gases through the nozzle produces thrust &
the inlet valve reopens as internal pressure drops.
- This engine has a provision to take in air for starting engine, from
an external compressed air supply.
- Versions of pulse-jets exist with no mechanical parts,
which uses non-linear airflow to achieve same effect.
Advantages  Disadvantages
- Produce thrust at 'O' speed  - High noise pollution
- Extremely simple  - Max speed is < 500 kts 2

- High reliability  - Poor fuel economy

VSTOL Engines
VSTOL Engine Requirements
- Static thrust for vertical takeoff must exceed aircraft weight + 20%.
- Power plant thrust distribution must be around aircraft CG.
Types of VSTOL Engines
- Vectored Thrust: Thrust generated by the engine is vectored
down during takeoff/landing & is parallel to flight during cruise.
- Remote Lift: Fans are fitted on wings or on airframe & are run
by an engine located elsewhere on aircraft.
- Tilt Rotors: Turboprop engines are attached to swivel pods on
- Tit wing: baird takeofilanding, the whole wing til upwards
with the propellor attached to them.
- Compound Systems: Helicopter rotors are used for takeoff. For
cruise, conventional aerofoil is used.
VSTOL Aircraft Control
- Aircraft stability during the transition from VSTOL to cruise has
to be controlled. Various systems used are:
- Puff Pipe: System bleeds air from engine & ducts them to
nozzles at 4 extremities of aircraft.
- Differential Engine Throttling: Engine is throttled separately,
or thrust is vectored for rapid response.
- Differential Thrust Spoiling: Thrust of engines is varied on
either side of the aircraft to maintain stability.
- Multiple Engines: Small & light engines are suitably placed
on the airframe.

• Terms & Definitions
Valance Shell: It is the outermost electron shell of an atom. Some
materials have a free electron in their valence shell & this electron can
easily move from one atom to another.
Conductor: Any material having a valance electron is a good conductor.
Insulator: Any material with electrons firmly bound to its nucleus offering
high resistance to the flow of current is an insulator. e.g. glass.
Principles by Which Electricity is Produced:
Thermo-couples  Compression Piezo-electricity
Photo-electricity  Chemical  Batteries
Friction Static electricity  Magnetism  Generators
Thermocouples: It consists of 2 different electrical conductors forming
an electrical junction. When this junction is heated, it produces a
Photo-electric Effect: Exposing some materials to light of a certain
wavelength can produce electron emissions from them, e.g., Zinc
will release electrons if exposed to UV light. Similarly, electrons
applied on a zinc screen will produce light (CRT monitor).  Electrics
Static Electricity: It is an imbalance of electrical charges in a material,
caused due to the transfer of electrons due to friction between 2
bodies, especially if 1 of them is an insulator.
Piezo-electric Effect: When a mechanical force is applied to some
crystals, a charge will be developed in the other axis. Similarly, AC
(alternating current), when applied across a crystal, will make it
vibrate, e.g., quartz crystal.
J  C = 1amp x 1sec
Charge: Unit - Coulomb (C)
- Property of a body to experience force, when placed in an EM field.
- Protons have (+)ve charge & Electrons have (-)ve charge.
1 A = 1C / 1sec
• Current (I): Unit - Ampere (A)
- It is the flow of charge (electrons) through a conductor in 1 second.
- Direction of flow of current is opposite to direction of flow of electrons.
- Current flowing in a circuit is directly proportional to voltage and
inversely proportional to resistance. It is measured by an ammeter
Microamp - one millionth of an ampere (1pA)
- one thousandth of an ampere (1mA)
• EMF or Potential Difference: Unit - Voltage (V)
- EMF is the pressure difference between 2 points, due to which
current flows. It is measured by a voltmeter.
- In a water tank, if the pressure decreases, flow decreases. Similarly,
in electrics, if the EMF 1 then the flow of electrons 1, voltage l.
- By increasing voltage, flow of electrons past any point in a circuit 1.
Microvolt - Millionth of a Volt (1uV)
Millivolt - Thousandth of a Volt (1mV)
Kilovolt - Thousand Volts (1kV)
Power: Unit - Watts (W)
- Power = Rate of doing work. W (Watt) = V (Volt) x I (Current).
Energy: Power consumed per time. Unit - (Watt Hr)

Inductor / Coil / Choke / Reactor  (See also: AC > Inductive Circuit)
- It is a two-terminal component that stores a magnetic field when
current flows through it.
- It consists of an insulated wire wound into a coil, around a core.
- DC experiences no resistance through an inductor.
- AC experiences Inductive Resistance through an inductor.
- In an AC circuit with an inductor, current 'lags' voltage by 90°.
Inductance: Unit - Henry
- It is the property of a current-carrying conductor/coil to store a
magnetic field & oppose a change in current. It occurs only in AC
• Capacitor  (See also: AC > Capacitive Circuit)
- It is a two-terminal component that stores an electric field.
- It consists of 2 metallic plates separated by a dielectric insulator.
- DC does not flow through a capacitor.
- AC experiences Capacitive Resistance through a capacitor.
- In an AC circuit with a capacitor, current 'leads' voltage by 90°.
- Factors affecting capacitance:
- Property of the dielectric material;
- Area of plates & distance between plates.
Capacitance: Unit - Farad
- It is the property of a capacitor to store an electric charge & the
property of a circuit to oppose a change in AC voltage.
Capacitance in parallel : C = C1 + C2
Capacitance in series : 2=21* 02
• Resistance: Unit - Ohm (Q)  V=IxR
- It is the reluctance for the current to flow.
- If 1 volt produces a current flow of 1 ampere, resistance is 1 ohm.
- Conductance: Inverse of resistance.
Resistance in series: R = R1 + R2 = 20Q + 200  R = 400
Resistance in parallel: 1 - 11+ F2 = 20 + 20 = 10 R = 100
Microhm (1 p2)  • One millionth of an ohm

Kilohm  - One thousand ohms

Reactance (See also: AC > Inductive/Capacitive Reactance)
- It is similar to Resistance, but Reactance is fq-dependent,
whereas Resistance is fq-independent with a fixed value.
- Reactance is only applicable to AC circuit with an inductor/capacitor.
- DC circuit has only resistance & no reactance.
- Inductive Reactance = resistance offered by an inductor in AC circuit.
- Capacitive Reactance = resistance offered by a resistor in AC circuit
Impedance
- It is the total Resistance in an AC circuit = Ohmic Resistance +
Inductive Reactance + Capacitive Reactance.
- Impedance occurs in AC, whereas resistance is a concept used in DC.
- Resistance & impedance have different fundamental origins even
though calculations for their value is the same: R = V / I
Resonance: As frequency 1, inductive reactance † & capacitive reactance J.
For a combination of a capacitor & inductor, at a particular AC frequency,
capacitive & inductive reactance being anti-phase, cancel out each other.
This fq is called Resonant Frequency. (See also: AC > Resonant Circuit)

- A Solenoid or a Relay uses the property of 'right-hand

Generator: A machine that transforms movement into electricity.
Electrics  Alternator: A generator that makes AC.

Diode: A two-terminal electronic component that conducts current only in

Triode: A three-terminal valve containing an anode, cathode, and control
grid. Any change in charge on the control grid controls the flow from
cathode to anode.
Semiconductor (Transistor): Materials that have conductive
properties in-between that of a conductor & an insulator.

Magnetism
(See also: Navigation > Earth's Magnetism)
(See also: Instruments > Magnetic Compass > Aircraft Magnetism)
• Introduction
- Magnetic Field: It is an area of lines of force
(flux lines) around a magnet.
- Flux lines of a magnet emerge from its north
pole & re-enter its south pole.  Unlike poles attract  Same poles repe
- Flux lines are always continuous & never
intersect one another.
- Both poles of a magnet will have equal strength.
- Same poles repel; opposite poles attract.
- A freely suspended magnet seeks N-S pole.
- Temporary Magnet: Soft Iron. Easily magnetised & de-magnetised.
- Permanent Magnet: Hard alloy steel. It is difficult to magnetise but
retains magnetic properties longer.
- Permeability: A magnetic property, where-in flux lines concentrate
through a soft iron body when it is placed in a magnetic field.
- Saturation: A body is unable to accept any further magnetisation.
- Retentivity: Amount of residual magnetism in a body when the
external magnetic field is removed.
• Magnetism can be induced by:
- Placing a ferro-magnetic material in a magnetic field, then vibrate/
hammer it. This is the main cause of aircraft magnetism.
- Repeatedly stroking an iron bar in the same direction.
- Placing an iron bar in a solenoid.
- Aligning an iron bar with magnetic lines of force in a magnetic field.
Demagnetisation is done by:
- Shock: Place an iron bar 1 to the earth's magnetic field and strike it.
- Heat: If you heat an iron bar to 900°C, magnetism doesn't return
when cooled.
- Electric Current: Passing an electric current through it will
demagnetise it.

Battery

terminal & current flows from +ve to -ve terminal.

Types of Batteries
Lead Acid: Old type of battery. Its capacity is determined by the surface
area of electrode plates placed inside the electrolyte. E.g. Car battery.
Alkaline Nickel-Cadmium Ni-Cd
- It has a nominal voltage of 1.2 V when fully charged.
- NiCd gives constant voltage output until almost fully discharged.
- Thermal Runaway. NiCd batteries suffer from low thermal
capacity. It may explode during charging or during multiple
successive engine starts on battery due to excess current draw.
Alkaline Lithium-lon Li-ion
- It has a nominal voltage 3.6 V when fully charged.
- It has higher energy density & lower maintenance than NiCd.
- During discharge, its anode (graphite) undergoes oxidation and
loses electrons through an electrolyte into its cathode.
- Different variations of Li-ion cathode (Li-Manganese, Li-phosphate,
etc.) offer different voltage, energy density & charging cycles.

AC Alternating Current
oo Introduction
- In AC, polarity of voltage & direction of current changes continuously.
In DC, neither polarity of voltage nor direction of current changes.
- Cycle: 1 complete process of a waveform in AC. 1 Cycle = 1 Hertz.
- Phase: Angular variation of a sine wave. 1 Cycle = 360°phase change.
- Amplitude: Maximum sine wave value.
- Frequency: Number of waves (or cycles) in a second.
- Period: Time taken for 1 cycle. It is the reciprocal of frequency.
- RMS Root Mean Square: It is the effective value of AC, calculated
by comparing it to DC, which provides the same heating effect in
identical conditions. RMS = (Peak-value/V2); or Peak value x 0.707.
- AC Frequency is determined by the generator RPM & no. of poles.
f Frequency = No of poles x-RPM  fr  Period = 1 seconds
(Hertz)  60  (T)
Q. Find the AC frequency of 8 Pole generator at 6000 RPM?
Ans. AC Fq = 8/2 × 6000/60 = 400 Hertz.
Electrics
•o Advantages of AC
- AC generators are simpler, more robust in construction & more
reliable than DC generators.
- Power to weight ratio of AC machines is better than DC machines.
- High voltage AC systems require less cable weight than comparable
DC systems.
- AC voltage can be changed to a higher/lower value with 100%
efficiency with a transformer.
- Any DC voltage can be obtained simply by using an AC transformer
rectifier unit.
- 3 phase AC motors which are simpler, more efficient than DC motors,
can be operated from a constant frequency source (AC generators).
- AC machines do not suffer from commutation problems associated
with DC machines. They are consequently more reliable, especially
at high altitudes.
Power Factor
- Power Factor = Real power / Apparent power
- Real Power = Voltage x Current x Power factor
- Apparent Power = RMS voltage x current in one half cycle.
- True Power = Apparent power when voltage & current in phase.
True Power =0 when voltage & current 90° out of phase (COS 90° = 0)
- In a pure resistive circuit, Phase angle = 0, RP = AP = PF = 1

AC Generator / Alternator
°o AC Generator
- A Generator produces AC by using a rotating armature & a stationary
magnetic field.  (See also: Electro-Magnetic Induction)
- It is simply a single wire loop armature, rotating inside the magnetic
field of a permanent magnet. Thus, EMF (voltage) is produced inside
the armature due to electro-magnetic induction.
- Armature is connected to a continuously rotating slip-rings.
- In one 360° rotation, voltage in the armature will rise to a maximum
value, fall to 0, then rise to the maximum value in the other direction.

- Most aircraft use an alternator than a generator due to its better power

5 - 12
AC Motor
Introduction
- AC motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
- In it, AC is applied to a stator, which generates a rotating magnetic
field, which in turn causes the rotor to turn.
- Advantages
- Less troublesome than DC motors.
- Better suited for constant speed applications.
AC Synchronous Motor
- Synchronous motors are AC Alternators operated as motors.
- For starting, its rotor is energised by DC to line it up with a magnetic
field in the stator. Then a 3 Phase AC is applied to the stator.
- Thus, rotation of the rotor is synchronised with the rotating field set
up in its stator; hence it is called 'Synchronous Motor'.
- Synchronous motors are single speed motors, and the speed of the
motor is proportional to the frequency of the supply.
- They are generally used in engine RPM indicators.
- Reversing the two phases will cause the motor to run in reverse.
- If 1 phase fails, motor will run at ½ speed & will not start next time.
- RPM of synchronous motor = 1200 x Fa/No. of Poles
e.g. a 4 Pole Synchronous Motor @ 400 Hz will rotate at 1200 RPM.
- Disadvantages:
- Synchronous motors are not self-starting.
- It needs induction winding for initial rotation.

AC Induction Motor (Asynchronous Motor)
- It is a 3 phase AC Motor.
- In it, a rotating magnetic field applied to the stator, which induces an
AC in its rotor. Hence it is called Induction Motor'.
- Speed of motor determined by fq of the supply & load on the motor.
- Rotor of an AC Induction Motor is called a Squirrel-cage Rotor. It
consists of a cylindrical laminated iron core with longitudinal copper
windings.
- Induction Motor never achieves true synchronous speed. If it did,
the squirrel cage bars would not cut any lines of force, & thus will
not produce induced voltage. Hence, Induction Motor is also known
as Asynchronous Motor.
- Difference between synchro-speed & rotor-speed is called slip. -5%
- Induction Motor is commonly used due to its simplicity & low cost.
- Induction Motor has slip rings but no brushes.
- Disadvantage: Synchronous motors are not self-starting.

DC Generator
°o Construction
- A DC Generator is essentially an AC Generator. In it, a single wire
loop armature is rotated inside a magnetic field of a permanent
magnet. This produces an EMF inside the armature due to electro-
magnetic induction. This produces AC.
- Now to make DC, slip rings of the AC Generator is replaced with a
split-ring commutator, which are conductive half-rings with an
insulator electrically separating each half.
- As armature rotates 0° - 180°  , +ve brush is in contact with left-split-
ring, & -ve brush with right-split-ring (refer to the diagram).
From 180° - 360°, +ve brush is in contact with right-split-ring & -ve
brush with left-split-ring. The result is that, every 180°, armature
terminals are reversed, producing DC.
- Commutator Ripple: It is the phenomenon of voltage rise & fall in
a DC generator, in a 360° turn. This problem is solved by increasing
no. of coils in the armature, thus making DC output voltage steady.
- An Alternator uses a Rectifier, which are solid-state blocking diodes
(electrical non-return valves) that are used to convert AC to DC.

Armature
Armature Reaction
- As load on the generator t, current flowing through its armature 1.
- This causes a magnetic field in the armature that interacts with the
main field, causing a distortion, thereby shifting the neutral plane to
where no voltage is induced, in the direction of rotation.
- Inter-poles counteract armature reaction.
Field Coil
- It is an electro-magnet (a coil wrapped around a conductor), whose
magnetic field strength is controlled by the current supplied in it.
- It is used to control the generator output voltage irrespective of the
armature speed.
- A field switch is used to shutoff the field & switch off the generator.
Voltage Regulator
- It is a 'variable-resistor', connected in series with the field coil.
- It senses generator/alternator output voltage & adjusts current in field
coil to maintain correct voltage irrespective of RPM or electrical load.
- Generally, it is a 14V/28V system for 12V/24V battery respectively.
===== [avh 0267]
5 - 14
- It permits generator voltage to build up to a preset value before the
circuit is closed. This prevents the battery from feeding current back
into the generator if generator voltage is below battery voltage.
- In a 28V system with 24V battery, the cut-out closes at 26V.
Over-voltage Protection Unit: It is used to guard against any dangerous
voltage rise in the Bus-Bar (~ > 16.5V for 14V system).
Types of DC Generators
1. Externally Excited Generators: In a generator with no residual
magnetism, a battery is needed to supply the initial current to
the field coil, to start the generating process.
2. Self Excited Generators: Due to residual magnetism, as soon as the
generator is rotated, a voltage is produced. Some of this voltage can
be applied to a field coil to increase voltage output.
2a. Self Excited Series Wound DC Generator
- In this, armature, field coils & external circuit are in series.
- Since field current is same as load current, which is large, required
mag flux is obtained with relatively less no. of turns in field winding.
- As load draws more current from the generator, this additional current
1 field strength & generates more voltage in armature windings. But
saturation is soon reached in field coils.
- Since constant voltage is needed in aircraft systems, Series Wound
DC generators are not used in aircraft.
- However, these are used in piston engines, during start.
2b. Self Excited Shunt Wound DC Generator
- In this, armature is parallel to field coils. Thus, current through the
field coil is determined by the terminal voltage & resistance of the field.
- Shunt windings have large no. of turns, thus, it needs only a small
current to produce the required field. When started, build-up time to
rated voltage is short because the field current flows through the
coils even if the circuit is open.
- There is minimal voltage drop from no-load to full-load, thus, it is
used where constant voltage is needed.
- Terminal voltage is controlled by a voltage regulator, which is
connected in series with the shunt field coils.
2c. Self Excited Compound Wound DC Generator
- It has both series & shunt windings. It is designed to overcome the
voltage drop in a shunt generator when load is increased. Series field
1 total magnetic flux when load is 1, thus, has constant voltage outpur.

5 - 15
DC Motor
Introduction
- DC motor also converts electrical energy to mechanical energy.
- There is no difference in construction between a generator & motor.
- DC Motor uses Flemings Left Hand Rule.
Back EMF  (See also: Lenz's Law)
- Movement or a conductor in a magnetic field induces an EMF in it
(as per 'Lenz's Law), which opposes the rate of change of magnetic
flux produced in it, i.e., induced voltage opposes supply voltage.
- Back EMF is proportional to motor speed. Motor speed 1 = Back
EMF 1.
- But 'back EMF' never f as much as the supply voltage. Difference
between applied EMF & 'back EMF' is such that current can flow in
the conductor & produce motion.
Types of DC Motor
Series Wound DC Motor
- In it, armature & field coils are in series.
- Since field current is the same as load current, which is large, the
required magnetic flux is obtained with a relatively small no. of turns
in the field windings.
- As load on the motor 1, it slows down & back EMF I, which allows
armature & field current to J, thus providing a heavier torque.
- Series motor runs slow at heavy loads & fast at low loads. Thus,
over-speeding of the motor is possible. So, it is not ideal for
constant speed motors, where loads may be intermittent.
- It has high starting torque, so it must never be started without a load.
- It is used mainly in electric actuators, landing gear actuators, etc.
Shunt Wound DC Motor
- In it, armature is parallel with field coils, directly across the voltage
source, & the shunt windings have a large no. of turns.
- Thus, current through the field coil is independent of the load & the
armature current.
- Torque developed varies directly with armature current.
- If load on motor 1, motor slows down, back EMF I, armature current
1, torque 1. If load on motor l, motor speeds up, back EMF 1,
armature current j, torque l.
- There is minimal speed drop (10%) from no-load to full-load; thus
they are used in constant speed motors.
- It can be started with no-load, e.g., fans, centrifugal pumps, etc.

• Starter Generator
- It is a compound wound Generator that is used as both a starter-
motor & a generator.
- For starting, it is used as a compound motor. When engines are
running, it is used as a generator with a voltage regulator.
- Disadvantage: Inability to maintain full output at low RPM; hence
generally, it is used in a turbine engine.
Motor Actuators
- They are small reversible motors, coupled with a gearbox.
- Travel range of these actuators are controlled by limit micro-
switches.
- They are fitted with electro-magnetic brakes to prevent over-travel.
- Clutches are used to prevent mechanical overloading.
- Rotary Actuators: Used in fuel shutoff/air-oil shutoff valves.
- Linear Actuators: Used where push-pull action needed. e.g., flaps,
undercarriage

Transformer
°o Introduction
- A transformer is used to step-up or step-down AC voltage.
- It consists of 2 separate coils wound over iron laminations to form a
common core.
- Primary winding is connected to an AC supply, and output is taken
from its secondary winding.
- Alternating voltage & current in the primary winding creates an
alternating flux across secondary winding, which sets up an EMF.
- Output voltage has 180° opposite phase.
†  Transformation (r) = N2 - E2  N2, N1 = No. of turns in 2nd, 1st coil
Ratio  E2, E1 = Voltage induced
- If ratio is > 1, it is a step-up transformer.
- If ratio is < 1, then it is step-down transformer.
- In a transformer, power output = power input.
- If there is no load on the output, current flow in the secondary coil
will be negligible.

° Inverter
- An inverter converts DC to AC.
- Rotary Inverter: DC is converted to AC by using a constant speed
DC motor, to drive an alternator, thus produce AC.
- Static Inverter: It is a solid-state device that contains oscillators,
diodes, transformers & capacitors to converts DC to AC.

5 - 18
Aircraft Power Systems
Di-Pole/2 Wire System
- In dipole circuit, current passes through 1 wire & returns in another.
- Current needs to complete circuit at the -ve terminal of a generator.
- Any short circuit in the wiring causes a component not to work.
- This system is used if fuselage is made of non-conductive materials.
Single Pole or Uni-Pole or Earth-return Circuit
- It is the most common type of system. It is used in an aircraft where
the metal airframe is used as the negative/ground terminal.
- Negative terminal of the generator is also connected to the airframe.
- Short circuit in a single-pole circuit is caused when wiring between
the supply & equipment goes to neutral/ground.
• Volt Meters: They have high internal resistance and are connected in
parallel to measure voltage.
• Ammeters: They have low internal resistance and are connected in
series to measure the current through the load.
- A shunt field may be fitted to f indicating range of the instrument.
- In a 2 engine aircraft, 2 ammeters (1 for each generator) are provided,
with 1 switchable voltmeter to indicate either the generator or
battery voltage.
• Bus Bar
- It is the power collection & distribution system in an aircraft.
- In a 2 engine aircraft, generators, batteries & inverters are
connected in parallel to bus-bars.
- For AC, a synchronising bus-bar is needed to match frequency, phase
& voltage.
- Bus bars can be classified as:
- Essential Bus: Systems vital for aircraft safety is connected to it.
- Non-essential Bus: Non-essential loads are connected to it.
- Hot Bus: Battery is directly connected to certain a/c equipment.
- AC Split Bus:
- Different AC buses are not interconnected, so it does not
need frequency, phase & voltage matching equipment.
- It can be automatically connected together if 1 alternator fails.
- If both alternators fail, all non-essential services are lost.
- Static Inverter in split bus supplies essential AC consumers.
Bonding
- Bonding prevents static electricity buildup on any part of
the aircraft, to reduce risk of spark/fire.
- It is done by joining up aircraft parts with wire strips.
- It maintains 0 potential difference between all metal components.
Static Discharger
- It reduces static build-up on airframe by discharging it to atmosphere.
- It is fitted on the trailing edges of the airframe.
- Static is discharged on touch-down by using high carbon tyres.
Screening
- Static charges are produced by aircraft electrical equipment, which
creates EM interference with other equipment & radio circuits.
- Screening is done to prevent this interference by using suppressors
in cables connected to source of interference.
- They are required for ignition systems, DC generators & slip rings
operating over 200 RPM.

Switches (Types)
- Toggle Switches: Normal ON/OFF switch.
- Switch Light: A 'press switch' with a light inside it, when ON.
- Guarded Switch: Switches that have a mechanical cover on them.
- Micro Switch: Switches for small connections, e.g., for doors
closing/landing gear indication.
- Bi-metallic Switch (Thermal): Used for fire detection.
- Proximity Switch
- Capacitive: Fuel quantity sensors.
- Magnetic: RPM sensor on gears.
Circuit Protection Devices
0:30
• Fuse
- A fuse opens the circuit before full fault current is reached.
- A fuse has a low melting point. It operates when the current flowing
through it is sufficient to melt the element. They have to be replaced
when they are blown.
- They are fitted in series with the load.
- Fuses are rated in Amps. A fuse rating is selected as per the power  Electrics
requirement of the circuit.
- Current Limiter is a fuse with a high melting point.
- Types - Cartridge Fuse: Normal glass cylinder fuse.
- HRC High Rupture Capacity: More accurate, used for
high rated circuits.
• CB Circuit Breaker
- It opens the circuit when full fault current is reached.
- It is fitted in series with the load.
- It does functions of both fuse & switch.
- They can be reset.
- They are used for circuit isolation also.
- Both CB & its device should be able to withstand full fault current for
a short duration.
- Types
- Non-trip Free: CB can be held IN under fault circumstances &
circuit will be completed.
- Trip Free: CB cannot be held IN if the fault still exists. CB can
be reset only after the fault is cleared.
- Reverse Current CB: Gives protection against reverse current.

Basic Computer
• Parts of a Computer
- Input Devices: Mouse, keyboard, etc.
- Output Devices: Monitor, printer, etc.
- CPU Central Processing Unit: Its main parts are:
- ALU Arithmetic & Logic Unit: Performs calculations in binary.
- Shift Register: Temporary store of the data being processed.
- Control Unit: A computer clock, synchronising operations.
- Memory
- ROM: Read Only Memory. It is non-erasable memory.
- PROM: Programmable Read-only Memory
- It is a memory that is programmable by user.
- EPROM: Erasable Programmable Read-only Memory.
- EEPROM: Electronically Erasable Programmable ROM.
- RAM: Random Access Memory.
- Volatile RAM: Data is lost when power is turned OFF.
- Non Volatile RAM: Data persists even with power OFF.
• Binary Logic Types:
- Positive Logic: Binary, 1 by +5V, 0 by OV.
- Negative Logic: Binary, 1 by OV, 0 by +5V.
- Computer language with base-16. It uses hexadecimal values
(numbers 0-9, then alphabets A-F).
- Computer language with base-8 uses octal values (numbers 1-8).

6 - 3
•° Pitot System
Pitot Tube (Senses Dynamic Pressure)
- Pitot is a tube fitted in front of an aircraft. In normal flight attitude, its
mouth should open parallel to airflow. To sense dynamic pressure
correctly, it must be positioned outside the boundary layer.
- It should have a de-icing provision and drain holes.
Static Vent (Senses Static Pressure)
- It is a vent placed on an airframe, with its mouth perpendicular to
the airflow. No component of dynamic pressure should enter it.
Principle of Pitot System (See also: Aerodynamics > Static/Dynamic Pressure)
- Dynamic Pressure: It is the air pressure along the forward-facing
parts of a moving aircraft, and corresponds to ½ p v2.
- Static Pressure: It is the air pressure at that altitude, denoted by'S'.
- Total pressure inside a Pitot tube = Dynamic (½ p v2) + Static (S).
- Pitot system supplies static + dynamic pressure to ASI & machmeter,
and only static pressure to the altimeter & VSI.

Position Error
- Position Error occurs when there are disturbances in the
static air around the aircraft, which is influenced by:
- Position of pitot & static  - Configuration: u/c, flaps, etc.
- Angle of attack  - Sideslip
- Aircraft speed  - Presence of shock-waves

- Position error is also increased during 'Ground Effect.
- It can be reduced by careful design and positioning of static vents.
- It doesn't matter where Static vents are placed on an aircraft; as long
as they sense static pressure correctly, instruments will read correctly.
- 2 interconnected static vents on either side of the aircraft fuselage
will balance out errors caused by sideslipping or yawing.

===== [avh 0276]
6 - 4
°° Altimeter
Introduction
- Altimeter is an instrument that senses the outside static air pressure
and converts it into altitude information.
- Altitude displayed by an altimeter may not be the actual altitude of
aircraft due to variations in outside atmospheric pressure at that time.
- However, since all altimeters are calibrated on the same datum
(standard ISA conditions), a safe vertical separation is achieved
between 2 aircraft maintaining the same altimeter setting (QNH/QNE).
- During preflight checks, QNH must be set on the altimeter. Maximum
error from aerodrome elevation must be within t75' (DGCA) or
160' (ICAO).
Construction
- An altimeter consists of a thin corrugated partially-vacuum
metal capsule, which is prevented from collapsing, by a spring leaf.
- Static pressure from the static vent is fed into the altimeter casing &
changes in static pressure make the capsule contract or expand.
These movements are fed to the altimeter dial by mechanical
linkages.
- A bi-metallic strip is used to compensate for any capsule movement
that occurs due to changes in temperature within the casing.
- QNH/QNE is set on an altimeter by a sub scale knob (Kollesman
Window). When QNH is set, altimeter reads the elevation of aircraft
Instruments  above the MSL. When QNE (1013) is set, it reads the Flight Level
(Pressure Altitude).
- Altimeter errors must be < +30' at sea level.
- Altimeter has decreased sensitivity above 60000' due to the low
pressure/density of air at that altitude.
- A Sensitive Altimeter may have 2 or more capsules. Thus, it is
more accurate.
- A Servo Assisted Altimeter is even more accurate. A position
control servo system is used instead of mechanical linkages to
control pointer movements. Lag error is virtually eliminated in this.

Lag Error
- Occurs because capsule/linkage movement is not instantaneous..
- Altimeter under-reads during climb, over-reads during descend.
- This error can be eliminated by using servo altimeters.
Instrument Error: Error due to manufacturing tolerances.
- A capsule under stress will have imperfect elastic properties.  Errors in Altimeter
- It causes delayed reading when levelling out from climb/descend.
Position/Pressure Error: It is caused due to interference of dynamic
pressure at static vent. It always cause altimeter to under read.
This can be caused due to 2 reasons:
- Wrong positioning of the static vent, eliminated by placing 2
static vents, on opposite sides of the airframe.
- Manoeuvre Induced Error: Caused by aircraft manoeuvres.
Temperature Error (High - Low - High error)
- Cold air mass is denser than standard air & thus, pressure levels
are more closely spaced. So when an aircraft is flying where it is
colder than ISA conditions, altimeter will over read.
- This error is 'O' at sea level & increases with altitude.
- This error can be compensated for, by using:
Altimeter Cold Temperature Corrections
(Ref: Doc 8168 > Flight Procedures > Altimeter Cold Temp Corrections)  Instruments
Altitude must be corrected by +4% for every 10°C below standard ISA
temperature (till -15°C), as measured at the altimeter setting source.
Barometric Error (High - Low - High error)
- Occurs if the actual atmospheric pressure is different or if a
wrong QNH is set on the altimeter sub-scale.
- When flying from a high-pressure area to a low-pressure area,
altimeter will over-read & actual aircraft altitude will be less.
- This can also caused due to the type of terrain below the aircraft.
Air sweeping around hills cause low pressure on the leeward side.
• Types of Measured Altitudes (See also: Meteorology > Density > Density Alt)
- Pressure Altitude: Altitude displayed on altimeter when 1013 is set.
- Density Altitude: Altitude, at which, a given density occurs in ISA.
It is an altitude figure used only for engine performance calculations.
T = ISA temperature difference
†  DA = PA ‡ (118 x T)  PA = Pressure altitude
- True Altitude: Actual height of aircraft above the ground.
TA = PA + (PA x *3.5 x T) / 1000; or
PA + 1% per 2.5°C ISA deviation; or
PA + 4' per °C ISA deviation per 1000'
(*If height > 10000', multiply by 4)
- At standard ISA conditions, Density alt = Pressure alt = True alt.
Q. Aircraft is at FL180 & temperature is ISA -10°C. Find True Altitude?
* Ans. TA = 18000 + (18000 × 4'x -10 / 1000) = 17280'; or
(1% x -10) / 2.5 = -4%. -4% of 18000' = -780', or TA = 17280*.  so if QNE 1013 is set, then at FL180 your True Altitude is 720' lower.

• VSI - Vertical Speed Indicator
Construction
- VSI displays the vertical speed of an aircraft by measuring the
difference between the static pressure supplied into a capsule inside
the VSI & the metered delayed static pressure fed into the VS! casing.
- Static changes with aircraft altitude & delayed static lag behind. By
sensing the difference between them, vertical speed is measured.
- A 'capillary & orifice metering unit' inside the VSI capsule compensate
for pressure & temperature variations.
- Pressure difference across the capillary 1 with f in altitude &
temperature. The reverse is true for the orifice. This is because
airflow through a capillary is laminar & the orifice is turbulent. Thus,
pressure is compensated at a constant temperature.
- Pressure difference across capillary with 1 in temperature. The
reverse is true for the orifice. Airflow through a capillary is directly
proportional to temperature & inversely proportional through the orifice.

Transonic Jump: VSI indicates a climb at transonic speeds, because
of the lower pressure behind the formation of shock waves.
IVSI Instantaneous VSI
- IVSI consists of an inertial mass, balanced by a spring, which has
an immediate response to the departure of aircraft from level flight.
It also has an accelerometer built into it.
- As soon as an aircraft climbs, inertia causes the mass to move,
thus, moving the VSI needle. After a few seconds, this effect dies
away, and the normal metering unit takes over.
- In IVSI, lag & manoeuvre induced errors are eliminated.
- In IVSI, instrument, position & turning errors still persists (bank > 40°)
- Sometimes, an IVSI may be too sensitive, and indications may
fluctuate during steep turns or turbulence.

• ASI - Air Speed Indicator
Introduction
- Total pressure on an aircraft in a pitot tube = Dynamic + Static.
- Therefore Dynamic pressure = Total pressure - Static pressure.
- ASI is a pressure gauge to measure this dynamic pressure, & as
per Bernoulli's theorem, it remains constant in any part of the stream.
- Thus, a pitot tube can be placed anywhere on an aircraft, where the
airflow is at a higher or a lower speed than that of the aircraft.
- Provided static source is placed correctly (without airflow interference
& gives true atmospheric pressure), ASI will always read correctly.
Construction
- Pitot pressure is supplied into a capsule & static outside it.
- The resultant movement of the capsule is connected to a
needle by a mechanical linkage.
- But, dynamic pressure is directly proportional to aircraft velocity V2. So,
pointer movement is not equal for an equal amount of speed change.
: ASI is calibrated to show equal graduation of speed on its dial.
- Servo ASI: In it, the mechanical linkage is replaced by electric
means, and thus, is more accurate.

°° Machmeter
(See also: Aerodynamics > Supersonic AD > Mach Number)
Introduction
- Speed of sound changes only with temperature. Temp 1 = LSS 1
- Air molecules at higher temperature have more energy, thus, can
vibrate faster & sound waves can travel more quickly.
- Speed of sound is 661 kts (343 m/s, 1236 kmph) at sea level.
- At absolute 0 (-273°C), sound cannot propagate.
- Air is compressible. Mach no., or the speed of sound, is a measure
of that compressibility, and is measured by a machmeter.
- As altitude 1 = temperature J, density J = LSS I.
- Thus, when climbing with constant TAS, mach no. † with altitude, or
climbing with constant IAS, TAS 1, Mach no 1 (in normal lapse rate).

Construction
- Machmeter displays a ratio of dynamic pressure to static pressure.
- It has 2 capsules. 1 work as an ASI, the other as an altimeter.
- Readings from the ASI via a 'ratio arm' is transferred to the altimeter
arm, before displaying it on a needle.
- Thus, as altitude f, for the same speed, a higher mach no. is displayed.

Since mach no. is a ratio, density & temperature errors are cancelled out.
Why is mach no. more important than TAS at high altitude?
Mach no. = TAS/LSS. LSS | with t in altitude. Thus, at constant TAS, mach no.
1 with altitude. If McRIT is exceeded, shockwaves form & will cause aircraft stability
issues. Also, at higher altitudes, ASI is not that reliable.
Why is aircraft limited by IAS in low altitude & mach no. at high altitude?
Aircraft is limited by both IAS (Vo) & mach no. (Mo). At low altitudes, the
speed of sound is high, so aircraft is limited by its IAS. At higher altitudes, the speed
of sound is low, so aircraft will be limited by its mach number. While climbing, at a
particular point, a pilot must switch from remaining under the IAS limit to remaining
under the mach limit.

• Magnetic Compass (Direct Indicating Compass)
(See also: Navigation > Earth's Magnetism)
(See also: Electrics > Magnetism)
Requirements of an Aircraft Magnetic Compass
- Aperiodicity/Deadbeat: Compass card should settle down quickly.
- Sensitivity: It must seek the horizontal component 'H' of the earth's
magnetic field.
- Horizontality: It must lie horizontal to the aircraft & must not be
affected by the vertical component (Dip) of the earth's magnetic field.
- Accuracy minimum needed: Magnetic compass ‡10°
Remote indicating compass: +1°
Requirements of Compass Liquid
- Low expansion coefficient  - Low freezing point  - High boiling point
- Low viscosity  - Transparency  - Non-corrosiveness
Errors in a Magnetic Compass
• Acceleration Error
- It occurs due to the inertia of the magnet & the magnetic 'Dip'
acting on it (effect of earth's vertical component 'Z').
- AP Acceleration causes an apparent turn towards nearest Pole.
Deceleration causes an apparent turn towards nearest Equator.
- This error is maximum at poles due to f in Dip, and is zero near the
magnetic equator (no Dip).
- No acceleration/deceleration errors exist when
the aircraft is flying in north/south direction.
• Turning Error
- During a turn, magnet CG swings out and creates a couple with Dip.
- PU Turning through Pole: Compass Under reads.
Turning through Equator: Compass over reads.
- This error is maximum at poles due to f in Dip, and is zero near the
magnetic equator (no Dip).
- No turning error exist when the aircraft is turning through east/west.
- Liquid Swirl: Caused by the swirl of the liquid inside the compass
casing, when an aircraft turns. In the northern hemisphere, liquid swirl
error 1 when turning through north, I when turning through south.
Total Errors (Acceleration Error + Turning Error )
- APPU: Acceleration causes compass turn towards nearest Pole,
Turning through Pole causes compass to 'Under-read'.

6 - 10
Aircraft Magnetism
- Aircraft magnetism is the cause of Compass Deviation.
- Aircraft 'soft-iron' is due to the changing vertical component - dip
(z) and horizontal (h) magnetic fields of the earth. It varies with
magnetic heading of the aircraft.
- Aircraft 'hard iron' magnetism is the permanent magnetism in an
aircraft, and varies with magnetic latitude. It is not affected by
external fields.
• Compass Swing
- It is done to check & reduce 'deviation' in an aircraft magnetic
compass, after a:
- Replacement of compass components;
- Large change in aircraft operating latitude;
- Periodic inspection;
- Lightning strike;
- Prolonged aircraft ground storage on a single heading;
- Significant modification of aircraft/electrical components.
Compass Swing Procedure
When the aircraft is on ground, its compass readings are measured
on cardinal & inter cardinal headings, and is compared with a
reference compass. Then the total deviation is calculated as follows:
Coefficient B = (Dev E - Dev W) / 2
- It is the Deviation caused due to aircraft magnetism on its
longitudinal axis, and varies as per the SIN of aircraft heading.
Instruments  - It is maximum when the aircraft is flying E/W, 'O' when flying N/S
- Corrections are done on an easterly heading, by setting up a local
magnetic field, by adjusting micro-screws on the compass.
Coefficient C = (Dev N - Dev S) / 2
- It is the Deviation caused due to the aircraft magnetism on its
lateral axis, and varies as per the COS of aircraft heading.
- It is maximum when the aircraft is flying N/S, 'O' when flying E/W.
- Corrections are done on a northerly heading, by setting up a local
magnetic field, by adjusting micro-screws on the compass.

• Aircraft magnetism on longitudinal Axis  • Aircraft magnetism on longitudinal Axis
