Coefficient A
- It is the remaining Deviation of the whole aircraft magnetism.
- Coefficient A = Deviation (N+NE+E+SE+S+SW+W+NW) / 8
- It is the deviation due compass defects, lubber line misalignment.
- It is corrected by adjusting the lubber line.
Any residual deviation is corrected by providing a 'Deviation Card'
Total Deviation on any hdg = A + B (SIN heading) + C (COS heading)

Flux Valve Theory
- A coil placed across magnetic flux lines produces 0 induced current
& a coil placed along flux produces max induced current in it. At any
other angle, the induced current is proportional to COS e between
coil axis & magnetic field (or aircraft heading & earth's magnetic field).
- Thus, this induced current in the coil changes as per the aircraft
heading and is sensed by the flux valve.
But there are 3 problems:
- (a) Voltage induced in the coil depends
on the rate of change of flux.:. once a
heading is established, there is no more
change in flux & no more induced current.
- (b) Hdg ambiguity: 000°/180° & 090/  Current in each pick-up leg
270° will have the same induced current. changes with heading of aircraft
- (c) As latitude 1, horizontal component J. This reduction is due to
the change in aircraft heading or change in latitude.
Problem (a) is solved by
- Applying an alternating current at coil centre (C). This produces an
induced current in the top & bottom legs of the flux valve (in legs
A & B - red & blue). They are at the same frequency & amplitude,
but are in anti-phase. The resultant flux (green line) is 'O', and no
current is induced in the pick-up coil. If earth's flux were present
in the background, total flux (AC + Earth), would start from a
different baseline (dotted line), which would not be zero. Thus,
an EMF is produced, proportional to the amount of flux cutting
the coils, in the direction of the earth magnetic flux (COS).
Problem (b) & (c) are solved by
- Using a 3 legged flux valve. Resultant of the vector pickup on all
3 legs shows the direction of the magnetic flux.
- Latitude problem is also solved, as only the magnitude of
vectors is reduced, but the direction still points north.

Construction of a Flux Valve
- Flux valve is a pendulous magnetic detecting element positioned at
the wingtips or tail of an aircraft. It is mounted on a 'Hooke's Joint,
which can swing +25° in pitch & roll, but cannot rotate in azimuth.
- If there is a difference between the flux valve output & gyro, a slaving
motor is activated until both are in sync. Corrections are at 3°/min.
- During initial system start, the slaving rate will be faster.
Types of Slaving/Error Correction in Gyro Magnetic Compass
- Step Function: Error correction occurs at a fixed rate.
- Linear Function: Correction rate is proportional to the error amount.
But problems arise when corrections are large, especially during
startup, which demands a high rate.
- Step Linear function: Correction rate is proportional to the error,
less for a small correction but maximum restricted to 2°/min.
• Advantages of Gyro Magnetic Compass  Disadvantages
- No drift, no manual sync required  - Heavier
- No turning errors  - More expensive
- Can be used as DG at poles  - Requires electricity supply
- Multiple outputs from one flux valve  - Complicated construction
- True heading can be obtained
by setting a 'variation control'
• Errors in a Gyro Magnetic Compass
Detector Tilt Error: Correct output occurs only if flux valve is maintained
in the horizontal plane. Tilt is caused due to various reasons:
Instruments  - Turning: Caused due to prolonged turns at slow speeds.
- Coriolis: A/c flying relative to spherical earth follows a spherical
- Venice lovement v  path & this force acts on the pendulously suspended flux valve.
- Vehicle Movement: When flying a true or rhumb line track, the
aircraft must turn to maintain a constant track with reference to
converging meridians. It is similar to Coriolis error.
- Acceleration: Caused due to aircraft acceleration.
Northern Instability: Heading oscillations experienced by a high-
speed aircraft flying straight & level, near the magnetic poles.
Hang-off Error: Errors due to all types of wander, real & apparent.
Gimbal Error: Errors due to gimbal lock in a GMC.
Transmission Error: Overall system accuracy.

00  Gyroscopes
Gyroscope is a device used for measuring or maintaining orientation and
angular velocity. It is a spinning wheel or a disc, mounted on a frame. Its
spin axis is free to assume any orientation by itself. Its 2 properties are:
1. Rigidity: It is the reluctance of a rotating mass to change its plane of
rotation. Due to the conservation of angular momentum, the direction &
axis of rotation of a gyro stays the same in inertial space irrespective
of displacement of the frame on which gyro is mounted. It depends on:
- Rotor RPM (higher RPM = more rigidity)
- Moment of inertia (1 radius or 1 mass of rotor = larger m.o.i)
2. Precession: If a torque is applied about an axis 1 to the rotor spin axis,
the rotor will precess about an axis 1 to both axes of rotation & torque. In
other words, torque is precessed by 90° in the direction of rotor rotation.
- Precession continues as long as the torque is applied.
- Rate of precession is directly proportional to the applied torque
and inversely proportional to the moment of inertia & rotor RPM.
Q = Angular velocity (precession)  / = lorque
0 =  J = Angular velocity (rotor RPM  1 = inertia = mr
Topple: Movement of the gyro spin axis in earth's vertical plane.
Drift: Movement of the gyro spin axis in earth's horizontal plane.
Wander: Change of orientation of gyro axis, over time. Types of wander:
Total Drift = Real Wander + Apparent wander + Transport wander
Real Wander: Gyro axis moves with respect to inertial space.
- It is caused by rotor imperfections, imbalance, friction, etc.
- It causes both drift & topple.  Axis  Spin axis progressively
aligned  misaligned due to
Apparent Wander: Gyro axis seems to  North  earth's spin
move w.r.t. an observer on earth's surface.
- Caused by earth's rotation at 15.04°/hr.
- Rate of apparent wander: 15 x SIN Lat/hour.
- V.A Gyro: Max topple at equator.  Earth's rotatio
- H.A Gyro: Max topple at equator, Max drift at pole.

Transport Wander: It is the apparent change in the gyro axis, which
occurs when physically moving a gyro to another latitude, due to the

- No transport wander occurs if a/c moves N-S along same meridian.

Types of Gyro
Displacement Gyro: It has 2 gimbals & 2 degrees of freedom, e.g. AH.
- Space Gyro: It has full freedom to wander, with no restoring force.
- Tied Gyro: If it wanders, it is brought back by an external force.
e.g.: DG corrected by a flux valve; AH corrected by gravity.
- Earth Gyro: A type of Tied Gyro. Wander is restored by gravity
Kate Gyro: It measures angular rate, only 1 degree freedom, e.g., TSI.

DG - Directional Gyro
DHAT2
• Introduction
- Gyro Type: Horizontal Axis Tied-gyro, with 2 degrees of freedom.
- Principle: Rigidity for direction, Precession for gyro control.
- RPM: 12000
- DG provides a stable reference for maintaining the heading of an
aircraft, but it must be manually synchronised with a compass.
- It has no magnetic element; hence, it does not suffer from compass
turning/acceleration errors.
- Gyro rotor RPM is maintained either pneumatically by air-jets, or
electrically.
- A caging knob is provided to:
- Re-erect a toppled gyro;
- 'Cage it' before manoeuvres;
- Synchronise it with a compass.
- A 'Lat-nut' connected to its inner gimbal, is used to correct for
transport wander.
- Modern DGs can have up to 85° pitch & roll limits.
Errors in a Directional Gyro
Gimbal Error: It is caused by the geometry of the gyro gimbal system,
in which the alignment of the gimbal axis gets disturbed from the
aircraft axis due to aircraft manoeuvres.
- Maximum errors occur on inter-cardinal headings & during a
Instruments  combined pitch & roll change on any heading.
- Gimbal Lock: A gimbal error where one gimbal gets aligned
with another gimbal axis.
Cross-Coupling: It occurs when an aircraft turns with a 90° bank,
during which movement in one gyro axis is sensed in another axis.
Real & Apparent Wander: Explained in the previous chapter.
RPM: Less RPM = less rigidity

TSI - Turn & Slip Indicator
• Introduction  • THAR1
- Gyro Type: Horizontal Axis Rate-gyro, with 1 degree of freedom.
- Principle: Secondary Precession
- RPM: 4500  †  Angle of Bank = JAS. + 7
- TSI indicates rate-of-turn. Rate 1 = 3/sec  Rate 2 = 6°/sec f  Rate of Turn = _9TAN 0
Principle of Operation
- When an aircraft yaws about the vertical axis (Z), TSI rotor axis wants
to maintain the same axis (due to rigidity). But it cannot do so because
it has no freedom of movement in that axis.
- This force undergoes Primary Precession and acts along (Y) axis.
- If there was nothing to stop this precession, the rotor would continue
to precess. However, a calibrated spring holds it back. But this spring
tension causes a secondary precession, which acts along the initial
yaw axis of the aircraft, thereby assisting the initial force.
- When spring tension = secondary precession, the rotor stops there,
and a pointer attached to the rotor shows the rate-of-turn.
- TSI does not need any self-righting mechanism because as soon as
the yaw is over, precession is 0, spring tension straightens the rotor.

• Slip Indicator
- It is a ball, sealed in a curved glass tube which contains a liquid.
- It shows the interaction between gravity & aircraft centrifugal force.
- It indicates whether the aircraft is skidding or slipping, in a turn.
- When a/c skids, ball moves outward (centrifugal force has more effect
on it). When a/c slips, ball moves inward (gravity has more effect on it).
- If aircraft is in a right turn & slipping into the turn, the ball will be to
the right, RAF will be from the left & TSI needle will be to the right.
Errors in a TSI:
Rotor RPM: RPM | = precession | = indication l.
Spring Tension: TSI spring must have linear tension, else TSI will show
non-linear indication of turn. But this is not mechanically possible.
Pitching Error: Occurs due to 'cross-coupling', when aircraft is pitching
up & turning at the same time. Usually, an aircraft pitching up/down
is about the TSI rotor axis, with no effect on gyro. But if the gimbal
is tilted (due to turn) before the pitching commences, movement in
pitching plane causes additional precession. Thus, TSI will over-read.

Artificial Horizon
• Introduction  O: AVE2
- Gyro Type: Vertical-axis Earth-gyro, with 2 degrees of freedom.
- Principle: Rigidity for aircraft attitude, with respect to pitch & bank.
- RPM: 22500 (Electric), 15000 (Pneumatic)
- It has 360° freedom for roll, 85° freedom for pitch.
• Construction
- In level flight, the horizon bar is in the centre.
- During climb/descend, the rotor remains rigid, and the pitch gimbal
moves with the aircraft. This is transmitted to the horizon bar
through a guide pin in a curved slot, thus indicating pitch.
- During a bank, the rotor remains rigid & the roll gimbal moves with
the aircraft. Amount of bank is indicated on a curved scale.

Gyro Control
- It consists of lateral & longitudinal mercury levelling switches
(curved tubes containing mercury) & 2 torque control motors.
- Lateral switch detects roll & corrects it through a 'pitch torque motor'.
- Longitudinal switch detects pitch & corrects it through a roll torque
motor'.
• Errors in an Artificial Horizon
Acceleration Error (for an AH with rotor spinning clockwise)
- It is caused when the Artificial Horizon is subjected to acceleration
in the fore-aft axis. It shows a pitch-up & bank to the left during
acceleration & a pitch-down & bank to right during deceleration.
- In order to ensure rapid initial erection, AH is made bottom heavy.
But during acceleration, due to inertia, the bottom of the rotor
tends to move backwards. This force precesses through 90°, and
its base moves to the left and indicates a bank to the left.
- Acceleration also causes mercury in the levelling switch to move
back, which is interpreted as top-of-rotor moving towards the
pilot. Torque motor compensates by showing an apparent climb.
- Similarly, AH shows a descend & roll to right during deceleration.
- This error no longer exists after twice the 'time of acceleration'.
- An electric AH does not suffer from acceleration errors because:
- Rotor has high speed, thus, making it more rigid;
- Rotor is less bottom-heavy;
- It has a pitch cut-out switches: for acceleration > 0.18g;
- It has a roll cut-out switch: for bank > 10°.
===== [avh 0289]
6 - 17
Turning/Erection Error
- It occurs due to the displacement of the 'roll levelling switch' due
to a centrifugal force & thus causing a departure of the rotor axis
from vertical.
- This centrifugal force experienced by gyro is constant and at 90°
to the instantaneous heading of aircraft.
- Because of this, the top of the gyro will trace a circular path, 90°
ahead of the aircraft's nose, e.g., when an aircraft puts on a bank
to the right, due to centrifugal force, mercury in the levelling
switch gets deflected to the left and activates the torque motor &
tilts the rotor top to the right (because mercury switch senses a
rotor tilt to the lett).
- Turning Error Correction:
- Erection Cut-Out: Cutting off the power supply to the mercury
switch when the bank exceeds 10°.
- Pitch Bank Compensation: Above 10° bank, the bank switch
is disconnected. However, the pitch switch corrects for the
varying pitch & bank errors.
- Inclination of Gyro Spin Axis (1.6° to 2.5°): If an arrangement
can be made for the top of rotor axis to describe a circle
about itself, there would not be a variety of errors, but a
single constant error, which can be removed by a construction
modification.
Instruments
Good judgment comes from experience.
Unfortunately, experience usually comes from bad judgment.

°° Radio Altimeter
Introduction
- A radio-altimeter shows the instantaneous height of an aircraft
above the ground beneath it.
- It uses an FMCW (Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave) radar
in SHF band on 4300 MHz (4200 MHz - 4400 MHz).
- Since it is a CW radar, it needs one antenna for transmission and
another for reception.
- A standard radio altimeter shows altitude from 0' - 2500'.
- Radio altimeter accuracy is +3% of height or ‡1', whichever greater.
- Radio altimeter indication is compensated for displaying the height
of the lowest aircraft wheel from ground level.
Principle of Operation
- To calculate height, a radio altimeter determines the time taken for a
radio wave to travel from the aircraft to the ground beneath it & back.
During this time, transmission frequency changes at a known rate.
- By comparing the received frequency and the current transmission
frequency, it calculates the time delay, and thus, distance.
- Transmission beam has a width of 30° fore/aft & 60° sideways (to
cater for aircraft bank angles).

Errors in a Radio Altimeter
- Fixed Error: Errors in transmission frequency changes the height
calculation.
- Mushing Error: Occurs when the transmission & reception antenna
are not on the same plane (e.g., when aircraft climbs/descends).
- Aircraft Installation: Radio altimeter antenna & its settings need to
cater for the height from wheels to fuselage & the cable length from
receiver to avionics bay. This is called 'Residual Height. This distance
is different for different types of aircraft.
Advantages
- Radio altimeter gives the actual height of aircraft above the ground.
- No QNH setting is required.
- No pitot/static blockage errors.
- It can be coupled with auto-landing systems.
Limitations
- It cannot provide vertical separation between aircraft.
- It cannot provide warning of any terrain ahead of aircraft.

• Aerodynamic Alert Devices
Altitude Alert
- It is a system that warns a pilot when the aircraft is
approaching a pre-selected altitude or when it deviates
from an autopilot set altitude.
- When approaching 900' to a selected altitude, a 'white box' appears
around it in the PFD Primary Flight Display. When the aircraft is
within 300' of selected altitude, the white box disappears.
- Altitude alert is inhibited when the aircraft is on an ILS glide-slope or
if the aircraft configuration is 'flaps with undercarriage down'.
- If an aircraft deviates +300' from the selected altitude, then:
- Master caution + aural warning comes ON;
- EICAS caution message "ALTITUDE ALERT" appears;
- Altitude box in PFD becomes amber in colour.
- Altitude Alert is mandatory for all turbine engine aircraft & all
turboprop aircraft with AUW > 5700 kg or passenger > 9.
Overspeed Warning
- It alerts the crew if the aircraft speed is approaching Vo.
- Its indications are:
- Master warning + aural warning ON;
- EICAS caution message "OVER SPEED" appears.
Stall Warning
- Stall warning comes ON when the aircraft speed is within
Instruments  5 kts or 5% of its stall speed, whichever is more.
- Indications: visual, aural or sensory (stick shaker) warning.
- Stall warning system process information from the following inputs:
- Angle of attack indicator;
- Flap/slat position;
- Landing gear position;
- Airspeed.

- They are of various types:
- Probe Type: A slotted probe extends outside the aircraft, with a

pressure variations corresponding to the AOA, which is sensed.
- Vane Type: It is similar to probe type, & senses aircraft AOA.

Temperature Gauge
Expansion Type:
- Principle: Expansion of solids/liquids due to the rise in its temperature.
• Electrical Type (Thermocouples)
- Works on the principle of 'Seebeck Effect.
- It uses a bi-metallic strip of dissimilar properties. If it is heated at its
junction, free electrons are produced on both strips. This causes an
EMF between them, which can be measured.
- This system doesn't need an external electricity supply to work.
Instead, it converts heat energy into electrical energy. It is of 2 types:
- Surface Contact Type: Fitted on cylinder heads, to measure CHT.
- Immersion Type: Used for liquid/gas, to measure JPT/EGT. 2 types:
- Rapid Response: Used where exhaust gases are slow-moving.
- Stagnation Type: Used where exhaust gases are fast-moving.
- For accurate measurements, cold zone is placed on aircraft skin, so
that difference b/w hot & cold zone is not affected by change in OAT.
- CHT is measured at the hottest cylinder.
- EGT is measured at the LP turbine outlet.
Electrical Type (Resistance - Wheat Stone Bridge)
- It works on the principle of Ohm's Law.
- As the temperature of a conductor (metal) increases, its resistance/
conductivity changes, which is measured.
- This type of system is used to measure oil temperatures.  Instruments
• Radiation Pyrometer
- It works on the principle that the 'wavelength of radiation' emitted by
a body is proportional to its temperature.
- Radiation pyrometer directly senses the turbine blade temperature
(radiation frequency & wavelength) without any physical contact. It
then compares the measurement with a database of calibrated
values & indicates its temperature.
- Drawbacks: It is prone to sooting, and measurement is accurate
only at its calibrated value.

===== [avh 0295]
6 - 23
Torque Meter
Introduction
- A torque gauge measures the power generated by the engine.
- Torque = Force applied at a distance to a turning point.
- Power = Torque x RPM.
• Electric Torque Meter
- It consists of a torque meter assembly and a phase detector.
- A torque meter assembly has 2 concentric shafts:
- An Inner shaft, connected to the engine reduction gearbox;
- An outer shaft, connected to the engine output.
- Additionally, on both shafts, there are 2 toothed gears with pickup
heads (permanent magnets on top of a coil) attached on it.
- When there is no load, both shafts turn together & there is no
relative motion between them.
- When there is a load on the inner shaft connected to the gearbox, it
will twist slightly along its length and the toothed gears will have a
slight angular displacement between them.
- Pickup heads on both shafts pickup this angular difference and the
difference, proportional to the torque generated, is displayed.
Oil Torque Meter
- It consists of a helical gear placed along the engine shaft.
- This helical gear tries to moves axially when it is used to transfer
the power generated by the engine. The amount of this movement
is proportional to the thrust transferred.
- But this gear cannot be allowed to move axially, because then, their
teeth will no longer mesh together & the drive will fail. The gear is
kept in place by counteracting it with an oil pressure.
- This required oil pressure is proportional to the amount of thrust
generated, and it is sensed & displayed on an indicator.
Helical Gear

Vibrations on an aircraft are measured with 2 accelerometers.
- Frequency of the vibration is proportional to RPM, and the amplitude
of the vibration is proportional to the damage, if any.

°° INS - Inertial Navigation System &
IRS - Inertial Reference System
IRU Inertial Reference Unit
- It is a self-contained system, comprising of gyros & accelerometers.
- Each IRU has 3 gyros/RLGs (for the stabilising platform) & 3
accelerometers (for measuring the acceleration on 3 different axes).
- A typical INS/IRS system will have 3 such IRUs for redundancy.
INS & IRS
- INS needs its initial position to complete its alignment. This position
can be updated only on the ground and aircraft has to be stationary.
- INS computer calculates later aircraft positions from this initial
position. By programming waypoints, this system can navigate the
aircraft on a predetermined track.
- INS provides attitude, heading, acceleration & angular rate to FMS.
- INS position accuracy degrades with time. This is known as drift.
- If an INS is switched OFF & ON in flight, it can only be used in ATT
(Attitude) mode, which gives attitude & heading information only.
Old system  New, more powerful, integrated
Used mechanical gyros  Uses strap down RLG
Platform held stable mechanically  Platform stable mathematically
Components of an INS/IRS
- Gyro: To stabilise the platform on which accelerometers are mounted.
- Accelerometer: Aligned with reference axis N-S, E-W & up-down.
- Integrator: Integrates acceleration to get velocity in ground speed,
which is further integrated to get the distance.
Principle of Operation
- An INS works on Newton's Laws of Motion:
- Every action has an equal and opposite reaction;
- Acceleration is proportional to the force acting on the body.
- Accelerometers are kept level by 3 gyro stabilised platforms (in x, y,
z axes) to correct for aircraft roll, pitch & yaw. Thus accelerometers
always point N-S, E-W & up-down, to detect acceleration in these
directions, respectively.

===== [avh 0297]
6 - 25
00
INS Alignment
- An INS alignment, which is achieved independent of any
external data is known as Self Alignment. This process
can be sped up with Reference Alignment Method or by manually
updating the position.
Self Alignment:
- Warm-up Period (3-4 mins): Operating fluid is heated to ideal
temperatures.
- Coarse Levelling & Alignment: Pitch & roll motors are driven
until they are 90° to each other. The platform is roughly aligned
in azimuth to t1°.
- Gyro Compassing: In this, self-alignment is accomplished
without any external reference, by using the inertial platform's
accelerometer to slave it to earth's gravity vector & by employing
one of the gyros to seek the true-north by sensing the rotation of
the earth. This takes about 15 minutes.
- Vertical: Acceleration due to gravity is always perpendicular
to the earth's surface. This provides the vertical reference,
allowing the output for attitude.
- Latitude/True North: Once a vertical reference is attained, &
if aircraft is stationary, by detecting earth's rotation (15.04°/hr),
local latitude & true north can be determined. The problem is
that, sensing true-north requires knowing current latitude &
determining the latitude requires knowing the true-north. This
problem is solved using successive approximations of both
data. Fortunately, this process is convergent, and stops when
the desired precision is achieved. This process is quicker at
the equator (~10 mins), and takes more time at the poles.
Entering the latitude info manually will speed up this process.
- Longitude: INS needs longitude input. Usually, the system
memory will contain the last shutdown position, & if the
aircraft has not been moved since, this position can be used
to speed up alignment.
Reference Alignment Method
- Transferring gyro alignment from an external gyro.
- Synchro Memory: Storing aircraft switch-OFF position.
- HUD Alignment: Position input from a HUD/runway threshold.
Modes of INS Operation: OFF, STBY, ALIGN, NAV, ATT
- STBY: System is powered up & aircraft position info can be entered.
- ALIGN: Start gyro-compassing (aircraft has to be stationary).
- NAV: Start navigation. INS must be selected to 'NAV', before the
aircraft moves from its parked bay.
- ATT: Only attitude and heading information are available.
Advantages of INS
- High accuracy  - Passive: No radiation
- Autonomous: no external input needed  - Self contained system
- All weather operation  - Global use
===== [avh 0298]
6 - 26
oo Errors in an INS
Real Drift: These are errors due to construction imperfections.
- This error is compounded when the velocity is integrated
into distance, causing a position drift of up to +2 nm/hr.
- This error reduces if the INS position is updated from GPS.
Apparent Drift/Transport Wander
- It is an apparent drift that occurs due to the convergence of
meridians, when physically moving from one latitude to another.
- This error can be corrected by a 'Lat Nut' on the INS.
Schuler Loop: As an inertial platform accelerates in one plane, it not
only detects the linear acceleration, but the platform will also tilt
and detect a component of gravity (like somatogravic illusion). The
opposite occurs during deceleration. 'Schuler tuning' caters for this,
but this correction never fully catches up with the system.
Theoretically, anywhere on earth, maximum error occurs at 42.2
minutes, and error reduces to 'O' at 84.4 minutes. Practically this
error grows with each loop.
Coriolis: This error occurs because when the aircraft is flying 'straight
and level', it is actually flying a curved path, parallel to the curved
surface of the earth. This error is known & can be compensated for.
Earth's Rotation: When an aircraft is flying, the earth is rotating
under it. The rate of this error is known can be catered for.
Another Method of Classification of Errors
Inherent Errors: Errors due to construction, balance & complexity of
the instrument.
Instruments  Bounded Errors: These are errors due to -
- Platform tilt due to its misalignment;
- Accelerometer bias: Slight output even if aircraft is stationary;
- 15t stage integrators errors;
- Schuler Loop - Errors that build-up to maximum & return to zero
within 84.4 minutes.
Unbounded Errors: These are cumulative track/distance errors,
which increases with time. They are:
- Initial azimuth misalignment;
- Azimuth gyro wander;
- Levelling gyro topple;
- 2nd stage integrators errors.
Kalman Filter
- It is a system used to improve the accuracy of an INS.
- This system knows the individual error rates of position information
of different sources. e.g., INS is accurate in the short term, but it
drifts 2 nm in 3 hrs. Beyond 3 hrs, a VOR/DME is more accurate, etc.
- A computer algorithm calculates this position error by inputs from
various sources, corrects the error & gives the best hybrid position
information at that time, to the pilot.

• RLG - Ring Laser Gyro
• Principle of Operation
- In 1913, one Mr Sagnac observed that the frequency of two counter
propagating waves in a cavity would be shifted by an amount that is
proportional to its angular velocity.
f = frequency,
c = f A but f = n/t Therefore c = n N/t  n = no. of cycles
1 = Wave length
- So if t' reduces because of rotation, to  t = time
keep 'c' constant, 'I' has to 1 & 'f' has to 1.  c = speed of light
- By sensing this frequency shitt, angular velocity can be calculated.
• Construction
- RLG has a resonant cavity with 3 or more mirrors, in which a laser
can travel continuously along an optical route, in both clockwise and
anti-clockwise directions.
- A laser is used because it is monochromatic, coherent & directional.
- The cavity is filled with ionised helium-neon gas, which provides a
good gain over a very narrow bandwidth. By carefully controlling the
gain, only 1 resonating frequency of the laser will be sustained.
- If RLG is stationary, the frequency of the clockwise & anti-clockwise
beams will be the same. If there is angular rotation, the laser path
length will † & frequency will I, which is measured by the formula:
A = Area enclosed
J Fq difference Af = 4AQ/AL  - = Length of path
1 = Wave length
- Fibre Optic Gyro: It is an improvisation on RLG,  Q = Rate of rotation
& uses a circular fibre optic cable, instead of mirrors.

RLG Errors
- Thermal Errors: Heating of the cavity causes path expansion.
- Null Shift: Without any angular rotation input, you may still get

- Scale Factor: Laser is passing through a gas, not vacuum, thus,

===== [avh 0300]
6 - 28
• Autopilot
Introduction
- Autopilot gives aircraft guidance in speed, altitude, heading & VOR
radial holding. It also gives aircraft stabilisation in pitch, wings level
& yaw damping. Auto-trim is available in the pitch axis only.
- If an autopilot is engaged without any mode, automatic stabilisation
is provided & auto-trim may be available.
- When crossing overhead a VOR 'cone of confusion', the autopilot
maintains the last heading, till the VOR radial is re-captured.
- Crossing the last waypoint, the autopilot changes to heading mode.
- Changing altimeter sub-scale after all-hold will not change a/c altitude.
- A synchronisation unit will prevent an unserviceable autopilot
engagement & prevents snatching during auto-pilot disengagement.
- During a go-around, autothrottle opens power to TOGA & aircraft
pitch is raised 15°. Landing gear has to be manually raised up.
- Single pilot 'night IFR operations' need an autopilot that can hold
heading & altitude.
Yaw Damper
- It is a part of the autopilot. It senses aircraft yaw rate & moves the
rudder in the opposite direction, in proportion to the rate of yaw.
- It also prevents a 'Dutch Roll'. (See also: Aerodynamics > Dutch Roll)
Autothrottle
- Autothrottle automatically adjusts the engine power, to maintain
aircraft performance as demanded by the autopilot.
- It is used to maintain constant engine power during takeoff & climb.
Instruments  - It also maintains a constant airspeed or mach no., during cruise.
Autoland  (See also: Air Regulations > Precision Approach)
- Semi Auto-land: Autopilot maintains the speed & attitude on approach
till DH; thereafter, a manual landing is carried out.
- Auto-land: Autopilot approach (ILS) + Auto-land + Auto-rollout (with
or without Auto-brakes)  (See also: Airframe > Brakes > Auto-brakes)
- ILS Cat 3A: Auto-land is completed at the start of the landing roll.
- ILS Cat 3B: Auto-land process is completed when the pilot
disconnects the autopilot, at the end of the landing roll.
- Fail Passive Autopilot: A system with 2 auto-pilots. If one fails,
there is no significant out-of-trim conditions or deviation from flight
path, but landing will not be done automatically.
- Fail Operational: A system with 3 or more autopilots. If one fails
below the alert height, the system will function as normal & continues
for autolanding, but will function as fail-passive from then on.
Autoland Sequence
- 2500': Radio altimeter becomes operational.
- 1500: Glideslope and localiser is captured.
- Offline autopilot is engaged to provide protection.
- Flare mode is armed.
- 330': Stabiliser trims nose-up, elevators move down to counterbalance.
- 50': ILS glide-slope is disconnected.
- Flare-mode takes over pitch. ROD is reduced to 2'/sec.
- Autothrottle retards thrust.
- 5: Auto-flare disengages, a/c touches down, roll-out mode engages.
- On Touchdown, elevators brought down to keep nose wheel down.
- Autothrottle disengages, reverse thrust engages.
- Auto-pilot stays ON until the pilot disconnects it.
===== [avh 0301]
6 - 29
° EFIS Electronic Flight Instrumentation System
Introduction
- EFIS presents aircraft attitude information on an EADI (Electronic
Attitude & Direction Indicator) and nav-information on an EHSI
(Electronic Horizontal Situation Indicator), in an ergonomic format.
- 3 levels of messages appear on CDU: warning, caution & advisory.
Colour Coding:
- White: Current data, present status, ranges/scales.
- Green: Selected data, engaged modes, autopilot mode.
- Magenta: Headings, pointers, active route, FDS commands.

• FMS - Flight Management System
Introduction
- FMS is an integrated suite of sensors, receivers & computers (FMC
Flight Management Computer), coupled with a nav-database.
- It improves navigation, fuel efficiency & reduces crew workload.
- It has 2 CDUs for pilot interface & to input data into the FMC.
- Dual Mode: FMCs process info independently & compares the result.
- Single Mode: In case 1 FMC fails, the other takes over.
- Functions - Flight Planning  - Guidance & auto-pilot
- A/c performance calculations - Position determination
- FMS navigation accuracy is .05 nm/hr.
- FMS Navigational Database: Consists of ATS routes, STAR, SID,
aerodrome/nav-aid information, etc. No RT frequencies are included.
Database is valid for 28 days & can only be updated on the ground.
- FMS Performance Database: Optimum flight levels, cruise speeds.
Sequence of FMS CDU Pages on Startup
- IDENT Page: On startup, aircraft model, configuration,
- POS INIT Page: To initialise UTC & heading/position of IRS.
- RTE Page: To insert the route waypoints - origin, route, destination.
- PREF INIT: Current performance: a/c weight, fuel, altitude, cost index.
- CLB Climb: VNAV, LNAV & timing functions.
- CRZ Cruise: Cruise climb options.
- DES Decent: Aircraft descent profile.
LNAV: Normally, FMS flies 'great circle' tracks between 2 waypoints.  Instruments
- Route Navigation is done by LNAV, by inputs from INS, VOR, DME,
ADF & GPS. It normally relies on a GPS or a DME/DME fix.
- Most accurate position is by a DME/DME fix (DME errors are < .3nm).
- Maximum DME range FMC uses for determining position is 25 nm.
- FMC combines short term accuracy of INS with the long term
accuracy of external references.
VNAV: Entering cost index 'O' provides economy speeds & maximum range.
- Performance management is done by VNAV & ATM (Automatic
Thrust Management)

between 2 signals or 2 corresponding points in

It bends toward the denser medium.
Frequency 1 = refraction J.

Radio Nav-aids  fluctuations in the ionosphere. It usually happens during dawn/dusk,

Attenuation: It is the gradual loss of signal strength as it travels outwards.
It depends on:
- Frequency: Frequency 1 = attenuation 1. VLF has maximum range.
- Absorption: Radiation energy is absorbed & scattered by air, water
vapour, dust, etc. Frequency 1 = absorption 1.
- Depth of Penetration: More penetration 1 = attenuation †.
- Type of Surface: Higher attenuation on land, less attenuation at sea.
- Polarisation: Vertical polarisation = minimum attenuation.

===== [avh 0307]
7 - 5
•• Propagation
1. Ground Wave (Non-lonospheric Propagation) is of 2 types:
1a. Surface Wave
- It occurs for fqs between 20 kHz - 50 MHz (upper VLF - lower VHF)
due to the diffraction of waves moving along the earth's surface.
- For a surface wave, frequency 1 = range l. Power 1 = range 1.
1b. Space Wave: It is further sub-divided into 2 types:
1b i. Ground Reflected Wave: Surface wave reflected off the ground.
1b ii. Direct Wave: These are frequencies with direct line of sight
reception (VHF, UHF). Due to atmospheric refraction, VHF
ranges are generally 7% more than the actual line of sight range.
Super Refraction (Duct propagation):
- It is a phenomenon in which VHF waves experience a
downward bend, increasing their range up to 40%.
- Pre-conditions: Inversion layer: pronounced radiation cooling;
- High pressure, causing subsidence;
- High humidity.
Sub Refraction: A phenomenon that is rarer than 'super refraction'.
- It causes a reduction in VHF ranges, by up to 20%.
- Its pre-conditions are opposite to that of super refraction.
2. Skywave (lonospheric Propagation):
- Skywave occurs for frequency between 2 MHz - 30 MHz (HF).
- Solar radiation in UV & short-wavelength ionise the air molecules in
stratosphere & above, thus changing its refractive index.
- These ionisation layers cause radio waves to reflect back to earth.
- Highest ionisation of the atmosphere occurs at 1400 hrs.
- lonisation layers are: D layer (between 50 - 100 km), E layer
(100 km - 150 km) & F1, F2 layer (200 km - 250 km).
- Diurnal Effect: At night, solar radiation stops. This causes D layer
to disappear, E to move up, and F1 & F2 to combine. This 1 height
of ionisation layer, causing skip distance to 1. So, at night, HF fqs
are decreased to reduce skip distance & maintain same HF ranges.
- Frequency 1 = critical angle 1, skip distance 1, dead space 1.
Critical Angle: Angle b/w 1 to transmitter & 1st skywave return. Any
angle < CA will escape into space. CA for 3 MHz = 0°, 30 MHz = 90°.
Skip Distance: Distance between transmitter & 1st skywave reception.
- Max skip distance (nm) = 1.43VH (height of ionosphere in km)
Dead Space: Distance between ground wave range & 1st skywave.

000 Modulation
Modulation: It is the process of impressing a modulating wave
(information) onto a carrier wave (carrier).
Amplitude Modulation: Keeping the frequency constant, the amplitude
of the carrier is modified as per the amplitude of the modulating wave.
Modulation Depth: Extend to which carrier is  Edulated, excessed 1% = Amplitude of samier
Frequency Modulation: Keeping the amplitude constant, the frequency
of the carrier is modified as per the amplitude of the modulating wave.
- FM has reduced ranges, but better signal quality than AM.
- It has a simple transmitter & a complex receiver.
- FM is unsuitable below VHF band.
- Pulse Modulation: In this, transmission is sent out in short bursts.
it can be used in both AM & FM, & is used in radars, data exchange
in communication systems, etc.
Phase Modulation: Keeping amplitude & fq constant, phase angle of the
carrier wave is changed. Used in digital transmission, e.g., MLS, GPS.

ooo Sidebands: All forms of modulation produce sidebands, of trequencies
higher & lower than the carrier frequency. Modulating a 900 kHz
carrier with a 1 kHz audio creates components of 901 kHz USB Upper
Sideband & 899 kHz LSB Lower Sideband along with the original
carrier 900 kHz. This full range of frequencies (899 kHz - 901 kHz) is
called its Bandwidth. So, a receiver should be capable of admitting
adequate frequency range on either side of the carrier frequency
because in an AM/FM modulation, it is the sidebands (USB & LSB)
that carry the information & not the original carrier wave.
VA, WIDSB Double Sideband Tx: In this, the full bandwidth (USB + LSB+
carrier) is transmitted. All VHF & UHF transmissions are DSB.
- SSB Single Sideband Tx: In this, the transmitter removes the carrier
wave & one of the sidebands before transmission. These are added
back at the receiver using a BFO. All HF transmission (JE) is SSB.

000 Communications
LF: LF has up to 2000 km & VLF 5000-20000 km transmission ranges.
- Disadvantages:
- LF has high static. The lower the frequency, the more is the static.
- High power is needed for its transmission.
- High cost of installation.
- Uses large aerial, with length min ½ wavelength of tx frequency.
HF (SSB) (JE): HF communication is between 2 - 25 MHz.
- HF communication uses Amplitude Modulation.
- HF has lesser static than LF.
- Due to the presence of sky waves, HF has longer ranges than VHF.
- HF datalink is used in Oceanic Control. It uses USB for data.
- The higher the HF frequency, the higher is the attenuation.
- The higher the HF frequency, the more is the skip distance.
- At night, E layer moves up. So fqs are | to cater for f in skip distance.
MUF Max Usable Frequency: MUF is the highest frequency that
can be used for transmission between 2 points via sky waves, under
prevailing ionospheric conditions, at a specified time.
- OUF Optimum Usable Frequency = 0.85 x MUF.

- Time of day  - Seasons

sporadic E layer, thereby causing disturbances.
SELCAL: A system used in HF transmission, that employs an audio

Types of Transmissions
- Simplex: Comm b/w 2 stations happen one at a time (walkie-talkie).
- Duplex: Both stations can talk at the same time (mobile phones).
- Semi Duplex: Simplex at one end, duplex at the other end.
Parts of a Simple Transmitter
- Microphone/Audio Oscillator: Information signals are produced.
- Speech Processor: Extreme frequencies are removed. Amplitude
variation is reduced to make low volume parts of speech more audible.
- Pre-amplifier: Signals are amplified until it is strong enough to pass
through the remainder of the transmitter components.
- RF Oscillator: RF carrier wave is generated in an oscillator, whose
fq is controlled by quartz crystals and a semiconductor circuit.
- Mixer/Modulator: Carrier wave is modulated by the modulator.
- Power Amplifier: RF signal is amplified again before transmission.
Heterodyne Receiver. The term 'heterodyne' was coined by Mr Fessenden,
its inventor, from the Greek word 'hetero' meaning different & 'dyn'
meaning power. It is used to shift 1 frequency into another. A Heterodyne
receiver contains a BFO. Incoming signal from the antenna is mixed
(heterodyned) with a signal from a local oscillator (LO) to produce a fixed
lower frequency signal called intermediate frequency (IF). IF signal is
amplified, filtered & is applied to a demodulator that extracts audio signal.

Characteristics of a Receiver
- Selectivity: Ability to select a particular fq while rejecting others.
Radio Nav-aids  - Sensitivity: Reproduce strong sound even if incoming signal is weak.
- Fidelity: Faithfully reproduce entire fq range received at the antenna.
What is a BFO Beat Frequency Oscillator?
In a radio receiver, a BFO is an oscillator used to create an audio frequency
signal from morse-code radio-telegraphy (CW), to make them audible. or to
demodulate single-sideband (SSB) (HF)  signals, by restoring the carrier that
was suppressed at the fransmitter. A BFO produces a radio signal close to the
frequency of the received signal. When a mixer mixes the BFO & the received
signal, 2 'beat frequencies, equal to the sum & difference of these two
frequencies are created.
idits a dans elver is tuned to a morse code signal, fiF 40000 Hz. That means
dahs' are pulses of a 40000 Hz signal, which is inaudible. To make
them audible, the frequency needs to be shifted into audio range faudio 1000
Hz. To achieve this, the desired BFO frequency is fBFo = 41000 or 39000 Hz.
When fir is mixed with fero, it creates two other frequencies or heterodynes.
(fiF - fBFO), and (fF + fBFO). The difference in frequency (fIF - fBFO) 1000HZ, IS
also known as beat frequency. The other, the sum frequency, (fr + for) =
81000 or 79000 Hz, is removed by a lowpass filter.
By varying BFO frequency around 41000 or 39000) Hz, the listener can
vary the output audio frequency & correct for small differences between tuning
of transmitter & receiver.

Antenna: It is a structure designed to transmit a radio wave when it is

supplied with opposite phases of an AC. When energised, it
generates an electric field primarily & a magnetic field secondarily.
Loop Antenna: A loop of wire, when energised, generating a magnetic
field primarily & electric field secondarily.
Yagi-Uda Antenna: It consists of -
- Driven Element (one). Connected to a transmitter or a receiver.
- Directors (one or more). Slightly shorter than driven element.
- Reflectors (longer than driven element). They are not connected
to transmitter or receiver. Reflectors absorb
& re-radiate radio waves from driven element
with a different phase & enhance radiation in  Reflector
a single direction. It substantially † antenna
gain when compared to a simple dipole.
ow Antenna Gain: It is the ratio between 'radiation intensity' in a given
direction, to that produced by an ideal antenna that transmits in all
directions. It is expressed in decibel. In a transmitter antenna, it is how
well it converts input power into radio waves, in a specified direction.
In a receiver antenna, it is how well it converts radio waves arriving
from a specified direction into electrical power.
Decibel dB = 10 x log watt.  100 watt = 10 x log100 = 10 × 2 = 20 dB

- VDF facilitates an ATC controller to provide a pilot with bearings to

aircraft is used to find its direction.
- Bearing measurement for VDF (QDMs & QTEs) takes place at the

Factors Affecting VDF Accuracy
- Propagation: Aircraft transmission is reflected by terrain before it
reaches the receiver, giving wrong indications.
- Aircraft Attitude: VHF transmissions are vertically polarised. Best
reception occurs when the aircraft is flying straight and level.
- Cone of Confusion: Poor bearing accuracy when the aircraft is
overhead the nav-aid.
- Multiple Transmissions: When 2 aircraft transmit together, it
causes interference and reception error.
VDF Approach: Pilot interprets the VDF bearings, calculates the drift,
applies it to his heading & follows a published approach procedure.
QGH Homing and Controlled Descent: Controller interprets the VDF
bearings & pass headings for a pilot to fly along a published path.

7 - 12
000 ADF Automatic Direction Finding
Introduction
- ADF is the aircraft-side equipment for receiving NDB transmissions.
- It gives a direct indication of the aircraft's relative bearing with respect
Qg) to an NDB. This is unlike a VOR, wherein the aircraft VOR receiver
decodes and displays radials on the RMI, as it was encoded and
transmitted from a VOR station. (See also: VOR)
* Although NDBs transmit only between 190 kHz - 450 kHz, ADF
receivers can tune between 190 kHz - 1750 kHz so that it can receive
AM radio frequencies also. (See also: NDB)
* Principle of Operation: Bearing by Loop Theory. P
Loop Aerial
- A voltage is developed in both arms of ADF loop aerial, because of
the phase difference between the incident NDB signal on each arm.
- When this loop is rotated & becomes parallel to NDB transmission,
maximum phase difference occurs, which induces max voltage in it.
When the loop is perpendicular to transmission, there is no phase
difference in the loop arms & 'O' voltage is induced. As the loop
continues to rotate, voltage develops & drops continuously.
- Polar Diagram thus formed is a figure of '8', with '8' pointing to the
direction of NDB transmission. But then, there is a 180° ambiguity.
Sense Aerial
- To resolve the '180° ambiguity', a 'sense aerial' is added. Its
reception forms a polar diagram in the shape of a circle.
- Both the polar diagrams are superimposed & a Cardioid is formed.
- This Cardioid has a single 'null' position, indicating the direction of
NDB transmission. Accurate 'null' is obtained when the loop aerial is
rotated clockwise to provide maximum Cardioid strength.
- In reality, there is no physical rotating loop aerial in the aircraft. It is
electronically done by 4 fixed coils that simulate a rotation.

Why is NDB not transmitted on an HF frequency for better ranges?
NDB is not transmitted in HF frequency because NDB signals are meant to be
intercepted by the vertical arm of the ADF loop aerial. HF operates in skywave,
and skywave signals will be intercepted by horizontal arms too, which will
cause erratic direction readings.
===== [avh 0315]
7 - 13
Factors Affecting ADF Accuracy
DOC Designated Operational Coverage:
- Beyond DOC range, NDBs may have higher bearing errors.
Station Interference
- Due to congestion in LF/MF bands, there may be a possibility of
interference from adjacent stations.
- Remedy: Do not use NDB for navigation beyond its DOC.
Static in Precipitation
- Static is caused by the collision of water drops & ice on aircraft.
- This increases the signal to noise ratio, and in extreme cases,
masks the NDB signals.
- Indications: A wandering NDB needle.
Static in Thunderstorms
- Lightning causes discharges in MF/LF, causing the ADF needle
lock towards lightning.
- NDB needle may also lock towards CB cells.
Mountain Effect
- Mountains can cause reflections and diffraction at low altitudes.
- Remedy: Fewer errors occur if aircraft is flying at high altitudes.
Night Effect/Skywave Interference
By day, MF propagates by surface waves.
- During night, D-layer disappears, E-layer moves up & starts
refracting MF signals back to earth as skywave.
- Thus, ADF receiving loop will get 2 signals - from surface wave
& skywave. This degrades 'cardioid null'.
This can cause errors up to 30° beyond 70-100 nm from an NDB.
- Max errors occur at dusk & dawn, when ionosphere is in transition.
Coastal Refraction
- It is the error caused due to refraction of the wave & its bending
away from the normal, when it crosses coast into the sea.  Radio Nav-aids
- No refraction occurs when the bearing is 90° to the station.
- Remedy - Use NDB located closer to the coastline.
- Fly at high altitudes.
- Take a fix only when the  WDB Signal
aircraft is 90° to NDB.
Land  NDB
Angle of Dip
- Vertically polarised signals will induce errors if aircraft is banked.
- This error is only present when the aircraft is not in level flight.
Quadrantal Error
- Polar diagram of the loop aerial may be distorted by the
airtrame, which produces a strong fore-aft field.
- Maximum error occurs when aircraft is flying a relative bearing of
045°, 135°, 225° & 315° to the NDB.
Loop Mis-Alignment
- Occurs when loop aerial is not aligned to the aircraft fore-aft axis.
- This error is equal to the amount of misalignment.
Lack of Failure Warning System
- Unlike a VOR, an error in ADF signals gives no warning to a pilot.
===== [avh 0316]
7 - 14
000 VOR VHF Omni Directional Range
Introduction
- Principle: Bearing measurement by phase comparison.
- VOR Frequency Range: All even decimals 108.0 MHz - 112.0 MHz
(108.0, 108.05, 108.2...) 40 channels, & all decimals from 112.0 MHz
- 117.975 MHz (112.0, 112.05, 112.1...) 120 channels.
- VOR signal is horizontally polarised & require a horizontal antenna.
- Since VOR is in VHF band, it is free from static and night effect.
- Beacon Identification: A 3-letter VOR designator 'keyed morse
code' is encoded in the beacon signal at least once in 10 seconds.
VOR can also encode voice ATIS info in its beacon identification.
Principle of Operation
- VOR transmits 2 signals at a different phase difference.
- Omni-directional Reference Signal: It is a constant phase, 30 Hz
EM signal on a 9960 Hz carrier. The 30 Hz component of the signal
is used as the reference in the aircraft. Aircraft receives the same
phase 360° around the VOR. Its polar diagram is a circle.
- Directional Signal: A rotating AM directional signal is generated by
electronically rotating the signal 30 times per second, clockwise
(thus giving it a characteristic of 30 Hz) by 50 antennae placed in a
circle, each with a progressive phase difference. Its polar diagram is
a figure of '8', rotating 30 times a second.
- The resultant of both polar diagrams is a rotating LIMACON.
- 30 Hz FM reference signal is synchronised with 30 rev/sec AM signal
such that they are in phase at 000° direction. In any other direction, the
phase difference between them will give the magnetic bearing to the
VOR. e.g., a phase difference of 227° between the reference &
directional signals means the aircraft is on radial 227°

Types of VOR
BVOR (Broadcast): Transmits voice ATIS info in beacon identification.
CVOR (Conventional VOR): Old type VOR.
DVOR (Doppler VOR)
- It is a 2nd-gen VOR, developed to improve accuracy, as, in C-VOR,
as, the AM (variable signal) was prone to diffraction & site error.
- In D-VOR reference signal is 30 Hz AM & directional signal is FM
(transmitted by the 2 opposing antenna elements electronically rotating
30 times/sec, causing a Doppler effect & an apparent FM modulation).
- This simulated rotation of directional signal is also anti-clockwise
- D-VOR is more accurate that C-VOR, & is free from site error.
- No change in aircraft equipment is needed.
TVOR (Terminal): It is a low power (50 watts) VOR, with range < 50 nm.
VOT Test VOR: It is used for testing the aircraft VOR receiver.
- VOT (usually on 108.0 MHz) broadcasts '000° radial' all around.
- When VOT fq is tuned, RMI needle should indicate radial 180°.
- VOT test accuracy on ground must be < t4°.

Advantages of a VOR
- Cockpit indications easy to follow, with left/right indications on a CDI.
- A system failure waring is available on the HSI.
- It has a small receiver antenna.
- It is free from static & night effect.
- VOR can be paired with a corresponding frequency of a DME.
Radio Nav-aids
Factors Affecting VOR Accuracy
- Beacon Misalignment: It is monitored by the site-monitor.
- Site Error: Caused by terrain/obstructions around the transmitter.
Error +2°. Site error is reduced by using a DVOR.
- Propagation Error: Errors after signal leaves transmitter. Error ‡1°.
- Interference Error: Interference from other VOR stations. It is
removed by enforcing DOC (Designated Operational Coverage).
- Airborne Equipment Error: Maximum error permitted is ‡3°
- VOR transmission accuracy must be within +3°, 95% of time.
- Combined with airborne equipment, error must be < +5°, 95% of time.
- Form airborne check point: Maximum error permitted t6°.
- From a ground checkpoint or VOT test: Maximum error permitted t4°.
Factors Affecting VOR Range (same as VHF transmission)
- Tx Power: En-route VOR of 200 watts gives ranges up to 200 nm.
- Transmitter & Receiver Altitude: VOR works on 'line of sight'.
- DOC: Unlike NDB, for a VOR, DOC is promulgated for day & night.

000 DME Distance Measuring Equipment
Introduction
- Principle: Secondary radar.
- DME works in UHF band, 962 MHz - 1213 MHz, at 1 MHz spacing.
This provides 252 channels. 126 for interrogation & 126 for reply.
- If a DME is co-located with a VOR, DME ground transponders must
be within 100' of a VOR in a TMA, & within 2000' outside a TMA.
Principle of Operation
- Aircraft DME interrogator transmits omni-directional pulse-pairs &
its receiver searches for a reply from any ground station.
- These pulse-pairs are transmitted at random intervals. This ensures
uniqueness. A/c will only accept replies that match this randomisation.
- In initial search mode, aircraft transmits 150 pp/sec for 100 secs. If
there is no lock-on with any DME, transmission is reduced to
60 pp/sec. In case of lock-on, aircraft transmission is at 25 pp/sec.
- On reception of the aircraft signal, DME ground transponder retransmit
this pulse-pair, 63 MHz removed, and after a delay of 50 ps.
- Aircraft receiver identifies its own unique pulse-pair (transmitted
pulse ‡ 63 MHz), measures the time gap between its transmission
& ground reply & calculates the distance.
Beacon Saturation
A DME station can service maximum 100 aircraft at one
time. Assumption is, 95% of aircraft are in tracking mode
(95% of 25 = 24 pp/sec), & 5% is in search mode (5% of 60
= 3 pp/sec). Thus, an average of 27 pp/sec per aircraft is
expected to be received at ground station. So, DME outputs
a constant 2700 pp/sec even if there is no interrogation
from any aircraft. When DME receives more than 2700 pp/
sec (> 100 aircraft transmitting), it reduces its gain so that
only the strongest 100 aircraft signals are responded to.  Radio Nav-aids
A typical DME
Advantages of DME  transmitter
- It provides an accurate (but slant) range.
- It can convert the range into ground speed & EET.
- It is not affected by rain (because it works in UHF).
- Approach procedures can be developed (DME arc).
Errors of DME
- DME accuracy: ‡0.25 nm or ‡1.25% of the range, whichever greater.
• Ground speed will be accurate only if a/c flying towards or from station.
- Distance shown is a slant range. When aircraft is overhead, it shows
the height of the aircraft.

000 ILS Instrument Landing System
Introduction  (See also: Air Regulations > Precision Approach)
- Principle: Approach guidance by lobe comparison.
- Beacon identification: A 4-letter designator starting with the letter i.
- If ILS is installed for both runways, only one will be operational at a
time to avoid interference.
- If glideslope fails, that approach becomes an NPA. If localiser fails,
ILS approach is not authorised.
Parts of an ILS: 3 parts  (See also: Air Regulation > Approach Lighting)
1. Visual Information: Approach lighting & runway centreline lighting.
Localiser is a Yagi aerial transmitter, located 1000' upwind end of the r/w.
- It transmits 2 overlapping lobes along the centreline of a runway.
Left lobe is at 90 Hz (yellow), right lobe is at 150 Hz (blue).
- If depth modulation between these 2 lobes is 'O', it indicates a/c
is on centreline. Depth modulation increase away from centreline.
e.g. if aircraft is on the left, it receives more of 90 Hz modulation.
- Localiser Frequency Range: All odd decimals from 108.1 MHz
to 111.9 MHz (108.1, 108.15, 108.3... etc.), on VHF, 40 channels.
- Localiser Coverage: +35° till 17 nm (*10 nm) & ‡10° till 25 nm
(*18 nm), of the centreline (*reduced coverage).
- Localiser is adjusted to give full-scale deflection when 700' from
the threshold.

• MLS Microwave Landing System
Introduction
- MLS was developed to overcome the limitations of ILS.
- It works in SHF band, 5030 MHz - 5090 MHz, & has 200 channels.
- It uses a 'Time Reference Scanning Beam' for providing guidance.
Principle of Operation
MLS employs 'time division multiplexing' where only 1 frequency is
used on a particular channel. Transmission of the two guidance
beams (Az Azimuth & GS Glideslope) & transmission from the other
components are synchronised to assure interference-free operation.
Information Transmitted in an MLS Signal
Azimuth: A beam scans side to side at a uniform speed, with the time
interval between them proportional to the angular position of aircraft
in relation to centreline. Pilot can also choose to fly a predetermined
approach at any angle to the runway, not just the centreline.
- Coverage: Horizontal: 20 nm +40°, Vertical: 0.9°-15°, upto 20000'
- Accuracy: +20' horizontal, +2' vertical.
Glideslope: Glideslope signal is transmitted on the same frequency
(time-shared) & in the same area covered by the azimuth transmitter.
Pilot also can select any particular glide angle.
Back Azimuth: It is used for overshoot/departure guidance.
- Coverage: Horizontal: 10 nm, +20°  °, Vertical 15°, up to 10000'.
Flare: It provides 'flare information' (before touchdown) to the aircraft.
DME: MLS DME has an accuracy of 100'.
Auxiliary Data: Station ident, runway condition, weather information etc
Advantages of MLS
- It is also possible to program segmented/curved approaches.
- It has increased azimuth. Aircraft can choose their own glide path.
Radio Nav-aids  - It is compatible with conventional ILS & EFIS. Its control unit is a
combined multimode ILS/MLS/GPS receiver.
- Cockpit display similar to ILS, with indication relative to selected course
- No issue with back course transmission, up to +20° of c/l, 15° elevation.
- Operates in SHF band & can be used in hilly terrain, no interference.
- It has 200 channels available.
- It has a built-in DME.

300 Primary Radar
Introduction
- Primary radar works on reflected energy. Only one frequency is used.
- It uses 'echo' principle for range & 'searchlight' principle for bearing.
- Radar transmitter & receiver share the same antenna.
- Radar frequencies are VHF & above.
- An actual radar pulse is not a square wave. Its strength rises & falls.
- Pulse Width: Time between the leading & trailing edges of a single
pulse, where the pulse is at 50% strength.
Pulse width  Beam width
- Beam Width: Angle in which transmitted
power is > 50% of the peak power.  obe
Pulse:  Pulse
- PRF Pulse Recurrence Frequency:  50%  decay
rise strength
time  time  Side

- PRI/P Pulse Recurrence Interval/Period:

pulse transmissions. J  Pulse Width
- Lower wavelength = narrower beam,  PRI
shorter pulse, causing efficient reflection from objects.
- Larger the antenna = narrower the beam = more accurate bearing.
- An FMCW Radar has no minimum range limitation, & its max range
is depended on its max power output.
Principle of Operation
Range: It is calculated by timing the transmission pulse & its return.
- Max Range of a radar is determined by its PRF. PRF 1 = range 1.
- Min Range is determined by pulse width. PW I = min range l.
- Radar Range also depends on:
- Transmission power. To double range, power has to 1 16x.
- Characteristics of reflecting objects/Radar Cross Section.
- Target height & height of radar head: 1.23 (VHTx + VHRx).
- Radar wavelength & wave attenuation.
- Atmospheric conditions: super/sub-refraction.
- Restoration Time: Time required for a receiver to re-activate
after a pulse transmission.

Range Resolution: If pulse width is high & 2 targets are close to each
other (one behind the other), the reflected pulse will engulf both
targets & the radar will see both target as 1.
Bearing Resolution: If beam width is high & 2 targets are close laterally,
the reflected pulse will engulf both targets & radar will see both as 1.
Terminal Surveillance Radar uses a 10, 23, or 50 cm wavelength radar.
Aerodrome Surveillance Radar uses a 3 cm or a 10 cm radar
Precision Approach Radar uses a 3 cm wavelength radar.
===== [avh 0324]
7 - 22
Doppler Radar
Principle of Operation
- This phenomenon was discovered by Dr Christian Doppler, in 1842.
- Doppler Shift is the apparent change in frequency of a wave in
relation to an observer who is moving relative to the wave source.
- If there is relative motion between the transmitter (aircraft) & target
(ground), there is a Doppler shift, proportional to their relative velocity.
- Doppler navigation systems measure this 'Doppler shift' to calculate
aircraft ground speed & drift.
- These systems work on 8.8 GHz or 13.3 GHz, in SHF band.
- Doppler system is accurate within 0.3%, for ground speed and drift.
f = Original frequency
f = ¼. If there is any relative motion (v)  fR = Frequency received
Derivation  between radar & target, then fR = (c + v)/¼; or  fo = Doppler shift
fR = C/A + V/A  =>  fR = f + V/A;
or Doppler shift (fp) = V/¼
® Depression
In a radar, where transmitter & receiver is moving forward,  Angle
fr = f + 2 x v/ (beam goes out & comes back).
For a down-looking radar, fr = f + 2 x Vcose / A.
Vcose = component of the aircraft velocity along the depressed beam.
For small 0, fo is large, but energy loss is maximum. Large 0 gives good retums
but less doppler shift. 67° is calculated to be the best Depression Angle.
Doppler Applications
Ground Speed: Doppler beam is reflected off the ground & the
doppler shift is measured, which is proportional to ground speed.
Drift: Doppler beam is rotated & the doppler shift is measured in all
directions. Direction in which doppler shift is maximum is the direction
of drift. Difference between this & aircraft heading is the drift angle.
Doppler Systems
Radio Nav-aids  Single Beam: Most basic. 1 beam used to measure groundspeed & drift.
2 Beam Non Janus
- 2 beams are at a fixed angle between them, looking forward.
- When there is no drift, fo is the same for both. If there is drift, fo
of one beam will be more than the other. Thus drift is calculated.
3 Beam A-Janus
- 2 beams form a quadrant, and is depressed by 67°.
- 3rd beam is depressed down 85°-97°. It has less fo, but good retums.
- All 3 returns are electronically compared to calculate total fo.
- ROD of aircraft can also be calculated.
3 Beam T-Janus: Uses 3 beams in a T - configuration.
4 Beam X-Janus: Uses 4 beams. It is very accurate.

7 - 23
Doppler Advantages
- It is a self-contained independent air-navigation system.
- It is very accurate.
- It has worldwide coverage & usage.
- No warm-up time needed.
Doppler Disadvantages
- It is prone to 'jamming'.
- There is a probability of interception by the enemy.
- It needs position information updates for long-range navigation.
Errors in Doppler Systems
Height Hole Error
- A pulse Doppler radar cannot transmit and receive at the same
time. So it is possible that the reflected pulse is lost if it arrives
back when another transmission is being made.
- It occurs at a particular aircraft height, dependent on its PRF.
- There are more chances of this occurring over very flat ground/sea.
- It can be avoided by varying PRF/modulation of frequency.
Sea Bias Error
- 'Beam returns' from beam trailing-end reflect more than leading-
end. Amount of energy reflected back depends on the angle of
incidence. Higher the angle, the better the return signal strength.
- But, over a smooth sea, a large part of the transmitted energy is
reflected away, and calculated ground speed reduces by 2-3%.
Sea Movement Error
- Doppler measures drift & ground speed relative to a fixed terrain.
- But over the sea, sea-surface itself moves due to currents & tides.
- This can cause measurement error up to 7-8 kts.
Flight Path & Pitch Error
- Doppler beam is depressed at an angle, pointing down. So when  Radio Nav-aids
the aircraft pitch changes (climb/descend), beam angle 1/.
- This error can be removed by using a gyro stabilised beam.
- Janus systems do not have this error.
Roll Error
- This error is more prominent in a single beam radar.
- It is similar to the pitch error, but is caused due to roll.
Aerial Misalignment
- This error occurs if the aerial is not aligned correctly with aircraft.
- It does not affect the ground speed measurement, except in
single aerial systems.
Computational Error
- As aircraft climbs higher in altitude, angle of the flight path arc
remains the same, but length of the arc increases.
- This increment in length causes an error in nav-computation, up
to 1 nm at the poles; less at the equator.
- Doppler computer takes feed from the altimeter & compensates
for this error.
===== [avh 0326]
7 - 24
Pulse Doppler Radar
- It is essentially a pulse radar; however, its receiver is very sensitive
& can measure the doppler shift in the received pulse.
- Thus, it combines properties of both a pulse radar & a doppler radar.
- Ambiguity: If the return echo lies beyond 'half PRF length' on either
side, then there is an ambiguity as to which pulse the doppler shift
belongs to. Is it a doppler shift of a closing target from the 1st pulse?
or is it the return from the 2nd pulse of a receding target?
2V = PRE Therefore, velocity ambiguity max (v) = PRF XA
: to increase max ambiguous velocity, the radar PRF is increased.
- But increasing PRF increases ambiguity in range. So:
- High PRF is used when good velocity into is needed.
- Low PRF is used when good range info is needed.
Synthetic Aperture Radar
- To get good resolution at high ranges, we need a large antenna (for
a narrower beamwidth) & use low frequencies. But this is not
practically possible on an airborne radar.
Synthetic length of
- A synthetic aperture radar uses the forward motion
of aircraft to 'apparently increase' radar aperture.
- Multiple scans are stored & is processed together.
- Advantages:
- Very high resolution is possible at large ranges.
- Wavelength & fq is within transmitter limitation.
- Ground mapping is possible, even at night.
- Disadvantage: Radar can only scan sideways.
Phased Array/Electronic Scanned Array
- It uses the concept of 'beam steering', to overcome disadvantages
of a parabolic antenna (reaction time, mechanical error, etc.).
- In it, multiple small fixed antenna transmitters are arranged in an array.
- Altering the phase of transmission in each transmitter changes the
direction of the beam axis.
- Higher the A (phase), the greater is the angle the beam can be tilted.
- But beyond 60°, the beam will get distorted.
• = d Sin 0 x 2 I  d = distance between array
+ = Phase shift  0 = Beam Tilt
Types of Electronic Scanned Array
Passive: Array receiver is fed from a single common transmitter.
- Beam steering is achieved by delaying the signal reaching the
individual array from the common transmitter.
Active: Each array element is a transmitter in itself.
- Each element transmission is controlled, thus achieving beam steering.
- It is more complex than Passive ESA. In this, one radar can operate
in multiple modes since each element can transmit individually.
Advantages
- No physical rotation of the antennae is needed.
- If some elements are u/s, others can still function.
- Rapid beam steering is possible.
- One radar can do multiple tasks - part air
scan, part ground scan.
- Radiation pattern is finely controlled.
Beam steering in an ESA

°° Weather Radar
Introduction
- Weather radars are pulse Doppler radars.
- It uses 'searchlight' principle for bearing & 'echo' principle for range
measurement of weather.
- Weather antenna scans t60° of aircraft heading & t15° in pitch.
- Radar auto stabilisation limits are +25° in pitch, and t40° in roll.
- Weather radars usually have a pencil beam (beam width 3° - 5°).

Types of Weather Radar Antenna:
Parabolic: Conic/pencil beam for detecting weather at 60nm+.
Flat Plate: Cosecant/fan beam for ground mapping, at short range.
Weather Mode: It uses a conic/pencil beam for weather detection.
'Ground Clutter Suppress' mode is used to reduce ground clutter.
Ground Mapping Mode: It uses a cosecant beam (fan-shaped beam,
85° vertical, 3.5° azimuth) for even representation of surface features.
In it, transmission power is progressively increased as the distance
increases & power at the closest object is minimum. This reduction in
power is a function of cosecant of depression angle, hence the name.
Gain (Auto gain/Swept gain/STC Sensitivity Time Control): Auto-Gain
Control reduces the sensitivity of the echo received from nearer
objects. It ensures constant brilliancy of radar display, independent
of the echo range. Radar gain should normally be set to 'auto'.  Radio Nav-aids
Manual Gain must only be used for signal amplification & for cloud
detection at 70-120 nm. It is also used for signal reduction. By slowly
reducing gain, relative intensity between CB cells can be done, to
see which areas are still red, & highlight turbulent/embedded cells.
Predictive Wind Shear: Advanced weather radars use doppler shift
to measure the movement of particles in a microburst. However, it
cannot detect sand storms, lightning or CAT.
- Predictive wind shear mode is automatically activated below
2300' even if radar is OFF or STBY.
- Wind shear scan is done for t90°
ahead of the aircraft, but wind shear
processing is only done for t45°.
- Wind shear warning is displayed as
red and black bands towards the
direction of the wind shear.
- Advisory: WS is 5 nm & 1500' below.
- Caution: WS is 3 nm & 1200' below.
- Warning: WS is within 1.5nm.

Weather Radar Frequency:
- Optimum frequency of any radar is a frequency comparable to the
size of object that radar is intended to detect.
- For a weather radar, I frequency (1 wavelength) will not highlight
areas of turbulence, and 1 frequency will create returns from smaller
water drops & cause unnecessary clutter.
- A frequency of 9375 MHz (3 cm wavelength) is optimum for a weather
radar as they will detect large water droplets & wet hail found in
convective clouds.

000 SSR Secondary Surveillance Radar
Introduction
- A primary radar relies on reception of a reflected pulse, on same fq.
- In an SSR, the transmitter & receiver frequencies are different.
- An SSR transmits a pulse, to which an aircraft transponder replies
in another frequency. e.g., DME.
- SSR needs participation from the target aircraft to function.
- Interrogation is in on 1030 MHz, aircraft reply in on 1090 MHz.
- An aircraft with a serviceable transponder must operate it at all
times irrespective of ATC instructions.
- Pilots should squawk IDENT' only if ATC requests for it.
Principle of Operation
- Ground interrogator has 2 antennae. The directional antenna (main
beam) transmits 2 pulses (P 1 & P3) 8 usec apart, on a narrow beam
(2° - 3°). The omni-directional antenna transmits P2, 2 usec after P1.
- On receiving this interrogation, the airborne transponder (aircraft)
transmits 2 framing pulses (F1 & F2) 20.3 usec apart, in all directions.
- Between F1 & F2, 12 info pulses (212 = 4096 combinations) could be
transmitted back. Thus, 4096 squawk codes are possible.
- Squawk codes use digits 0 to 7 only. Squawk code 5678 is not valid.
- A further pulse SPI Special Position Indent may be transmitted
after F2 pulse while squawking 'IDENT'. SPI continuously transmits
for 20 secs, 4.35 usec after Fz.

===== [avh 0330]
000 7-28
Modes of Operation
- Mode A: Aircraft identification (P1 & P3 IS 8 usec apart)
- Mode B: Stand-by for mode A (P1 & P3 is 17 sec apart).
- Mode C: Aircraft ident + Altitude in 100's of ft. (P) & Ps is 21 usec apart).
- Mode S: To overcome limitations of Mode C (P 1 & P3 is 3.5 usec apart).
- It has selective calling & data link options.
- 16 million identifier codes are available instead of 4096 codes &
allow for unambiguous aircraft identification.
- It is reverse compatible with modes A and C.
- Altitude is reported in 25' intervals, not 100's of feet.
- It eliminates fruiting and garbling errors.
Advantages of SSR
• It is independent of the radar cross-section of an aircraft.
- It has higher ranges than a primary radar. With much less transmitting
power, ranges are available up to 250 nm.
- Additional information can be included in aircraft response, e.g.
squawk, altitude information, etc.
- No errors due to ground reflection or weather. Less clutter.
Disadvantages of SSR
- Availability of Codes: Only 4096 codes (not applicable to Mode S).
- No reply will be received from an aircraft without a transponder.
Errors in SSR
- Garbling: Spurious indications due to the overlapping of replies
from 2 or more aircraft transponders within 1.7 nm from each other,
(20.3 us = 1.7 nm), which are on a same or nearly same bearing
from the ground station.
- Fruiting: Interference received at an interrogator, caused by replies
from a transponder replying to another interrogator.
- Ghosting: Aircraft replying to interrogator side lobe transmissions
will cause it to appear in more than one location on the radar screen.
Radio Nav-aids  Special SSR Codes
- 0000: Transponder un-serviceable.
- 0033: 5 min before paradrop, until all paratroopers on the ground.
- 2000: Aircraft is in area of radar cover, but squawk is not allotted.
- 7000: Aircraft is in area of radar cover, but it is not under its service
(VFR in CTA).
- 7004: Training, practice or aerobatic display in progress.
- 7500: Unlawful Interference.
ATC may check with the pilot on RT about 7500. If the pilot doesn't
reply, ATC assumes unlawful interference & takes action accordingly.
- 7600: RT failure.
- 7700: Mayday. Unlawful interference can also be 7700 if it warrants.
- If the aircraft is already radar-identified, re-squawking 7700 may delay
re-identification. So, old squawk may be retained. ATC will continue RT
for the safe conduct of flight & will not expect any reply from the pilot.
- ATC will hand over that aircraft to adjacent ATS unit without requiring
pilot communication.
- Information about an aircraft in emergency will be transmitted to all
other aircraft in the vicinity, unless it is unlawful interference.

000 GNSS Global Navigation Satellite System
NAVSTAR (GPS) (United States) Datum WGS84 World Geodetic Survey 1984
GALILEO (Europe) Datum ETRS89 European Terrestrial Reference System 1989
GLONASS (Russia) Global Orbiting Nav Sat System PZ90 Parameter for earth 1990
GPS Segments
Space Segment (GPS Satellites)
- It consists of 24 satellites (21 operational & 3 stand-by) placed in
6 orbits at 55° inclination. Orbital height is 20180 km.
- Orbital period for each satellite is 12 hrs.
- Each satellite has 4 clocks compared internally, average is sent out.
Control Segment
- Master control station is in Colorado Springs, USA, and the
backup control station is at Onizuka, USA.
- 5 monitor stations at Colorado Springs, Ascension, Diego Gracia,
Kwajalein & Hawaii monitor satellite posn & its clock every 12 hrs.
- They upload satellite orbital correction data & ephemeris message
into the satellites, for their re-transmission to the GPS receivers.
User Segment (GPS Receivers)
- Sequential Receiver: 1 receiver scans the satellites sequentially.
- Multiplex Receiver: It has more than 1 receiver channel to
move quickly between satellites. This provides a faster 1st fix.
- Multi Channel: It can monitors several satellites simultaneously.
It is very accurate and is the preferred type for aviation use.
- PPS Precision Positioning Service: For dedicated military use.
- Satellites transmit P-code (precision) which has 16m accuracy.
- To maintain secrecy, it has a SA (selective availability) feature.
- SPS Standard Positioning Service: For normal civillan use.
- It uses CA-code (coarse acquisition). Accuracy in horizontal
plane is 13m for 95% time, in vertical plane is 22m for 95% time.
GPS Principle of Operation
- GPS satellites transmit PVT data (position, velocity, time), ephemeris
correction data and almanac info on UHF 1575.42 MHz.  Radio Nav-aids
- Receiver determines which satellites are visible for tracking based
on stored almanac into. If no such data exists, it will attempt to
locate any random satellite and download this information from it.
- When a satellite is acquired, receiver downloads the almanac info.
This takes ~12.5 mins. Using this data, receiver locks on to 4 satellites,
downloads PVT data & its range, and calculates its own position.
- Since receiver clock is not in sync with satellite clocks, this range is
called 'pseudo range'. The calculated position will be a 'cocked hat'.
- The receiver then solves a '4 simultaneous equations with 4 unknown
variables', to reduce this error, & provide a valid fix.
- Best fix is obtained when 1 satellite overhead with 3 others 120° apart.
