000 7 - 30
GNSS Integrity Monitoring: It is of 3 types -
ABAS/RAIM Air-based Augmentation System/Remote Autonomous Integrity
Monitoring
- GPS satellite signals within themselves do not include any information
about the integrity of their signals.
- RAIM is the capability of GPS receiver to perform integrity monitoring
on itself by ensuring adequate satellite signals are available for a
given time & phase of flight & warn the crew of unreliable signals.
RAIM function needs 5 satellites with acceptable geometry or 4
satellites + barometric altitude input (baro-aiding).
- Predictive RAIM: Based on stored almanac info, the receiver knows
when sufficient satellite coverage will be available for RAIM to work.
- FDE Fault Detection & Exclusion: Some receivers have enhanced
RAIM function called FDE. They can not only detect a faulty
satellite, but also exclude that signal from the navigation function.
FDE needs 6 satellites with acceptable geometry or 5 satellites +
barometric altitude input (baro-aiding). FDE is critical for PBN.
- RAIM fault messages are of 2 types:
- There are not enough satellites for RAIM function;
- RAIM has detected a faulty satellite signal.
- Baro-Aiding: Augmenting GPS integrity by using a non-satellite
source for altitude information.
GBAS/LAAS Ground Based Augmentation System/Local Area Augment System
- LADGPS (Local Area Differential GPS) uses a ground station in the
airport area, which is surveyed to a high level of accuracy.
- This station also receives standard GPS signals & computes the
difference between GPS position & the surveyed position. Correction,
if any, are transmitted to aircraft via VHF or data-link, for use during
precision approaches and departures.
- GBAS ground equipment can service 26 - 48 aircraft at a time.
Radio Nav-aids  - Close proximity airports can use the same GBAS transmitter.
- GBAS accuracy is within 1 m in vertical & horizontal. Accuracy
reduces with increase in distance from the ground station.
- GBAS approaches are classified as precision approaches.
- Pilot indication for a GBAS eqpt is same as ILS; no training required.
- It is also used to increase the accuracy of Cat II/II approaches.
SBAS/WAAS Satellite Based Augment System/Wide Area Augment System.
- It is a network of ground stations that measure GPS signal errors &
the correction is transmitted to a master station.
- Master station then send these corrections to a WAAS satellite
(geo- stationary satellite), which re-transmits this information to a
WAAS enabled GPS receiver in an aircraft.
- SBAS accuracy is within 1 m laterally & 1.5 m vertically, 95% of time.
Although it suits precision approach CAT I requirements of 16 m
lateral & 4 m vertical accuracy, SBAS approaches are classified as
non-precision approaches.
- Prominent WAAS systems:
- GAGAN (India) GPS Aided Geo Augmented Navigation
- EGNOS (Europe) European Geostationary Nav Overlay System
- MSAS (Japan) Multi Function Satellite Augmentation System

Errors in GPS
Selective Availability
- It is the intentional degradation of GPS signal accuracy for civilian
use. However, SA was switched OFF on 01 May 2000, but the
USA reserves the right to turn it back ON anytime.
Satellite Position Error (Ephemeris Error)
- Satellite orbit is affected by the gravity of the sun, moon & earth.
This error can be predicted and is corrected for.
- But errors due to space debris/asteroids/orbit inaccuracies exist.
- There is also a delay before the MCS can upload corrected
ephemeris data. Any position fix taken meanwhile is inaccurate.
Satellite Clock Error
- These are the errors present in the satellite clocks, despite the
MCS Master Control Station updating it every 12 hours.
- Position accuracy degrades by up to 1.5 m.
Ionospheric Refraction
- Although UHF transmission is not significantly affected by
ionospheric refraction, even a tiny amount can cause satellite
signals to attenuate or take a longer route to reach a receiver.
- It is the most significant GPS error. Errors up to 5 m.  Radio Nav-aids
- This error is least when the satellite is directly overhead.
Tropospheric Refraction
- These are errors caused due to refraction & attenuation of GPS
signals in troposphere. This error is small (0.5 m) & is disregarded.
Multi-path Reception Error
- Reflected UHF signals arrive later and from a different direction
than the main signal & are usually disregarded by GPS receiver.
- But if the main signal was shielded, the receiver does not know
any better and will use the reflected signal, causing an error.
- This error can be rectified by using specific antenna designs that
can disregard signals coming from unusual angles.
GDOP Geometric Dilution of Position
- Best fix is obtained when 3 satellites are 120° apart.
- If such a geometry is not available, position accuracy may reduce.
- Errors up to 20 m.
Receiver Noise: Depends on the quality of receiver, 0.3 m error.
Solar Disturbance: Solar wind, radiation & EM disturbances cause
interference with satellite transmission.

ooo GPWS Ground Proximity Warning System
Introduction
- GPWS provides visual & aural warnings of proximity to terrain to a
pilot, but only with respect to terrain that is directly below the aircraft.
- It takes input from radio altimeter, altimeter, ILS & ADC.
- GPWS is mandatory for all aircraft with AUW > 5700 Kg or pax > 9.
- GPWS is operational when aircraft height is between 50' & 2450' AGL.
- In case of a GPWS warning in the cockpit, positive & immediate
action by the pilot is required: maintain wings level, open max
power, climb with Best Angle of Climb speed (Vx). Deviation from
this procedure is permitted only if the pilot is in VMC, or the reason
for the warning is positively identified & the aircraft is safe.
- Along with GPWS functions, an EGPWS monitors the aircraft track
& calculates if it is heading towards an obstruction in front of it also.
- It uses GPS + terrain database + enhanced features (TAD+TCF)
- If radio altimeter is un-serviceable, basic GPWS & TCF functions
are not available, but TAD is available.
- If terrain data is not available, only Basic GPWS functions are
available. Both TAD & TCF are not available.
TAD Terrain Awareness Display
- It has electronic terrain data & gives a warning of approaching
terrain +2000' of aircraft altitude in shades green, yellow & red.
- Pop Up: The display automatically changes to terrain mode with
10 nm range when a terrain warning is issued by EGPWS.
TCF Terrain Clearance Floor
- It provides an additional layer of protection to an aircraft, to
prevent its premature descend during an NPA.
- An alert is issued based on aircraft position & altitude with respect
Radio Nav-aids  to the nearest runway location, & provides increasing terrain
clearance envelop around airport and runway.
- It is active regardless of aircraft configuration.

ACAS Airborne Collision Avoidance System
(See also: RT Phraseology > ACAS)
Introduction
- ACAS provides TA (Traffic Advisory) & RA (Resolution Advisory) by
means of a visual/aural warning to a pilot, by calculating the relative
position (altitude, bearing, distance) of conflicting traffic.
- This system is independent of Air Traffic Control. In case of a conflict
between an ATC instruction & a TCAS warning, follow TCAS.
- Visually acquired traffic may be different from ACAS traffic. Be careful.
- ACAS is mandatory for all aircraft in RVSM airspace.
- Priority: Stall warning > Wind shear warning > GPWS > ACAS > ATC.
- During a GPWS warning, ACAS shifts to TA mode & no alert is issued.
TCAS I: It is the first generation of collision avoidance technology.
- It monitors bearing, range & altitude of other aircraft, up to 40 nm.
- It can display a TA, but cannot issue an RA.
- TCAS I is mandatory for all a/c with AUW > 5700kg or passengers > 9
TCAS II: It offers all benefits of TCAS I, in addition of a vocalised RA.
- Before issuing an RA to pilots, TCAS II will coordinate RA between
up to 3 aircraft, so that if one aircraft is instructed to descend, the
other will be told to climb, thus maximising separation.
- TCAS Il is mandatory for all a/c with AUW > 15000kg or passenger >30
TCAS II (Version 7.1)
- It provides 'RA reversals' in coordinated encounters, in case one
aircraft doesn't follow the original RA.
- It has improved handling of corrective/preventive annunciation.
- It replaces the ambiguous RA "Adjust vertical speed, adjust" with
"Level off, level off", to prevent improper response by pilots.
- It removes the 'green arc' when RA weakens, when the aircraft is
extremely low (1000' AGL or below) or high (near aircraft ceiling), to
prevent dangerous guidance to a pilot.
Radio Nav-aids  TCAS III: It provides horizontal advisory also - left/right turns. But its
development has stalled since the introduction of ADS-B/C.
Principle of Operation - TCAS II
- TCAS uses the SSR principle (1030 MHz- 1090 MHz) in air-air
mode & can only interact with aircraft with mode A/C/S transponder.
- It builds a 3D map of the airspace, with range (interrogation -
response time), altitude (as reported by the interrogated aircraft) &
bearing (direction of return signal sensed by 2 directional antennae).

7 - 36
• ADS Automatic Dependent Surveillance
ADS-B (Broadcast)
- In ADS-B, the aircraft continuously broadcasts its position, speed &
callsign every second. This information can be received by other
ADS-B equipped aircraft as well as ground stations.
- ADSB-out: ADS-B equipment that can broadcast ADS-B info.
- ADSB-in: ADS-B equipment that can receive ADS-B broadcast.
- ADS-B info is transmitted on 2 frequencies:
- 978 MHz, known as UAT Universal Access Transceiver
- 1090 MHz (integrated with SSR), known as ES Extended Squitter.
- Thus, ADS-B provides improved air-air & air-ground surveillance.
- However, ADS-B traffic information may be incomplete due to the
presence of non-ADS aircraft flying in the vicinity. Be cautious.
- ADS-B is not to be used as a traffic collision avoidance system. No
avoidance manoeuvres are to be initiated based on ADSB info.
ADS-C (Contract)
- Although names are similar, ADS-C & ADS-B are different. ADS-C
works like a SSR. A report is generated by an aircraft in response to a
request within the terms of ADS contract held by the ground system.
- Aircraft can also send non-requested ADS-C emergency reports to
an ATS unit that has an ADS contract with aircraft.
- Ground system can establish ADS contract without pilot action
provided that ADS-C in the aircraft system is not selected OFF.
- Up to 5 ground systems may request ADS contracts with 1 aircraft.
- Pilot can cancel all contracts by selecting ADS-C to OFF.
- ADS Contract Types
- Periodic Contract: Specifies time interval for a/c to send a report.
- Demand Contract: Request a single ADS-C report. It does not
cancel/modify any other ADS contracts that may be in effect.
Radio Nav-aids  - Event Contract: Request a report when a specific event occurs.
- Waypoint Change Event (WCE)
- Level Range Deviation Event (LRDE)
- Lateral Deviation Event (LDE)
- Vertical Rate Change Event (VRE)
Waypoint change event contract will trigger a report for all waypoint changes.
All other event contracts will trigger a report on the first occurrence only.

===== [avh 0340]
7 - 37
• ACARS Aircraft Communication Addressing & Reporting System
- It is a system prior to the introduction of modern datalink, used for
sending short messages between an aircraft & ground, in telex format.
- It works on a satellite datalink or a direct VHF frequency.
- It interfaces with FMS and acts as a communication system for flight
plan, weather, aircraft system status, etc.
- A flight deck printer may be provided along with a cabin crew terminal.
- 3 types of messages can be handled:
- ATC messages & clearances: Used for communication with ATC. It
is similar to datalink/CPDLC, but is not as robust.
- AOC (Aeronautical Operational Control): Used for communication
with operator/base regarding aircraft operations. e.g., NOTAMs,
ATIS, aircraft position, ETA, etc.
- AAC (Airline Administrative Control): For info of admin nature, e.g.,
equipment status, abnormal a/c situation, catering requirements, etc.
• CPDLC Controller Pilot Data Link Communication
- This system replaces ACARS-ATC.
- It provides a 2-way datalink by which ATC can transmit non-urgent
messages as an alternative to voice communication with an aircraft.
- Pilots can respond/request clearances. A tree text tormat is also provided.
- CPDLC should start and terminate with a voice message "Transfer to
Chennai oceanic control on datalink (position), monitor (VHF fq)".
- Pilot has to log on to CPDLC by sending a request through FMS to the
ATS unit, which approves the link. Aircraft will continue to maintain a
watch over voice radio despite CPDLC logon.
- When CPDLC messages are ambiguous, revert to voice RT to clarify.
- For ADS and CPDLC established aircraft, ADS will be the primary mode
of surveillance & CPDLC will be the primary mode of communication.
- SELCAL check is mandatory before using CPDLC.
- While filling a flight plan, fill COM/CPDLC in items 10 & 18.
- Following datalink services are available in CPDLC:
- DLIC (Data Link Initiation Capability): Between controller & aircraft.
- ACM (ATC Comm Management): To transfer ATC comm to datalink.
- AMC (ATC Microphone Check): To check voice RT.
- DCL Departure Clearance.
- DSC Down-Stream Clearance Service.
Benefits of CPDLC
- Pilot to Controller: Downlink of position & clearance requests.
- Controller to Pilot: Uplink of ATC clearances. All clearances can
be included: Taxi instruction, takeoff, climb, en-route, descent,
landing & supports emergency alerting.
- Less voice communication, safer frequency change-overs.
- Reduced probability of miscommunication.
- Increased airspace sector capabilities.
- ATC can deal with more pilot requests.
- A free text option also available.
CPD CPDL and fatan kire availabin Delhi, Chennal, Mumbai &
Kolkata FIR.
- ADS/CPDLC equipped a/c must login 20 min prior entering Delhi
FIR & 10 min prior oceanic FIR (Mumbai, Chennai & Kolkata).
- A/c leaving Delhi FIR must login to next FIR 15 mins prior leaving.
===== [avh 0341]
7 - 38
Other Nav-aids
TIS-B: Traffic Information Service Broadcast
- TIS-B is a broadcast of ATC derived traffic (ADSB + SSR) from the
ground to an ADSB-in equipped aircraft. This gives an aircraft a
more complete traffic picture in the cockpit.
TIS Limitations
- This info is advisory only & not intended for collision avoidance.
- TIS position update has a delay of 3 - 13 secs.
- TIS needs a SSR radar to function. It doesn't work with a
primary radar.
- Quality of information depends on the coverage of SSR radars.
- No alert is issued to the pilot when the aircraft is outside TIS
coverage area. He will not see any traffic information.
FIS-B: Flight Information Service Broadcast
- It is a system similar to TIS broadcast & works on 978 MHz.
- FIS-B equipped aircraft will see weather & aeronautical information.
TLS: Transponder Landing System
- It is a type of precision approach guidance.
- TLS ground equipment interrogates aircraft transponder to know its
position, based on which it broadcasts a specific ILS frequency to
guide an aircraft along a desired path, for approach and landing.
- No additional equipment is needed in the aircraft other than the
existing ILS receiver & a transponder.
- TLS can service only one aircraft at a time.
- TLS signals are valid only for the particular aircraft.
FANS: Future Air Navigation Systems
- FANS is not a single system, but a range of avionics to
provide ATC control in areas where radar is not available.
Radio Nav-aids  It is primarily used in oceanic airspaces.
- It was created by ICAO in 1983, to improve concepts of air traffic
management.
- It uses GPS to an define aircraft position & transmits it to a ground
station via VHF/Satcom datalink, creating a virtual radar environment.
Thus, separation between aircraft can be reduced.
- FANS improves aircraft navigation by:
- Surveillance through ADS;
- Communication through CPDLC;
- Navigation through RNP & GPS.
- FANS-1 is developed by Boeing, based on ADS & CPDLC & is
implemented through FMS. FANS-A is developed by Airbus.
FANS-1 & FANS-A are both interoperable.
- FANS 1/A: Aircraft & ground data link & communication service
standard to comply with FANS standard.
Free Flight Concept
- It is a future concept in which pilots will be allowed to fly their own
direct tracks without any speed/level/heading restriction by ATC.
- In this, collision avoidance is ensured by TCAS & ADS-B.
- Advanced avionics of FANS & RNP assist this concept.
===== [avh 0342]
7 - 39
Legacy Nav-aids
LORAN (Long Range Navigation)
- It is a hyperbolic line-ot-position (LOP) radio navigation
system developed during WWII by the United States.
- In this system, a receiver determines its position by using multi-
lateration to compare difference in reception time of LF signals
transmitted by a master & 2-3 sub stations placed 600 nm away.
- It worked on one of 4 LF frequencies 1.75, 1.85, 1.9 or 1.95 MHz.
- It had a range of up to 500 nm & accuracy within 100'.
- Soon US Navy began developing LORAN-B, but ran into difficulties.
- In 1950s, the US Air Force worked on a different concept (Cyclan),
which the Navy took over as LORAN-C. It worked on 100 kHz, and
had better ranges than LORAN.
- It was opened for public use in 1974.
- This system also was prone to propagation (skywave) errors by night.
- With the advent of INS, GPS, LORAN-C started losing its charm &
transmitters around the world were slowly shut down, last one in 2015.
Decca
- It is also a hyperbolic (LOP) radio nav system developed
during WWII by the Royal Navy, specitically for use during the
D-day landings. After the war, the system was released for public use.
- It was mostly used by mariners, and sometimes by aircraft.
- It worked on 2 VLF frequencies 70 kHz & 129 kHz.
- In this, the phase difference between VLF signals from a master
station & 2-3 linked sub-stations placed in a triangular pattern
60-120 nm away was compared & own position was triangulated.
- Ranges of up to 400 nm by day & 250 nm by night was achieved, &
had an accuracy better than LORAN systems.
- This system was prone to propagation (skywave) errors by night.
- With the advent of GPS, the system was shutdown on 31 Mar 2000.
Omega
It was the first global range hyperbolic (LOP) radio navigation
system, developed by the US in 1971, to overcome the medium
range limitations of LORAN-C & Decca.
- In this, the phase difference between time-shared VLF signals
(10.2, 13.6 & 11.33 kHz in that order, & a 4th signal unique to each
station) from 8 transmitting stations placed around the world was
compared.
- This system has had range of 6000 nm & an accuracy of 4 nm.
- It was shutdown in 1997, in favour of GPS.
- Alpha, also known as RSDN-20, was its Russian counterpart, was
operational up to 2006.

8 - 4
Day
Civil Day: Duration of a day, light to dark, mid-point is called 12:00 noon.
Apparent Solar Day: Duration between two successive sun transit
overhead. This duration varies between 23:44 hrs to 24:14 hrs.
Mean Solar Day: Duration of apparent solar days averaged for a year.
Max difference between mean & apparent solar day is 16 minutes.
Sidereal Day: Day duration measured w.r.t. a distant star. 23h:56m:04s.
- Rate of change of the length of a day/night is maximum during
equinoxes & least during solstices.
- The sun will always reach 90° overhead within 23° north/south latitude
& will at least rise & set within 66° north/south latitude every day.
- Beyond 66° N/S, continuous day/night exist for 6 months.
• Sun
- Theoretical sunrise is when centre of the sun crosses sensible horizon.
- Practical sunrise is when tip of the sun rises above visible horizon,
which is below the sensible horizon (due to refraction).
Centre of the sun is below its edge by 16' arc. Also, due to refraction, the
visual horizon (true position) is below sensible horizon (perceived position)
by an arc of 34'. Thus, we see the tip of the sun 3 minutes (16'+34' = 50'
arc) before the actual sunrise. That is why, at the equator, a day is 6
minutes more than a night (3 mins before sunrise + 3 mins after sunset).
- Factors affecting length of a day (duration of sunrise to sunset):
- Latitude of the observer: 1 in latitude = f in daylight time,
- Declination of the sun,
- Altitude of the observer: 1 in altitude = 1 in daylight time.
Sunrise will be earlier & sunset will be later than published.
- To have the longest day, an observer must be at the north pole (90°
lat) & sun at 23½° declination, giving 6 months of continuous day.

- Every day, moon rises 55 mins late since direction of rotation of the

• Twilight: It is the period of diffused light before sunrise & after sunset,
caused due to atmospheric refraction.
- Civil Twilight: Centre of sun travels 0° - 6° below sensible horizon.
- At the equator, duration of civil twilight is 21 minutes, which is the
time tip of the sun takes to travel 5°10'(6° - 0°50') below horizon.
- Duration of civil twilight increases as we move toward poles.

8 - 5
• Time
GMT Greenwich Mean Time: It is a time zone, time at 0° longitude.
UTC Co-ordinated Universal Time. It is a time standard, to match GMT.
LMT Local Mean Time: When the sun crosses a particular meridian, it is
12:00 LMT at that place.
IST Indian Standard Time: LMT at 85.4° E. (GMT +5:30).
360° Longitude = 24 hrs of time  1° Longitude (60' arc) = 4 minutes of time
15° Longitude = 60 minutes of time 1' Arc = 4 seconds of time

Leap Year: 1 Civil Year is 365.25 days. So every 4 years, 1 extra day is
added to correct for this. However, to be more accurate, a reduction of
3 days is required every 4 centuries. So, in every 'century year', if its
1st two digits are divisible by 4, then that year is a leap year. E.g.,
2100, 2200 & 2300 are not leap years. 2000 & 2400 are leap years.

- 24 zones at 1 hr interval & 16 zones at 0:30 or 0:45 min interval.  Navigation
- Zones A to M are east of GMT (omitting J), N to Y are west of GMT.

True North: Geographic north, where meridians converge.
Magnetic North: It is where a freely suspended magnet will point to.
Earth's magnetic pole rotates around earth's true pole at the rate of 1°
Compass North: Where compass points to, influenced by a/c systems.
Dip: It is the vertical component of earth's magnetic field. It is 0° at the
equator & 90° at the poles. As 'dip' becomes more vertical, horizontal
magnetic force reduces & Dip angle increases. So sensitivity of a 'direct
reading compass' decreases and it is unreliable above 70°north/south.

• Maps & Charts
Globe: It is the most accurate projection of the earth, as paper maps
lose accuracy due to distortion in their flat perspective.
Map: They contain graticule & have excellent feature representation.
- General Purpose Maps: Atlas, road maps, etc.
- Special Purpose Maps: Water level, soil representation, etc.
- Thematic Maps: Population/forest cover, etc.
- Topographic Maps: Large scale detail, relief (Survey of India maps).
- Celestial Maps: Sky, constellation representation, etc.
- Aeronautical: Air-nav, airspace boundaries, etc. (Jeppesen charts).
Chart: They are maps used for representing the sea. They also have
graticules printed on them, but have fewer ground features represented.
Globe  Map  Chart
Requirements of an Ideal Map
- Distance between 2 points must be accurate.
- Angles & bearings between 2 points must be accurate.
- Coordinates must be readily readable.
- Shapes & areas must be correctly represented (Orthomorphic). This
is achieved by maintaining latitude & longitude 1 to each other.
- Rhumb line must be a straight line (to cut latitudes & longitude at
equal angles), which will help in easy navigation.
- Great circles also must be straight lines.
- Adjacent sheets of the map should fit, coverage must be worldwide.
• Methods of Depicting Relief
- Contours: They are lines joining places of equal height. If the area
is not well surveyed, contours will be shown as broken lines.
- Hachure: Short tapered lines on maps radiating from high ground.
- Spot Height: Exact height of a hill feature is marked.
- Hill Shading: For 3D depth effect.  Navigation
- Layer Tinting: It helps in the indication of height. Different shades
of colour represent different heights.

• Plotting
- Fix: Position of an aircraft determined by means other than pinpoint.
- Pinpoint: Aircraft position determined by direct visual observation.
- Ground Position: Position of aircraft on the ground beneath it.
- Air Position: Air position of aircraft, assuming nil winds.
- DR Position: Aircraft position deduced from previous known posn.

METHODS OF PLOTTING LINES & FIXES
oo Principles of Map Reading
- Select a route that is easily identifiable on the map & ground. •
- Avoid mixing maps of different scales. Choice of scale depends on
the flying distance, flight altitude, aircraft speed & type of terrain.
- Take into account current visibility.
- Orient the map along the fore-aft axis of the aircraft.
- Visualise the physical representations & symbols on the map. Have
a composite mental picture & co-relate with features on the ground.
- Distinguish significant features en-route and remain undistracted by
irrelevant information. e.g., if flying along a coastline, look for inlets
or cliffs along the coastline, which will enable the position to be
identified with reasonable accuracy.
- Estimate distances & bearings between features on the map.
- Success in map reading at night will depend mainly on:
- Amount of natural illumination;
- Presence of artificial lighting on the ground;
- Presence of contrasting reflecting surfaces on the ground;
(water/land, snow-covered fields/woods, etc.)
- Visibility, height of aircraft & observer's night vision.
- Best features for pinpointing, especially at night: Large towns, Major
roads, Marine lights, Railways tracks, Water features.
oo Local Lost Procedure for a Pilot While Flying:
- Check compass & ASI to ensure aircraft is flying in the planned
direction & speed.
Navigation  - Fix using all available aids (VOR/NDB/GPS).
- If possible, climb up to increase radio/VOR ranges.
- Request for radar vectors if in RT contact.
- If penetrating a controlled airspace without clearance, squawk 7700.
- If doing visual navigation:
- Be careful not to fly into high terrain in poor visibility, climb
above MSA or RSA Route Safety Altitude.
- Plot a DR position with the time flown since the last fix.
- Then draw a 'circle of uncertainty' at that DR position with a
radius of 10% of the distance since the last fix.
- Now read 'map to ground. Aircraft should be within this circle
of uncertainty.
- If still in difficulty, consider turning towards a good visual line
feature (coast, railway line), then follow it until you reach a
definite visual checkpoint.

8 - 9
• The Earth
Introduction
- Shape of the earth is described as 'Ellipsoid' or 'Oblate Spheroid.
- Earth's polar diameter (12713 km) is less than equatorial diameter
(12756 km) by 23 nm (27 statute miles). Compression is 0.3%.
- 1 Nautical Mile is the distance subtended by 1 minute arc, at D
the centre of the earth, measured along a longitude. Length of
1 nm is 6076.1' (~6080"), 6048' at the equator, 6108' at poles.
- 1 Kilometre is 1/10000th average distance between equator & poles.
Latitude: Angle between equator & a point north or south, subtended at
the centre of the earth.
Longitude: Angle between prime meridian & a point east or west,
subtended at the centre of the earth.
Graticule: A network of meridians &
latitudes that are drawn on a map/chart.
Small
Small Circle: Any circle other than a Great Circle, Crete  Circle
which cuts the earth into 2 unequal parts.
Great Circle (GC)
- It is a circle that cuts the earth into 2 equal halves.
- It is the shortest distance between any 2 points on earth.
- It has the greatest radius possible, hence the least curvature.
- Only 1 GC can be drawn through any 2 points on the earth, unless
these 2 points are diametrically opposite, in which case, an infinite
number of great circles can be drawn through these 2 points.
- Radio waves always propagate along surface of earth in GC tracks.
- On a Mercator chart, GC is concave to the equator & Rhumb Line.
- On a Lambert's & Polar Gnomonic chart, GC is a straight line.
Rhumb Line (RL)
- It is a line that cuts all meridians at equal angles. Hence, its direction
& heading is constant, & thus following an RL helps in easy navigation.
- However, RL may not be the shortest distance between 2 points.
- All parallels of latitudes are rhumb lines.
- Equator & meridians are examples of GCs which are RLs also.
- On a Mercator chart, RL is a straight line.  Navigation
- On a Lamberts & Polar Gnomonic chart, RL is concave to poles & GC.

8 - 14
GEOREF Geographical Reference System
Disadvantages of latitude/longitude position reporting system
- 13 digit group is required for 1' accuracy, e.g. 51°36'45"N 165°25'55"W
- 1' lat & 1' long represent different distances, except at the equator
- Distance of 1' longitude decreases with an increase in latitude.
To overcome these disadvantages, GEOREF was developed.
- GEOREF divides the earth into 288 boxes with 15° sides. It has:
- 24 longitudinal boxes (360°/15°), each 15° wide, lettered A to Z
(omitting I & O), eastwards from 180° meridian; and,
- 12 latitudinal boxes (180/15°), 15° wide, lettered A to M
(omitting I), northward from the south pole (90°S to 90°N = 180°).
- These 2 letters are the 1st two characters of GEOREF.
- Each 15° box is now sub-divided into 225, 1° boxes.
- 15 longitudinal x 15 latitude boxes 1° wide, lettered A to Q
(omitting I and O), eastwards & northwards respectively from the
southwest corner. They form the 3rd & 4th characters.
- Thus, a 4 letter group can identify any 1° box in the world.
- Each 1° box is further sub-divided into 60, 1' boxes, numbered 00 to
59, eastwards & northward respectively from southwest corner.
- Thus, 4 letters & 4 digits give the position of any 1' quadrangle.
90°
75°  AL
60°
45°
30°
12 x 15° boxes
B
-75°  ABCDEFGAJKLMN PORSTUVWXYZIA
-90°
24 x 15° boxes
Advantages of GEOREF:
- It provides an easy and quick method of position reference.
- Smaller no. of alphabets than lat/long, to specify 1' accuracy.
- It is capable of universal application.
- More secure: Code letters can be changed easily.
Navigation  Disadvantages of GEOREF:
- This system can be confusing. Eastings are given before northings,
even in southern & western hemispheres.
- Like latitude & longitude system, a different scale has to be used to
measure of eastings and northings.
Converting Latitude/Longitude to GEOREF:
Q. Convert 55°05'N 010°25'W to GEOREF.
Ans. Using conventional signs N(+), S(-), E(+) & W(-), add 90 to latitude &
180 to longitude. Then, degree portions are divided by 15.
90 + 55°05 = 145°05
145° / 15 = 9, remainder 10  169° / 15 = 11, remainder 4
To obtain 15° box, add 1 to the quotients; 9+1=10, 11+1=12.
Letters corresponding to 10 & 12 omitting I & O is MK. (15° box)
To obtain 1° box, 1 is added to each remainder, 10+1=11, 4+1=5
Letters corresponding to 11 & 5 omitting I is EL. (1° box)
Final minutes portion of GEOREF is given directly taken, i.e., 3505.
Thus 55°05'N 010°25'W corresponds to MKEL 3505 in GEOREF
===== [avh 0357]
8 - 15
• Grid Navigation
Before FMS or GPS, long-range navigation in the polar regions was
difficult due to 3 reasons:
- Convergence of Longitude: Following a track that is anything but
directly (true) north or south requires a constant change in true
heading.
- Proximity of Magnetic Poles: Large & rapid changes in variation
make magnetic compasses unreliable, even over a relatively short
distance.
- Ground-based nav-aids were few and widely spaced.
To overcome these obstacles, Grid Navigation was developed in the
early 1940s and remained in use until late in the 20th century.
hich is alad parallel to a specific longitude. This grid is overaid on an
appropriate Polar Stereographic Projection navigational chart. The aircraft
compass is aligned to this grid. Although any longitude can be used as a
reference, the Prime Meridian is most commonly used as the datum
meridian. This grid is often referred to as "Greenwich Grid".
The great circle track between points A and B (black line) cuts each
longitude (blue lines) at a different angles (see diagram below). Thus, flying
with reference to True North would require a constant change in heading
to maintain track. However, if a grid is overlaid on the chart (red lines),
the required track cuts all the lines of the grid overlay at the same angle.
This means that if the aircraft gyro is aligned to the grid, the heading
required to maintain the track would be constant, making navigation
much easier.
Grid Variation (Grivation): Angle between grid-north & magnetic-north.

CP Critical Point
oo Introduction
- CP is the Point of Equi-time, where the time required to continue
to the destination or return to the departure aerodrome is the same.
- CP is independent of fuel onboard & endurance.
- For 'nil winds, CP will be at the mid-point of the route.
- For beam winds, CP will be at route mid-point, but time to CP will f.
- For any other winds, CP always moves into the wind direction.
- If GS or TAS is reduced, CP will move into the wind.
- For calculating engine failure CP, use reduced GS Home & GS Out.
- For calculating CP for a critical patient on board, use increased GS.
- To calculate time to CP, use normal GS.

8 - 18
Critical Line
CP represents the point of equi-time, on the track between A & B.
But if an aircraft is off-track, CP loses its significance. So Critical Point
must be replaced by a Critical Line. A critical line may be defined as
the locus of points from which an aircraft will take equal time to fly to B
or return to A. In nil wind conditions, it is a perpendicular bisector of
the track, representing a line of equi-time. To correct for winds, time
for the aircraft to fly from nil-wind critical line to either A or B at reduced
TAS is calculated. The critical line is then moved upwind by a distance
equal to the nil-wind air-time, multiplied by the wind speed.
Q. Total distance A-B is 1000 nm, reduced TAS 260 kts,
winds 060/60 kts. Find Critical Line.
Ans. Nil-wind critical line will be at 500 nm (mid-point of 1000 nm leg).
Nil-wind flying time from critical line to A or B with reduced TAS =
500/260 = 1.92 hrs. Thus critical line must be moved in direction
060°T by 1.92 × 60 (wind speed) = 115 nm. Thus, the new Critical Line
will be 615 nm from A.
Wore we New critical line
moved 060 direction
500 nm
615 nm  Nil-wind
Critical Line
Since wind affect on 'track to CP" & track to alternate from CP' are assumed to
be same, air distance measured on track will be in slight error. However, we
can disregard this, unless wind component is a significant proportion of the
TAS. To eliminate this ambiguity, ensure that Heading/TAS vector towards A or
B commences from the equi-line rather than track & ground speed vector.
Last Point of Diversion
Last point of diversion (LPD) is a special case of CP, in which,
beyond a point along the track'A-B', it is impossible for the aircraft to
reach the diversion aerodrome 'C'. Such a case will exist if the diversion
is so far from destination 'A' that aircraft cannot carry enough fuel to
reach the destination 'B', and then divert to 'C'.
Q. Find last point of diversion between departure 'A' & destination
Navigation  'B', with diversion as 'C'
Ans. Track A-B is extended to D (a pseudo diversion) such that A-D
represents the limit of safe endurance at the ground speed along that
track. C-D is joined, and a perpendicular bisector PQ is drawn (CQ =
QD), cutting A-D at P. PQ now becomes a nil-wind critical line between
aerodrome at 'C' & the pseudo aerodrome 'D'.
Now, similar to wind correction in a critical line (mentioned above), PQ
is moved in the direction of wind, by a distance equal to the nil-wind
flying time from P to C, using reduced TAS (if calculating engine
failure LDP) or normal TAS (for normal LPD), multiplied by the wind
speed. Where it cuts AB (x), will be the last point of diversion, to C.

diversion

CP Between Three Aerodromes
While flying, in case of an emergency, there may be an option of
diverting to an off-track aerodrome. In the diagram below, an aircraft is
flying from A to B, and C is an off-track aerodrome. Between 'A' & a
point 'L' along the route, it will be quicker to return to 'A'. From 'L' to a
point 'N', it will be quicker to divert to 'C', & beyond 'N' it will be quicker
to proceed to destination 'B'. Thus L and N represent two critical points.
Method of finding positions of L & N is graphical, & is based on the
'critical line' method. AC & BC are drawn, joining departure & destination
to diversion aerodrome. Perpendicular bisectors of these lines (LM &
NO) are drawn to cut AB at L & N. As L is equidistant from A & C, and
N is equidistant from B & C, L and N are nil-wind critical points.
To account for the wind effect, points L & N are moved upwind, in
the same manner as constructing a critical line, by an amount equal to
wind speed multiplied by time to fly from L and N respectively to C, at
reduced TAS. Critical lines are drawn through the ends of the wind
vectors, parallel to LM and NO, and where these cut the track

ROA is defined as the maximum distance that an aircraft can travel
out from an aerodrome along a specified track before returning to the
same or a different aerodrome, within a specified time. The time specified
IS called Patrol Time (dictated by fuel/operational requirements) & the
specified track that aircraft requires to maintain is called Patrol Track.
When the aircraft is on patrol, Time (out) + Time (back) = Patrol Time.

PSR Point of Safe Return
Also called PNR Point of No Return, if no reserve fuel is catered for.
oo Introduction
- It is the furthest point to which an aircraft can fly to, and return back
within a safe endurance limit.
- PSR depends on the fuel being carried onboard.
- Distance to PSR is maximum in nil winds. Winds in any direction
will reduce the distance to PSR.
- Distance to PSR will remain unchanged if winds are reversed.
- 10% more fuel = 10% more time to PSR.
- Better engine performance = More distance to PSR.
oo PSR formula:
A

0 = GS OUT to PSR  or T (Time) = O+H
H = GS HOME from PSR
= Time OUT to PSR  EOH
E-T = Time HOME from PSR  or PSR (Dist) = O+H

• Projections  (See also: The Earth)
Convergency = Change in longitude x SIN mean latitude.

Departure = Change of longitude x 60 x COS mean latitude.
Distance between 2 points (Departure)
Q. Position A is (45°N 45°15'E). B is 280 nm west of A. Find posn B.
Ans: Departure (nm) = Ch Long X COS Lat
:: 280 nm = Ch Long x COS 45 or Ch Long = 280/0.707 = 396' = 6°36'
:: B is (45°N 45°15'E) - (6°36) = 45°N 38°39'E
GC Track between 2 points (Conversion Angle)
Q. Find the GC track between A (60°N 120°W) & B (60°N 140°30'W).
Ans: GC track = RL track + Conversion Angle
CA = ½ Change in Long x SIN Mean Lat = ½ (20°30') x SIN 60° = 9°
Since A & B are on the same Lat, RL track between them is 270°.
.: GC track between them = 270° *+ 9° = 279°  * + in N Hemisphere
* - in S Hemisphere
RL Track between 2 points (Conversion Angle)
Q. Find the RL track between A (58°N 30°W) & B (51°N 20°W), if GC track
from A to B is 100° T.  Mean Lat = 58° - 51° = 54.5°
Ans: Difference between GC track & RL track is Conversion Angle
CA = ½ Change in Long x SIN mean Lat = ½ (-10°) x SIN 54.5° = -4.07°
: GC track = RL track -(-4.07°) => 100°-(-4.07°) = 104.07°T
Final Position (Departure)
Q. From position A (4°N 30°W), an aircraft flies RL track 700 nm each,
initially to S, then E, then N, then W. Find final position.
Ans: Using formula Departure (nm) = Ch Long X COS Lat for calculating posn,
700 nm true S of (4°N 30°W) = 700/60 = 11°40' change in Long.
: Position B is (4°N 30°W) + (11°40' S) = (7°40'S 30°W).
700 nm true E from posn B (along 7°40'S) is 11°46.3'
:: Position C is (7°40'S 30°W) + (11°46.3') = (7°40'S 18°13.7'W)
700 nm true N from posn C = 700/60 = 11°40' change in Long
:. Position D is (7°40'S 18°13.7'W) + (11°40' S) = (4°N 18°13.7'W)
700 nm true W from posn D (along 4°N) = (11°41.71'W)
:: Final Position = (4°N 18°13.7'W) + (11°41.71'W) = (4°N 29°55.4W)

Ans: Glide Slope angle = %/100 × 60 = (12/100) x 60 = 7.2°
ROD on ILS = GS/min x glide angle x 100 = 540/60 × 7.2 x 100 = 6480 fpm
Change in ROD = GS Change/60 × 7.2 × 100 = 30/60 × 7.2 x 100 = 360 fpm

Ans. {(300 - 270) x 15}/60 + 15  => 75 + 15  => 22.5 nm

Time by Speed Adjustment
The formula from which all speed adjustment is derived from is
"If aircraft speed is increased or decreased by a basic speed in 'speed/minute',
then 1 second is gained or lost for every minute of flighằi
Speed Correction
Old speed x Old time = New speed x New time
Q. Aircraft speed 200 kts. ETA 1230. Fix at 1200 shows aircraft is 100 nm
to destination. New ETA required is 1227. What is the new speed reqd?
Ans: 200 kts × 30 minutes = New speed × 27 minutes
New speed = (200x30)/27 = 223 kts
Bells Method
† or j speed by 'no. of knots' equal to 'no. of seconds' aircraft is
late or early & hold it for (GS/minute) minutes. Time for holding
that correction is constant (GS/minute) irrespective of being
early / late. It is generally applied for small corrections of time.
Q. At a checkpoint, aircraft is 5 seconds late. GS is 180 kts.
Ans: Increase speed by 5 kts, hold for 3 minutes (180/60)
Bells Method Inverse
If aircraft speed is 1 or 1 by (GS/minute), then the aircraft will
gain or lose that many seconds. It is used for larger time
corrections.
Q. At a checkpoint, aircraft is 25 seconds early. GS is 180 kts.
Ans: J speed by 3 kts (180/60), hold for 25 minutes.
Rule of 'n' / Rule of 5
1 or 1 speed by (GS/min) x 5, hold for (no. of secs early or late) / 5
Q. At a checkpoint, aircraft is 25 seconds late. GS is 180 kts.
Ans: 1 speed by 15 kts (180/60) x 5, hold for 5 minutes (25/5)
f X Factor = (GS/minute) x no. of seconds early or late
Time actually gone in minutes
It is used to address variation between calculated GS & actual GS observed.
X factor is usually applied at 1st checkpoint en route.
Q. Planned GS 180 kts. Set course time 1300. Checkpoint should have  Navigation
been at 1310:00, but was at 1309:30. What is the actual GS?
Ans: X factor = (180/60 x 30) / 9.5 = 9.47 ~ 9
Actual GS is 180+9=189 kts. So, from now on, maintain 171 kts
(180-9), after applying current error correction by rule on 'n'.
Speed Correction by Mental DR
IAS x Time (minutes) early or late at destination
1 or J speed by Time (minutes) remaining to make good ETA
Q. Aircraft speed is 360 kts. Flight time is 80 minutes. At 20 minutes,
aircraft is found to be 1 minute late. To make good ETA, what is the
new speed required?
Ans: After 20 minutes, aircraft is 1 minute late. If no adjustment is made,
aircraft will be late at destination by 4 minutes.
To make good ETA, reminder of the flight must be covered in
59 minutes. : Increase in speed required = 360 x 4/59 = 24 kts

Time by Distance Adjustment
t = time on each leg
Dog Legs: Alter heading to lose time
30° = ~ 25% t  60° = t
45° = ~ 50% t  90° = 45 secs
Proof COS 0 = AD/AB
AD = t COS e  DC = t COS e
(AB+BC) - (AD+DC) = 2t - 2 COS 6 = 2t(1-COS e)
Time to lose on dog leg = 2t(1-COS e)
t = No. of minutes to be held on dog leg
So 30° = 2t x (1-COS 30) = 2t x .1339 = .2679T ~ 25% t
45° = 2t x (1-COS 45) = 2t x .292 = 5T ~ 50% t
90° Dog Leg
60° = 2t x (1-COS 60) = 1 t
90° = 45 secs
But practically, it is 15 sec for a 60° dogleg, 10 sec for 45° dogleg & 5 sec for a 30°
dogleg, due to the additional time is required for roll-in for a Rate 1 turn.
So, reduce that much time on each leg.
Cutting Corner
A method of gaining time in which aircraft turns early before
reaching a waypoint and intercepts the next track
Proof: DF = t SIN ½ FE = t SIN /½
:. DE = 2t SIN ½  t SIN 8/2 F
G = 2t - 2t SIN ½ = 2t (1-SIN ½)
or T = G/2(1-SIN 0)  0 = angle between tracks  t SIN ½
G = time you want to gain
t = distance before turn
Precomputed Time Legs PCTL
A method of gaining time in which aircraft turns early before
reaching a waypoint and intercepts the next track
PCTL is a part of original navigation plan. Planned flight
track is ABC. If no time correction is required, then follow
ABC. If we need to lose time, follow ABDEC as per how
many minutes early.

Structural Mass Limitations: It is published by the aircraft manufacturer.
MZFM (Max Zero Fuel Mass): Max permitted mass, with TL+ unusable fuel.
MSTM (Max Structural Taxi Mass): Max permitted mass before taxi-out.
MSTOM (Max Structural Takeoff Mass): Max permitted mass for takeoff.
MSLM (Max Structural Landing Mass): Max permitted mass for landing.
Performance Mass Limitations: It is to be calculated by the operator.
PLTOM (Performance Limited TOM): Max takeoff mass limited by departure
aerodrome characteristics & obstructions. (See also: Takeoff Performance)
PLLM (Performance Limited LM): Landing mass limited by destination
aerodrome characteristics & obstructions.
Regulated Mass Limitation
RTOM (Regulated Takeoff Mass): Lower of MSTOM & PLTOM  Mass Balance  Performance
RLM (Regulated Landing Mass): Lower of MSLM & PLLM
Max Traffic Load (TL) is the lowest of the following:
- Structural Limited TL: MZFM - DOM
- Takeoff Limited TL: RTOM - DOM - FOB
- Landing Limited TL: RLM - DOM - Fuel remaining
Max Takeoff Mass is the lowest of the following:
- MZFM + Takeoff fuel
- RTOM (Least of MSTOM & PLTOM)
- RLM (Least of MSLM & PLLM) + fuel used in flight

• Mass & Balance Documentation
Prior to each flight: Mass & balance must be documented & accepted
by Commander with a signature. A 'last-minute change' procedure must
be established by the operator. If a passenger is boarding at the last
minute, mass & balance need not be recalculated, provided that, that
much extra fuel is burned-off before takeoff.
Mass & Balance documentation must contain the following details:
- Aircraft registration and type.
- Flight identification number and date.
- Identity of the Commander & person who prepared the document.
- Dry Operating Mass and the corresponding CG of the aircraft.
- Fuel mass at takeoff, trip fuel mass & consumables other than fuel.
- Components of load including passenger, baggage, freight & ballast.
- Takeoft mass, landing mass and zero tuel mass.
- Load distribution.
- Applicable aircraft CG positions.
- Limiting mass & CG values.
All aircraft must be weighed:
- On initial entry into service;
- Every 4 years after initial weighing;
- After aircraft alterations or modifications;
- Whenever DOM change exceeds more than 0.5% of MLM;
- Whenever CG position at DOM exceeds 0.5% of MAC.
Fleet Mass Weighing:
- It is a procedure for weighing random samples of aircraft in a fleet,
instead of weighing the entire fleet.
Performance  Mass Balance  - DOM of the fleet is calculated by weighing (n + 51) aircraft samples.
n = no. of aircraft in the fleet
- Fleet mass weighing is done every 9 years.
- If DOM of an aircraft moves outside fleet mass tolerances, that
aircraft has to move out of the fleet mass weighing system. That
aircraft has to be weighed separately, every 4 years.

• Centre of Gravity
Centre of Gravity
- CG is the 'point of balance', a point through which the entire
mass of the aircraft is considered to acts downwards.
- It is the point through which the three axes of the aircraft pass through.
- It is the part of a/c that follows the fight path & manoeuvres in the air.
- It is on a point along the aircraft's longitudinal axis, but not necessarily
between the nose & tail. It can be ahead of its nose or beyond its tail.
- CG is not fixed & moves during flight due to fuel burn, pax movement etc.
- Permitted range of CG movement is determined by the manufacturer &
It is the operator's responsibility to ensure CG movement is within limits.
- After a re-fit, new BEM & CG datum must be determined by the operator.
- CG position = Total moment/lotal mass.
- CG position determines how longitudinal stable or manoeuvrable a/c is.
- CG behind aft-limit may cause aircraft to be neutrally stable.
- CG of all aircraft must be mentioned in % MAC.

000 Declared Distances
Obstacle Clearance Plane: OCP starts along a line perpendicular
to the centreline of the runway, slopes up at 1.2% & is tangential
to (or clears) all obstructions. The width of OCP is:
- 200' either side of r/w centreline from start of the plane till end of r/w;
- Thereafter, increasing to 500' at 1500' from the start of the plane;
- Thereafter, 500' on either side of the centreline of the plane.
Screen Height/Reference '0': Height of an imaginary screen placed:
- At the end of TODR, at 35 above threshold height (Class A aircraft)
or 50' (Class B aircraft), during takeoft.
- At beginning of LDR, at 50' above threshold (all a/c class), for landing.
Stopway: An area at the end of TORA, where an aircraft can be stopped
during an abandoned takeoff.
- Its width & slope must be the same as that of the runway.
- It must have minimum 30% of the load-bearing strength of the runway.
Clearway: An area on ground/water, over which an aircraft may make a
portion of its initial climb, to the specified screen height.
- Clearway starts at the end of TORA.
- Its length is ½ of TORA or till the distance of the 1st obstacle that
can damage an aircraft, whichever is less. Its width is 150 m at the
runway end, expanding to 180 m by the end of clearway.
- Obstacles should not project a plane sloping up at end of r/w at 1.25%.

ASDR Acceleration Stop Distance Required
It is the distance required from standing start, to bring aircraft to a
complete stop, during a reject takeoff, assuming:
- Aircraft accelerates on all engines at takeoff thrust, till the point of
engine failure & thereafter with critical engine inoperative & remaining
engines at takeoff thrust;
- Engine failure is recognised at V1 & action is initiated to abandon
takeoff;
- Aircraft is retarded with all available means of retardation but without
using reverse thrust;
- Landing gear remains fully extended.

LDR Landing Distance Required
It is the distance required during a normal landing for an aircraft, from
a screen height of 50' (for all classes) above the threshold at speed
VREF & come to a complete stop (following a steady descend gradient
not more than 5% & speed not < VREF) on a dry level surface, under
ISA temperature conditions. LDR has to be multiplied by a regulatory
factor as shown below, while calculating performance requirements:
- LDR × 1.67 for Jets at destination (A/c will stop within 60% of 1.67 x LDR)
- LDR x 1.42 for props at destination (A/c will stop within 70% of 1.42 x LDR)
- LDR × 1.42 at diversion. (A/c will stop within 70% of 1.42 x LDR)
- LDR × 1.92 if runway is wet or a grass-runway. (115% of 1.62 x LDR)
- 10% increase in LDR has to be added for every 1% down-sloping
runway. No reduction in LDR is subtracted for an up-slope runway.

- Approach speed (10% high approach speed = 20% 1 in LDR).
- A/c height above threshold (50' higher than normal = 1 1000' LDR).

TORA Takeoff Run Available: It is the length of runway declared as

Takeoff/Landing performance with varying parameters
- 21% increase in takeoff weight = 10% increase in takeoff speed.
- 10% increase in takeoff weight = 21% increase in takeoff distance.
- Tailwind of 10% of takeoff speed = 21% increase in takeoff distance.
- Headwind 10% of takeoff speed = 19% decrease in takeoff distance.
- 10% increase in weight = 10% increase in landing distance.
- 21% increase in weight = 10% increase in landing speed.
- 10% increase in landing speed = 20% increase in landing distance.
- Takeoff performance is calculated with the actual temperature.
- Landing performance is calculated with the forecast temperature.

• V Speeds  'V' stands for Vitesse, French for speed.
All speeds mentioned in Flight Manual are IAS
All published V speeds' are CAS, except VO which is EAS. E
VMcG Min Controllable Speed Ground. It is the minimum CAS during
takeoff run at which if one engine becomes suddenly inoperative, it is
possible to recover directional control of an aircraft & continue takeoff
with rudder forces alone, not exceeding 150 Ibs; provided:
- Aircraft lateral deviation from runway centreline is not > 30';
- Max takeoff thrust is available on live engine;
- Aircraft has max AUW;
- Aircraft is in takeoff configuration;
- Nose wheel steering is not used;
- Landing gear remains extended;
- 7 kts crosswind from the inoperative engine side is assumed.
VCA Min Controllable Speed Air. It is the CAS at which if one engine
becomes suddenly inoperative, it is possible to maintain aircraft
directional control with rudder forces not exceeding 150 Ibs; provided:
- Bank is not exceeding 5° into the live engine;
- Direction loss is not exceeding 20°;
- Thrust on the live engine is not reduced;
- Aircraft is airborne and is out of ground effect;
- VMCA is less than or equal to 1.2 Vs.
VCA is demonstrated with CG at the rearmost point, with max AUW &
max continuous thrust on the live engine (other engine is windmilling).
During takeoff, with one engine inoperative, lift-off shouldn't be
attempted until aircraft speed is > VMCA, by specified safety margin.
V1 Takeoff Decision Speed. It is the CAS during takeoff run at which it is
possible, with the critical engine inoperative, to continue with takeoff &
achieve V½ by 35' within TODA; or to reject takeoff & bring aircraft to
complete stop within ASDA.
- V1 is more than or equal to VMCG
- V1 is less than or equal to VR
- V1 is less than or equal to VMBE
Increase in V1 will result in:
†ASDR, 1 TODR
- Improvement in obstacle clearance performance.

- 1 Mass = 1 V1  - Runway length, condition
1 Flaps = 1 Vł  - Engine thrust used for takeoff
- Tailwinds | & headwinds † V1  - Reverse thrust/brakes
VR Rotation Speed. It is the CAS at which rotation is initiated, such that
max rotation rate would attain VLOF, & aircraft will attain speed V½ by 35'.
- VR is more than or equal to V1
- VR is more than or equal to 1.05 VMCA
- VR is more than or equal to 1.1 Vs  Mass Balance  Performance

aircraft is rotated at VR.
- VLor is less than or equal to Tyre Limiting Speed.

00 9 - 10
V½ Takeoff Safety Speed. It is the speed that has to be achieved by 35'
height, during takeoff.
- It ensures a 15° angle of bank manoeuvrability.
- It gives a specified safety margin from stall.
- It ensures controllability of aircraft during an EFATO.
- V½ = 1.2 Vs OR  V2 = 1.1 VMCA, Whichever is higher.
Factors affecting V½:
1 Mass = 1 V2  - 1 Flaps = 1 V½
- Forward CG = 1 V2
- VMCA (which depends on Pressure Altitude & temperature)
Vx Best Angle of Climb Speed. Maintaining Vx during climb ensures
maximum height gain in the least forward distance travelled. But it
may take more time than maintaining Vy.
- Vx is the same as VIMD for jets, & slightly less than VMP for props.
- Vx is always < Vy. With † in altitude, Vx remains constant, Vy l.
- At the absolute ceiling, Vx = Vy.
- When lowering undercarriage or flaps, Vx J, Vy l.
Vxse Best Angle of Climb Speed with one engine inoperative.
Vy Best Rate of Climb Speed. Maintaining Vy during climb ensures
maximum height of climb in the least amount of time.
- Vy is slightly < VIMD for jets, & is slightly > VMP for props.
VysE Best Rate of Climb Speed with single engine inoperative.
VSR Stall Reference Speed. For a 'Class A' aircraft VS should not be:
- < 1G stalling speed; or
- < 2 kt / 2% (whichever greater) at which 'stick pusher' activates.
Vsw Stall Warning. Speed at which 'stall warning' must activate.
- Vsw must be 5 kts before stall or before stall speed + 5%;
- Vsw must be 3 kts or 3% more than VSR.
- Vsw must give sufficient time margin, to enable stall recovery.
VAPP Approach Speed. Speed specified for approach and landing.
This is the speed to be maintained on approach & gradually
reduced to VREF + gust, by 50' above the threshold. Maintaining
this speed avoid chances of undershooting on an approach, or
sudden high rate of sink. It gives the best compromise between
handling qualities (stall margin/controllability) & LDR.
- VAPP =
VREF + ½ of steady headwind + full gust value, limited to 20 kts; or
VREF + ⅓ of average headwind/gust-velocity limited to max 15 kts.
(See also: Air Regulations > Approach Speed)
VREF Landing Reference Speed or TTS (Target Threshold Speed) is the
speed to be achieved at 50' above the threshold, in a normal landing.
- VREF = 1.3 VS  - 1 Flaps = 1 VREF
- Forward CG = 1 VREF  - 1 Weight = 1 VREF

Other V Speeds
V1 MIN: The lowest Decision Speed, at which takeoff may be continued,
which will allow the aircraft to reach V½ (and 35 ft) after takeoff.
V1 BAL: Decision Speed, at which the 'Accelerate Stop Distance' is equal
to the 'Accelerate - Go Distance'.
V1 MAX: The highest decision speed, which will allow the aircraft to stop
within Accelerate Stop Distance Available, during a reject takeoff.
V2 MIN: Minimum Takeoff Safety Speed. It should not be less than 1.2 Vs1.
: Steady Initial Climb Speed, which the aircraft is assumed to have
after takeoff, with all engines operating. V3 = V2 + 10 kts.
V4  : Steady initial climb speed, with all engines operating, to the point
where acceleration to 'flap retraction speed' is initiated. This speed
should be attained by a height of 400 ft.
VA : Design Manoeuvring Speed. It is the recommended IAS in
moderate turbulence or for throwing the aircraft about. Va is the
maximum speed at which full control deflections can be made
safely, without exceeding the design wing loading. At or below
this speed, aircraft will stall first & thus reduce the aerodynamic
force on the wings,
† Altitude = 1 VA. 20% increase in weight = 10% increase in VA.
VAT  : Threshold Crossing Speed, usually, it is 1.3 Vso.
VATO  : Threshold Crossing Speed with all engines operating.
VAT1 : Threshold Crossing Speed with the critical engine inoperative.
VAT MAX: Maximum Threshold Crossing Speed, above which a go-around
should be initiated, to prevent exceeding the available landing
distance. VAT MAX = VATO + 15 kts.
: Turbulence Speed. Design Speed for Max Gust Intensity. Whereas
VA is a fixed value relative to Vs1 for all aircraft within the same
category, Ve is the recommended turbulence penetration speed.
When flying at Vs, aircraft gets max protection against structural
damage. When maintaining Vs, aircraft must be able to withstand
66 ft/sec vertical gust without crossing its 'g' limits.
VBR  : Best Range Speed. It is the speed that provides max L/D ratio,
thus minimum drag & minimum power required, & consequently,
greatest distance per litre of fuel. It usually utilises about 55%
power & decreases as aircraft weight decreases from MTOW.
Wind conditions also have to be taken into account.
: Best Endurance Speed. It is the speed that gives the greatest
airborne time per litre of fuel. It is usually around 75% of VBR &
speed is flown when flying a search pattern allowing maximum  decreases as aircraft weight reduces from MTOW. Usually, this  Mass Balance  Performance
time for area survey.
: Best (Power-off) Glide Speed. It is the speed that provides max
L/D ratio or maximum glide ratio, & consequently the greatest
glide distance during aircraft power-off glide, in a specified
configuration. It is same as the best range speed, and decreases
as the aircraft weight decreases from MTOW.
VCL. : Clean Configuration Safety Speed.
===== [avh 0381]
9 - 12
Vc  : Design Cruise Speed or Optimum Cruise Speed. It is the speed
giving most velocity (i.e., greatest distance per time) from a litre
of fuel, usually utilising 75% power at MTOW. When maintaining
Vc, aircraft must be able to withstand 50 ft/sec vertical gust without
crossing 'g' limits. Vc should not exceed max speed at 'MCT max
continuous thrust'. Vc should have a sufficient margin from Va.
Vo  : Design Diving Speed. It is the maximum speed considered when
assessing the strength of aircraft. When flying at Vc, and if the
aircraft goes into a dive, it provides a safety margin when the
pilot pulls-up to recover. When maintaining Vo, aircraft must be
able to withstand 25 ft/sec vertical gust without crossing 'g' limits.
VDF  : Demonstrated Flight Diving Speed.
VEF  : Speed at which the critical engine js assumed to fail during takeoff
for V1 calculations. It assumes aircraft accelerates after critical
engine failure. It is > 105% of VMC.
: Design Flap Speed.
: Maximum Speed for Stability (flight controllability) characteristics.
: Maximum Flaps Extended Speed. It is the top end of the white
arc on an ASI. Above this speed, extending flaps or flight with flaps
extended may result in distortion/damage of flaps or its mechanism.
: Flap Retraction Safety Speed. Lowest airspeed at which flaps
should be retracted.
VFTO  : Final Takeoff Speed.
VGA  : Go-Around Speed.
VH  : Max Level Flight Speed attainable utilising maximum continuous
engine power, which, for some engines, may be less than the
full-throttle power.
VHOLD: Holding Speed which gives the best endurance for a specified
configuration and altitude.
VLD MAX: Speed which gives greatest glide distance (max Lif/Drag ratio).
: Maximum Landing Gear Extension Speed. Speed at which the
landing gear can remain extended without risking damage.
: Maximum Landing Gear Operation Speed. Speed at which the
landing gear system can be operated. Different limits may exist
for extension and retraction.
VLL  : Maximum Speed for extending the landing lights.
VLOF  : Maximum Lift-off Speed, for normal takeoff (about 10% above VU).
VLS  : Minimum Selectable Airspeed for auto-pilot and auto-thrust.
VMAX  : Maximum attainable speed in level flight, at a specified altitude.
VMBE : Maximum Brake Energy Absorption Speed. Applying brakes
above this speed may cause damage to tyres.
VCL : Minimum speed at which aircraft can be controlled after a failure
Performance  Mass Balance  of the critical engine, in landing configuration (landing flaps, gear
extended) with go-around power set on the operating engine.
VMD  : Minimum Descent Speed. The speed that results in the lowest
sink rate in a power-off glide, providing the longest duration of a
glide, but less than the maximum gliding range. ~ 90% of VBG
VMIN  : Minimum Selectable Airspeed.
VMO  : Maximum Operating Limit Speed, of the aircraft.
VMS  : Minimum Speed in a Stall.
: Minimum Threshold Crossing Speed.
===== [avh 0382]
9 - 13
VU: Minimum Unstick Speed. Speed used in takeoff where it is
advisable to lift-off at lowest possible speed, to get the tires off
the surface (e.g. soft field, wet grass, etc.) and safely fly in
ground effect until Vross is attained, to allow climb-away.
VNE: Never Exceed Speed. The speed which must not be exceeded in
a glide or dive or other manoeuvres in smooth air. It is the red
line at the top-end of the ASI yellow arc. It is usually 90% of the
Design Diving Speed Vo, which Itself is usually 1.4 times Vo.
Vo: Maximum Structural Cruise Speed. It is the top-end of the green
arc on ASI. When cruising at or below Vo, the aircraft will not be
damaged by a 35 kt vertical gust. Flight above Vo should only
be conducted cautiously and in smooth air.
Vp : Pull-up Speed. The maximum speed at which the aircraft may be
pulled out of a dive, with instantaneous full control deflection.
VR : Rotation Speed. It is the speed at which rotation is initiated for
takeoff, such that maximum rotation rate would attain speed
VLOF, & aircraft will attain speed V2 by 35'.
VRA  : Rough Air Speed. VRA must be less than (VO - 35 kts) TAS, and
less than or equal to V.
Vs  : Stalling Speed. It is the minimum speed at which the aircraft is
controllable in air.
Vso  : Stalling speed in the landing configuration, at MTOW & with 1G
wing loading, with the CG at the most forward position allowed. It
is at the bottom end of the white arc on the ASI. Vso decreases
as the aircraft weight decreases from MTOW.
VS1  : Stalling speed, or the minimum steady flight speed, in a specified
flight configuration (usually in clean configuration), at MTOW &
with 1G wing loading. It is at the bottom end of the green arc on
ASI. Vs1 decreases as the aircraft weight decreases from MTOW.
It also means that if the pilot can reduce the wing loading below
1G by an 'unloading' (-ve G) manoeuvre, Vs1 is decreased.
Vs2G : Stalling Speed in a specified flight configuration under a 2G wing
VS15  : Stalling Speed in the specified flap configuration (flaps x°).
VSR  : Slat Retraction Safety Speed. It is the lowest speed at which the
slats should be retracted during a climb-out.
Vss  : Stick Shaker Activation Speed.
VSSE  : Safe Single Engine Speed (about 10% > VMc).
Vsw  : Stall Warning Speed.
: Threshold Crossing Speed.
VT MAX: Maximum Threshold Crossing Speed.
VTD  : Touchdown Speed.  Mass Balance  Performance
Vross : Minimum Takeoff Safety Speed. Speed to ensure that adequate
control will still exist during initial climb after takeoff, under
conditions of turbulence, or even engine failure. After lift-off aircraft
should not be allowed to climb away until Vross is attained.
Vu  : Utility Speed.
Vw  : Maximum Speed for Winch Launch (glider).
Vww  : Windshield Wiper Operation Speed.
VZF  : Minimum Zero Flaps Speed.
===== [avh 0383]
9 - 14
• Performance Definitions
DGCA is the authority to grant Certificate of Airworthiness to transport aircraft.
But since almost all commercial transport aircraft are manufactured abroad &
aircraft flight manuals are prepared according to regulations of the country of
manufacture, DGCA, in principle endorses 'Certificate of Airworthiness'
granted in the country of origin.
Performance: It is the capability of an aircraft in various stages of flight,
in terms of weight, altitude, speed, climb/descend gradient, rate of
climb, obstacle clearance, manoeuvrability, range, etc.
- Mandatory Performance: It is the minimum laid down performance
to be met by an aircraft, for grant of 'Certificate of Airworthiness' by
the appropriate authority. It is specified as:
- Gross Performance: It is used for certification purposes. It is
the average performance expected to be achieved by a fleet of
aircraft type & with average pilot skills.
- Net Performance: It is used for obstacle clearance purposes. It
accounted for, due to factors such as:
- Variation in operating techniques and maintenance practices;
- Ageing of aircraft;
- Deviation in environmental conditions.
- Demonstrated Performance: It is the performance recorded during
demonstration flights by manufacturer, for certificate of Airworthiness.
- Operational Performance: It is the performance specified by the
manufacturer for daily aircraft operations. It is more conservative
than Mandatory Performance & is given in the 'Flight Manual.
Gross Height: True height attained at any point in takeoff fight path using
gross climb performance. It is used for calculating 'pressure altitudes'
for obstacle clearance & height at which flap retraction is initiated.
Net Height: True height attained at any point in takeoff flight path using
net climb performance. It is used to determine the net flight path that
must clear all obstacles & comply with operating regulations.
Service Ceiling: Altitude at which theoretical ROC reduces to 100 fpm
for piston aircraft or 500 fpm for jet aircraft, with all engines at MCT.
Absolute Ceiling: Altitude at which theoretical ROC, with all engines
operating at MCT, reduced to 'O' fpm.
Aerodynamic Ceiling (Coffin Corner or Q corner): Altitude, in
unaccelerated 1G level flight, where basic stall speed (slow speed) &
Performance  Mass Balance  MCRIT (high-speed buffet) are coincident.
(See also: Manoeuvre Margin > Q Comer)
Performance Classes of Aircraft
Class A: 'Any turbo-jet aircraft' & 'all turbo-prop with AUW > 5700 kg or
passengers > 9'. It refers only to multi-engine aircraft. Class 'A'a/c shall
not have to force-land in case of an engine failure at any stage of flight.
Class B: Any "turboprop or piston a/c' with AUW < 5700 kg or passenger < 9.
Class C: Any piston aircraft with AUW > 5700kg or passengers > 9.
Unclassified: Aircraft with unique performance. e.g. seaplanes.

Takeoff Performance
Maximum Takeoff Weight is the lowest of:
1. Max Zero Fuel Weight + Fuel required;
2. Max Structural Limit Takeoff Weight;
3. Max Performance Limited Takeoff Weight; which in-turn is lowest of:
3a. Max Field Length Limit Weight
3b. Climb Limit Weight (Climb gradient required in takeoff flight path)
3c. Obstacle Limit Weight (Obstruction gradient in takeoff flight path)
4. Max Structural Limit Landing Weight + Burn-off Fuel;
5. Performance Limited Landing Weight; which in-turn is lowest of:
5a. Max Field Length Limit Weight (LDA)
5b. Max Climb Limit Landing Weight (Landing Climb gradient 2.1%)
5c. Obstacle Limit Weight (to clear obstacle by 35' during go-around)
6. Tyre Speed Limit Weight;
7. Brake Energy Limit Weight.

oo 3b. Climb Limit Weight  (See also: Aerodynamics > Steady Climb)

ROC (fpm)  Thrust - Co x 100%
TAS (kts)  Weight
Hence maximum climb gradient is achieved at best Co/CL angle of
attack, with minimum weight & when maximum thrust is available.

Field Limit TOW & Climb Limit TOW ensure adequacy of field length &
2nd segment climb gradient. However, with this climb gradient, net
takeoff flight path may not clear obstacles on the takeoff path by 35'.
In such cases, obstacles can be cleared only by I TODR and/or f
climb gradient capability. This is achieved by I TOW and/or 1 V1.
Thus, we arrive at Obstacle Limit Weight.
Though climb gradient by definition is not affected by wind, flight path
angle f with headwind resulting in better obstacle clearance. Thus,
with head wind, Obstacle Limit Weight t. When Obstacle Limit Weight
is less than Field Limit TOW, it can be improved to climb on the lines
as per 'improved climb' mentioned in earlier.

As long as V½/Vs ratio is 1.2, it is ensured that VLOF does not exceed

improving climb, VLOF corresponding to resulting V2 may exceed tyre
limiting speed. Thus TOW may be restricted by tyre speed limits,
especially in low flap configuration coupled with down-slope and/or
tailwind. Tyre Speed Limit Weight depends on the ground speed of
aircraft, which is higher for a given CAS, when air the density Is less.
Hence, Tyre Speed Limit Weight is reached at a lower VLOF, and
hence it J with † in Pressure Altitude/OAT, or in tailwinds.
For a given ASDA, a higher V1 calls for more braking action, thus,  Mass Balance  Performance
heating wheel brakes more. Thus, 1 in V1 beyond a value (VMBE) may
exceed Brake Energy Limit, in which case Vi has to be restricted to
VMBE, & TOW has to J accordingly. Braking action is related to aircraft
weight & ground speed. Hence, Brake Energy Limit is reached at a
lower CAS, when OAT, Pressure Altitude or tailwind components are
high. Similarly, a down-slope calls for a lower value of VMBE, since a
component of acceleration due to gravity has to be compensated by
additional braking action at a given ground speed. A higher flap
configuration provides f drag which helps braking action and thus 1 VMBE.

00 Balanced Field: (Effect of V1 on TORR, TODR, ASDR)
- Balanced Field Length by definition is where a V1 is chosen
so that ASDA = TODA; or Stopway = Clearway.
† V1 = 1 ASDR (higher abort speed = more runway length required).
1 V1 = 1 TODR (It is easier to continue takeoff with a higher V1).
- When you put these two values in a graph (refer to the graph below), the
point where they intersect defines 'Balanced Field Length'. Any further
variation of V1 results in a 1 in TODR or ASDR. If you 1 V1, ASDR will
T, and, if you J V1, TODR will †.
- So, a 'Balanced Field Length' represents the minimum runway length
that you need for a given aircraft weight; or the maximum weight you
can takeoff with, from a given runway length.
- An 'Unbalanced Field' is where clearway is factored into the calculation.
You can carry more weight from an unbalanced field than a balanced
field, by reducing V1. Unfortunately, this calculation is complex. You
need to calculate TODR, TORR, ASDR & Brake Energy Limits.
- The main benefit of using Balanced Field in planning boils down to its
simplicity (ease of performance calculations) at a small weight penalty.
In other words,
For a fixed TORA/TODA & unrestricted ASDA, V1/VR ratio | with
weight. On the other hand, if ASDA is fixed & if TORA/TODA is not
restricting, a lower value of V1/VR may enable f of TOW. Hence, for a
given runway length, there will be one maximum weight &
corresponding V1, such that in the event of a critical engine failure,
- Before V1 takeoff cannot be continued;
- After V1, takeoff cannot be abandoned;
- At V1, both options are available.
This criterion (when TODA = ASDA) is called 'Balanced Field Length'.
- In other words, stopway = clearway; or
- A runway that has no stopway or clearway is a balanced runway.
- If a runway has a stopway, but no clearway, then that runway
unbalanced.
If actual AUW is less than weight limited by TORA/TODA & ASDA,
there will be a minimum & a maximum value of V1 & an option to
select within these values. Thus, † in V1 will result in:
- Longer ASDR;
- Shorter TODR;
- Improvement in obstacle clearance.

Takeoff Flight Path and Gross Gradient Requirements
(incase of failure of the critical-engine on multi-engine aircraft)
Takeoff Path: It extends from the point of standing start of aircraft during
takeoff, until it reaches 1500' above MSL.
Takeoff Flight Path: It extends from 35' above MSL (at the end of TODR)
to 1500' above MSL.
Takeoff Gross Flight Path: Takeoff Flight Path at 3.2% climb gradient.
Takeoff Net Flight Path: It is the gradient of 'Takeoff Gross Flight Path'
reduced by a margin of 0.8% (for 2 engine aircraft), 0.9% (for 3 engine
aircraft) & 1.0% (for 4 engine aircraft). On Takeoff Net Flight Path, an
aircraft must clear all obstructions by 35' vertically or by 200' horizontally.

•• En-route Performance
En-route performance is applicable from:
Class A a/c: 1500' above takeoff surface to 1500' above landing surface.
Class B a/c: 1500' above takeoff surface to 1000' above landing surface.
En-route Gross Flight Path: It is the flight path along which, with one
engine inoperative & other at MCT (Max Continuous Thrust), actual
gradient of climb is available.
En-route Net Flight Path: It is the climb gradient of En-route Gross Flight
Path reduced by a margin of 1.1% (for 2 engine aircraft), 1.4% (for 3
engine aircraft) & 1.6% (for 4 engine aircraft). Net Flight path during
en-route segment must clear all obstructions within 5 nm of track by:
- 1000' during climb;
- 1000' over plains during cruise;
- 2000' over mountainous terrain during cruise;
- 2000' during descent.
At 1500' above landing surface, there should be a positive climb gradient.

Drift Down: During an engine failure, it may not be possible for an aircraft
to maintain altitude even with the live engine at MCT, due to reduced
engine performance at higher altitudes. Thus, aircraft has to lose height,
until it reaches a lower level (Gross Level-off Altitude), where level flight
on one engine is possible. For this, aircraft has to maintain the best o
ratio speed (which depends on weight) for it to cover maximum distance
with minimum height loss. Such a profile called 'Drift Down Profile' &
the speed to be maintained is called 'Drift Down Speed' (usually Vyse).
- Head/Tailwind does not affect drift down rate.
- Headwind | & tailwind † drift down distance.
Gross Level-off Altitude: It is the Pressure Altitude where thrust
available with one engine inoperative equals aircraft drag, when flying
best p ratio speed. It is not mandatory to follow the drift down profile,
but it must be followed if obstacle clearance is critical.

•° Approach Pertormance
Approach/Landing Climb Regulations
- During a 'go-around' after a missed-approach with both engines
operational, the minimum climb gradient required is 2.5%.
- In a 'go-around' after touch down (baulked landing) with takeoff
thrust available on both engines (after 8 secs of advancement of
throttle to takeoff position) with aircraft in landing configuration &
with landing gear extended, it should be possible to achieve a climb
gradient of 3.2%, without speed exceeding 1.3 Vs.
- If 'going-around' during approach with the critical engine inoperative,
with live engine at takeoff thrust & aircraft is in approach configuration
(flaps 1, landing gear up), it should be possible to achieve a climb
gradient of 2.1% (2 engine aircraft), 2.4% (3 engine aircraft), 2.7%
(4 engine aircraft) without speed exceeding 1.5 Vs.

• Manoeuvre Margins
Buffeting: It occurs at low and high speed regimes, as follows:
Pre-stall Buffet: It occurs close to stalling speed. It 1 with † in aircraft
weight, bank angle, forward CG position, PA & load factor, and !
with 1 in flaps.
Shockwave Induced Buffet: It occurs at McRIT. To allow for a safety
margin, a lower mach no. (Mo) is chosen as upper manoeuvre
limit. This mach no. marginally j with an increase in bank.
Low Altitude Manoeuvre Margin: At low altitudes, i.e., during takeoff &
approach for landing, speeds are low & upper limit mach no. is never
reached. At these altitudes, stick shaker speeds associated with various
flaps/slats configurations & landing gear have to be considered, taking
into account maximum bank requirements for obstacle avoidance, and
for following approach procedures.
High Altitude Manoeuvre Margin: At high altitudes, an aircraft is flown
in clean configuration & at high speeds. At the altitude selected for
cruise, there should be adequate manoeuvre margin, catering for a
bank angle corresponding to a load factor of at least 1.3 G. For other
altitudes, it is essential to know the following limits:
- Range of speeds at which mach no. buffet occurs at bank required
for normal manoeuvres;
- Max bank at which flight can be continued without occurrence of buffet.
• Coffin Corner (Aerodynamic Ceiling or Q corner)
- (1) For an aircraft, stall speed is the minimum speed required to
maintain level flight. Any reduction in speed will cause aircraft to
stall & lose altitude. Similarly, McRIT is the max speed at which
aircraft can fly without losing lift due to flow separation & shock
waves. Any 1 in speed will cause aircraft to lose lift, or to pitch
heavily nose-down & lose altitude. (2) Aircraft always stalls at the
same IAS. However, as altitude 1, for same IAS, stall TAS 1.
- Putting these 2 facts together, as the aircraft altitude increases, stall
TAS & MCRIT come closer. This region of flight is called the Coffin
Corner. The "Corner" refers to the triangular shape at the top of a
flight envelope where stall TAS & MCRIT are within a few knots of each
other, where it is difficult to

Meteorology  Why is the sky blue during day & red during the twilights?
Sunlight is scattered by particles in the atmosphere. Smaller wavelengths (blue
hues) scatter easier & gets diffused. Hence we see sky as blue. This is called
Raleigh Scattering. At sunset & sunrise, because of the angle of sun's radiation,
most of the blue & green wavelengths are scattered/absorbed before reaching
lower atmosphere, hence we see more of orange & red colours during twilight.

- Atmospheric Pressure is measured by a Barometer.
