• Classification of Pressure Regions
- Low is an area of low pressure, enclosed by an isobar.
- It is caused due to the rising of hot moist air (convection), due to
heating by the sun.
- A 'Low' is associated with bad weather, high winds, but good
visibility (except in precipitation).
- At a 'Low', air converges at low altitude, ascends and diverges
at high altitude.
- Winds are anti-clockwise in a Low, in the northern hemisphere.
- A secondary Low moves around the primary Low in a clockwise
direction and is more turbulent.
Trough of Low
- It is a tongue-like 'V-shape' outward extension of isobars from an
area of low pressure. It is associated with line squalls.
- Pressure rises on either side of a 'trough of Low'.
High
- It is an area of high pressure, enclosed by an isobar.
- It is caused due to subsidence of dry cold air.
- A 'High' is associated with good weather but poor visibility.
- At a 'High', air converges at high altitude, descend & diverge at
the surface.
- Winds are clockwise in a High, in the northern hemisphere.
Ridge of High
- It is a tongue-like 'U' shape
extension from a High.
- It is associated with fair weather.
Col
Col
- It is an area between two High  ugh
& two Low pressure areas.
- It is a region of relatively flat
pressure patterns & low winds.

• Temperature
Introduction
- Surface temperature depends on latitude, season, time of day,
cloud cover, winds & nature of the surface.
- Surface temperature by meteorological department is measured in
a shade, 4' above the ground.
- During the day, ambient temperature is < surface temp due to winds.
- Flying from high temp to low temp, altimeter reads high, true alt is low.
- If temperature < ISA, the altimeter will read high, true altitude is low.
Conduction: Heat is physically transferred to an adjacent body.
Convection: Heat transferred by the movement of hot air.
Advection: Heat is transferred due to the horizontal movement of winds.
Radiation: Heat is transferred without any medium.

Insolation
- It is the solar radiation per unit area received on the earth's surface.
- Earth is heated by sun's shortwave radiation & loses heat as IR
longwave radiation.
- 51% insolation is absorbed by the earth, and 19% by the atmosphere.
- On a clear day, up to % (83%) of the sun's heat reach earth's surface.
- Atmosphere is not heated by the sun, but by earth's re-radiated heat
(23%) & by latent heat: evaporation/condensation of water (77%).
That is why temperature is max near surface and as altitude †.
- Cloudy nights are warmer since it insulates earth's re-radiation.
- Insolation is max at equator & min at poles due to earth's inclination.
- Albedo: Reflection of sunshine. 26% sunshine is reflected back or
scattered by the atmosphere. Snow reflects 80% sunshine.

• 10 - 8
Inversion
- It is the phenomenon of increase of temperature with height.
- Presence of inversion or an isothermal layer indicates that
the air mass is absolutely stable.
- Inversion does not allow surface air to rise up & mix with the upper
wind. Hence, smoke, mist & fog stagnate, causing low visibility.
- Low level inversion is seen on winter nights due to night cooling of
earth.
- Tropopause Inversion occurs at a point where temperature stops
reducing with height and becomes isothermal. Air changes from
unstable troposphere air to stable stratosphere air.
- Stratosphere Inversion is due to solar radiation (ozone heating).
Types of Inversion
Subsidence Inversion
- Air descending at a high-pressure region (compressed &
warmed by weight of air above it) meets rising cool air (due to
insolation). Where they meet, subsidence inversion occurs.
- When an aircraft is climbing through a haze layer, and if QNH >
1013, sky above this subsidence inversion layer will be clear.
Valley Inversion
- Air cooled by cold mountain rock, descends into a valley at night.
Frontal Inversion
- Caused due to the temperature difference at a Front.
Friction Layer Inversion
- During the day, when there is slight turbulence close to the surface
(2000'-3000), mixing of hot surface air with cooler air (at 3000")
occurs, forming a friction layer cloud.

Diurnal Temperature Variation
- Minimum temp is just after sunrise; max temp is at 2 hrs after noon.
- Diurnal variation maximum with nil winds, minimum with low clouds.
- Diurnal variation is minimum over the sea (just 1°C).
Temperature Definitions
Heat is the total sum of all the kinetic energy in all the molecules in
the substance. A bucket of 60°C water will have more heat than a
cup of 100°C water.
Temperature is the average value of the kinetic energy of the molecules.
Specific Heat: Heat required to raise the temperature of a body by 1°C.
Latent Heat: It is the heat absorbed/released when water changes
state from ice to water to steam. When water vapour condenses to
Meteorology  liquid, latent heat is released. When snow melts, it absorbs latent
heat, cools the air around it, and slows further melting.

• Density
Introduction
- Dry air is most dense. Moist/humid air is less dense than dry air.
- Rate of change of density reduces with increase in height.
- Low density means poor engine takeoff/climb performance.
- Surface temperature is higher & density is lower at the equator than
the poles. So, at poles, flying low is better for engine efficiency.
- Temperature is lower & density higher at the equator tropopause
than the tropopause at poles. So, for better engine efficiency, flying
near equator-tropopause is better than pole-tropopause.
Density Altitude: It is the altitude at which a given density is found in ISA.
- It is an altitude figure used only for engine performance calculations.
- Higher density altitude means a lower density prevails & vice versa.
- At a given altitude, pressure 1 = density 1 = DA 1 (good for engine).
- At a given altitude, temperature 1 = density 1 = DA 1 (bad for engine).
- At a given altitude, humidity 1 = density J = DA † (bad for engine).
- For every 1°C rise in temperature above ISA, DA increases by 118'.

Introduction
- Humidity is measured by a Hygrometer or a Psychrometer.
- Dry air is most dense. Moist/humid air is less dense than dry air.
- On a rainy day, air density. = engine climb/takeoff performance 1 =
more runway length needed for takeoff.
- Saturated air, if forced to descend, will heat up less than dry air
since latent heat will be absorbed during evaporation.
- In saturated air (RH 100%): Dry bulb temp = wet bulb temp = dew pt.
- In unsaturated air (RH < 99%): Dry bulb > wet bulb temp > dew pt.
HMR Humidity Mixing Ratio = It is the weight of water vapour contained
in a unit mass of air.
SMR Saturation Mixing Ratio = It is the HMR, when air is saturated.
Absolute Humidity: Actual amount of water vapour in a given parcel of air.
Relative Humidity: Ratio of actual water vapour air holds, to max it can hold.
- RH is affected by the change in water
vapour content & temperature.  f RH = HMR x 100

- Air temperature 1 = RH J.
- If RH < 99.9%, air is considered to be dry. RH 100% = air saturated.
Wet Bulb Temperature: It is the lowest temperature air would
attain if water is evaporated into it, to saturate it.
Dry Bulb Temperature: Actual temperature of the air. It is the OAT.
Dew-point: Lowest temperature to which air must be cooled, to saturate it.
- Cooling air below its dew-point will condense the water vapour in it.
- Dew-point is affected only by changes in water content.
- 1 water content in air = 1 dew-point.

Visibility
• Introduction
- Visibility: It is the ability, as determined by atmospheric conditions,
to identify prominent unlighted objects by day & lighted objects by
night. Visibility reported by the Met department is the lowest in any
direction in an aerodrome.
- Visibility < 800 m is reported in steps of 50 m
- 800 m to 5 km in steps of 100 m
- 5 km to 10 km in steps of 1 km
- Visibility > 10 km is reported as 10 km only.
- Prevailing Visibility: It is the greatest horizontal visibility prevailing
in more than at least half the horizon circle, which need not be
continuous.
- Inflight Visibility: It is the average forward horizontal distance, as
seen from the cockpit.
RV Runway Visibility Value
It is the visibility for a particular runway measured by a transmisso-
meter. It is used in-lieu of visibility for determining minimums. It does
not take into account lighting systems.
• RVR Runway Visual Range
It is the horizontal distance a pilot in a moving aircraft will see down
the runway while making an approach. It also takes into account
runway lighting systems and lighting intensity. It is used in-lieu of
visibility, for determining minimums for a particular runway.
- RVR is measured by transmissometer (or a skopograph), which is
placed 76 m away from the runway centreline, at a height of 15'.
- RVR is reported when visibility drops below 1500 m.
- RVR < 200 m is reported in steps of 25 m,
- 200 m - 800 m in steps of 50 m,
- RVR > 800 m is reported in steps of 100 m.
- RVR is measured at 3 points along the runway:
- Touchdown Zone (TDZ)
- Midpoint (MID)
- Roll out area or end of the runway (END)
- If TDZ RVR < 550 m, MID RVR also shall be passed by ATC.
- If TDZ or MID RVR is < 300 m, END RVR also shall be passed.
(See also: Air Regulations > Precision Approach > RVR,
SVR Slant Visual Range
It is the distance a pilot in the final stages of approach can see the
runway markings or lights.
- In shallow fog (when fog is confined to ground layers), SVR is > RVR.
- In matured fog (density of fog increases with height), SVR is «RVR.

===== [avh 0401]
10 - 11
• Fog: Fog is a stratus cloud on the ground, caused due to condensation.
It is made of very minute water droplets or ice, suspended in the air.
- In fog, visibility is < 1,000 m, and RH is close to 100%.
Radiation Fog: It is caused by radiation (night cooling of the
ground by loss of heat). Preconditions for Radiation fog are:
- High Humidity: So that minimal cooling is required for the air to
reach dew-point.
- Clear Sky: To permit max radiation cooling of the ground at night.
- Light Wind (2-7 kts); It enables cooling to extend to a sufficiently
deep level to bring air temperature of all layers to the dew-point.
If there is no wind, ground cooling may not extend upwards, &
dew forms instead of radiation fog. If winds are too strong,
temperature may not drop sufficiently in the layer. In a stable
atmosphere, this mixing is confined to a shallow layer.
- Since minimum temperature occurs just at sunrise, fog formation is
most frequent at sunrise, between 500' - 800'. It dissipates 2-3 hrs
later by strong winds or insolation (heating of earth in the day).
- Radiation fog is frequently found when relative humidity < 100%,
due to the presence of condensation nuclei in the air.
- It forms after passage of a 'Western Disturbance', which causes rain.
- It also forms in a High or Col (no strong pressure gradient & winds).
- In India, radiation fog generally occurs during winters, only at night/
early morning & only over land.
Upslope/Valley Fog: Moist air that is forced up a mountainside is
adiabatically cooled to its dew point, and fog forms along the slope.
Advection Fog: It forms when relatively warm-moist-air (high RH)
from elsewhere blows over a cold ground. It can form over land
(during winters) or sea, day or night.
Steaming Fog (Arctic Smoke): Reverse of Advection Fog. It occurs
at high latitudes, when cold air flows over a warm sea surface, which
causes evaporation on the sea surtace. The vapour, on reaching the
cold overlying air, immediately re-condenses to form steaming fog.
- It is common over frozen land/ice in polar regions.
- Over the sea, it is also referred to as sea smoke.
- It can be up to 500' thick, and may blow onto adjacent land.
Precipitation/Frontal Fog: It forms due to saturation of air in an area
of continuous rainfall ahead of a warm front. This increases the
moisture content of the air and its dew-point is raised, causing fog.

• Mist: They are suspended water droplets in the air.
- In mist, visibility is 1000 m - 5000 m & RH is > 75%.
• Haze: In haze, visibility is 1000 m - 5000 m & RH is < 75%.
Smoke Haze: They are small particles of smoke in suspension. It

Dust Haze: It is caused by light winds kicking up dust. It is generally

is < 75%. At night, winds are calm, dust settles, visibility improves.

• Winds
Introduction
- Wind: Horizontal movement of air is called wind.
- Convection is upward & Subsidence is downward movement of air.
- Anemometer for wind measurement is placed 10 m above ground.
- Wind direction given by ATC is magnetic brg, by Met dept. is true brg.
- Winds given by ATC during takeoff is the surface winds along the
runway, & for landing is the surface winds at TDZ.
- Takeoff/Landing Winds are winds averaged for 2 mins.
- METAR winds are winds averaged for 10 mins.
- Veering: Winds turn clockwise. Backing: Winds turn anti-clockwise.
- In a low pressure in northern hemisphere, winds back (anti-clockwise).
Classification of Winds: (3 types)
- Planetary/Primary Winds
- Periodic/Secondary Winds
- Local/Tertiary Winds
1. Planetary Winds
These are winds that blow in the same direction throughout the
year. The main primary winds are: Easterly Trade winds, Subtropical
Westerlies & Polar Easterlies.  (See also: General circulation)
They are caused due to 2 main reasons:
Pressure Gradient Force
- Deferential heating between 2 areas cause change in air pressure.
Winds blow from high pressure to low pressure area.
- Closer isobars = higher PGF = faster winds.
•  Coriolis Force
- An 'apparent effect which cause objects moving on a
straight path, appear curved when viewed from a rotating earth.
- Wind in N hemis appear to deflect right & wind in S hemis to left.
- Any air moving towards the poles overtakes slow-moving
surface air & any air moving towards the equator lags behind
fast-moving surface air, e.g., easterly trade winds.
- Coriolis force increases with latitude. Nil at equator, max at poles.
- Wind speed is proportional to Coriolis. † Coriolis.= † winds.

Formation of Planetary Winds
Geostrophic Wind
- These are winds due to Pressure Gradient Force + Coriolis force.
This is a theoretical wind as there are other forces always present.
- Winds initially flow 1 to HP & LP. After that, Coriolis force takes over
& winds deflect 90° to the right (in N hemis). Eventually, when PGF
& CF are in balance, winds flow straight & || to straight isobars.
- These winds occur only above 3000' due to surface friction below 3000'
- Geostrophic winds are stronger at the equator than at poles.
- Geostrophic wind direction follows 'Buys Ballot Law'.

Gradient Wind
- These are winds due to PGF + Coriolis force + Centrifugal force.
- Gradient wind occurs when isobars are curved, causing centrifugal
forces. Thus Gradient winds are curved.
- Near a 'Low', centrifugal force opposes PGF, : actual wind speed J.
- Near a 'High', centrifugal force adds to PGF,: actual wind speed 1.

Cyclostrophic Wind
- These are winds due to PGF + Centrifugal, disregarding Coriolis.
- If Coriolis is negligible, Gradient wind = Cyclostrophic wind.
Classification of Winds by its Speed
Calm: Wind speed < 1 kt.
VRB (Variable): Wind speed 1-3 kts.
Gust: A rapid † in relative wind speed by 10 kts, for less than 1 minute.
Squall: † in wind speed >22 kts for > 1 min, with a change in direction.
Gale: Sustained winds > 33 kts for 10 mins or more.  Meteorology
Hurricane: Persistent winds with speed exceeding 63 kts.

Surface Wind: Below 3000', due to surface friction, Coriolis
force 1 & winds start blowing across isobars again.
- Due to this, in the northern hemisphere:
- Land: winds back 20°(40° by night), & speed 1 50% (70% by night)
- Sea: winds back 10°, & speed 1 30% (no change at night).
- Surface winds are generally east'ly at low lats & westly at mid lats.
- Surface wind is measured by an anemometer, 10 m above ground.
- Diurnal Variation - Wind veers & speed 1 by 1500 hrs.
- Wind backs & speed | 30 mins after sunrise.
- This helps formation of radiation fog by night & its dissipation by day.
- Variation over sea is small because of low temperature variation.

• Upper Winds: Winds due to PGF + Coriolis + Centrifugal - Surface friction.
- In N hemisphere, the upper wind veers & f speed as altitude 1 (due
to l in friction). E.g., at 20000' for same PGF, as per geostrophic wind
formula (V = PGF/20p SINe), wind speed is double, since p is half.
- Low surface temp (e.g. poles) leads to comparatively lower pressure
at same the higher altitude, compared to a higher surface temperature
(e.g. equator). Rate of drop of pressure is higher in colder areas.
- Due to this pressure difference at higher altitudes, air stars flowing
from high pressure (equator) to low pressure (poles). Now, due to
Coriolis, any poleward moving air will get deflected right in northern
hemisphere & become westerlies. So, Upper winds (incl. Jet-streams)
become progressively westerly with ht. Buys Ballot law also applies.
- Upper wind speed is maximum at tropopause & reduces above it.
- Upper-wind is measured by RAWIN (Radar Winds) or Pilot Balloons
Buys Ballot's Law
- It is a phenomenon that occurs due to Coriolis force.
- It is named after a Dutch meteorologist Mr Buys Ballot, in 1856.
- In the N hemisphere, if an observer stands with his back to the wind,
low pressure is on his left side (reverse is true in S hemisphere).
- Local winds do not follow Buys Ballot's Law, due to surface friction.

• 3. Local Winds: Winds that blow only during a particular period
of day or year. E.g.: Sea breeze, Foehn Winds, etc.
Sea Breeze
- It blows sea to land, few hrs after sunrise to few hrs after sunset.
- During the day, land gets heated faster, & a low pressure forms. This
causes a sea breeze of up to 12 kts, and blows up to 50 km inland.
- With sea breeze, temperature over land falls & RH increases.
- Sea breeze sometimes lifts up along the coast and forms a line of
cumulus clouds. This also helps as a navigation feature for pilots.
Land Breeze: Occurs during night. Land to Sea. Up to 5 kts, up to 5 nm.

Katabatic Winds
- At night, air cools & blows down along a hill slope.
- These wind speeds are not more than a few knots.
- It forms a pool of cold air, mist & fog, in the valley & low lying areas.
- If the mountainside is snow-covered, this can happen in daytime too.
Anabatic Winds
- During the day, mountain slope is heated by the sun, & air ascends.
- It is weaker than Katabatic winds, but maybe accented by sea breeze.

===== [avh 0406]
10 - 16
• General Circulation
Hadley's Cell
- ITCZ (Inter Tropical Convergence Zone): It is an area of Intense solar
radiation over the equatorial region. The landmass here heats up,
causes air to rise, form convective clouds & causes precipitation.
- Rising air creates a low pressure at surface, called Equatorial Low.
- Warm air rises until tropopause. But stratosphere air being stable,
cannot rise anymore. It turns horizontal and moves poleward.
- But due to Coriolis force, this poleward moving air becomes
westerlies. And as per conservation of angular momentum, these
winds get stronger with height & form Sub Tropical Jet-streams.
- To compensate for the rising air at equator, dry subsidence occurs
in the tropics. This inhibits cloud formation & causes large deserts over
30°N & 30°S. This area around 30°N - 40°N (Horse Latitudes) where
calm winds & high pressure prevails is called Subtropical High.
- A part of this sinking air, on reaching the surface, moves towards
the equator along earth's surface. Due to Coriolis force, this air lags
behind fast-moving surface air & turns west along the surface, forming
Easterly Trade Winds. These Trade Winds blow towards the thermal
equator, & change direction on crossing the geographical equator.
- Doldrums: An area of fair weather & light winds that exist at ITCZ,
when ITCZ is near the equator and pressure gradient is low.
(See also: Depressions > ITCL
Ferrel Cell
- Some of the subsiding air from Hadley's cell that diverges at
the surface moves poleward. Due to Coriolis, they become westerlies.
- At high latitudes, this surface wind overtakes slow-moving surface air,
& due to increasing Coriolis force, strengthen & form progressively
stormy westerly surface winds with increasing intensity, called
Roaring 40s, Furious 50s & Crying 60s.
- At 60°N, air rises, cools, condenses, forms clouds and precipitation.
- Reaching tropopause, this rising air moves poleward or equator-ward.
- This is the region of the Polar front. Polar Jet Stream forms here due
to Coriolis force, but at a lesser height due to low tropopause height.

===== [avh 0407]
10 - 17
• Jet Streams
Introduction
- Jet streams are narrow bands of high wind speeds of minimum 60 kts,
2000 nm long, 200 nm wide, 2 nm thick (ratio 1000:100:1). They
occur at the tropopause breaks between Hadley's/Ferrel/Polar cell.
- They form due to the large horizontal temperature gradient that exists
at these breaks (different air masses), which adds to the already
westerly upper winds, and the effect of Coriolis force.
- Jet Axis: Path of maximum airspeed, usually just below tropopause.
- Jet Core: Tubular area of maximum air volume around the Jet axis.
- Jet Streaks: Areas within the Jet axis with the fastest wind speeds.
- Wind speeds are not always uniform in a jet stream.
- Extensive sheet clouds (Cs, Cc on warm side & Ci on cold side) form.
- CAT (Clear Air Turbulence) occurs at the boundaries of jet streams.
- Max turbulence occurs near & below the cold (low pressure) side, left
of downstream in N hemisphere, with a 'secondary' above its axis.
- Jet streams have higher vertical wind shear (5 m/sec per km) than
horizontal wind shear.
Arctic Jet Stream: They are westerly jet streams that exist near the poles.
- It has a mean height of 7 km (20000'), with speeds of up to 120 kls.
Polar Jet Stream
- They are westerly Jet streams that exist near 50° N/S.
- It has a mean height of 9 km (30000"), with speeds of 100 - 140 kts.
- During the summer it moves to 70°N & J in speed. During winters, it
moves down to 30°N & t in speed due to higher temp differences.
Sub Tropical Westerly Jet Stream
- They are westerly jet streams that exist near 30° N/S.
- It has a mean height of 12 km (40000), with speeds of 150 - 200 kts.
- It moves with the movement of ITCZ, 25°N - 40°N.
- It arrives over North India at 27°N in October during winters, after
the withdrawal of monsoons & shifts down up to 22°N by February.
- With the onset of SW Monsoons (May), Tropical Easterly Jet forms,
& Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet moves north & disappears from India.
Tropical Easterly Jet Stream
• Easteries. Mean height of 15-16 km (50000), with speeds 60-80 kts.
- They occur only during summers, between 10°N - 20°N, over SE
Asia & Central Africa.
- It establishes over in South India with the onset of SW monsoons
(15°N in June to 12°N in Aug) & disappears by September.

===== [avh 0408]
10 - 18
• Clear Air Turbulence
Introduction
- CATs are a patchy phenomenon, less turbulent than thunderstorms.
- Turbulence classification: Light <0.5g, Moderate 0.5-1g, Severe > 1g.
- CAT can be caused due to:
- Wind shear
- Convective Turbulence
- Mountain Waves
Wind Shear: It is a sudden change in wind direction or speed > 25 kts
within 500, ≥ 40 kts within 1000', or > 50 kts within 1500', due to a:
- Topography: Wind shear due to mountains/manmade obstacles.
- Gust Front: Cold down-draught from a thundershower hits the
ground & spreads around.  (See also: Microburst)
- Microburst: (Low level wind shear) Concentrated down-draught, up
to 5 km wide, & lasts for up to 5 minutes.  (See also: Jet Streams)
- Jet Stream: CAT wind shear occurs along the edges of a jet stream.
CATs due to Jet streams occur in North & Central India due to STJS
(Oct - May, max in Feb), & in South India due to EJS (Jul - Aug).
- Front: Rapid change in temperature & wind at a front causes strong
winds and turbulence.  (See also: Fronts)
Convective Turbulence
- During the day, turbulence is due to heat convection & friction layer.
- It develops more easily when the lapse rate is steep.
- It doesn't develop over the sea or over smooth ground, where winds
are light & the lapse rate is stable.
Mountain Waves (Standing Waves)
Requirements for Mountain Wave Formation:
- A steady wind-flow, within +30° ahead of a mountain range,
(14 kts for small mountains & 30 kts for large mountains).
- Unstable atmosphere at low levels, stable (isothermal or inversion)
layer at mountain crest & unstable layer above that.
Mountain Wave Hazards
- Mountain waves have constant up-currents at its ridge & down-
currents at the leeward side, causing a dangerous sink. Adequate
terrain clearance is therefore a must before crossing a mountain.
- They extend up to 100 - 200 km laterally (a single wave up to 10 km),
& sometimes vertically, well into the stratosphere.
- Altimeter may not respond correctly due to height & temp fluctuations.

===== [avh 0409]
10 - 19
• Atmospheric Stability
Introduction
Any packet of air, when it rises (due to orographic lifting, convection,
frontal lifting, etc) expands & cools at the rate of ELR. After this initial
disturbance, depending upon whether this packet is warmer or cooler
(in effect lighter/denser) than surrounding air, it may continue to rise or
may come back down, causing atmospheric stability or instability.
ELR Environmental Lapse Rate:
- ICAO standard atmosphere ELR is 0.65°C/100m (2°C/1000')
DALR Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate: 1°C/100m (3°C/1000')
- Rate at which dry air (RH < 99%) cools as it rises.
SALR Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate: 0.6°C/100m (1.5°C/1000')
- Rate at which saturated air (RH > 99%) cools as it rises.
- DALR & SALR are theoretical values. ELR is the actual lapse rate.
DPLR Dew-point Lapse Rate: 0.16°C/100m (1.8°C/1000').
Why is SALR less than DALR? Saturated air, if forced to ascend, cools slower
as latent heat is released while water vapour condenses. This keeps the air
warmer. Similarly, saturated air, if forced to descend, will heat up
less than dry air, as latent heat is absorbed during evaporation.
Absolute Stability
If rising air (at ELR) cools slower than SALR, it means that the
rising packet will remain colder than the surrounding air, and so, will
nove down (because it is more denser than outside air). i.e., If ELR <
SALR (0.6°C/100 m), then atmosphere is stable. Inversion or isothermal
layer indicates absolutely stability. A stable atmosphere has:
- Very small lapse rate,
- Bad visibility due to suspended particles,
- Formation of stratiform (horizontal/layer) clouds,
- Intermittent/continuous precipitation.
Absolute Instability
If rising air (at ELR) cools faster than DALR, it means that the rising
packet will remain warmer than surrounding air & will continue going
up (because it is less dense than outside air). i.e., If ELR > DALR
(1°C/100m), then atmosphere unstable. An unstable atmosphere has:
- Lapse rate higher than normal.
Unstable
- Good visibility.  • Consonal Abodey
- Moderate turbulence.  Stable
- Cumuliform (vertical) clouds.  Absolutely  11000*
Unstable
- Showery precipitation.  DALRY SALR

Conditional Instability
If the actual ELR is b/w DALR & SALR, i.e., ELR is b/w 0.6°C to 1°/100 m,
then we have to see whether the rising packet of air is saturated or dry.
Atmosphere is stable if air is unsaturated, unstable if air is saturated.
Neutral Stability: If ELR is 1°C/100m & air is dry, atmosphere is neutrally
stable, i.e., rising air packet will stay where it is, neither rise or descend.

===== [avh 0410]
10 - 20
• Clouds
Introduction
- Air rises due to convection, orographic lifting, convergence,
turbulence etc.
- This rising air is subject to a decrease in pressure as it ascends,
causing it to expand & cool adiabatically. Thus, unsaturated air
becomes saturated, & clouds form at the condensation level.
- Inversion causes atmospheric stability & inhibits cloud formation.
- Cloud-base is measured by a Ceilometer or a Nephoscope.
†  Height of Cloud-base = (Surface temperature - Dew point)°C x 400'
Convective Cloud
- It forms due to heating of the land surface, rising air & instability. At
condensation level, it can spread out due to turbulence & can form Sc.
- It dissipates at night since insolation stops & clouds evaporate.
- Over mountainous areas, extensive vertical clouds may form due
to instability. Heavy precipitation can occur.
- Over sea, convective clouds cannot form. But when cold air moves
over a warm sea, air may get unstable & form convective clouds,
called Advection Cloud.
- Critical Temperature: Surface temperature required to lift a parcel
air up to condensation level.
- Cloud-base height will vary with surface temp, but cloud-top height
is limited by air mixing with & evaporating into a drier environment.
Orographic Uplift
- Air blowing at the windward side of a mountain will be forced to rise.
- If this air is dry, cloud forms above mountain top: Lenticular clouds.
- If air is humid, Sc/St clouds form below the mountain top & cause
precipitation. Cloud base on the leeward side will be higher.
- It also causes warm wind on the leeward side, called Foehn winds.
(See also: Mountain Waves, Winds)
Convergence Cloud
- Air converges at a low pressure trough, which causes lifting of air.
- This causes instability and formation of Cu/Cb clouds.
Frontal Uplift
- At a front, lifting of air occurs as warm air rises above cold air.
- Layer clouds form in stable air at a warm front & cumulus clouds
form in unstable air at a cold front.  (See also: Fronts)
Turbulence/Friction Layer Cloud
- In stable conditions, vertical movement of air is limited. But surface
friction up-currents sometimes pushes air up.
- If this air reaches dew-point temperature before reaching the top of
the friction layer, St/Sc forms. Since it is caused by surface turbulence,
it is called turbulence cloud.
- Usually, an inversion layer exists above the turbulence cloud.

descends

• Classification of Clouds (See also: Station Model, cloud symbology)
Low Clouds (clouds between 1000' - 6500)
Sc Stratocumulus: Large irregular puffy layer-clouds.
Cu Cumulus: Bulging cotton clouds that form due to convection.
- They indicate fair weather. No precipitation occurs.
- Thermal currents & turbulence exist below a Cu, smooth above.
Cb Cumulonimbus: Dense clouds with great vertical extent.
- It causes +SH, TSRA, SQ & severe turbulence in its upper parts.
- Tcu Towering Cumulus: Cb that extends up to the tropopause.
- Cb Capilatus: Cb with anvil at tropopause. It shows wind direction.
- Winds at 10000' influence the movement of a Cb cell.
St Stratus: Grey sheet clouds. It causes -RA, DZ, ice, & snow.
- Usually, it is the lowermost cloud layer. It forms 1000 - 2000' AGL,
with a maximum thickness of 1000' - 1500'.
- Stratus clouds on the ground is called fog.
Ns NimboStratus: Dark-grey rain-bearing stratus-clouds, with cloud
base up to 6500' AGL. It causes continuous rain, snow (60 min+).
Medium Clouds (clouds between 6500' - 20000', may extend up to 23000)
As Altostratus: Thick As cause rain/snow. Sun may be dimly visible.
Ac Altocumulus: White grey sheet-layer clouds. No precipitation.
Ac Lenticular (Lens Shaped): Forms at leeward of mountain waves.
Ac Castellanus: Bubbly Ac. It shows instability at medium levels.
High Clouds (clouds between 20000' - 60000')
Ci Cirrus: Fibrous filament hairlike clouds, made of ice crystals.
Cc Cirrocumulus: Thin white wavy puffs of ice crystals.
- Ci & Cc causes no precipitation or airframe icing.
Cs Cirrostratus: Whitish cloud veil, made of ice crystals. No icing.
- May cause snowfall, which is confined to upper levels.
- Covers a wide area, causes halo around the sun due to ice crystals.
Nacreous Cloud (Mother of pearl clouds)
- Seen in high latitudes in winters.
- Forms in upper stratosphere, 15 - 25 km.
- Made of ice crystals/dust.  Nacreous  Noctilucent
Noctilucent Cloud (Night shining clouds)
- Forms in the mesosphere, above 70 km.
- Seen at 50°- 65° latitudes in summers. Made of ice crystals.

Precipitation
• Introduction
Drizzle: Intermittent precipitation that occurs from an Sc, St or As.
Rain  : Continuous precipitation that occurs from Ns.
Shower: Precipitation that occurs from heap clouds Cu, Cb, Tcu.
Snow : For snow to reach the surtace, air temperature must be < 4°C.
Wet snow occurs if the temperature is between 0°- 4°C.
Sleet  : It is a rain that freezes, as it falls.
Hail  : Occurs when drops freeze & strong winds carry them higher
into the cloud, forming more ice around it, making it bigger.
Thunderstorm is reported when thunder is heard along with a Cb.
Rainy Day: A day in which rainfall received is > 2.5 mm.

Precipitation Theories
Ice Crystal Theory: In cold clouds (whose top portion extends above
treezing layer), supercooled water drops & ice crystals co-exist. They
grow bigger when water vapour sublimates on it, & fall as ice/rain.
Coalescence Theory: Ice crystal theory fails to explain rain falling
from warm clouds (below freezing layer). As per coalescence theory,
when small drops fall, they coalesce to form larger drops. Convection
& updrafts increase coalescence.
Giant Nucleus Theory: In a maritime environment, presence of small
salt particles from a 'salt-spray' absorb moisture & form condensation
nuclei, on to which water vapour sublimates, to form water drops.

What is the smell of Rain?
The smell of rain is called Petrichor, it is caused due to 3 reasons:
- Rain water brings down with it ozone molecules, which contribute to the scent
- Certain oils produced by plants during dry weather is released into the air.

===== [avh 0414]
10 - 24
• Icing
Freezing Level
- Altitude, where ambient temperature is 0°C is called freezing level.
- In clear air, freezing level is at 3°C/1000' (DALR) until 0°C reached.
- In a convective cloud, it is at 1.8°C/1000' (DPLR) until 0°C reached.
- Clouds formed due to orographic lifting (mountainous area) lowers
the freezing level & increases the severity of icing.
- With an inversion, there could be 2 freezing levels.
SWD Supercooled Water Drops
- They are water droplets that exist in liquid form at temperature < 0°C.
- Disturbing an SWD will trigger them to freeze immediately.
- Large SWD form if OAT is 0° to -20°C, Small SWD b/w -20° to -40°C.
No SWD can form if OAT is below -40°C; hence no icing possible.
Airframe Icing: It occurs when SWD freeze on contact with the airframe.
- 180th portion of supercooled drops freezes per 1°C below 0°C.
- Greatest concentration of SWDs is near the base of Cu, Cb clouds,
between freezing level & 25000', where it is warmest. Severe Icing
is experienced here.
Severe Icing : 0°C to -7°C  Light Icing : -12°C to -20°C No icing possible
Moderate  : -7°C to -12°C Very Light : -20°C to -40°C below -40°C
- Rate of Icing on Airframe depends on:
- 1 Speed of aircraft = 1 icing
- Thin aerofoil (thin chord) = More icing.
- 1 Size & concentration of SWD (Cu, Cb clouds) = 1 Icing
- Kinetic heating (/100)2 may warm airframe out of, or into icing range.
- Anti-icing must be ON if OAT < 10°C & precipitation is visible in air.
Hoar Frost: It occurs when temperature of airframe < 0°C. It can happen
on the ground (at night) or in the air, when descending to a lower altitude.
- It is caused by sublimation (vapour to ice), forming needles/scales.
- It dissipates quickly & is not a serious threat.
Rime Ice: Moderate Icing that occurs when medium to small SWD freeze
on contact with airframe. Moderate Rime 0°to-10°C, Light -20° to -40°C.
- This icing is not very heavy, but may interfere with control surfaces.
- It can occur in As, Ac, Sc, St & Ns clouds.
Glaze Ice: Sever icing occurs when Large SWDs freeze on contact with the
airframe. But latent heat is released which, delays freezing, giving water
drops enough time to spread across top wing surface to form clear ice.
- It's a severe hazard, 1 aircraft weight & distorts airframe surface.
- It occurs mostly on airframe leading edges. It builds up fast.
- Large SWDs forms in Ns, Cu & Cb clouds, from 0°C to -20°C.
Rain Ice/Glazed Frost: Occurs when SWD falls from an inversion layer
above (lower level is below freezing point). SWD freezes over airframe,
Meteorology  making ice. It is a rare occurrence, e.g., when flying into a warm front.
Engine Icing: It can happen when OAT < 5°C.
(See also: Airframe > Ice Protection)
(See also: Engines > Carburettor Icing)
===== [avh 0415]
10 - 25
Thunderstorms
• Introduction
- TS forms in coastal areas due to land/sea breeze & in valleys due
to anabatic/katabatic winds. It generally occurs at night/early morning.
- Over the sea, TS is more frequent at night.
- In the tropics, and over plains, convection causes Cu/Cb clouds to
form, which cause rainfall in the afternoon/evening. This is more
frequent during summers than in winters.
- Winds at 10000' influence the movement of a Cb cell.
- Thunderstorm is reported when thunder is heard along with Cb.
Frontal Thunderstorm
- Frontal thunderstorm forms 100 - 300 km ahead of a fast-moving
cold front or occlusion & moves in the direction of the front.
- In temperate latitudes, frontal TS is more frequent in winters, caused
by cold fronts. E.g. rain in NW India after the passage of a WD.
- It is more frequent in winters & occurs over land or sea, day or night.
Air Mass Thunderstorm
- It forms in summer due to heating & convergence due to low pressure.
- It forms only over land, during the day & clears up by night.
- It also forms when cold air passes over a warm sea.
- It is weaker than frontal TS.
Dust Storm/Sand Storm
- Dust storms form the same way as a normal TS, but their vertical
growth is restricted by low humidity (RH < 75%).
- Due to high surface temperatures, the atmosphere becomes highly
unstable & convection occurs. However, precipitation evaporates
before reaching the ground due to high temperature & low humidity.
- It occurs over North India, during pre monsoons/summers, during
afternoon hours.
- During a dust storm, strong surface winds of more than 20 kts raise
dust. Vigorous up-draughts carry dust & sand to great heights.
- Visibility reduces < 5000 m.
- Dust storm approaches like a high wall of dust/sand.
- Lifecycle of a dust storm is lesser than that of a TS.
Light DS  up to 21 kts  Visibility 500 m - 1000 m

• Tornado
- It is a high instability phenomenon associated with thunderstorms.
- It is caused due to circulating updraft that exist under a Cb.
- It generally has a diameter of 50 m - 200 m.
- Wind speeds can be up to 150 kts.
Conditions for Cb Cloud Formation
- Steep lapse rate: Helps development of cloud's vertical extent.  Meteorology
- An adequate supply of moisture from below.
- A triggering mechanism: Convergence; or
- Convection/Orographic lifting; or
- Radiation/Katabatic cooling.
===== [avh 0416]
• 10 - 26
Life Cycle of Cb Cell (2 - 3 hours)
Cumulus/Initial Stage (15 - 30 mins)
- One or more cumulus clouds begin to grow into large
cumulus. Vertical up-draught speeds of 1000 - 2000 fpm exist.
- This up-draught sustains drops/ice crystals in the cloud.
- Drop size continue to grow, until up-draught can't sustain them.
- Moisture inflow continues from its bottom and sides.
Mature Stage: (20 - 40 mins)
- It begins with the fall of precipitation - rain or hail.
- Continuous evaporation of falling drops keeps the air saturated.
- Both up & down-draught exist. Turbulence exists below & inside Cb.
- Down-draught up to 2400 fpm & up-draught up to 10000 fpm occur.
- Down-draught close to the ground spreads horizontally & forms
a gust-front (Microburst).
- Lighting & thunder can occur due to static electricity buildup.
Dissipating Stage: (1.5 - 2.5 hrs)
- Entire lower portion of the Cb has down-draught.
- Heavy precipitation occurs. Turbulence exists below & inside Cb.
- An anvil may form at the tropopause because no more lapse
rate exists & unstable air cannot rise any further.

- It is a localised column of severe concentrated down-draughts D

- Intense precipitation occurs. Air column moves downward until it

- It usually lasts for 5 mins. Wind shear up to 50 - 90 kts can occur.
- Macro-burst: A smaller event in a larger area (10 km).
- Virga: Dry downburst due to evaporating rain. It may occur under a

10 - 27
Thunderstorm Hazards
- Turbulence: Moderate to severe turbulence exists in
up/down-draught in a TS.
- Wind shear: Sudden change in wind speed & direction is dangerous,
especially during takeoff/landing.
- Squall: Wind speeds of 40 - 100 kts exist at a gust front.
- Icing: Severe icing can occur when OAT is 0° to -20°C, between
freezing level to 25000', due to the presence of large SWDs.
- Hail: Damaging hail can exist up to 45000' in a Cb cell & at any
height under an anvil.
- Lightning is likely at ‡5000' of freezing level & if OAT is between
+20°C to -10°C.
Thunderstorm Avoidance
- Consider flying in the mornings, before afternoon-heat triggered
storms form.
- If winds above 18000' are southwesterly, expect storms to form.
- Visual Avoidance: If a Cb/Tcu is visual at any altitude, avoid it by
10 nm laterally & an anvil top by 5000' vertically.
- On a weather radar:
- If a Cb is detected, avoid it by 5 nm (until FL200), by 10 nm
(FL200 to FL250), by 15 nm (FL250 to FL300), or by 20 nm
(above FL 300).
- Avoid scalloped edges, hooks, figure 'U' or '6' & protrusions
seen in a weather radar by 10 nm.

Flying Technique in CBs/Thunderstorms
- Postpone takeoff/landing if TS is reported within 20 nm of aerodrome.
- Select a FL above 25000' or below the freezing level. That band is
worst for hail & icing.
- Avoid flying under/over a Cb cell.
- Never climb inside a Cb cell.
- When inside a Cb cell, never attempt turns.
- If flying through a Cb:
- Fasten seat belts;
- Reduce aircraft speed to turbulence speed;  Meteorology
- Engage autopilot;
- Let aircraft ride the storm.

- Abrupt changes in temperature & humidity are found at boundaries

10 - 29
• Fronts
Introduction
- The edge of the mixing of 2 dissimilar air masses is called a front.
- Contrasting temperatures & humidity at a front cause cloud formation.
- When 2 fronts meet, warmer air will always rise above colder air.
- Frontogenesis: Tightening of temp gradient, to produce fronts.
- Frontolysis: Dissipation or weakening of a front.
Warm Front
- It occurs when warm air overtakes colder air.
- It is slow-moving air (15 kts), with a slope ratio of 1:150.
- In it, Ci, Cs clouds form, and as the front gets closer, Ns, As form.
- A frontal fog always exists ahead of a warm front.
- As front approaches, drizzle, low St & poor visibility occurs.
- After a warm front passes, temp & pressure is steady & the sky clears.
Cold Front
- It occurs when cold air overtakes warmer air.
- Its speed is 30 kts (2x faster than warm front). Steeper slope of 1:50.
- Cold front is associated with thunderstorms, squalls & instability.
- A Line Squall occurs 100 km - 300 km ahead of a cold front.
- Precipitation occurs 30 - 50 km before & after a cold front.
- Fog occurs after a cold front.
- As a cold front comes and goes, altimeter 1, then l.
Stationary Front: Boundary between 2 airmass, neither strong
enough to replace each other.
Occluded Front: They are of 2 types:
- Warm Occlusion: In it, cool air overrides colder air at a warm front.
- It occurs in winters, and is less common.  _Warm Front
- Heavy showers & hail exist.  .Cold Front
- Cold Occlusion: In it, cold air undercuts cool  Stationary
air at a warm front.  . Occluded
SYMBOLOGY
- It occurs in the summers.
- It will have CBs embedded in Ns clouds.

Main Global Fronts
- Arctic Front: Occurs at the boundary between Arctic & Polar mass.
- Polar Front: It is the front between Polar easterlies & mid-lat
westerlies at 60°N.  (See also: General Circulation > Polar Front)
- Mediterranean Front: Front between cP air from Europe & cT air
from North Africa.
- ITCZ: Also known as Equatorial Front. (See also: Depressions > ITCZ)
- It can then be interpreted as a front along the leading edge of
the equatorial air mass.
- It is an area where both the NE & SE trade winds converge at
the thermal equator. They have the same temperature.
- India is not affected by any fronts except in WD (Wester Disturbance),
during winters, which is caused by an occluded front.
(See also: Monsoons > Western Disturbance)

10 - 31
• Depressions
Frontal Depression
- In a stationary front, both air masses are in equilibrium. But, if warm
air starts to replace cold air, a wave is generated.
- Surrounding pressure drops & forms a 'Low', &
further intensifies to form a depression.
- It is marked by poor visibility.
Orographic (Lee) Depression
- When airflow meets a mountain range at a large angle, there is a
marked tendency for it to flow around the edge than above it.
- Depression occurs on the lee side due to comparative lack of air there.
Thermal Depression
- As surface air heats, it expands and rises, result in an
upward & outflow of air at the top.
- This in turn causes surface pressure to drop & air rises anti-cyclonically.
- It causes the formation of Cb, Cu, heavy showers & turbulence.
ITCZ Inter Tropical Convergence Zone: One of the main global fronts.
- Also called ECZ Equatorial Convergence Zone or Equatorial Front.
- It is the 'thermal equator' & lies along equatorial low pressure area.
• It shifts 20° north to 20° south, and back, with seasons.
- Doldrums: If the pressure gradient is weak, ITCZ is slack between
5°N - 5°S. This area is characterised by fair weather & light winds.
- ITCZ has mT, cT to the north of it & mT, mE to its south.
- Air on both sides of ITCZ (NE & SE trades) have same temperature.
- Active ITCZ has high pressure & instability, causes Cu, Cb, TS, +SH.
- Air convergence from both sides at ITCZ causes clouds up to 50000'.
- When air is stable, ITCZ has As & Ns clouds, causing continuous rain.
- Most TRS form at the edge of ITCZ, when furthermost from equator.
Summer ITCZ
Winter ITCZ
Peninsular Discontinuity
- Depression that forms over Central India in pre-monsoons (Apr-May).
- It has cT air from North India & cool moist mE air from Bay of Bengal.
- It gives rise to afternoon TS/heavy shower & squall.
- It lasts for 3 - 4 days before dissipating.
Tropical Depression  (See also: Monsoons > Monsoon Depression)
* They form along ITCZ frequently & originate at the boundary between
mT & cT air mass, with a minor surge of mE air.
- Surge: A sudden strengthening wind of the same air mass. This
surge distorts the ITCZ and can start a tropical depression.
- Conditions for formation of a TD:

• Tropical Revolving Storm/Cyclones
Introduction
- Most TRS form in the months Aug - Sep, when the sea is warmest.
- They form in the Tropics, over the sea, at the edge of ITCZ, when it
is furthermost from the equator.
- It then moves west due to the easterly trade-winds, moves away
from the equator & increases in strength due to Coriolis force.
- They then recurve east due to prevailing westerlies at mid-latitudes.
- TRS gets their energy from the release of latent heat of moisture
over the oceans. This release of heat further expands air & reduces
pressure, creating convergence, causing more moisture to rise, cool
& release more latent heat. This is a self-feeding system, with ever
increasing intensity.
- Only when crossing mid-latitudes or when coming over the land will
a TRS lose its energy, since there is no more moisture influx.
- In the north-west Pacific ocean, TRS happens throughout the year.
- TRS never form in the South Atlantic as ITCZ never cross 5°S.
- TRS is called Hurricane in North America, Typhoon in North Pacific
& Cyclone in Asia/China.

Tropical Revolving Storms in India
- In India, TRS occurs in pre-monsoon (Apr - May) & maximum in
post-monsoon (Oct - Nov).
- No cyclones form during the monsoon season because, then, the
land is cooler & there is not enough temperature gradient to form a
circulation. Also, during the monsoon, ITCZ is over the Asian sub-
continent & not over the sea.
- In winters (Jan - Feb), depressions are first noticed over the
Andaman Sea (wind speed up to 15 kts). They move west along
ITCZ, across the peninsula (at 10 kts over the land) and into the
Arabian Sea. When mE is cut, they slow down and recurve NE.
- Tropical cyclones that form over the Arabian Sea & Bay of Bengal
are of small lifespan, as they pass over waters only for short
periods, thus is immature while striking the coast.
Meteorology  - They last an average of 3-5 days, max 6-7 days for recurving storms.
- Recurving ones are more severe as they spend more time over sea.
- Low latitude tropical cyclone crosses Tamil Nadu or South Andhra
Pradesh & weakens over land. They may emerge at the Arabian
Sea, intensify, & recurve NE and hit Maharashtra/Gujarat coast.

10 - 33
• Conditions for Formation of TRS
- Latitude: TRS forms only between 5°N - 25°N. Below 5°N,
there is not enough Coriolis force & above 25°N, waters are cool.
- Temperature: Over warm tropical waters, the temperature is
> 26°C until 60 m depth, thus supplies adequate moisture.
- Instability is needed for the vertical development of TRS.
- Humidity: Air needs to have high humidity.
• Stages of a TRS
Tropical Depression: Winds are variable. SQ, RA occur over a large
area. Pressure drops, winds pick up 20 - 34 kts.
Tropical Storm: Storm gets more organised & has a circular rotating
appearance. Winds are 35 - 64 kts. A name is given for the TRS at
this stage.
13 member nations of WMO (World Meteorological Organisation) & ESCAP
(UN Economic & Social Commission for Asia & Pacific), shortlist name for
each TRS. Once used, the name is not repeated. The rules for naming are:
- It must be neutral to politics, religion, culture & gender;
- It must not hurt the sentiments of any group of population;
- It must be short (8 characters) & must be easy to pronounce.
Tropical Cyclone: The pressure continues to drop. The eye forms.
Wind speeds are now > 64 kts.
Parts of a TRS
Calm/Eye: 20-50 km diameter. Lowest pressure, light winds & clear sky.
Eye Wall: 50-60 km diameter, with hurricane winds of 64 kts or more.
- Wall is the most dangerous and violent part of a TRS.
- It will have violent rains under a circular wall of clouds.
Outer Storm Area: 400 km diameter, wind speed decreases outwards.

• Monsoons & Indian Climatology
- Monsoons are seasonal winds blowing due to the 'summer
low pressure' & ITCZ, in concert with the trade winds.
- Most of world's rainfall is caused by ITCZ & its associated Monsoon.
- Monsoon rains are of continuous nature from stratus clouds & not CBs.
- Rainfall occurs all over the country during monsoons.
- Monsoon season is the most hazardous season for flying: low visibility,
low cloud ceiling, heavy precipitation, strong surface winds, wet runway.
March - May: Pre Monsoon, Summers
- Pressure: Subcontinent gets heated, causing low pressure over land.
A trough of low (Monsoon Trough) form over the Indo-Gangetic plain.
- Visibility: Good, except in dust storms which are common in
Rajasthan during this period.
- Jet Stream: Sub Tropical Jet Stream weakens and moves north.
South India experiences fairly violent TS of conventional origin (Cb).
- Norwester (Kalbaishakhi): They are Isolated TS occurring in
afternoons/evenings in NE India during this period due to intense
insolation. They continue till monsoons establish.
June - September: SW Monsoon, Rainy Season
- Pressure: Monsoon Depression is a low pressure area within the
monsoon trough over Arabian Sea & Bay of Bengal during monsoons.
- Rain distribution depends upon the position of Monsoon Trough.
- It is associated with cyclonic circulations, extending up to solo.
It lasts 3-5 days. Wind speeds are 17-33kts, moves N-NW into land.
- Worst weather in MD is in SW sector, there is steady heavy rain.
- Fair weather in Assam during monsoon indicates intensification
or formation of monsoon depression & vice versa.
- Visibility: Good visibility exists except in precipitation.
- Jet Stream: Easterly Jet stream forms, 16 km high, 70-80kts.
- Onset of Monsoons:
Monsoon forms when ITCZ moves north & crosses the equator.

10 - 36
El-Nino & La-Nina
El-Nino (Spanish for little boy') & La-Nina (Spanish for little girl') are 2
opposing conditions of the ENSO (El-Nino Southern Oscillations) that
causes fluctuation in Sea Surface Temperature SST (1°C to 3°C) in the
tropical pacific ocean. This affects global weather significantly (rainfall,
agriculture & fishing). This phenomenon is thought to have been occurring
for thousands of years, in an irregular cycle between 2 to 9 years.
Normal Conditions: During normal conditions, trade winds blow west
along the equator, taking warm waters from South America towards
Asia. To replace this warm water, cold water rises from the depths
(called upwelling), which bring up nutrients & phytoplankton, and is
crucial for marine life.
El-Nino: During El-Nino, SST is warmer, due to which trade winds
weaken or reverse & warm water is pushed back east, towards the
west coast of America. This causes the Pacific Jet stream to shift
south from its normal position and causes increased tropical cyclones
in the pacific and reduced rainfall in India & Southeast Asia. Upwelling
also reduces, disrupting marine life.
La-Nina: During La-Nina, SST is cooler, and trade winds are stronger
than usual, pushing more warm water towards Asia. Pacific Jet stream
shifts north, causing heavy rains and flooding in Australia.

10 - 37
Contrails
Introduction
- Contrails are 'condensation trails', that form at the exhaust or the
wingtips of an aircraft, due to the condensation of water vapour.
- It may or may not form, depending upon the RH of the air.
Types of Contrails
Wingtip Trails
- These are contrails that sometimes form aft of wingtips, especially
during high-lift conditions, due to the reduction in pressure,
expansion & consequent cooling & condensation of the water
vapour in the air.
- It may not form if the air already is dry or cold.
- They are short in length & is insignificant.
Exhaust Trails
- Water vapour exists in the exhaust gases of an aircraft.
- When an aircraft is flying, this sudden addition of extra water
vapour into an air packet that already has a high RH, cause it to
saturate and condense immediately.
- Exhaust trails are long and persistent if:
- Ambient air has high RH, causing its quick saturation.
- Flight altitude is below Maxtra level.
- High throttle setting (high water vapour in the exhaust).
- Low/moderate wind speed (so that contrails do not dissipate).
Distrails
- They are the opposite of contrails.
- The heat of engine exhaust dissipates/evaporates the clouds
that the aircraft is flying through, thereby cutting a channel
through the clouds.
Contrail Formation Requirements
It is possible to calculate the critical temperature (OAT) at which
contrails can form.
Mintra: No contrails can form below this temperature. (OAT~ -45°C).
Drytra: Flight Level above which Contrails will form, irrespective of its
RH. It is ~ 2 km above the Mintra level.
Maxtra: Level above which contrails will not form. In the stratosphere,
temperature 1 with altitude. So after a particular height, contrails
stop forming.
Water vapour &  Turns into  Contrails
sulphur particles  ice

SPECI Special Report / Aviation Selected Special Weather Report
- It is issued whenever there is a sudden deterioration or improvement
in weather (improved conditions should last minimum 10 minutes).
- SPECI is also appended with a TREND, uses same codes as METAR.
It is issued when:
- Mean wind speed change > 10 kts (Gusts).
- Change in wind direction > 60° & spd before/after change 10 kts.
- Visibility/RVR passing through 800 m, 1500 m, 3000 m.
- Onset/change of intensity of FL, FZFG, DS, SS, TS.
- Clouds below 450 m, † to BKN/OVC, or back to SKC/FEW/SCT.
- Cloud BKN or OVC at 30 m, 60 m, 150 m, 300 m, 450 m.
- Sky OBC & vertical visibility changes 30m, 60m, 150m or 300m.
- Surface temperature has increased 2°C from the last observation.
TREND: It is a short-range landing forecast, valid for 2 hrs, appended to
a METAR & SPECI. It is issued only by a Class-1 Met Officer
- Used only for changes in visibility, surface winds, weather & clouds.
- PROB is used in a TAF, but is not used in TREND.

• Satellite Picture Interpretation
Visible Image
- They indicate amount of sunlight reflected by clouds/earth surface.
- Cloud-free areas will typically be dark, clouds/snow appear bright.
- In a visible satellite image, thicker clouds appear brighter than
thinner clouds. However, it is difficult to distinguish between low &
high-level clouds. For this, IR images are used.
- Visible images can not be taken during night time.
IR Image
- They represent the IR radiation or temperature (wavelength 10.5 um
- 12.5 um), emitted by the clouds/earth surface.
- In an IR picture, warmer objects appear darker than colder objects.
- Cloud-free areas will typically be dark, but also very low clouds and
fog may appear dark.
- High clouds are brighter than low clouds due to their low temperature.
- Thick prominent white spots on IR images are CB clouds because
of their very low cloud top temperature.
Water Vapour Image
- They represent water vapour content in the mid & upper atmosphere.
- They are useful for identifying regions of moist & dry air.
- White regions represent more moisture than dark regions.
How to interpret a Visible & Infrared images of the same place.

absorbs sunlight.  Sea, being colder appear bright.

reflects sunlight.  8. Clouds are bright, meaning they are cold,
3. Forests appear dark.  and hence high clouds. In the visible image,
4.  Faint clouds.  they are not easily seen (8), thus they are
thin clouds. They are probably high cirrus.
Meteorology  1. Thick layer of white clouds seen.  3. Thick white clouds on visible image (1) are not
2.  Thin strip of white clouds are seen  seen in IR, which means it is not much colder

10 - 45ł
Practical Meteorology for an Aviator
Atmosphere
- Tropopause is important for aviation because all weather, clouds,
jet streams & CAT form below it.
- Temperature is lower & density is higher at the equator tropopause
than the tropopause at poles. So, for better engine efficiency, flying
near the equator-tropopause is better than pole-tropopause.
Pressure
- If QNH at departure & destination are the same, but true altitude is
T, the destination is warmer.
- If QNH at departure is low & QNH at destination is high, and true
altitude = indicated altitude, then the destination is warmer.
- I QNH than ISA, but indicated & true alt same, temp is 1 than ISA
- If QNH 1 than ISA, but indicated & true alt same, temp is _ than ISA.
- If OAT > ISA, then true altitude > indicated altitude.
- Low QNH = bad weather & high winds. But visibility will be good,
- High QNH = good weather, but bad visibility due to subsidence.
- QNH reducing from higher than ISA value (1013) means visibility
will improve. But so will turbulence & up-draught. Cloud base will
rise. QNH dropping lower than ISA means winds will start picking
- Max QNH is at 1000 hrs & 2200 hrs. Minimum at 0400 hrs & 1600 hrs.
Temperature
- Cloudy nights will be warmer since the clouds insulate the earth's
terrestrial re-radiation.
- During day, ambient temperature will be < surface temp, due to winds.
Density
- Rainy day = low air density = poor engine climb/takeoff performance
= more runway needed for takeoff.
- Max humidity (max RH) & min temp will be ½ hour after sunrise.
- Min humidity (min RH) & max temp is at 1500hrs.
Visibility
- Since minimum temperature occurs just at sunrise, fog formation is
most frequent, or it thickens at sunrise. It dissipates in 2 - 3 hours
after sunrise.
- Radiation fog happens at night, during winters (due to night cooling).
However, there should be light winds & a clear sky.
- Fog is stratus cloud on the ground, when surface OAT = dew-point.
- Visibility reported by the Met department is the lowest in any direction.
- Low level inversion is common during winter nights, due to night
cooling. During the day, it can occur when slight turbulence occurs
close to the surface at 2000'-3000'. This phenomenon also occurs
in high pressure areas due to subsidence. Low level inversion does
not allow surface air to rise up & mix with upper-wind. Hence smoke,  Meteorology
mist & fog stagnate close to the ground, causing low visibility.
- Haze due to subsidence inversion layer: while climbing through a
haze layer & if QNH > 1013 (high pressure) & there is a clear sky
above, it means you just climbed through a 'subsidence inversion'.
===== [avh 0436]
10 - 46
Winds
- Coriolis Force: Air moving poleward will deflect east (jet streams),
& equator-ward moving air will deflect west (easterly trade winds).
- Upper winds (in the northern hemisphere) are generally westerly
due to Coriolis force.
- Surface wind (3000' & below) in the northern hemisphere back 20°
& weaken 50% than upper winds, due to surface friction.
- Winds by Met department is true bearing. Winds by ATC is magnetic.
- Sea breeze blows sea to land, in day time & cools the land.
- In the mountains, cold katabatic winds at night cause fog in valleys.
- During day, anabatic winds cause cloud formation on mountain tops.
- Subtropical jet streams are at 40000, with speeds of 150 - 200 kts.
They are at 25°N in Oct, moves south to 22°N by Feb (winters).
- Easterly jets occur at 50000' during SW monsoons. Speed 60-80 kts.
- Max turbulence in jet streams occur below & left of its downstream.
Icing
- Freezing level: In clear air, it is at 3°C/1000' (DALR) until 0°C reached.
In a convective cloud, it is at 1.8°C/1000' (DPLR) until 0°C reached.
- Clouds formed due to orographic lifting (mountainous area) lowers
the freezing level & increases the severity of icing.
- Anti-icing must be ON if OAT < 10°C & precipitation is visible in air.
- Severe airframe icing can occur if OAT is between 0°C to -20°C.
- Greatest concentration of SWDs is near the base of Cu, Cb clouds,
between freezing level & 25000', where it is warmest. Severe Icing
is experienced here.
- 1 Speed of aircraft; or 1 size & concentration of SWD = † icing.
- Stratus is usually the lowermost cloud layer, with thickness 1000-1500.
- Cumulus clouds are an indication of thermal up-currents.
- Turbulence occurs below and inside a Cu. Above it will be smooth.
- An anvil will form on top of a Cb at the tropopause, as clouds
cannot rise any further. Its direction will be along the prevailing winds.
- Winds at 10000' influence the direction of Cb/TS movement.
- Lenticular cap clouds on top of hills indicate turbulence.
- Rotor clouds present at the same level on the leeward side of a
mountain will have maximum turbulence.
- Sea breeze sometimes lifts up along the coast and form a line of
cumulus clouds. It helps as a navigation feature.
- Cloud base height = (Surface temperature - Dew Point) × 400'.
Precipitation
- Monsoon rains are of continuous nature (60 min+), from an Ns.
- Intermittent light rain occurs from stratus Sc/St.
- Showers occur from cumulus Cu, Cb, Tcu.
- Fair-weather Cu in the morning indicates instability & chances of
formation of Cb by evening.
- Snow will reach the ground only if the surface temperature is < +4°C.
Meteorology  - Lightning is likely at t5000' of freezing level & if OAT +20°C to -10°C.
- Virga (Evaporating rain) is an indication of a microburst.
===== [avh 0437]
10 - 4ł
Thunderstorm
- Over the sea, TS is more frequent at night.
- Over coastal areas, they generally occur at night/early morning due
to land/sea breeze & in valleys due to anabatic/katabatic winds.
- In the tropics & over the plains, convection results in Cu/Cb clouds
& cause rainfall in the afternoon/evening.
Thunderstorm Avoidance
- Consider flying in the mornings, before afternoon-heat triggered
storms form.
- If winds above 18000' are southwesterly, expect storms to form.
- Visual Avoidance: If Cb/TS is visual at any altitude, avoid them
laterally by 10 nm & the anvil top vertically by 5000'.
- On a weather radar: If a Cb is detected, avoid it by 5 nm (until
FL200), by 10 nm (FL200 to FL250), by 15 nm (FL250 to FL300), or
by 20 nm (above FL 300).
- Avoid scalloped edges, hooks, figure 'U' or '6' & protrusions by
10 nm.

SEVERE  Steep gradient

severe thunderstorm
- Postpone takeoff/landing if TS is reported within 20 nm of aerodrome.
- Select a FL above 25000' or below the freezing level. That band is
worst for hail & icing.
- Avoid flying under/over Cb cells. Never climb inside a Cb cell.
- When inside a Cb, never attempt turns.
- If flying through a Cb:
- Fasten seat belts;
- Reduce aircraft speed to turbulence speed;
- Engage autopilot;
- Let aircraft ride the storm.
TRS Avoidance: On whatever course a cyclone is in, strong winds from  Meteorology
the left indicates that the storm's centre is ahead. Alter course until the
winds are from the right & is weakening.

===== [avh 0439]
11 - 3
Human Performance Limitations
• Central Nervous System
- Human brain is only 2% of the bodyweight but consumes 20% of its
total energy needs.
- The brain can only deal with one conscious decision at a time.
- 70% of the information processed by the brain is from visual channel.
- Visual Constancy: It is the process of recognising familiar objects
in unfamiliar conditions.
- Expectancy or Perceptual Set: To some extent, we perceive what
we expect to perceive. Perception is a highly subjective process.
- Top-down processing use previous knowledge to modify mental model.
- Bottom-up processing use sensory info to start building a mental model
- Westbound long flights are easier to cope with than eastbound.
• Circulatory System
- After donating blood, a 24-hour rest is mandatory.
- Average adult resting heart rate is 72 bpm.
- Human heart pumps approximately 5 litres of blood every minute.
- Normal adult blood pressure is 120(systolic)/80(diastolic).
• Respiratory System
- Henry's Law: The amount of gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional
to the air pressure over the liquid.
- Dalton's Law: Total pressure of a gas = sum of its partial pressures.
- Tidal Volume: Normal respiration volume of lungs, ~ 500 ml.
- Inspiratory Reserve Volume: Additional volume that can be
inhaled forcefully, ~ 3000 ml.
- Expiratory Reserve Volume: Excess volume of air that can be
expelled by force breathing out, after tidal volume, ~ 1100 ml.
- Residual Volume: Minimum air that remains in lungs, come what
may, ~ 1200 ml.
- Average adult breathing rate is 16 times a minute.
- Women have 25% less lung volume than men.
- Level of CO2 in blood controls the respiration rate.
Carbon Monoxide: It is an odourless poison. Haemoglobin in the blood
has 250x more affinity for carbon monoxide than oxygen. Symptom of
CO poisoning is tightness across the forehead or a headache.
Effects of Vibration
1 - 4 Hz: Breathing Interference.
4 - 10 Hz: Chest & Abdominal pain.
8 - 12 Hz: Backache.
10 - 20 Hz: Headache, Eye strain, muscular tension.
Miscellaneous
- 73% of all aviation accidents are attributed to 'human factors'.
- Body Temperature is maximum at 1700 hrs & minimum at 0500 hrs.
- Not eating breakfast can cause hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar).
- Abdominal Distension: Gas formation in abdomen.
- BMI Body Mass Index:  BMI < 25%  25% - 30%  BMI > 30%
Weight (kg)  Healthy  Overweight  Obese
Height (m*)

===== [avh 0440]
11 - 4
Arousal: It is the reaction level of a pilot.
- Optimal arousal has a positive influence on one's performance.
- Low/extremely aroused (anxious) pilots will perform significantly less.
• Human Memory
- Sensory Store
- Iconic Memory: Short term memory that has a span of 1 sec.
- Echoic Memory: Recall events that occurred 2 - 8 secs earlier.
- Short Term Memory
- It is the memory of events in the last 10 - 20 secs.
- This memory can recall only about 7 ‡ 2 unrelated items at a time.
- It is highly sensitive to interruption.
- It can be improved by memory improving methods like chunking,
association, mnemonics, etc.
- Long Term Memory
- Semantic: Memory of worldly knowledge.
- Episodic: Memory of events that occurred in one's life.
- Motor Memory: Muscle memory, e.g., playing the piano.

11 - 5
Stress
Introduction
- Stress in a person is cumulative.
- Stressors: Any event or situation that induces stress.
- If there is no stress, pilot will be slack in cockpit. High stress can cause
a pilot to break down. Optimum stress results in best performance.
- Psychosomatic Illness: Physical illness due to psychological causes.
• Types of Stress
- Physiological Stress: Stress caused due to environment, heat,
noise, aircraft emergency, lack of training/experience, hunger, thirst,
lack of sleep, pain, etc.
- Cognitive Stress: It occurs when a person is placed in an unknown
problem. Its effect depends on his training & experience.
- Personal Stress: Stress caused due to domestic issues, children,
family problems, etc.
- Imaginary Stress: Anxiety.
- Organisational Stress: Management pressure, pressure from seniors.
Methods to Cope with Stress
- Action Coping: The person does something about the stressor.
- Cognitive Coping: Thinking positive, Have a positive attitude,
- Symptom Directed Coping: Use of drugs, chocolate, smoking, etc.
• Managing Stress
- Experience level of a pilot reduces his stress in the cockpit.
- Learning/system knowledge reduce stress for inexperienced pilots.
- CRM cockpit resources management (share the workload in cockpit).
Sleep
• Introduction
Circadian Rhythm: A free-running body clock has a natural sleep-
wake rhythm cycle of 25 hours.
- Sleep Cycle: 1 sleep cycle (4 stages of sleep) lasts tor 90 minutes.
Sleep Credit
- Sleep credit & debit is cumulative, carrying forward to the next day.
- +2 points for every sleeping hour, -1 point for every waking hour.
- Max sleep credit that can be accumulated is 16 points (8 hours sleep)
•  Stages of Sleep
- REM Sleep: Brain is active while sleeping. Eye movement &
dreams occur during REM sleep. It occurs 4-5 times a night.
- Stage 1: Light sleep in the initial 10 mins of falling asleep.
- Stage 2: Early sleep lasting 20 mins, before entering stages 3 & 4.
- Stage 3 & 4: Slow-wave or orthodox sleep. Eyes are stationary.

11 - 6
Eye
Parts of the Eye
- Sclera: The white of the eye.
- Cornea: It is a clear protective outer layer, covering iris, pupil & lens.
- Iris: It is the pigmented muscular curtain, between cornea and the
lens. It controls the amount of light entering the eye.
- Pupil: Hole in the centre of Iris. Lens is behind the pupil.
- Retina: Light sensitive area on the back wall of the eyeball.
- Fovea: Central part of the retina. It gives central vision.
- Choroid: Vascular layer of the eye, containing connective tissues,
lying between the retina and the sclera.
- Cones: Light sensitive cells on the retina used for day/colour vision.
It can sense up to 1000 different colours. Each cone is connected to
a single neuron.
- Rods: Used for night/peripheral vision. I's maximum density is at
10° from the fovea. Several rods are connected to a single neuron.
- Visual Acuity: Sharpness of vision.
• Defects that occur in the eye
- Myopia: Nearsightedness caused by a longer eyeball. This can be
corrected by a concave lens.
- Hypermetropia: Farsightedness. It is corrected by a convex lens.
- Presbyopia: It is a type of hypermetropia. It is the inability of the
lens to adjust and change shape. It is caused due to old age.
- Colour blindness occurs in 7% of men, but only 0.1% of women.
• Types of Vision
- Central Vision
- It is used for object, size, shape, texture & colour recognition.
- Peripheral Vision
It helps us with orientation while flying in good visibility.
- It helps us in placing an object.
- During night flying or when in clouds, peripheral vision is cut
out, and chances of disorientation increase.
- If disoriented, use central vision & get onto instrument flying.
Photopic Vision (Colour Vision): Day vision using 'Cone' cells.
- Mesopic Vision: In low light conditions, both cones & rods are active.
- Scotopic Vision (Night Vision): Black/white vision, using 'Rod cells.
Night Vision adaptation time is 30 minutes for Rod cells.
• Adequate carbohydrate intake before a night flight reduces
the effect of hypoxia on the rods and enhances night vision.
Factors affecting night vision:
- Hypoxia  - Vitamin 'A' deficiency
- Alcohol and smoking  - Hypoglycaemia.

11 - 7
Ear
• Introduction
- Human hearing range is from 20 Hz to 20000 Hz.
- The ear is also the organ that supplies acceleration, orientation &
body-balance intormation to the brain.
- Otitic Barotrauma: Ear pain due to pressure changes in atmosphere.
- Sinus Barotrauma: Pain in nasal sinuses due to pressure
differential in the sinus cavity and the atmosphere.
Parts of the Ear
- Outer-ear/Pinna
- It collects external sound and sends it through the Auditory
Canal to the eardrum.
- Eardrum (Tympanum): It transmits sound waves to middle ear.
Middle-ear (Tympanic Cavity): it is filled with air. It contains:
- Otolith Organs or Ossicles (3 bones - malleus, incus & stapes)
These bones senses linear acceleration of more than 0.1 m/s2,
and transmit sound from the eardrum to the inner ear.
- Eustachian Tube: It is used for equalising pressure in the
middle-ear, across the eardrum.
- Inner-ear: It is filled with fluid. It contains:
- Cochlea: A hollow, spiral-shaped bone that plays a key role in
the sense of hearing & in the process of auditory transduction.
- Semicircular Canals: It senses angular acceleration.
- The 3 semicircular canals are placed at 90° to each other. It
is filled with fluid & has ciliary hair in it.
- Depending on the orientation of angular acceleration, the fluid
in the corresponding canal moves, causing the ciliary hair
Inside it to move, which is sensed as angular acceleration in
heir respective 3 axes.
- Any movement below its sensing threshold of 2°/sec is not
registered. This is the primary cause of disorientation.
• Defects that occur in the ear
- Presbycusis: Hearing loss due to old age.
- Noise Induced Hearing Loss: Caused due to extensive exposure
to loud noises > 90 dB, reducing the sensitivity of auditory cells.
- Temporary Noise Induced Hearing Loss:
< 90 dB Unlikely  140 dB Pain
120 dB Discomfort  > 160 dB Drum Rupture
- Conductive Deafness: Caused due to any problem in transferring
sound from outer ear, tympanic membrane (eardrum), or middle ear.
- Sensorineural Deafness: Hearing loss due to damage in inner ear.

Acceleration
Factors that affect acceleration on the human body
- Magnitude, duration & direction of acceleration;
- Rate of application;
- Area & site of application.
Human Tolerances
Gx (Front/Back) : 3.5 g in relaxed flight, 45 g during impact
Gy (Sideways)  : 6 g - 9 g in flight, 25 g during impact
+Gz (Up)  : 4.5 g - 6 g for 5 secs, 8 g with g-suit.
Height (not strength or gender) is the most important factor in a pilot's ability to
tolerate G. Since women have a smaller body mass, the shorter distance
between their heart & brain makes it easier for them to counteract G-forces.
Overall G tolerance depends on physical fitness.

- Empty stomach
- Hypoxia
- Hyperventilation
- Poor physical state

- Lack of current flying practise at high 'g' manoeuvres
- Worry and fear
- Experiencing negative 'g' before positive 'g'

- Tensing of abdominal muscles

11 - 9
Spatial Disorientation
• Introduction
Spatial disorientation occurs when a pilot can't correctly perceive the
attitude of his aircraft & doesn't know which way is UP. During good
visibility, eyes & vestibular organs (ears) are in sync. But during
marginal visibility, input from the eye reduces & the brain relies more
on input from vestibular organs for orientation. These may be erroneous
& may give rise to confusing signals in the brain, causing disorientation.
Orientation Triad
- Eyes: They provide 90% of the orientation cues.
- Central vision (30° visual cone) concerns with object recognition
(what) & identification of an object.
- Peripheral vision gives general orientation (where).
- Ears: Semicircular canals detect angular & otolith organs detect
linear acceleration (see also: Ear > Semicircular Canals, Otolith Organs)
- Muscles, skin, joints: Kinaesthetic/proprioceptive receptors in the
skin, joints and muscles are influenced by the forces acting on
the body. This is also called 'seat of the pants' sensation.
• Pre-disposing factors to disorientation
- Personal traits  - Weather  - Inexperience  - III health
- Fatigue  - Time of day  - Alcohol  - Emergencies
- Emotional state - Phase of flight  - Medication  - Insomnia
- High Gz forces  - Glare & Dazzle  - Hypoxia  - Anxiety
- Unnecessary head movements
• Types of Disorientation
- Type 1 Unrecognised: Pilot does not know that he is disoriented.
- Type 2 Recognised: He knows he is disoriented & takes corrective
action, due to his experience and his trust in cockpit flight instruments. R
- Type 3 Incapacitated: He knows he is disoriented, but cannot
correct for it. e.g. 'Giant Hand' phenomenon.
Remedy for Disorientation
- Constant flying practice
- Reduction of predisposing factors
- Reduce orientation conflict, have complete faith in instruments
- Inform co-pilot, hand over controls if disoriented
- Inform ATC
- Use of auto-pilot
- Bring aircraft to straight and level for at least 60 seconds
- Control breathing, do not panic.

• Illusions
1. Gyral Illusions (Semicircular Canal Illusions):
1a. Somatogyral: In a turn, during initial angular acceleration, the
ciliary hair in the semi-circular canals move. But when a constant
rate of turn is achieved after about 20 secs, the ciliary hair may
become stationary. When the aircraft finally rolls out, the ciliary
hair moves in the other direction, which now causes a sensation
that the aircraft is banking in the other direction.
1b. Occulogyral: It is the visual effect of somatogyral illusion. The pilot
feels a false sense of motion of the stationary objects in front of him.

1d. Leans: When angular acceleration or rate of increase of aircraft

is straight and level, the pilot feels he is banked to the other side.
1e. Graveyard Spin: It is the term used to describe the result of an
incorrect recovery from a spin caused by a Somatogyral illusion.
Applying rudder to stop the spin will cause ciliary hair to move in
the opposite direction, causing an illusion of opposite spin, to which
a pilot applies rudder in the initial direction, which aggravates spin
in the original direction.

11 - 11
2. Acceleration Illusions (Otolith Organ Illusions):
2a. Somatogravic: During low visibility, linear otolith organs
perceive a sense of pitch-up during takeoff/acceleration
& sense a pitch-down during landing/deceleration.
2b. Occulogravic: Visual effect of somatogravic illusion. It creates a
sensation of apparent upward movement of lights outside the
aircraft, from its actual position. However, during good visibility, it is
not of much consequence as the eyes compensate for it & orientate.
3. Vision Illusions
3a. Shape Consistency
- Up-sloping Runway: Pilot will feel steep on approach & makes
a shallow approach.
- Down-sloping Runway: Pilot will feel shallow on approach &
makes a steep approach.
3b. Size Consistency
- Narrow Runway: Pilot will feel steep on approach, makes a
shallow approach & flares out low.
- Wide Runway: Pitot will feel shallow on approach, makes a steep
approach & flares out high.
Normal Runway: Correct Approach  Normal Runway: Correct Approach

Down-slope Runway: Steep Approach  Wide Runway: Steep Approach
3c. Black Hole Approach: On a normal approach at night, the
touchdown spot remains fixed on the windscreen & the visual
angle increases as the aircraft descends. Just before touchdown,
the runway nearly fills the windscreen.
Normal Approach
But if the runway is in the centre of a dark patch of land, the pilot
feels that he is making a steady approach, but the illusion compels
him to fly on an arc of constant visual angle, causing the aircraft to
move on a path below glide path. Approach becomes increasingly
shallow & dangerously close to the ground without the pilot realising
Black-hole Approach
