• 11 - 12
Other Visual Illusions
- Parallax: Head movement causes distant objects to move relative
to each other.
- Perspective: Parallel lines converge, e.g., railway tracks
- Empty-field Myopia: If there is nothing outside for the eyes to
focus on, it focuses a point 1 - 2 m ahead. It can occur when flying
over featureless areas like the sea, desserts, etc.
- Auto-kinesis: Apparent movement of a point of light in a dark sky.
- White-out: It occurs when flying over snow covered area, causing
problems in judging distance.
- Aerial Perspective: When flying in fog, judgement of distance
ahead is distorted. Scattering of light makes distant objects appear
blue.
- Haze/Rain: Due to refraction of light, pilot feels steep on approach,
and will make a shallow approach.
- Poor Visibility: Tendency will be to make a steep approach.
- Leans on the Sun: We are accustomed to seeing a bright sky and
darker earth. But when flying in weather, this may be reversed,
thereby disorienting a pilot as to where actually the sky is.
- False Horizon: It occurs when seeing sloping clouds and confusing
its border with horizon & with aircraft attitude.

11 - 13
• Decompression Sickness
Introduction
- Decompression sickness occurs when the body is suddenly
decompressed from a higher pressure to lower pressure.
- It is most likely to occur above 30,000', if the duration of stay above
this altitude was more than 10 minutes.
- If cabin altitude is < 25000', decompression sickness is not likely.
- In case of cabin decompression, wear an oxygen mask & descend
below 10000' immediately.
- Do not fly for 12 hrs after scuba diving, using compressed air.
- Do not fly for 24 hrs if the dive depth was more than 30 ft (10 m).
Symptoms of Decompression Sickness
- Bends: Release of nitrogen from blood, causing pain in joints
- Creeps: Tingling, itching on the skin
- Chokes: Formation of bubbles in the lungs
- Hallucinations/central nervous system symptoms
- Effects on vision
- Neuro-circulatory collapse due to shock of above symptoms
Predisposing Factors of Decompression Sickness
- Rate of ascent
- Final altitude & duration at that altitude
- Outside temperature
- Obesity
- Age
- Individual susceptibility
- Lack of physical exercise/body fitness
Prevention of Decompression Sickness
- Pre-pressurisation of the body
- Reducing time spent at high altitudes
- Breathing of 100% oxygen
- Pre-oxygenation (de-nitrification) of the individual, to remove
maximum nitrogen from the body.
Types of Cabin Pressurisation
- Hyperbaric: Cabin pressure maintained at ground level pressure.
- Isobaric: Cabin pressure is maintained at 8000' (passenger aircraft).
- Hypobaric: Cabin pressure is maintained at 25000' (combat aircraft).
Rapid De-compression
- It is the sudden loss of cabin pressure in flight, occurring within
seconds. Effects of rapid decompression are:
- Misting of cabin air
- Sudden drop in temperature
- Sucking out of objects from the aircraft
- Injuries due to flying objects
Aeromedical  Factors
===== [avh 0450]
11 - 14
• Hypoxia
Introduction
- Hypoxia is caused due to inadequate supply of oxygen by the blood
to body tissues.
- Smoking causes carbon monoxide to attach on to haemoglobin,
thereby reducing its efficiency. A smoker may start to experience
hypoxia at a height 4000'-5000' below the threshold of a non-smoker.
- In case of doubt between hypoxia vs hyperventilation (symptoms for
both are similar), then assume it is hypoxia. However, if the aircraft
is below 10000', it is hyperventilation.
- Hypoxia-induced unconsciousness can lead to death. A person will
always recover from hyperventilation induced unconsciousness.
Oxygen Requirement for Aircrew
- Additional oxygen is required from 4 km (12000') upwards.
- 100% oxygen is required from 11 km (34000') upwards.
- Pressure breathing is essential from 14 km (41000') upwards.
- Ebulism (boiling of body fluids) occurs at 20 km (63000').
- A sealed cabin is essential above 25 km (75000*).
(See also: Air Regulations > Aircraft Equipment Requirements > Oxygen)
Types of Hypoxia
- Hypoxic Hypoxia: It is caused due to the lack of oxygen in higher
atmosphere (> 10000'), when flying in an unpressurised aircraft.
This is the most common type of hypoxia experienced by pilots.
- Anaemic Hypoxia: It is caused due to lack of oxygen-carrying
capacity of the blood. It can be caused by anaemia, haemorrhage,
haemoglobin abnormalities, sulfa drugs, nitrites, or carbon
monoxide poisoning (due to aircraft heater malfunctions, engine
manifold leaks, or cockpit contamination with exhaust).
- Stagnate Hypoxia: It occurs due to inadequate circulation of blood,
when the body is exposed to cold temperatures because of decreased
blood flow to the extremities or during rapid decompression.
- Histotoxic Hypoxia: It occurs when toxic substances present in the
cell (alcohol, narcotics, cyanide, etc) reduce its oxygen absorption
ability from the blood.
Stages of Hypoxia
- Indifferent Stage: Occurs up to 10000' altitude, no effect on the body.
- Compensatory Stage: Mild symptoms occur from 10000' - 15000'.
The body compensates by increasing breathing and heart rate.
- Disturbance Stage: Occurs from 15000' - 20000'. The body cannot
compensate any further.
- Critical Stage: Occurs above 20000'. It severely affects the body &
finally will lead to unconsciousness.
Factors Affecting Hypoxia
- Rate of ascent;  - Smoking & alcohol consumption;
- Duration at altitude;  - Illness;
- Ambient temperature;  - Emotional state;
- Physical fitness.

11 - 15
Prevention of Hypoxia
- Care of aircraft and personal oxygen equipment, and their use
whenever required.
- Ensure availability of sufficient oxygen before the sortie.
- Check serviceability of oxygen mask.
- Keep one-self fit.
Symptoms of Hypoxia
- A person is never provided with any warning of Hypoxia. The severity,
effect and sequence of symptoms may vary from person to person.
- Awareness of breathing;
- Sense of suffocation;
- Fatigue, depression or euphoria;
- Spots before eyes and dimming of vision, especially night vision;
- Impairment of hearing, touch and pain;
- Emotional outbursts - crying, laughter;
- Impairment of memory, intellect and concentration;
- Lack of sound judgment and self-criticism;
- Development of fixed & erroneous ideas & tendency to commit errors;
- Slow thinking & reaction.

===== [avh 0452]
11 - 16
• Hyperventilation
Introduction
- It is a purely physical phenomenon to start with, but may reach a
harmful state due to the reduction of CO2 from the body.
- Increased rate & depth of breathing release excess CO2 from the
blood. Thus blood pH increases & becomes less acidic than normal.
- This leads to blood alkalosis & affect both cardiovascular system &
central nervous system. It causes arteries to contract, resulting in
less oxygen circulation.
- The immediate effects are 1 heart rate, I blood pressure, J blood
flow to the brain.
- Hyperventilation may lead to unconsciousness, but a person will
always recover from it.
Causes of Hyperventilation
- Fear;
- Apprehension;
- Hypoxia;
- Pressure breathing;
- Over exercise;
- Temperature variation.
Symptoms of Hyperventilation
- Nausea, dizziness, faintness, lethargy;
- Numbness, tingling, tremors;
- Tightening, stiffness of muscles, convulsions;
- Facial spasm;
- Poor judgement, discretion or orientation;
- Cold, clammy skin, pale cyanosis, weak pulse.
Prevention of Hyperventilation
- Control of breathing;
- Use of oxygen above 10000'.
Hypoxia or Hyperventilation ?
The natural body reaction to oxygen shortage is to breath faster & deeper. A
hypoxic individual may hyperventilate to get more oxygen. During flight it can be
difficult to distinguish symptoms of Hypoxia & Hyperventilation. Pilots must assume
the worst and take action accordingly if they are at an altitude where Hypoxia IS
a possibility. However, when flying below 10000 ft, significant symptoms of hypoxia
are unlikely & hyperventilation may be assumed.
DO NOT ASSUME HYPERVENTILATION IF IT COULD BE HYPOXIA
HYPERVENTILATION - AFTER UNCONSCIOUSNESS - RECOVERY
HYPOXIA - AFTER UNCONSCIOUSNESS - DEATH
After leaving a regulated life in the Navy, a friend of mine, a retired officer took
a civilian job, but had trouble getting into work on time. Finally, his boss asked him,
"what would they have said to you in your previous job, about being late?
My friend answered him "Good Morning Admiral*.

DGCA CPL/ATPL Application Procedure
DGCA policy for CPLATPL may change from time to time.
For the latest procedure, please visit pariksha.dgca.gov.in.
Computer Number
- A computer number is necessary tor you to apply tor DGCA exams.
- Visit pariksha.dgca.gov.in, read the 'Flight Crew User Manual PDF'
carefully & prepare the required documents as mentioned in it, in
physical & soft copy (scanned PDF in specified size). They include:
- Passport photo & signature
- Date of birth proof
- X & XIl pass certificate, mark sheet & board verification
- Adhar card & Permanent address proof
later, you can download the verification online instantly. Got to
resultsarchives.nic.in > select the year > click Class X/XII exam
results > enter your roll number. Take a printout & get it attested.
Offline verification process is time-consuming & involves sending a
copy of your mark sheets to any of the 10 CBSE regional offices
with a DD of Rs.500. This procedure is mentioned on their website.
- Now visit pariksha.dgca.gov.in again, register for your ID (New
Candidate) at validate your email & mobile number. Log in, fill the
application form & upload the scanned PDF of your documents. On
successful upload, you will get your Temporary Computer Number.
- Ensure that the physical application with all enclosures (attested
copies) reach CEO, DGCA, within 10 days of the online application.
When it is verified, your 'Computer Number' will be emailed to you.
Apply for Exams
Online exams are conducted every 3 months & their schedule is
published on pariksha.dgca.gov.in. There are a total of seven
exams and two viva-voce. (List of exams on the next page).
- When the online application portal opens, apply for your exam,
preferred exam centre & pay the fees online. The fee is Rs.2500/-
per exam.
- For Navigation & Radio-aids, once you pass the online exam, you
also need to clear its respective viva-voce. Dates for the viva are
published about 2 weeks after the announcement of the results of
the online exam. If you fail in your 1st viva attempt, you can attempt
it twice more in subsequent exam cycles. In this case, apply for the
viva separately in the same way you applied for the online exam. An
additional fee (Rs.500/-) needs to be paid online.
- You can appear for all exams in one go. But, if you aren't constraint
by time, for ease of preparation, I recommend 3 attempts:
- Air-Regs + Meteorology
- Radio Aids + Navigation (and its corresponding 2 viva)
- Tech General + Tech Specific + Tech performance
- Military Pilots appearing for ATPL: For you, Meteorology, Radio-
aids & Navigation exams are combined into a single composite
exam and its corresponding single viva. Also, Tech General exam is
waived-off. That leaves just four exams. Air regulations, Composite-
paper, Tech Specific & Tech Performance. Cheers!

eGCA ID
- Register your eGCA ID at dgca.gov.in & start filling your online
e-logbook. This is a time-consuming process, especially if you are
applying for an ATPL. An eGCA ID is also required for applying for
Medicals, FRTOL and your final ATPL application.
RTR (A) Radio Telephony Restricted - Aero
• A valid RTR (A) license from DoT is required for getting your FRTOL
A comprehensive description of RTR (A), its application
procedure and syllabus are given in subsequent pages.
Class 1 Medicals
- Log-in at eGCA portal > Medicals > Apply for class 1 medicals. Select
your preferred Air Force centre & date. The type of tests that need
to be done (blood test, ENT, eye, etc.) will be mentioned in the
instructions.
- Pay the fee at bharatkosh gov.in as a non registered user, payment
head: 'Medical - CAR Section 7 : Issuance of Medical Class I'.

FRTOL Flight Radio Telephony Operator Licence
- An RTR (A) COP & valid class 1 medicals are pre-requisite for FRTOL.

- For this, you will need to apply directly with any DGCA approved
establishment (list available at DGCA website) that conducts an
ELP course. The syllabus is for a fixed number of hours, at the end
of which, you will have to undergo a test.
- DGCA has exempted military pilots from undergoing the ELP
syllabus/course. They can appear for the ELP test directly.
- It is a practical test to check standards of your pronunciation,
structure, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension and interactions.
- Depending upon your performance, you get an ELP level from 1 - 6.
Level 1,2, 3 - You have failed the test; further training is required.
Level 4 is valid for 3 yrs, Level 5 for 6 yrs & Level 6 is valid for life.
Skill Test (procedure for military pilots)
- Once you have cleared all exams, class 1 medicals, FRTOL & ELP
and have the required flying hours, take an appointment with a
Defence DE (Designated Examiner) & send the application to DGCA
FSD (Flight Standards Directorate) for approval to appear for skill test.
Final application
- After completing the skill test, log-in at eGCA portal > Licenses >
Apply for ATPL, and upload the required documents. Ensure that
the required documents are sent to DGCA for verification.
That's it! I everything is in order, you will finally receive your ATPL :)

A -7
Attempting the Viva
Dress
- Wear good fitting formals.
- Be well groomed.
First Impression
- Greet the examiners individually.
- Wait till you are offered a seat.
Positive Attitude
- Be enthusiastic.
- Maintain a good body language.
- Don't look stressed.
Language
- Speak confidently.
- Have a good command over the language.
- Don't use slangs.
Introduction
- Be prepared for giving a short introduction about yourself.
Answering Questions
- Take a few seconds to compose your answer.
- Try to reply in this sequence (as applicable):
- Full form of the term.
- Its brief development history: year, country, what was the issue
being faced till then, what problem did it solve, did any aviation
accident trigger its development, etc.
- Introduction to the topic, working principle, frequency of use:
- How is it useful for a pilot.
- Draw its diagram (bring a clip board & a plain paper).
- Its various types.
- Its advantages & disadvantages.
- Be polite in your response. Don't try to show-off your knowledge.
- Prepare for possible sub-questions that will be asked from the main
question.
- If you do not know an answer, it is alright to say so. Do not guess.
They know better.
Before Leaving
- Give a firm handshake and thank them for their time.

A -8
RTR (A) CoP Application Procedure
Radio Telephony Restricted (Aero) Certificate of Proficiency
Applying for RTR (A) Exam
Unlike DGCA exams, RTR exams are conducted by the
Department of Telecom. 6 exams are conducted in a year, in one city
at a time, once every 2 months. The application procedure & tentative
exam schedule are published at their website rlo-mumbai.in.
You have to register for your ID and apply for the exam there. A
fee of Rs.500 has to be paid at bharatkosh.gov.in. After the online
application, the physical application along with its supporting documents
needs to be sent to the address mentioned on the website within 10
days. Once approved, the admit card will be available for download.
The full procedure is mentioned on their website.
Conduct for the Exam: RTR (A) exam consists of 2 parts.
- Practical RT Transmission Technique (25 minutes, 100 Marks)
- Viva: It is conducted by 2 examiners
- WPC (questions on radio theory & principles)
- DGCA (questions on air regulations & procedures).
Results of the practical RT test is announced immediately & those
who clear this test proceeds for the viva, which is also conducted on
the same day. Due to the unique nature of this examination, passing
the practical RT test is generally more difficult, and hence, during
exam preparation, more focus must be given to this, than the viva.
After Passing the Exam
The results of the viva is published on their website after about a
month. Once you have passed the exam, apply for your RTR CoP
license. The procedure is mentioned on their website. The fee for a
iifetime' RTR license is Rs. 10,000/-.
There are many online coaching classes that offer to train you in passing RTR (A)
exam, for a fee. This may actually save you a lot of time and trouble.

A - 9
CPI-ATPL- RTR
RTR (A) Practical RT Transmission Test
Refer 'Air Regulations > RT Phraseology'
for RT calls that needs to be prepared for the practical RT test.
This exam is conducted over an intercom RT circuit, with an examiner sitting
behind you. Correctness of your RT phraseology & transmission technique will be
assessed. While replying over the intercom, you will also have to write both the
transmitted and received RT calls on your answer sheet.
The exam consists of 5 questions of 20 marks each (sample question papers
included in subsequent pages). First 4 questions will be based on various phases
of a simulated flight, from start-up (including SID), en-route (including emergency
handling, diversion, weather deviations, etc.) & approach/landing (including
STAR/IAP). You will also be given hypothetical route charts (included in
subsequent pages) relevant to your question paper. The fifth question will be of
general nature, abbreviations, fill in the blanks, etc.
Time Management
- The difference between a candidate who passes & one who fails in
this exam is 'Time Management' & 'Exam Technique'.
- During your exam preparation, practice writing & transmitting your
call at the same time. This will save precious time.
Before getting the question paper
- Set a timer on your watch for 21 minutes. This will give you an
indication of when to attempt Q.5.
- Carry out RT check with examiner "Carrying out RT check 1 2 3 4 5,
how do you read meạẠạ
- Quickly prepare your answer sheet by drawing margins & headings
This is not mandatory, however, it makes it more presentable & can
be helpful as you can refer to them during your RT call.
Immediately after getting the question paper
- Start your timer for 21 minutes.
- Read questions 1 to 4, to know the setting of the hypothetical route.
Don't waste much time on it as your exam time has started.
- Fill the 'prepared top portion' of the answer sheet by writing down
important details about the sortie.
Callsign: As per question paper, If it is an Airbus or Boeing, suffix
'heavy' after callsign, in all RT calls.
ETAs: Fill hypothetical ETAs for each question by adding half an hour
to the takeoff time given in the question paper, e.g. 0900/0930/
1000/1030. These will be the time of RT call for each question.
POB: Use hypothetical POB. Boeing/Airbus 120, ATR 70, Cessna 4,
Challenger/Bombardier 30. For general aviation use 5.
Speed: Use hypothetical speed. Airbus/Boeing 450 Kts, ATR 350 kts.
Endurance: As given in the question paper.
Flight Level: As given in the question paper.
- Start with question 1, by saying attempting Q.1
Attempting the question paper
- Write hypothetical time of RT Call as per ETAs against each question.
- Log the 'received call in the next line (on the other half) of the
answer sheet from your transmitted call.
- Draw a horizontal line after each question.

A - 10
CPL ATPL RTR
- Long RT calls: Repeat your callsign again at the end of the call.
- In case of stopping on the taxiway or rejecting takeoff, give a full call.
"callsign, frequency, position, & stopping slowly abeam Link C,
request taxi instructions"
- Time management for Q.5 is very important. It will be an easy scoring
20 marks. If you are still stuck in Q.4 when your watch timer goes
off, say "Sir, I am attempting Q.5 & & start Q.5". While answering
Q.5, don't read aloud the question, just say "A.answer..., B.answer...
Remember standard call format:
- Whom are you calling (ATSU & fq)
- Who are you? (your c/s, neavy)
- Where are you? (position, time, FL)
- What do you want? (information)
- Who are you? (your c/s, heavy)
Standard Mechanical calls: Don't miss out on scoring standard mechanical
calls like start, taxi, ATC clearance, AIRPROX, wind shear, air report,
microburst, descend, distress, etc., by using the correct RT format.
Calling correct ATSU & its frequency is very important. When attempting
a question, put a point on the route chart to see where you are & what
is your height. TWR and CTRL are generally not confusing. But in
some places in the route chart, APP upper limit is ambiguous*. It may
be written as ™A/50. In this case, the upper limit of APP has to be read
in conjunction with the lower limit of CTRL, in this example - FL100
TWR : CTR  APP: 100 orồỗẠIMA  GTRL: 40 or IMA
Some places (e.g. Lucknow) chart indicates LLK TMA, but in Fq box, LLK does
not have any CTRL. So you will have to call LLK APP and not LLK Control.
- First call to any ATSU should contain the 'frequency' of that ATSU also.
- Start and taxi clearance are given by GRND, departure clearance
and takeoff is given by TWR.
- If the examiner doesn't reply, you are probably calling a wrong ATSU.
- If the examiner says "call appropriate authority" you must call the
next ATSU. The reply should be "Changing to Mangalore Control on
112.7, VUBFT" (& not repeating the call "Call appropriate agency,
VUBFT"). Immediately after, give a call to the new ATSU "Mangalore
Control, VUBFT on 112.7,...
Abbreviated callsign: VTUBA = VBA. Use it only if examiner abbreviates
it first. 1st call to the next ATSU should always be the full callsign.
Pronunciation: Be very particular about 9 (niner) 3 (tree) 5 (fife) & 8 (Ait)
Read back clearances: Do not waste time in writing down 'read back'
clearances in the TX column. However, you do have to read back on
RT. But for logging, just write "Kochi Tower VUBFT ..  Ị and draw
an arrow towards it, from the RX column.
Local flying before setting course: RT Call: "request local flying between
radials 070 - 090, 20-50 nm 5000 ft before setting course".
In case of RCF: During climb, maintain current FL for 20 minutes, give a
blind call to that effect. At 15 minutes, repeat position call. At 20 minutes,
climb to the previously cleared level.
MayDay: If no intention is given in Q paper & aircraft is not under control,
give a call "force landing straight ahead". If landed safely on the runway
after a PanPan & Mayday, give a 'cancel MayDay' call after landing.
Interception: Call the ATSU you are with, but use frequency 121.5 MHZ.
===== [avh 0463]
A - 11
SID/STAR/Missed Approach:
- Easiest way to answer a SID, STAR or a missed approach question
is to follow its text portion printed on the chart.
- Keep in mind speed and FL restrictions on the chart.
- Keep giving SID calls at each event, do not waste time for the
examiner to reply. He may or may not say ROGER, e.g.:
- Reached 2500', turning Left;
- "Reporting LOXIR, climbing to FL70".
Changing IFR/VRF: At the point of commencing VFR, take permission
from the appropriate ATSU to change to VFR, pass new ETAs & FL if
applicable. If the question indicates visual approach at the destination,
but visibility is below VFR minima, the call will be "cancelling VFR at
_, request ILS approach...
De-Conflict traffic at your level/reporting point: Call will be "Will
arrange to reach FL300 at (+15 mins) after/before" conflicting traffic.
If traffic ahead/above is climbing slow, and you want to climb, contact
the aircraft on inter-pilot 123.45 MHz & request him to climb faster.
Inter pilot calls: When calling other aircraft, always use inter-pilot 123.45
MHz. Don't use the ATSU frequency.
If unsure of which action to take while answering a question, e.g.
- Which ATS unit should I contact?
- Which diversion? Primary or Alternate?
- Alter Track (which new route should I take?)
- Which side should I deviate for weather (left or right)?
take a hint from the next question & see where & what you are doing.
Diversion: Read the question for a hint. If CTRL is available, divert to
primary diversion in the same CTRL. If CTRL is un-available, divert to
the 2nd alternate in another CTRL.
Weather
- On Takeoff: Deviate heading 15 degrees left/right.
- On Finals: Go around.
- Air Report: To be given whenever you encounter a drop in visibility,
turbulence, CAT or icing. In case of severe turbulence, follow it with
an "unable RVSM" call.
- En-route: Almost always, there will be a hint in question as to what to
do (deviate, unable to maintain FL (unable RVSM) or re-route flight).
- If working Fq busy: 'PanPan' call to gain the attention of controller.
- In case of a microburst or wind shear on finals, give a 'microburst/
wind shear report followed by "initiating go around & missed
approach procedure" & not just a "initiating missed approach" call.
Standard Terminology for Logging Answers
Inadvertently: By mistake I did something.
Observed: I saw something happening.
Sighted: Seen another aircraft or airfield. Don't say "visual with..."
Reporting: I'm telling you (waypoint/FL/clearance compliance).
Negative contact with: Cannot contact....
Egpt not responding or Eapt U/S: Equipment is not working.
Experiencing: Going through (e.g. weather).
Changing to: Changing ATSU. Don't say "over to ..." or "Contact ...
Pass your message: If someone calls you in flight. Don't say "go ahead
Deviation required: For deviation 20 - 30 nm from original ATS route.
Alter track: New ATS route required, Give full estimates & new FL.

Sample RTR (A) Question Paper 1  CPL ATPI
Time: 25 minutes  Maximum marks: 100
Aircraft identification: IC 517 Type of Aircraft: Airbus
Departure: VECC  Destination: VOMM
Level FL 280  Route: via VEBS & VEVZ
SELCAL: ALCH
Q 1. Before Departure from Kolkata obtain the following:
(i) Startup clearance
(ii) Taxi Instruction
(iii) Takeoff clearance
Departure Time 1400
Q 2. Over the Kolkata-Chennai FIR boundary, you have received a
SELCAL indication. Take action.
Q 3(a) When crossing DOCKET, you observed fire on the left engine and
decided to make a force landing. Take action.
(b) The fire was minor. You are able to extinguish the fire and decide
to proceed as per the flight plan. Take action.
Q 4. When you are 30 DME from Chennai, request for a visual approach.
Q 5. Transmit the following phrases as per radiotelephony procedure.
(a) Wait, I shall call you.
(b) Establish radio contact.
(c) My transmission has ended, and I expect no answer from you.
(d) Examine a system or procedure.
(e) Continue in accordance with clearance.

SELCAL: CMJL

===== [avh 0477]
B - 1
Aviation Formulae
Physics
Weight  = m (mass) x g (gravity)  Work = F (force) x s (displacement)
Momentum = m (mass) x v (velocity)  Power = Work / Time
= M (mass) x a (acceleration)
Kinetic Energy = ½ m (mass) x v (velocity)2
Potential Energy = m (mass) x g (gravity) x h (height)
Aerodynamics
Lift = CL ½ p V2 S  CL Coeff of lift
Drag = CD ½ p V2 S  CD = CDI +CDP  Co Coeff of drag
Parasite Drag Dp = ½ pV2 CDP S  CoP Coeff of parasite drag
Induced Drag DI = ½ pV2 CDI S  Cor Coeff of induced drag
Stall Speed: VB2 = VB1 JW1  VWz  or VB1 Vg (Tum) or VB1 Vcos e (Bank angle)
VSTALL increases by a factor of Vg (load factor) AOB 30°: VsB x 1.07
AoB 45°: VsB x 1.2
4g wing loading = 2x VsB
AoB 60°: VsB × 1.41
Load Factor = Liff/Weight = cos e  AoB 75°: VsB x2
Magnetism, Compass
Coeff B = Dey E - Dey W  Coeff B is due to Longitudinal Magnetic Component 'P'
Coeff C is due to Lateral Magnetic Component Q
Coeff A is due to fixed mis-alignment, independent of hdg.
Coeff C = Dev = Dev s
Radio & Radar
C = FA  C = Speed of light, F = Frequency, 1 = wavelength
Optical Range (nm) = 1.05 VHeight (ft)
Max Skip Dist. (nm) = 1.43 VHeight of ionosphere (in km)
VHF Range (nm)  = 1.23 V(Tx (ft) + Rx (ft)) or 12VFL if VOR at MSL
NDB Range (nm)  = 2 x VP (land), 3 x VP (sea) P = NDB Power output (Watt)
Radar Min Range =  C x PW  PRP = Range x 2
2
Radar Max Range = C x PRI  PRF = Range x 2. or PRF
Radar Duty Cycle = PW Pulse Width (Sec) x PRP Repetition Frequency (Hz)
70 x Wave length
Radar Beam Width (Degrees) = Antenna diameter
Electrics
Voltage (V)  = Current (I) x Resistance (R)
Power (P)  = Voltage (V) x Current (I)
Fq of AC (hertz)= (No of poles / 2) x (RPM / 60)
RMS  = Peak sine wave value x 0.707
===== [avh 0478]
B - 2
Meteorology
Cloud base = (Surface temperature - Dew point)°C x 400'
Cloud height above aircraft (ft) = (Tilt - ½ Beam width) × Range (nm) × 100
DALR = 3° / 1000'  At sea level (1013 mb) = 27ft/mb
SALR = 1.5° / 1000'  At 18000' (500 mb) = 48ft/mb
CP, PNR
CP = OH PNR = EOH  H = Reduced TAS Home D = Distance
O+H
O = Reduced TAS Out  E = Endurance
*If actual headwind or tailwind is known
HW = Headwind  TW = Tailwind
Projections
Departure  = Change of Longitude x 60 x COS mean Latitude
Convergency  = Change of Longitude x SIN mean Latitude
Conversion Angle = ½ Convergency
Scale at Equator  = Scale at Latitude x COS (Latitude)
360° Longitude = 24 hrs of time  1° Longitude (60' arc) = 4 mins of time
15° Longitude = 60 mins of time 1' Arc = 4 seconds of time
Climb, Descend, Turn, Range
Climb Grad = ROC  Climb Angle = ROC x 0.6 ROC = Excess of power
TAS  TAS  Weight
Time to Climb (sec) = Ht Diff (ft) x 60. Dist to Climb (nm) =Ht Dif (ft) x GS (Kts)
ROC (fpm)  ROC (fpm) x 60
Radius of Turn = (NS m; or 11.26 TAN 6  V2 (TAS)  - ft; or GS (TAS) nm (diameter)
STAN e
Rate of Turn = 1091 x TAN 0 o/sec Angle of Bank (rate 1 turn) = TAS + 7
V (TAS)
TAS
Specific Air Range = Fuel consumption SFC x Drag
ILS
Height (ft) above ground on ILS: Dist (nm) x Glide angle x 100
Why 100? As per 1 in 60 rule, 1° at 1nm (6000') = 6000/60 = 100'
ROD on ILS: Ground speed per min x Glide angle x 100
- Change in ROD = Change in GS/60 x Glide angle x 100
- For a 3° GP, ROD = GS/60 × 3 x 100 = GS X 5
Glide Path % = TAN (glide angle) × 100  Glide Path ° = %/100 × 60
Altitude
Density Altitude = Pressure Altitude + (118 x T) T = ISA Temp difference
True Altitude = PA + (Pressure All/1000 x 3.5 x T) If ht > 10000', multiply by 4
PA + 1% per 2.5°C ISA deviation
PA + 4' per °C ISA deviation per 1000 ft
===== [avh 0479]
B - 3
Speed
a. EAS = TAS x Vrelative density  e.g at 40000 ft, density is ¼.
b. TAS = RAS + (RAS/60) x 1000's of feet  OR
RAS + 1.75% RAS x 1000's of feet
c. TAS from Mach No: Multiply mach no. x 600. Then,
If mach is no. less than 0.6, +1 for every 1000' below 25000'
-1 for above 25000'
If mach is no. more than 0.6, +2 for every 1000 below 25000'
-2 for above 25000'
d. Mach Number: TAS LSS = Local speed of sound = 39VT (661 kts sea level)
LSS T = Kelvin scale temperature
- Altitude 1, Temperature † = Density J = IAS / CAS 1 = TAS †
- Temperature 1 = LSS 1 = M.no. 1
EAS lAS  ẠỊEASIAS TAS  EASAS M NOTAS
VE VIV

Layer→
• Speed  Speed  Speed
Changes in EAS, IAS, TAS & M No with f in altitude
Temperature
TAT = Total Air Temp
a. TAT = SAT + (TAS/87)2 (Kinetic heating or Ram Rise)  SAT = Static Air Temp
M = Mach no.
TAT = SAT (1 + 0.2M2 x R)  R = Recovery factor =1
Total Air Temp = Indicated Air Temp = Ram Air Temp
True Air Temp = Static Air Temp  = Outside Air Temp
00  Wind
a. Triangle of Velocities
- Track Required = Heading ‡ Wind correction drift.
b. Wind Calculation
- For constant GS, max drift is when wind is 1 to heading.
- For constant TAS, max drift is when wind is 1 to track.
c. Head / Tailwind Component = COS (wind angle) x Wind Speed.
d. Crosswind Component = SIN (wind angle) x Wind Speed.
Crosswind speed thumb rule (1 in 60 rule):
• - for 30°crosswind, headwind = ½ of wind speed
- for 45° crosswind, headwind = ½ of wind speed
- for 60°crosswind, headwind = 90% of wind speed
e. A/c Drift Angle = SIN (wind angle) × Max Drift  75°  Angle
97% ***  60°  between
f. Max Drift = (Wind Velocity / TAS) x 60  aircraft &

===== [avh 0480]
B - 4
Distance
a. 1 in 60 Rule: 1° at 1 nm = 60nm.
b. Distance off-track from required radial
= (Bearing change from aid x Distance from aid) / 60
Abbreviations  c. Distance to touch-down in a DME arc
= Length of arc remaining + final approach distance.
=> (Bearing change (current radial - final approach radial) x arc radius)/60
+ Arc distance (final approach distance)
GS x minutes flown
d. Distance to Aid =
Bearing change from aid
• This formula works if a constant heading is maintained
• It is not applicable if bearing change > 45°, or if aircraft is too close to aid
e. Nautical Ground Mile NGM: Distance flown at GS / distance flown on chart.
f. Nautical Air Mile NAM: Distance flown at TAS.
NAM = IAS  - In nil winds, NAM = NGM
NGM  GS  - NGM less than NAM for headwinds.
Track
a. Standard Closing Angle (SCA) = 3600 / GS
Alter heading by SCA for no. of minutes, as per no. of nm off-track.
b. Track Error: Angle between 'track required' & 'track made good'.
TE = Distance off-track x 60 CA =  Distance to go x 60
Distance gone  Distance remaining
Correction = TE + CA
Time by Speed Adjustment
a. Speed Correction: Old speed x Old time = New speed x New time
b. Bells Method
† or I speed by 'no. of knots' equal to 'no. of seconds' aircraft is late or
early & hold it for (GS/minute) minutes. Time for holding that correction is
constant (GS/minute) irrespective of being early / late. It is generally
applied for small corrections of time.
c. Bells Method Inverse
If aircraft speed is 1 or 1 by (GS/minute), then the aircraft will gain or lose
that many seconds. It is used for larger time corrections.
d. Rule of 'n' / Rule of 5
1 or 1 speed by (GS/min) x 5, hold for {(no. of seconds early or late) / 5)
e. 'X' Factor
It is used to address variation between calculated GS & actual GS observed.
X factor is usually applied at 1st checkpoint en route.
X Factor =  (GS/minute) x no. of seconds early or late
Time actually gone in minutes
f. Speed Correction by Mental DR
1 or l speed by lAS x Time (minutes) early or late at destination
lime (minutes) remaining to make good ETA
Time by Distance Adjustment
a. Dog Legs: Alter heading from track to lose time.
30° = ~ 25% t  60° = t
45° = ~ 50% t  90° = 45 secs

B - 11
Q Codes
Q codes were originally used in the olden days' as brevity codes for ease of communication
during aircraft HF transmission. It was transmitted in 'Morse Code'.
QAA - QNZ are reserved for Aeronautical use
QOA - QQZ are reserved for Maritime use  Formulae &  Abbreviations
QRA - QUZ are reserved for Common use
